Asimov memory tests: the outliers, why they looked wrong, and the tests we added

Written 2026-11-08 from the histories of the two analysis sessions (asimov-04 and asimov-be), Jesse's README files for results 001 to 012, the run plans and the four report pages. Every number was checked against the result files by the verification pass; numbers marked est. are derived, not measured. Generated by gen_outliers.py.

Short version. Across six rounds of emulator runs, 50 measured results did not make sense at first sight. Each one led to a question, a hypothesis and a new test in the next round. 18 are now explained, 18 are narrowed to a named cause with a test still to run, and 14 are open.

0. The request, as written

This is the prompt that asked for this page, copied without edits. It states what the page must contain.

At this and peer sessions, many tests have run. The pattern is, scoping of a test's result opened suspicious outliners in that their data did not make sense and in order to clarify, we add more tests to provide insights. And each round we gain more insights.

1. Architecture overview

1.1 The blocks

Asimov is an Arm SoC under test on a Palladium emulator (a hardware emulator that runs the chip's RTL cycle by cycle). One hemisphere holds five clusters. Each cluster is a DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit) with two Arm C1-Nano cores. The diagram below is the map used for every outlier in section 4: the blocks involved in an outlier are highlighted in orange.

  • Cores. Ten C1-Nano cores, CPUs 0 to 9. CPUs 0 and 1 run the kernel. CPUs 2 to 9 are isolated for the tests. A C1-Nano is an in-order core that issues two 128-bit loads per cycle [C1-Nano Software Optimization Guide, section 2.33; README 011].
  • L1. Each core has a 32 KiB data cache and a 32 KiB instruction cache with 64-byte lines, and a 16-entry L1 data TLB (the table that translates addresses) [sysinfo.txt of bootF1 lines 101 to 102]. The way count is not in any source on disk (sysfs prints 0).
  • L2. One 128 KiB L2 per cluster, shared by its two cores [sysinfo.txt line 103]. So the L2 is a cluster cache here, not a per-core cache.
  • L3. One 256 KiB L3 per cluster, one slice [sysinfo.txt line 104]. It has two modes. In snoop-filter-only mode the L3 RAM keeps only the snoop filter (the list of lines held by the cores) and stores no data. In full mode it stores data. The stock firmware put only cluster 0 in full mode, so on runs 1 to 3 and boots A to D the L3 of the measured cores held no data. Boot E's rebuilt SCP firmware put all clusters in full mode [README 006 and 010].
  • CME. Each cluster has one CME (the Arm C1-SME2 unit) shared by its two cores. It runs the streaming-mode (SME) instructions. It has its own 64 KiB, 4-way L1 data cache with two 512-bit read paths, a 24-entry TLB and its own prefetcher. Its path to memory is CME L1D, then the cluster's L3, then the mesh. The core's L1 and L2 are not on that path [C1-SME2 TRM as cited on the CME page; cme_test output].
  • Mesh. The clusters, home nodes and memory bridges sit on a CMN S3 mesh, a 6 by 6 grid of crosspoints. Each cluster has one mesh port (RN-F). A request travels 1 to 5 crosspoint steps to a home node [README 004, mesh map].
  • Home nodes, SLC and OCM. Five home nodes (HN-S) own all addresses; a DRAM address belongs to one of them by a hash, so a buffer spreads over all five. Each home node has 1 MiB of SLC (System Level Cache) in 16 ways. The firmware locks 4 ways of each node as a 256 KiB OCM region (On-Chip Memory, addressable SRAM at 0xE0000000 plus n MiB). The other 12 ways, 768 KiB per node and 3.75 MiB in all, cache DRAM lines [README 004 Platform facts].
  • DRAM. About 2 GiB of memory behind the mesh's SBSX bridges. On the emulator it is four Cadence AXI memory models, not real LPDDR. Every delay control on the four models is zero and the native response is 3 ns. Of the 52.7 ns a random load costs from the core, 23.7 to 24.2 ns is the home-node round trip and about 29 ns the leg beyond the home node, of which about 20 ns is RTL pipeline by Jesse's stage count (est.) [README 011, memory model answer].
  • Clock. The cores run at 2.0 GHz nominal (2.003 GHz from the 4 KiB row: 4.01 cycles per 2.002 ns load). The timer runs at 1 GHz, so one tick is 1 ns and 2 cycles. The emulator is cycle-exact with no frequency scaling [README 004 and 011].

General ranges: UVM CS2210 memory-hierarchy notes (L1 about 3 cycles, L2 10 to 15, L3 30 to 45, memory 150 to 300 at 3 GHz) and Chips and Cheese on the Cortex-A510 (L1 4 to 5 cycles, L2 9 to 13), both read 2026-11-08. 2. Prefetchers

A prefetcher is hardware that fetches cache lines before a load asks for them. It watches the addresses of recent loads or misses, detects a pattern (a stream of consecutive lines, or a fixed stride), and issues its own reads ahead of the program. The prefetchers shaped more outliers than any other block, because they change what a row measures without changing the row.

2.1 Which levels have one

  • Core, L1 side. A prefetcher fills the core's L1 data cache. Its fills are counted by event 0x81BC (L1 refills a hardware prefetcher asked for) and 0x0111 (L2 refills made for the L1 prefetcher's requests). On the 8 MiB sequential chain with every line flushed, both read 1.00 per load: every line entered the L1 at the prefetcher's request [boot A latency-dram-seq rows, 005].
  • Core, L2 side. A second prefetcher fills the L2. Its fills are counted by 0x81BD. On the one-line-per-page OCM chains it fetched up to 2.98 extra lines per load while 0x81BC read 0 [boot A latency-ocm-region4-vary-cpu8.csv]. The Arm PMU lists five named data prefetchers for this core family: correlating, spatial, offset, stride and TLB descriptor (events 0x00D9 to 0x00DB, 0x010F, 0x0110). Which one fills which level is not stated in the sources on disk.
  • Cluster L3. The predecessor core's manual (Cortex-A520 TRM) names L3 stride and offset prefetchers, and the C1-Nano PMU has event 0x0123 (L3 refills by L2-side prefetches). That event was never counted in these runs, so an L3-side prefetcher is neither shown nor excluded. Insufficient data: counting 0x0123 beside the refill set would show it.
  • CME. The CME has its own prefetcher with 128 streams, indexed by instruction address. It fills the CME's L1D and the cluster L3, works in virtual addresses and keeps its own TLB [C1-SME2 TRM, as cited on the CME page]. Its fills are counted by CME event 0x32B2.
  • SLC, OCM, DRAM. No prefetcher is documented at the home nodes or the memory models in the sources on disk.

2.2 How a prefetch relates in time to the load

The prefetcher does not run at the same time as the load it helps. It runs ahead of it. It trains on the first loads or misses of a pattern, then issues reads for lines the program has not reached yet, independently of the demand loads. The demand load then finds the line in the cache, or finds it on its way in. The measurements below show the three cases.

  • Before the load (a stream or stride). On the sequential chain every line still comes from DRAM once (1.00 L2 refills per load), but the load costs 2.49 ns instead of 52.7 ns. The lines arrive in the L1 before the chain reaches them [boot E, 010; boot C with the L3 off: 6.92 ns per load]. On the one-line-per-page OCM chains the L2-side prefetcher reacts to the page stride, not to the line offset inside the page: it fetched 1.8 to 2.2 extra lines per load with a fixed offset and 1.2 to 1.7 with a varying one [boot A, 005].
  • Never (a random dependent chain). The next address is inside the line being read, so there is no pattern. Boot B (prefetchers off) is within -5.6 to +5.3 % of boot A on all 24 random chase rows from 4 KiB to 32 MiB. The chain latencies in section 1.2 are therefore the levels' own [latency-dram-small.csv and -large.csv of 005 and 006].
  • Partly before (a random chain over a small region). On the per-region OCM chains of runs 1 and 2 (256 KiB, dense) the prefetcher fetched neighbours of the missed line that the chain used later: 0.74 to 0.96 L3 read refills per load instead of 1.00, so a quarter of the loads hit a line already brought in. That is why run 3 moved to one line per page [outliers 4.4 and 4.19].
  • Against the load (the CME). Through the CME a random chain that fits the CME's 64 KiB L1 gets slower from 8 KiB on with the prefetcher on: 21.4 ns at 4 KiB, 24.9 at 8 KiB, 45.6 at 64 KiB, with 14 prefetched lines per load at 32 to 64 KiB. The prefetcher's fills evict the chain. With it off (boots B and F2) the chain reads 21.0 to 21.2 ns up to 64 KiB [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 012; outlier 4.27].
  • Software hints. A PRFM hint 4 lines ahead raises the plain loop from 2.38 to 6.33 GB/s with the hardware prefetchers off, adds 1.5 to 3.8 % with them on and the L3 off, and slows the loop with the L3 on (24.9 to 20.2 GB/s) [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 006, 007, 010; outlier 4.41].

  • Arm's documented limit for the predecessor core. The Cortex-A520 TRM gives the core's L2 interface 31 outstanding read transactions (single-slice L2). The C1-Nano and C1-DSU manuals are not on disk, so Asimov's own limits per core, per cluster and for the CME are Insufficient data. The measurement that would give them: the home nodes' read-queue occupancy event (PMU_HNF_POCQ_OCCUPANCY) around the same one-core read on an L3-on and an L3-off boot, proposed for run 7 [follow-up-run-plan.md section 14].
  • What the L3 changes. With the L3 on the same stream keeps about 20 lines in flight instead of 7.5, with the same refills per line and 0.975 times the mesh requests. So the L3's full mode lets more read requests stay open, by a mechanism not yet measured [outlier 4.33].

2.4 How the prefetchers were turned off

  • Boots B, D and F2 ran a rebuilt TF-A (0.35.0-pfoff.1). At the end of every power-on of CPUs 2 to 9 it sets IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bit 48 (ALLPFDIS: disable all data-side prefetchers) and IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 (PF_DISABLE for the CME prefetcher), reads both back and prints one line on the console [README 006, which quotes uart_1.log lines 104 to 111].
  • The check that it worked: boot B's sequential chain reads 52.76 ns per load against boot A's 6.92 ns, and the prefetch refill columns read 0.0000 in 558 of 559 latency rows [006 latency-dram-flushed.csv and the latency files].
  • Linux cannot make these writes itself: the registers are EL3-only, so the change needed firmware.

4. The outliers

In order of first appearance. Each item has four parts: what looked wrong, why it looked wrong (the expectation it contradicted), the tests added, and what they showed. The small diagram marks the blocks involved. The full verified record with every number and source folds out under each item.

4.1 Flushed DRAM rows read DRAM latency, not SLC (DC CIVAC reaches the SLC)explained

Run 1 flushed 1 to 3 MiB rows read 52.7 ns per load (the DRAM value), not the expected 23.8 to 25.4 ns SLC value.

What looked wrong

  • Run 1 had flushed DRAM rows at 256 KiB, 1, 2, 3 and 8 MiB. [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • "Flushed" means every line was cleaned and invalidated with DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate-by-address instruction) before one timed pass. [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • The flushed 1, 2, 3 and 8 MiB rows read 52.716, 52.714, 52.713 and 52.711 ns per load on run 1 (best of 3 reps, the lowest of three repeated passes). [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:12, :17, :22, :27]
  • The fresh 32 MiB chain (a random pointer chain walked once, never flushed) read 52.300 ns per load on run 1. That is the DRAM value. [001 latency-dram-large.csv:46]
  • Fresh chains of 512 KiB to 2 MiB read 23.075 to 23.998 ns per load on run 1. The fresh 3 MiB chain read 25.449 ns per load. [001 latency-dram-large.csv:6 to :22, :26]
  • The flushed 256 KiB row read 35.689 ns per load on run 1, with 0.78 to 0.90 L3 read refills per load. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:4 to :7]
  • That is a separate defect (prefetch on a re-walked chain) and is not covered here. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:4 to :7]

Why it looked wrong

  • The SLC (system level cache, the cache in the CMN mesh, Arm's coherent mesh interconnect) that caches DRAM is 3.75 MiB. A 1 to 3 MiB footprint fits in it. [001 README.md:23]
  • The flush was meant to clear only the core caches: L1, L2 and the DSU L3 (the L3 in Arm's DynamIQ Shared Unit).
  • So the 1 to 3 MiB flushed rows were expected at the fresh-chain values of those sizes, 23.8 to 25.4 ns per load.
  • The refill counters (the count of lines a cache fetched from the next level) showed 1.00 L1, L2 and L3 read refills per load on every flushed row from 1 MiB up on run 1. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:9 to :26]
  • Every timed load missed every core cache. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:9 to :26]
  • The flushed rows' time per load matched the 32 MiB fresh chain within 0.42 ns on run 1. [001 README.md:36, run1-report.html:471]
  • So DC CIVAC also removed the DRAM-backed lines from the SLC, and the timed pass read DRAM. [001 README.md:36, run1-report.html:471, RUN2-PLAN.md:74 to :76]
  • Such a row cannot stand for an SLC hit. [RUN2-PLAN.md:74 to :76]

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (membench-jibin-001, Jesse's results dated 2026-10-31), analysed 2026-11-01 and 2026-11-02

What looked wrong. Run 1 had flushed DRAM rows at 256 KiB, 1, 2, 3 and 8 MiB. Flushed means every line was cleaned and invalidated with DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate-by-address instruction) before one timed pass. The 1, 2, 3 and 8 MiB flushed rows read 52.716, 52.714, 52.713 and 52.711 ns per load (best of 3 reps) [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:12, :17, :22, :27]. The fresh 32 MiB chain (a random pointer chain walked once, never flushed) read 52.300 ns per load [latency-dram-large.csv:46]. The fresh 512 KiB to 2 MiB chains read 23.075 to 23.998 ns per load [latency-dram-large.csv:6 to :22], and the fresh 3 MiB chain 25.449 ns [latency-dram-large.csv:26]. The SLC (system level cache, in the CMN mesh) that caches DRAM is 3.75 MiB [membench-jibin-001 README.md:23]. A 1 to 3 MiB footprint fits that SLC. So the 1 to 3 MiB flushed rows were expected near the fresh-chain values of the same sizes (23.8 to 25.4 ns), not at the DRAM value. The 256 KiB flushed row read 35.689 ns with 0.78 to 0.90 L3 read refills per load, a separate defect (prefetch on a re-walked chain) [latency-dram-flushed.csv:4 to :7].

Why it looked wrong. The flush was meant to clear only the core caches (L1, L2, DSU L3). The refill counters show that each timed load missed every core cache: 1.00 L1, L2 and L3 read refills per load on every flushed row from 1 MiB up [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:9 to :26]. The time per load equals the 32 MiB fresh chain within 0.42 ns. So DC CIVAC also removed the DRAM-backed lines from the SLC, and the timed pass read DRAM [membench-jibin-001 README.md:36; run1-report.html:471; RUN2-PLAN.md:74 to :76]. Such a row cannot stand for an SLC hit. OCM rows were unaffected (OCM lines are locked SLC ways; see the OCM-mode entry).

Tests added.

  • Shrink the flushed DRAM rows to one 8 MiB row, run as a fresh chain plus flush (latency --cpu 2 --perf --fresh 3 --flush --sizes 8M), and keep it as the DRAM reference. Drop the 256 KiB and the 1 to 3 MiB flushed rows. Run 1's flushed rows had used --flush --reps 3 (fresh=0: a chain already walked twice in warm-up); run 2's row is fresh=3 [run_asimov.sh:24 to :32, :114 to :115; membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:1; membench-jibin-002 latency-dram-flushed.csv:1]. The SLC is taken from the fresh chains instead. [run 2 (membench-jibin-002, commit 8ae533c; the run 2 commits were f81eb51, 94572c5, 7ba4c5b, 89552a1, 8ae533c) [RUN2-PLAN.md:5 to :6, :221, :494]]: whether the flushed 8 MiB row reads within 1 ns of the 32 MiB fresh chain (the acceptance criterion) [RUN2-PLAN.md:104, :290]

What the tests showed. Run 2: the flushed 8 MiB row read 52.712 ns per load [membench-jibin-002 latency-dram-flushed.csv:6] and the fresh 32 MiB chain 52.233 ns [latency-dram-large.csv:46], a gap of 0.48 ns, inside the 1 ns criterion [RUN2-PLAN.md:502]. The flushed 8 MiB row has stayed the DRAM reference on every later run: 52.711 ns (control run 003), 52.738 (run 3, 004), 52.739 (boots A, B, D), 52.657 (boot C, 007 bootC/latency-dram-flushed.csv:7), 52.659 (boot E, 010 bootE/latency-dram-flushed.csv:7), 52.658 (boot F1, 011). The SLC is quoted from the 2 MiB fresh chain: 24.053 ns on boot C [007 bootC/latency-dram-large.csv:23] and 24.177 ns on boot E [010 bootE/latency-dram-large.csv:23]. The core page states it as 'from the SLC in 24.2 ns and from DRAM in 52.7 ns (every line flushed)' and its table 4.1 labels the 2 MiB fresh row 'SLC (mesh cache)' and the 8 MiB flushed row (52.659 / 52.738 / 52.657 ns on E / run 3 / C) 'DRAM' [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, short version and table 4.1]. 4.2 Flushed OCM rows stay at 19 to 26 ns: way locking or CMN OCM mode?explained

Flushed OCM rows in run 1 still read 18.8 to 25.5 ns per load, not the 52.7 ns DRAM value the same flush produced.

What looked wrong

  • Every flushed OCM (on-chip memory, 256 KiB per region) row in run 1 read 18.8 to 25.5 ns per load on its best row. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv]
  • Over all nine single reps the range was 18.8 to 26.0 ns per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv]
  • The flush was DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction, which pushes lines out of the core caches). [001 README.md line 36]
  • The same flush pushed DRAM-backed lines out of the SLC (system level cache, held in the CMN mesh home nodes). [001 README.md line 36]
  • The flushed DRAM rows of 1 to 8 MiB in run 1 read 52.7 ns per load, the DRAM value (best rows 52.716, 52.714, 52.713, 52.711 ns). [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • The 256 KiB flushed DRAM row in run 1 read 35.7 ns per load best (reps 44.7, 39.0, 35.7 ns). Some of its lines were prefetched. So this row understates a single read. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv, 001 README.md line 34]
  • The L3 read refill count on the 256 KiB flushed OCM rows in run 1 was 0.77 to 0.91 refills per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]
  • A value of 1.00 would mean every load left the DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, a 2-core cluster). [001 README.md line 34]

Why it looked wrong

  • The expectation was that a clean-and-invalidate flush empties the SLC for the flushed range. The DRAM rows behaved that way in run 1 (52.7 ns per load). [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • The OCM rows stayed at 18.8 to 25.5 ns per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • The open question was how the OCM lock is set up. [run1-report.html line 491]
  • A plain locked range (set by the registers hnf_slc_lock_ways and lock_base) and the CMN OCM mode (a mode of the Arm CMN S3 mesh) behave differently on a flush. [run1-report.html line 491]
  • The Arm CMN S3 TRM (Technical Reference Manual) says a CleanInvalid of an OCM-mode line does nothing in the SLC. [run1-report.html line 491]
  • It also says a locked line in a normal range can be pushed to memory by a non-allocating request. [run1-report.html line 491]
  • No memory sits behind OCM. If the flush had removed the OCM lines from the SLC, the data would have had nowhere to come back from. [README.md lines 40 to 46, run1-report.html line 491]
  • Run 1 showed that the data stayed. So the question was about interpretation and not about safety. [README.md lines 40 to 46, run1-report.html line 491]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Question to Jesse, answered from the SCP firmware source and address mapotherReads the lock mode of the OCM regions and the home-node id of each region from the SCP (System Control Processor) firmware source and the address map. No chip measurement is involved. OCM mode would mean a flush leaves the line in the SLC. A plain locked range would mean a flush can push it out. The source is program_ocm in asimov_physical_sam.c lines 458 to 490 (writes HN_LOCK_WAYS, four HN_LOCK_BASE registers, then HN_CFG_CTL |= HN_OCM_EN) and sam_map.yaml lines 208 to 212 (routes ocm0 to ocm4 to one home node each, "No HN subordinate"). Answered 2026-11-01, before run 2. [memory note asimov-run1-facts.md, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 60 to 66, CMN S3 TRM page 292]
Run 2 per-region OCM rows from CPU 2, fresh chain plus flushrun 2Measures ns per load on a chain never walked before (the --fresh 3 --flush options), after DC CIVAC. Counts the requests received at each of the five home nodes (the cmncount counter hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all) around each row. OCM-speed latency after the flush would confirm that the lines stay in the SLC. A request count concentrated on one home node per region would confirm the node ids. Ran 2026-11-02. [002 latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv, 002 cmn-counts.csv]

What the tests showed

  • OCM is CMN OCM mode. The home node sends no requests to memory. A CleanInvalid or CleanShared terminates in the SLC and does not invalidate the line. [Jesse's agent reply of 2026-11-01, checked against the SCP source and the TRM: memory note asimov-run1-facts.md, README.md lines 40 to 46, RUN2-PLAN.md line 63]
  • The CMN node ids 88, 160, 216, 288 and 344 hold OCM0 to OCM4. [README.md line 37, RUN2-PLAN.md line 64, 002 README.md line 70]
  • Run 2 confirmed the flush result on the chip. [002 latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv]
  • The per-region rows from CPU 2 with a fresh chain plus a flush read 18.46 to 22.00 ns per load (best rows OCM0 to OCM4: 19.770, 18.456, 21.355, 21.535, 22.001 ns). [002 latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv]
  • Run 1 had read 18.78 to 23.17 ns per load on the same five regions. [002 README.md section Against round one]
  • Run 2 confirmed the node ids on the chip. In each of the 20 per-region rows the region's own home node received 111,468 to 123,460 mesh requests. [002 README.md section Mesh counts, cmn-counts.csv]
  • Each other node received 9,042 to 10,576 requests. [002 README.md section Mesh counts, cmn-counts.csv]
  • The flush-based OCM rows are safe by design. The flush does not remove the OCM data. The rows therefore measure OCM and not DRAM. [README.md lines 40 to 46]
  • The four generated pages (asimov-c1nano-perf.html, asimov-cme-perf.html, asimov-c1nano-run4.html, asimov-cme-run4.html) carry the node ids only. They do not mention the lock mode. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html line 231]
  • The lock-mode claims live in README.md lines 40 to 46, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 60 to 66 and the memory note.

Still open

The claim that OCM mode needs a power-of-two number of home nodes is not in any file in this folder. The CMN S3 TRM text is not in refs/. A copy of the TRM section on OCM mode (page 292 is the cited page) would settle whether that claim exists and whether five home nodes meet it.

4.3 OCM write and copy rows at 7.2 and 12.0 GB/s timed the flush, not the writepartly explained

Run 1's OCM write row at 7.2 GB/s timed the cache flush rather than the stores. The fixed row reads 20.4 GB/s.

What looked wrong

  • One core (CPU 2) wrote OCM1 (OCM is the on-chip memory, and region 1 is 256 KiB) in one pass with --flush-after. The row read 7.18 GB/s in run 1 [membench-jibin-001 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, log.txt:29].
  • The same core copied OCM1 to OCM2 (256 KiB, --flush-before and --flush-after) at 11.96 GB/s in run 1 [001 bandwidth-ocm-copy.csv:7, log.txt:30].
  • Four cores writing one OCM region each read 29.2 GB/s in total, 7.2 to 7.4 GB/s per core, in run 1 [001 bandwidth-ocm-4core.csv:11-14].
  • The same core writes DRAM at 30.6 to 32.0 GB/s at every footprint from 16 KiB to 32 MiB in run 1 [001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11,26,41,56,71,86].
  • The write row took 36.5 to 36.6 us (262,144 bytes at 7.16 to 7.18 GB/s). 256 KiB of stores at 32 GB/s take 8.2 us [001 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:4-6].
  • The copy row took 43.8 us (524,288 bytes at 11.965 GB/s) [001 bandwidth-ocm-copy.csv:5].

Why it looked wrong

  • The expectation was a store rate near the core's 32 GB/s DRAM write rate from run 1 [run1-report.html section 5a].
  • Instead, with --flush-after the timed span held the 256 KiB of stores plus one DC CIVAC (clean and invalidate by address) for each of the 4,096 lines [bandwidth.c:248-254, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 77-81].
  • The stores take 8.2 us at 32 GB/s. The remaining 28.3 us is the flush, about 6.9 ns per line (est., run 1) [run1-report.html section 5a].
  • So 7.2 GB/s is the rate of stores into the core caches plus a serial write-back to OCM, not a streaming OCM write rate [run1-report.html section 5a].
  • The copy row's 43.8 us is about 16 us of loads from OCM1 plus about 28 us of flush of OCM2 (est., run 1). The 4-core write row has the same defect [run1-report.html section 5a].
  • A 256 KiB buffer also fits in L2 plus L3 (384 KiB in total). The lines never leave the cluster during the timed pass [run1-report.html section 5a, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 121-127].
  • Jesse's README lists three OCM row kinds timed without a flush first. Its own rule says every timed OCM pass starts flushed [001 README.md line 35].

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Streaming OCM write, one core, 1.25 MiB over five regions, flush beforerun 2, control run, run 3, boot F1Measures the one-core OCM write rate with the flush outside the timed span (bandwidth --threads 1 --cpus 2 --mem ocm --ocm-regions 0,1,2,3,4 --bytes 1280K --kernel write --flush-before --passes 8 --reps 3). The 1.25 MiB buffer is 3.3 times the 384 KiB of L2 plus L3. Lines then reach OCM by eviction. The flawed write, copy and 4-core rows were dropped. A rate near 32 GB/s would mean run 1 timed only the flush. A lower rate would mean one core writes OCM slower than it writes DRAM [002 log.txt:59, RUN2-PLAN.md lines 121-127 and 228-232].
Streaming OCM write through the CME, same flags, mesh counters onrun 3Measures whether the CME's (the cluster's streaming unit that issues loads and stores for the cores) store path reaches a higher OCM write rate than the core's, with the same command plus --cme. A higher CME rate would mean the core's 20.3 GB/s is not a limit of OCM itself [004 log.txt:117, CME-plan.md line 102, test 7].
Both OCM write rows with the L3 on, then prefetchers offboot F1, boot F2Measures whether the L3 (run 3's command set rerun on the L3-on firmware) or the data prefetchers (turned off in boot F2) change the core's or the CME's OCM write rate. A changed rate would mean that unit takes part in the write path [011 and 012 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7].

What the tests showed

  • Run 2: one core writes OCM at 20.3 to 20.4 GB/s over three reps, best 20.433 GB/s. This is the first row free of the flush defect [002 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:4-7].
  • Jesse noted it sits below one core's 32.0 GB/s store rate to DRAM [002 README.md line 86].
  • The run 1 write-then-flush row, the copy row and the 4-core OCM write row were dropped from run 2 onward [RUN2-PLAN.md lines 107 and 228-232].
  • run1-report.html section 5a proposed 4 passes. The plan and the run used 8 [RUN2-PLAN.md lines 107 and 228-232, 002 log.txt:59].
  • Control run (run 2's code on run 1's firmware): 20.338 GB/s. Run 3: core 20.326 GB/s, CME 19.795 GB/s [003 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, 004 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, 004 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7].
  • In run 3 the CME writes DRAM at 62.0 to 63.9 GB/s at every footprint from 16 KiB to 32 MiB [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11,26,41,56,71,86,101,116].
  • In run 3 the core writes DRAM at 30.1 to 32.0 GB/s. So both write OCM slower than they write DRAM [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv:11-86].
  • Boot F1 (L3 on): the core's OCM write stays at 20.326 GB/s, unchanged to three decimals from run 3 [011 bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7].
  • Boot F1: the CME's OCM write rises to 30.659 GB/s by the bracket and 30.977 GB/s in span, 1.549 times run 3 [011 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, README.md line 317, asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.6].
  • Boot F2 (prefetchers off): CME 30.994 GB/s by the bracket, 31.327 GB/s in span [012 cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv:7, README.md line 133].

Still open

Why one core's OCM streaming write sits at 20.3 GB/s (run 2 through boot F1), below its 32.0 GB/s DRAM store rate, is not explained in any primary file. The OCM and DRAM write rows differ in page size (OCM in 4 KiB pages, DRAM in 2 MiB pages). They also differ in flush state (OCM flushed once before its 8 passes per rep, DRAM never flushed). A run that changes one of these at a time would settle which one matters [004 README.md line 84, CSV header lines].

4.4 256 KiB OCM rows count fewer than 1.0 L3 refills and more than 1.0 L2 refills per load (prefetcher fills)explained

256 KiB flushed chains counted 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills per load, below the 1.00 a dependent chain should need.

What looked wrong

  • Run 1: every 256 KiB flushed row (five OCM region rows and one DRAM row) counted 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • The same rows counted 1.14 to 1.34 L2 refills (event 0x17) per load. [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • Run 1 rows of 1 MiB and more counted 1.00 of each.
  • DRAM flushed 1 to 8 MiB read 1.0001 to 1.0012 refills per load. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • OCM all-five flushed 1.25 MiB read 1.0004 to 1.0012 refills per load. [001 latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv]
  • The run 1 DRAM 256 KiB row got faster as its L3 count fell.
  • It read 44.698, 39.031 and 35.689 ns per load at 0.9043, 0.8459 and 0.7839 L3 read refills per load. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv reps 0 to 2]
  • Run 2 fresh chains (never walked before the timed pass) did not change it.
  • Run 2's 40 passes on 20 per-region rows counted 0.76 to 0.95 L3 and 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load. [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 002 README line 66]
  • In 19 of 20 rows the faster pass had fewer L3 read refills. [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 002 README line 66]
  • Run 3 sparse chains (one member line per 4 KiB page) counted 1.92 to 3.78 L2 refills per load over 140 passes. [004 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 004 README line 111]
  • The same passes counted 0.47 to 1.14 L3 read refills per load. [004 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 004 README line 111]

Why it looked wrong

  • A dependent chain (each load's address comes from the previous load) asks for one cache line per load. So each cache level should show at most 1.00 refills per load.
  • Fewer than 1.00 L3 read refills per load means 9 to 23 % of the lines (1 minus 0.91, 1 minus 0.77) were already inside the cluster when the load asked for them.
  • More than 1.00 L2 refills per load means the L2 filled lines the chain never asked for.
  • The run 1 to run 3 counter set (0x03 L1 refills, 0x17 L2 refills, 0xA2 L3 read refills) counts fills by level, not by cause. [common.h line 336]
  • So a hardware prefetcher was a hypothesis, not a measurement, until run 4.
  • On runs 1 to 3 and on boots A and B the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data (snoop-filter-only mode). [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]
  • So an L3 read refill on these rows means a demand read that left the cluster. The early-arriving lines sat in the L2. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Fresh chains with flush on every per-region OCM rowrun 2Each timed pass walks a chain never walked before (CSV header fresh=3 flush=1, two timed passes per row, fresh1 and fresh2). A count that stays below 1.00 L3 read refills per load would mean an unseen chain does not remove the early-arriving lines. [002, commit 8ae533c, 2026-11-02]
Sparse chains (one member per 4 KiB page) plus dense all-five controlrun 3Per-region latency when no neighbouring line is a chain member (chain c uses line 8c+4 of every page, 7 timed passes of 64 loads per region). The dense all-five control row (run 2's all-five arguments) checks that the platform repeats run 2. [004, commit ba834c0, 2026-11-03, latency.c lines 21 to 22]
Prefetch refill events on every OCM row plus sequential 8 MiB chainboot AHow many fills per load each prefetcher made, using events 0x81BC (L1D refills requested by a hardware prefetcher), 0x81BD (L2 refills by prefetchers targeting the L2) and 0x0111 (L2 refills from the L1D prefetcher's requests). The --seq 8 MiB sequential chain is the stimulus that shows whether the new events count at all. [005, commit e8e4580, 2026-11-04, common.h lines 329 to 336, latency-dram-seq.csv]
Data prefetchers off on CPUs 2 to 9 and their CMEsboot BDemand-only refill counts and latency on the same rows, with TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1 (commit 5a9e2a8) setting IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bit 48 ALLPFDIS and IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 PF_DISABLE at every core power-on. So any remaining extra fill would not come from a prefetcher. [006, commit 7921962, 2026-11-04/05, README lines 16 to 23]

What the tests showed

  • Runs 2 and 3: fresh chains did not remove the early-arriving lines (0.76 to 0.95 L3 and 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load). [002 README line 66]
  • Sparse rows did not count closer to 1.00 (1.92 to 3.78 L2 refills per load). [004 README line 111]
  • The dense all-five control read 25.340 ns per load, 0.166 ns under run 2's 25.506 ns per load, with 1.00 refills per load at L1, L2 and L3. [004 README line 110]
  • Boot A: the new events count. On the sequential 8 MiB chain (6.917 ns per load) 0x81BC and 0x0111 each read 0.9999 per load beside 1.0000 L1 and L2 refills per load. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.1]
  • There 0xA2 reads 0.0001 per load. So 0xA2 does not count prefetch fills. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.1]
  • A prefetched line lowers the L3 count below 1.00.
  • Boot A: on every OCM row, L2 refills minus 0x81BD equal the L3 read refills. [table 3.4, 005 CSVs 218 rows recomputed]
  • Row means differ by -0.022 to +0.000 per load, and single 64-load passes by -0.125 to +0.016 per load (one pass counts in steps of 1/64 refill per load). [table 3.4, 005 CSVs 218 rows recomputed]
  • So the extra fills come from a hardware prefetcher that targets the L2.
  • Boot A 0x81BD row means per load: dense per-region 0.236 to 0.459, sparse 1.112 to 2.223, vary 1.152 to 2.980, all-five sparse 1.051 to 1.066, all-five dense 0.000. [table 3.4, 005 CSVs]
  • The L1 prefetcher made none: 0x81BC and 0x0111 read 0.000 per load on every OCM row. [table 3.4, 005 CSVs]
  • Boot B: every prefetch refill counter reads 0.0000 per load (rounded to four decimals) in all 559 counted rows, and exactly 0 on the OCM rows. [006 README line 7, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.5, 006 CSVs]
  • The one non-zero value, 1.907e-06 per load (one refill in 524,288 loads), is on the first pass of the 32 MiB row of latency-dram-large.csv. [006 README line 7, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.5, 006 CSVs]
  • Sparse rows count 1.002 to 1.007 L2 and 1.011 to 1.022 L3 read refills per load (row means). [006 README line 7, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.5, 006 CSVs]
  • Boot B against boot A (median of passes): dense OCM rows +9 to +18 % slower, vary rows +2 to +30 %, sparse rows -10 to +6 %. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.2, tables 11.2 and 11.3, 006 README line 49]
  • The sequential 8 MiB chain read 52.762 ns per load on boot B against 6.917 ns per load on boot A. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.2, tables 11.2 and 11.3, 006 README line 49]
  • So the L2 prefetcher helps a dense chain. It does nothing for a sparse one.

Still open

Which prefetcher (stride or spatial) reacts to a one-line-per-page chain is not named. The per-prefetcher refill events 0x00D9 to 0x00DB, 0x010F and 0x0110 would answer it. They were not run. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, H2 paragraph]

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (membench-jibin-001), ran 2026-10-31 [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 3]; counted again on run 2 (002, 2026-11-02), run 3 (004, 2026-11-03), run 4 boots A (005, 2026-11-04) and B (006, 2026-11-04/05)

What looked wrong. Every 256 KiB flushed row in run 1 (the five OCM region rows and the DRAM 256 KiB row) counted 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load and 1.14 to 1.34 L2 refills (event 0x17) per load [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, latency-dram-flushed.csv]. Rows of 1 MiB and more counted 1.00 of each (DRAM flushed 1 to 8 MiB: 1.0001 to 1.0012; OCM all-five flushed 1.25 MiB: 1.0004 to 1.0012). Run 2's fresh chains (a chain never walked before each timed pass) did not change it: the 40 timed passes of the 20 per-region rows counted 0.76 to 0.95 L3 and 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv]. In 19 of those 20 rows the faster pass is the one with fewer L3 read refills [002 README line 66]. Run 3's sparse chains (one member line per 4 KiB page) counted 1.92 to 3.78 L2 refills and 0.47 to 1.14 L3 read refills per load [004 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 140 passes; 004 README line 111]. Why it looked wrong. A dependent chain asks for one line per load. So each cache level should show at most 1.00 refills per load. Fewer than 1.00 L3 read refills means 9 to 23 % of the lines were already inside the cluster when the load asked for them (1 minus 0.91, 1 minus 0.77). More than 1.00 L2 refills means the L2 filled lines the chain never asked for. The run 1 to run 3 counter set (0x03 L1 refills, 0x17 L2 refills, 0xA2 L3 read refills) counts fills by level, not by cause [common.h line 336]. So a hardware prefetcher was a hypothesis, not a measurement, until run 4. A second fact only run 4 boot B showed: the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data on runs 1 to 3 and boots A and B (snoop-filter-only mode), so 'L3 read refill' on these rows means a demand read that left the cluster, and the early-arriving lines sat in the L2 [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1].

  • --sparse chains (one member per 4 KiB page, at line 8c+4 of every page for chain c [latency.c lines 21 to 22]), 7 timed passes of 64 loads per region, plus a dense all-five control row (run 2's all-five arguments) [run 3 (004, commit ba834c0, 2026-11-03)]: per-region latency when no neighbouring line is a chain member; the control checks that the platform repeats run 2
  • Prefetch refill events on every OCM row: 0x81BC (L1D refills requested by a hardware prefetcher), 0x81BD (L2 refills by prefetchers targeting the L2), 0x0111 (L2 refills from the L1D prefetcher's requests) [common.h lines 329 to 336], plus the --seq 8 MiB sequential chain as the prefetch stimulus (latency-dram-seq.csv) [run 4 boot A (005, commit e8e4580, 2026-11-04)]: how many fills per load each prefetcher made, and whether the new events count at all
  • Boot B: data prefetchers off on CPUs 2 to 9 and their CMEs (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1, commit 5a9e2a8, sets IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bit 48 ALLPFDIS and IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 PF_DISABLE at every core power-on) [006 README lines 16 to 23] [run 4 boot B (006, commit 7921962, 2026-11-04/05)]: demand-only refill counts and latency on the same rows

What the tests showed. Run 2: fresh chains did not help (0.76 to 0.95 L3, 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load) [002 README line 66]. Run 3: sparse rows were not cleaner (1.92 to 3.78 L2 refills per load); the dense all-five control read 25.340 ns per load against run 2's 25.506 ns, a 0.166 ns gap, with 1.00 refills per load at L1, L2 and L3 [004 README line 110]. The dense all-five chain is the OCM number the pages quote [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Short version]. Boot A: the three new events count (on the sequential 8 MiB chain 0x81BC reads 0.9999 and 0x0111 0.9999 per load beside 1.0000 L1 and L2 refills, at 6.917 ns per load) [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.1]. On every OCM row, L2 refills minus 0x81BD equal the L3 read refills: the row means differ by -0.022 to +0.000 per load [table 3.4]; single 64-load passes differ by -0.125 to +0.016 (one pass counts in steps of 1/64) [005 CSVs, 218 rows recomputed]. So the extra fills are made by a hardware prefetcher that targets the L2: 0x81BD per load, row means, dense per-region rows 0.236 to 0.459, sparse 1.112 to 2.223, vary 1.152 to 2.980, all-five sparse 1.051 to 1.066, all-five dense 0.000 [table 3.4]. The L1 prefetcher made none: 0x81BC and 0x0111 read 0.000 on every OCM row [table 3.4; 005 CSVs]. Also, 0xA2 does not count prefetch fills: on the sequential chain it reads 0.0001 per load while L2 refills read 1.0000 [table 3.1], which is why a prefetched line lowers the L3 count below 1.00. Boot B: every prefetch refill counter reads 0.0000 per load (rounded to four decimals) in all 559 counted rows; the one non-zero value is 1.907e-06 (one refill in 524,288 loads) on the first pass of the 32 MiB row of latency-dram-large.csv [006 README line 7]; on the OCM rows all are exactly 0 [006 CSVs]. Sparse rows count 1.002 to 1.007 L2 refills and 1.011 to 1.022 L3 read refills per load (row means) [section 11.5; 006 CSVs]. By the median of passes the dense OCM rows read +9 to +18 % slower than boot A, the vary rows +2 to +30 %, the sparse rows -10 to +6 % [section 11.2, table 11.3; 006 README line 49]. So the L2 prefetcher helps a dense chain and does nothing for a sparse one. Which prefetcher (stride or spatial) reacts to a one-line-per-page chain is not named: the per-prefetcher refill events 0x00D9 to 0x00DB, 0x010F and 0x0110 were not run [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, H2 paragraph].

4.5 OCM latency 18.8 to 23.2 ns per region against asimov-bench's 14.42 nsopen

Our flushed OCM chase reads 18.8 ns per load at best, 4.4 ns (30 %) above asimov-bench's 14.42 ns on the same region.

What looked wrong

  • In run 1, CPU 2 ran a flushed chase (dependent loads, one per 64-byte line, after a cache clean) of OCM1 (on-chip memory region 1).
  • The best row read 18.782 ns per load, with 0.8157 L3 read refills per load [001 latency-ocm-region1.csv, rep 2].
  • The five OCM regions read 18.782 to 23.165 ns per load in run 1 [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows].
  • In run 2, with fresh chains, CPU 2 read 18.456 to 21.355 ns per load from the three regions one crosspoint away (OCM0 to OCM2) [002 latency-ocm-region0..2-cpu2.csv, best rows].
  • It read 21.535 to 22.001 ns per load from the two regions three crosspoints away (OCM3, OCM4) [002 latency-ocm-region3..4-cpu2.csv, best rows].
  • asimov-bench (the other team's benchmark) measured 14.42 ns per load on the same OCM1 region (0xE0100000).
  • That chase covered 64 KiB (16 pages) after DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction), on RTL 6da3026 [001 README, cross-check table].
  • Our fastest row (18.782 ns per load, run 1) sits 4.4 ns (30 %) above asimov-bench's 14.42 ns per load.

Why it looked wrong

  • Both numbers are chase averages that start flushed. Both run on the same CMN (the mesh interconnect) and the same C1 core logic.
  • The RTL differs only elsewhere. So the two numbers should agree [001 README, cross-check].
  • Jesse's README gives one reason the gap could be real. asimov-bench's 14.42 ns per load is below its own 20.0 ns waveform read of one SLC line (system level cache) [001 README, SLC row].
  • So that chase counts some lines fetched before their load [002 README, cross-check].
  • A second reason: asimov-bench's 16-page set fits the core's 16-entry L1 data TLB (the translation cache) [002 README, cross-check].
  • Each of our regions spans 64 pages [004 README, Caches].
  • Our own per-region rows are also not one home-node read per load. They count 1.14 to 1.34 L2 refills and 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills per load in run 1.
  • So some lines reach the cluster before their load, most likely by hardware prefetch [001 README, Reading the numbers].

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Fresh-chain per-region OCM rows from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8run 2OCM latency per region and per crosspoint distance. Whether a fresh chain removes the lines fetched before their load.
Sparse per-region rows plus a dense all-five controlrun 3A chase in which every load is a demand miss to a flushed line (one line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads a pass, best of 7). The dense all-five row is the clean one-read-per-load number.
Boot B: data prefetchers off, route rows under crosspoint countersboot BHow much of the per-region spread the L2 prefetcher causes. A distance fit with no prefetch.
Boots C and D: 64 KiB OCM translations with TLB eventsboot C, boot DWhether the 16-entry L1 data TLB explains the gap. TLB refills and chase time with 64 KiB translations (contiguous hint) against 4 KiB pages.
Boots E and F1: the DSU L3 on for CPUs 2 to 9boot E, boot F1The same OCM rows with the cluster L3 holding data.

What the tests showed

  • Run 2: the per-region bests order by mesh distance. They average 19.64 ns per load at 1 crosspoint (8 rows), 21.82 ns at 3 crosspoints (10 rows) and 24.58 ns at 5 crosspoints (2 rows).
  • That is about 1.1 to 1.4 ns per crosspoint [002 README, OCM and SLC latency by mesh distance].
  • The fresh chain did not remove the early fetches: 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills and 0.76 to 0.95 L3 read refills per load [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 20 best rows].
  • Run 3: the sparse rows from CPU 2 at one crosspoint read 22.969, 21.359 and 22.297 ns per load (OCM0 to OCM2, best of 7) [004 latency-ocm-region0..2-cpu2.csv].
  • Over CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8 the one-crosspoint bests are 20.141 to 22.969 ns per load (mean 21.58 ns).
  • The dense all-five row from CPU 2 reads 25.340 ns per load with 1.0009 L3 read refills per load [004 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv].
  • The README calls the gap to 14.42 ns 'still not explained' [004 README, line 135].
  • Boot B (prefetchers off): the route rows fit 20.75 ns + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step, within 0.09 ns rms (root mean square error, derived).
  • So a one-crosspoint OCM read with no prefetch is about 21.7 to 22.7 ns per load (est., from the fit) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 6, Distance].
  • Boots C and D (64 KiB translations): on boot C, CPU 2's L1 data TLB refills fell from 0.66 to 0.77 per load on boot A to 0.17 to 0.20 per load.
  • The sparse TLB-set rows on boot C read 23.297, 22.109, 21.469, 24.484 and 24.594 ns per load. Boot A's read 23.719, 24.062, 24.266, 25.312 and 24.531 ns per load [005 and 007 latency-ocm-region0..4-tlb-cpu2.csv].
  • The sparse TLB-set rows are 0.950 times boot A's by geometric mean, the core OCM rows 0.977 times.
  • So the TLB explanation accounts for about 1 ns per load at most, not the 4 ns gap [007 README, line 52].
  • Boots E and F1 (L3 on): on F1 the sparse rows from CPU 2 at one crosspoint read 20.297, 18.656 and 19.516 ns per load, with only 0.31 to 0.52 L3 read refills per load in the best pass.
  • So part of each row is served inside the cluster [011 latency-ocm-region0..2-cpu2.csv].
  • On boot E the dense OCM1 chain from CPU 2 reads 14.847 ns per load with 0.4365 L3 read refills per load [010 latency-ocm-region1-dense-cpu2.csv].
  • That matches asimov-bench's 14.42 ns per load. But the page says such rows sit below the true OCM latency [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, OCM paragraph and table 4.2].
  • The gap to 14.42 ns per load (derived): 4.36 ns on run 1's OCM1 row (18.782 ns), 4.24 ns on F1's OCM1 row (18.656 ns).
  • The gap is 6.9 to 8.5 ns on run 3's sparse one-crosspoint rows from CPU 2, and 10.9 ns on run 3's dense all-five row.
  • The F1 README still calls it 'the large gap round three's README notes' [011 README, line 142].

Still open

Hypothesis, not shown by these sources: asimov-bench's chase may have run on a core whose L3 held data. The stock SCP (the system control processor firmware) enables the full L3 for cluster 0 only [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Platform]. Or it may have counted lines fetched before their load. The measurement that would settle it: asimov-bench's chase re-run on this image from CPU 2 with the L3 read refill counter (event 0xA2) open, or our dense OCM1 chain run from a cluster 0 core.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (membench-jibin-001), 2026-10-31; the run 3 README (004, 2026-11-03) and the F1 README (011, 2026-11-06) still call the gap unexplained

What looked wrong. In run 1, CPU 2's flushed chase (a chain of dependent loads, one per 64-byte line) of OCM1 read 18.782 ns per load at best, with 0.8157 L3 read refills per load [001 latency-ocm-region1.csv, rep 2]. The five regions read 18.782 to 23.165 ns [001 latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows]. In run 2, with fresh chains, CPU 2 read 18.456 to 21.355 ns from the three regions one crosspoint away (OCM0 to OCM2) and 21.535 to 22.001 ns from the two three crosspoints away (OCM3, OCM4) [002 latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv, best rows]. asimov-bench, the other team's benchmark, had measured 14.42 ns per load for a 64 KiB (16-page) chase of the same OCM1 region (0xE0100000) after DC CIVAC, on RTL 6da3026 [001 README, cross-check table]. Our fastest row sits 4.4 ns (30 %) above it.

Why it looked wrong. Both numbers are chase averages that start flushed, on the same CMN and C1 logic (the RTL differs only elsewhere), so they should agree [001 README, cross-check]. Jesse's README gives two reasons the gap could be real but not a CMN difference. First, asimov-bench's chase reads below its own 20.0 ns waveform read of one SLC line, so it counts some lines already fetched before their load [001 README SLC row; 002 README cross-check]. Second, asimov-bench's 16-page set fits the core's 16-entry L1 data TLB (the translation cache), while each of our regions spans 64 pages [002 README cross-check; 004 README, Caches]. Our own per-region rows are also not one home-node read per load: they count 1.14 to 1.34 L2 refills and 0.77 to 0.91 L3 read refills per load, so some lines reach the cluster before their load, most likely by hardware prefetch [001 README, Reading the numbers].

Tests added.

  • Fresh-chain per-region OCM rows from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8 (latency by mesh distance) [run 2 (002)]: OCM latency per region and per crosspoint distance; whether a fresh chain removes the lines fetched before their load
  • Sparse per-region rows (one line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads a pass, best of 7) plus a dense all-five control [run 3 (004)]: a chase in which every load is a demand miss to a flushed line; the dense all-five row as the clean one-read-per-load number
  • Boot B: data prefetchers off; route rows under crosspoint counters [run 4 boot B (006)]: how much of the per-region spread the L2 prefetcher causes; a distance fit with no prefetch
  • Boots C and D: OCM mapped in 64 KiB translations (contiguous hint), with the L1 data TLB refill and walk events [run 4 boots C (007) and D (008)]: whether the 16-entry L1 data TLB explains the gap: TLB refills and chase time with 64 KiB translations against 4 KiB pages
  • Boot E and boot F1: the DSU L3 on for CPUs 2 to 9 [run 4 boot E (010), run 6 boot F1 (011)]: the same OCM rows with the cluster L3 holding data

What the tests showed. Run 2: the per-region bests order by mesh distance. They average 19.64 ns at 1 crosspoint (8 rows), 21.82 ns at 3 (10 rows) and 24.58 ns at 5 (2 rows), about 1.1 to 1.4 ns per crosspoint [002 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv, 20 best rows; 002 README, OCM and SLC latency by mesh distance]. The fresh chain did not remove the early fetches: 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills and 0.76 to 0.95 L3 read refills per load. Run 3: the sparse rows from CPU 2 at one crosspoint read 22.969, 21.359 and 22.297 ns (OCM0 to OCM2) [004 latency-ocm-region0..2-cpu2.csv, best of 7]; over all four CPUs the one-crosspoint bests are 20.141 to 22.969 ns (mean 21.58). The dense all-five row from CPU 2 reads 25.340 ns with 1.0009 L3 read refills per load [004 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv]; the README calls the gap to 14.42 ns 'still not explained' [004 README, line 135]. Boot B (prefetchers off): the route rows fit 20.75 ns + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step within 0.09 ns rms (derived) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 6, Distance]. So a one-crosspoint OCM read with no prefetch is about 21.7 to 22.7 ns. Boots C and D (64 KiB translations): CPU 2's L1 data TLB refills fell from 0.66 to 0.77 per load (boot A) to 0.17 to 0.20 per load, but the sparse TLB-set rows read 23.297, 22.109, 21.469, 24.484 and 24.594 ns against boot A's 23.719, 24.062, 24.266, 25.312 and 24.531 ns [005 and 007 latency-ocm-region0..4-tlb-cpu2.csv]. The core OCM rows read 0.977 times boot A's by geometric mean, the sparse TLB-set rows 0.950 [007 README, line 52]. So the TLB explanation accounts for about 1 ns at most, not the 4 ns gap. Boot E and F1 (L3 on): the sparse rows from CPU 2 at one crosspoint read 20.297, 18.656 and 19.516 ns with only 0.31 to 0.52 L3 read refills per load in the best pass [011 latency-ocm-region0..2-cpu2.csv], so part of each row is served inside the cluster. The dense OCM1 chain from CPU 2 on boot E reads 14.847 ns with 0.4365 L3 read refills per load [010 latency-ocm-region1-dense-cpu2.csv], which matches asimov-bench's 14.42 ns, but the page says such rows sit below the true OCM latency [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, OCM paragraph and table 4.2]. The F1 README still calls it 'the large gap round three's README notes' [011 README, line 142]. Hypothesis, not shown by these sources: asimov-bench's chase may have run on a core whose L3 held data (the stock SCP enables the full L3 for cluster 0 only [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Platform]), or may have counted lines fetched before their load. The measurement that would settle it: asimov-bench's chase re-run on this image from CPU 2 with the L3 read refill counter (0xA2) open, or our dense OCM1 chain from a cluster 0 core. The gap itself: 4.4 ns on run 1's OCM1 row (18.782 against 14.42), 4.2 ns on F1's (18.656), 6.9 to 8.5 ns on run 3's sparse one-crosspoint rows, 10.9 ns on the dense all-five row.

4.6 DRAM chase at 52 ns is too short for DRAM: the memory model has zero configured delayexplained

DRAM chain loads cost 52 ns on every boot, too short for real DRAM: the memory model's delay controls are all zero.

What looked wrong

  • The 32 MiB random chain (a pointer chase: each load's address comes from the previous load), walked once, read 52.181 to 52.875 ns per load on all ten boots, 001 to 011. [latency-dram-large.csv row dram,33554432,best of each run]
  • The lowest was boot A (005). The highest was boot E (010).
  • The flushed 8 MiB random chain (its lines evicted with DC CIVAC before the walk) read 52.657 to 52.739 ns per load on the same ten boots. [latency-dram-flushed.csv row dram,8388608,best]
  • The unflushed 8 MiB chain read 45.0 to 45.3 ns per load. The unflushed 16 MiB chain read 50.6 to 50.8 ns per load. [latency-dram-large.csv rows 8388608 and 16777216]
  • The 2 MiB chain fits in the SLC (system level cache) and measures the core-to-home-node round trip alone.
  • It read 24.096 ns per load on run 3 (004), 24.177 ns on boot E (010) and 23.714 ns on boot F1 (011). [latency-dram-large.csv row dram,2097152,best]
  • So the memory behind the home node adds only 28.5 to 28.9 ns est. per load.
  • That is 28.482 ns on boot E (52.659 minus 24.177), 28.642 ns on run 3 (52.738 minus 24.096) and 28.944 ns on boot F1 (52.658 minus 23.714). [derived from the two CSV rows, and 011 README.md line 250 gives 28.9 ns]
  • For comparison, the CRB (the Arm reference board: a Neoverse V3AE core at 2.8 GHz with DDR5-8000 memory) reads 148 ns per load for a DDR5 random read. [message-to-bill.md line 41, a row not in this tree's crb-validation CSVs, whose largest flushed row is 97.127 ns at 8 MiB]
  • asimov-bench (the earlier Asimov benchmark) read 31.65 ns per load on RTL 6da3026 and 53.3 ns per load on RTL bc5596aa, both on host-model DRAM.
  • Run 1's README called the 52.3 ns close to the 53.3 ns figure and did not flag it. [001 README.md line 50]

Why it looked wrong

  • A random read on LPDDR5X (the low-power DRAM type a real chip would use) costs about 50 ns est. inside the chip alone. That covers precharge, activate and column access, before the controller and the wires.
  • This figure is the session's estimate. No external source is named in the files. [message-to-bill-52ns.md lines 5-6]
  • A 29 ns est. memory leg is shorter than one row cycle (the time a DRAM bank needs to open a row, read it and close it). [message-to-bill-52ns.md lines 7-8 and message-to-bill.md line 10]
  • Bill's reading of the 52 ns was "too good to be true". The replies to Bill are dated 2026-11-04 by file time. [message-to-bill-52ns.md line 1]
  • The date of Bill's own message is not in the primary files.
  • Two readings were possible. Either a prefetcher (hardware that fetches cache lines before the core asks for them) served some of the chain's loads early. Or the memory is a fixed-delay model.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Prefetch counters on the 32 MiB and flushed 8 MiB chains, prefetchers onboot AIt counts prefetcher refills per load (event 0x81BC for L1 refills by the hardware prefetcher, event 0x81BD, and L2 refills from L1 prefetches). A non-zero count would mean a prefetcher served some loads early. Zero would mean every load was a demand miss.
Address-order 8 MiB chain (--seq, flushed) beside the random chain, prefetchers onboot AIt checks that the prefetch counters and the --seq row work. A much lower time in address order with a prefetch count near 1 per load would mean the prefetcher is active and counted.
Address-order against random 8 MiB chain, data prefetchers offboot B, boot DWith the data prefetchers off on CPUs 2-9 through a TF-A hook (bit 48 of IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 set), it tests row-buffer behaviour (real DRAM serves address order faster than random order). Equal times would mean the memory has no row behaviour.
Question to Jesse: the memory model's configured delaynot runIt asks what delay controls the memory model behind the home node has in the image's RTL (asimov-rtl 0d9e214eb43b). Controls at zero would mean the 52 ns is a fixed pipeline cost and not a DRAM timing.

What the tests showed

  • Boot A (005): the flushed 8 MiB chain read 52.739 ns per load with 0.0000 prefetch refills per load in all three prefetch columns and 1.0001 to 1.0002 L3 read refills per load. [005 latency-dram-flushed.csv rows fresh1 and fresh2]
  • The 32 MiB chain read 52.181 ns per load with 0.0000 prefetch refills and 1.0000 L3 read refills per load. So every load was a demand miss. [005 latency-dram-large.csv rows dram,33554432]
  • Boot A (005), prefetchers on: the address-order chain read 6.917 ns per load with 0.9999 L1 prefetch refills per load. So the counters and the --seq row work. [005 latency-dram-seq.csv]
  • Boot B (006), prefetchers off: address order read 52.762 ns per load and random order 52.739 ns per load, a 0.023 ns difference. [006 latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv rows dram,8388608,best, and 006 README.md line 7]
  • Boot D (008) repeated it at 52.763 ns per load. [008 README.md line 9]
  • So the memory serves address order no faster than random order. It has no row behaviour.
  • Jesse's answer in the boot F1 README: the AP DRAM is four embedded Cadence AXI memory models, one per SMS lane (XMS lanes 32-35). [011 README.md line 247]
  • Every delay control is zero: read latency 0, write-response latency 0, READY delays and burst gaps 0, and no bandwidth or refresh scheduler.
  • With the controls at zero the model answers 3 lane-clock cycles (3 ns at the 1 GHz lane clock) after it accepts a read. That 3 ns was checked only in the repo's Xcelium test, not on the Palladium build. [011 README.md line 249]
  • By a count of RTL stages (an inference, not a measurement), the SN node's read request to the first data beat takes 20.0 to 20.5 ns est. on SMS ports 0-2 and 19.0 to 19.5 ns est. on port 3. [011 README.md line 250]
  • The rest of the about 29 ns est. leg is inside the CMN: home-node miss handling, mesh steps to the four SMS SN nodes, and the SBSX CHI-to-AXI conversion. [011 README.md line 251]
  • Nothing in the tree configures that part. Nothing on the path models banks, rows, page hits or refresh.
  • The DRAM rows on the pages are labelled as the emulator's memory model, not silicon. The pages carry no CRB DRAM row. [message-to-bill-52ns.md line 18]
  • The core page's run 6 section reports Jesse's answer. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 'The memory model's delay, answered']

Still open

The core page is inconsistent. Its section 5 still says the model's delay 'was asked of Jesse and is unanswered [message-to-jesse-round4.md]'. Its run 6 section says answered. And message-to-jesse-round4.md is not in the tree [asimov-c1nano-perf.html stripped line 176 against line 85]. The 3 ns model response (Xcelium test only) and the 20.0 to 20.5 ns est. pipeline count (an inference) were not measured on the Palladium build. A measurement of the model's response time there would settle how the about 29 ns est. leg splits between the model and the CMN pipeline.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (001), run date 2026-10-31 [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 3]. Jesse's run 1 README compared the 52.3 ns with asimov-bench's 31.65 ns and 53.3 ns and called it close to the 53.3 ns figure, so it did not flag it as too low [README.md line 50]. The doubt is Bill's review. The replies to Bill are dated 2026-11-04 by file time [message-to-bill.md 18:55, message-to-bill-52ns.md 19:01]. The date of Bill's own message is not in the primary files. Jesse answered the memory-model question in the F1 README (question dated 2026-11-06) [results/membench-jibin-011/README.md line 245].

What looked wrong. The 32 MiB random chain, walked once, read 52.181 to 52.875 ns per load on every boot from run 1 to boot F1 (ten boots; 52.300 on 001, 52.233 on 002, 52.297 on 003, 52.185 on 004, 52.181 on 005, 52.248 on 006, 52.238 on 007, 52.249 on 008, 52.875 on 010, 52.212 on 011) [latency-dram-large.csv, row dram,33554432,best, of each run]. The flushed 8 MiB random chain read 52.657 to 52.739 ns on the same boots [latency-dram-flushed.csv, row dram,8388608,best]. The unflushed 8 MiB and 16 MiB chains read lower, 45.0 to 45.3 ns and 50.6 to 50.8 ns [latency-dram-large.csv rows 8388608 and 16777216]. The 2 MiB chain fits the SLC and measures the core-to-home-node round trip alone: 24.096 ns on run 3 (004) and 24.177 ns on boot E (010) [latency-dram-large.csv, row dram,2097152,best]. So the memory behind the home node adds only 28.5 to 28.9 ns (52.659 minus 24.177 = 28.482 ns on boot E; 52.658 minus 23.714 = 28.944 ns on F1; 52.738 minus 24.096 = 28.642 ns on run 3). The CRB (a Neoverse V3AE board at 2.8 GHz with DDR5-8000) reads 148 ns for a DDR5 random read [message-to-bill.md line 41; not in the crb-validation CSVs of this tree, whose largest flushed row reads 97.127 ns at 8 MiB]. asimov-bench read 31.65 ns on RTL 6da3026 (a 64 KiB, 16-page chase after DC CIVAC) and 53.3 ns on RTL bc5596aa (one line per page after DC CIVAC), both on host-model DRAM [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 50].

Why it looked wrong. A random read on LPDDR5X costs about 50 ns (est.) inside the chip alone: precharge, activate and column access, before the controller and wires [message-to-bill-52ns.md lines 5-6]. A 29 ns memory leg is shorter than one row cycle [message-to-bill-52ns.md lines 7-8; message-to-bill.md line 10]. Bill's reading: too good to be true [message-to-bill-52ns.md line 1]. Two readings were possible: a prefetcher served some of the chain's loads early, or the memory is a fixed-delay model. The 50 ns LPDDR5X figure is the session's estimate and names no external source in the files.

4.7 All-five OCM rows read 1.1 to 1.5 ns above an SLC hitpartly explained

A pointer chain over all five OCM regions reads 1.1 to 1.5 ns per load slower than a chain that hits in the SLC.

What looked wrong

  • The all-five OCM chain is one 1.25 MiB pointer chain over all five 256 KiB OCM regions.
  • On run 1, CPU 2, that chain read 25.219 ns per load fresh and 25.512 ns per load flushed. [001 latency-ocm-all5-fresh.csv, latency-ocm-all5-flushed.csv, rows best]
  • The 2 MiB fresh DRAM-backed chain (an SLC hit) read 23.980 ns per load on the same run and CPU. [001 latency-dram-large.csv size=2097152 row best]
  • So the OCM row sat 1.24 ns per load (fresh) and 1.53 ns per load (flushed) above an SLC hit.
  • Run 2 repeated the pair from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8.
  • On every CPU the all-five row sat 1.12 to 1.48 ns per load above that CPU's 2 MiB row (CPU 2: 25.506 against 24.382 ns per load). [002 latency-ocm-all5-cpu*.csv, latency-dram-large.csv, latency-dram-slc-cpu*.csv, rows best]
  • Run 3's dense all-five controls showed the same gap on CPUs 2, 4 and 8 (1.24, 1.51 and 1.46 ns per load).
  • CPU 6 showed a smaller gap (0.64 ns per load). [004 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu*.csv, latency-dram-large.csv, latency-dram-slc-cpu*.csv, rows best]

Why it looked wrong

  • OCM (on-chip memory) is 4 of the 16 ways of each home node's SLC array, locked by the firmware. [001 README.md line 23]
  • So an OCM read should cost about the same as an SLC hit, not more.
  • The OCM rows run on 4 KiB pages (/dev/ocm maps a region in 4 KiB pages). The DRAM rows run on 2 MiB huge pages. [001 README.md, Jesse's note]
  • So the OCM chain can miss the TLB (translation lookaside buffer) where the DRAM chain does not.
  • A difference in mesh distance between the five OCM home nodes and the home node of the 2 MiB buffer is the other candidate.
  • This is a hypothesis. No file states the 2 MiB buffer's home node.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
All-five and 2 MiB SLC chains, four CPUs, refill countersrun 2OCM against SLC on each CPU. Also whether each load is one home-node read (a refill count of 1.00 at L1, L2 and L3 means yes).
Dense and sparse all-five rows from the same four CPUsrun 3Whether run 2's rows repeat. Also how much a sparse chain (one line per 4 KiB page) adds over the dense chain.
Dense all-five rows, CPUs 2 and 8, five OCM page-setting bootsboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EHow much of the gap the OCM page size carries. A smaller gap on C (64 KiB translations) than on A (4 KiB pages), and on D than on B, means the page size carries that much.
Dense all-five and 2 MiB SLC rows, four CPUs, L3 onboot F1Whether the gap remains when the DSU L3 holds data. A gap of the same size means the L3 setting is not the cause.

What the tests showed

  • Run 2: both rows count 0.998 to 1.001 refills per load at L1, L2 and L3. [002 all-five and 2 MiB CSVs, columns l1d/l2d/l3d_refill, README.md line 65]
  • So each load is one home-node read on both rows.
  • The run 2 rows order the CPUs by mean mesh distance to the five home nodes: CPUs 2 and 6 (1.8 crosspoints), CPU 4 (2.6), CPU 8 (3.4). [002 README.md line 31]
  • CPU 8 reads 2.19 ns per load behind CPU 2 on the OCM row and 1.87 ns per load on the SLC row. [002 CSVs rows best]
  • Run 3: the dense controls repeat run 2 within 0.17 ns per load (-0.166 to +0.009 ns). [004 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu*.csv, README.md line 110]
  • The sparse all-five rows read 0.45 to 1.16 ns per load above the dense ones. [004 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu*.csv, latency-ocm-all5-cpu*.csv, README.md line 110]
  • Run 4, CPU 2: the 2 MiB row stayed at 23.89 to 24.18 ns per load on all five boots. [005 to 008 latency-dram-large.csv, rows best]
  • With the OCM in 64 KiB translations the gap fell from 1.92 ns per load (boot A) to 0.91 (boot C), and from 1.67 (boot B) to 1.07 (boot D). [005 to 008 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv, latency-dram-large.csv, rows best]
  • The page size carries est. 0.6 to 1.0 ns per load of the gap (A minus C 1.01 ns, B minus D 0.60 ns). This comes from the boot pairs rather than a TLB counter.
  • About 0.9 to 1.1 ns per load remains on boots C and D, not attributed.
  • Run 6 boot F1 (L3 on): the gap stays.
  • It is 1.82 ns per load on CPU 2, 1.10 on CPU 4, 1.06 on CPU 6 and 1.50 on CPU 8. [011 latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu*.csv, latency-dram-large.csv, latency-dram-slc-cpu*.csv, rows best]

Still open

About 0.9 to 1.1 ns per load of the gap on boots C and D is not attributed. No all-five row was ever run under the TLB counter set. An all-five row with the TLB counters would settle the page-size share. A stated home node for the 2 MiB buffer would let the mesh-distance hypothesis be tested.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (membench-jibin-001), 2026-10-31

What looked wrong. The 1.25 MiB all-five OCM chain (one chain over all five 256 KiB regions) read 25.22 ns per load fresh and 25.51 ns flushed on run 1. The DRAM-backed 2 MiB fresh chain, which sits in the SLC, read 23.98 ns on the same run. So the OCM row sat 1.24 ns (fresh) and 1.53 ns (flushed) above an SLC hit. Run 2 repeated the pair from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8. On every CPU the all-five row sits 1.12 to 1.48 ns above that CPU's 2 MiB row (CPU 2: 25.51 against 24.38 ns). Run 3's dense controls show the same gap on CPUs 2, 4 and 8 (1.24, 1.51 and 1.46 ns) and a smaller one on CPU 6 (0.64 ns).

Why it looked wrong. OCM is 4 locked ways of each home node's SLC array (the firmware locks 4 of 16 ways per home node as OCM). So an OCM read should cost about the same as an SLC hit, not more. Two differences between the rows could carry the remainder. The OCM rows run on 4 KiB pages (/dev/ocm maps a region in 4 KiB pages) and the DRAM rows on 2 MiB huge pages, so the OCM chain can miss the TLB where the DRAM chain does not (Jesse's run 1 README names this). A difference in mesh distance between the five OCM home nodes and the home node of the 2 MiB buffer is the other candidate (hypothesis; no file states the 2 MiB buffer's home node).

Tests added.

  • All-five rows from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8 beside 2 MiB SLC chases from the same CPUs, both with L1, L2 and L3 refill counters [run 2 (002)]: OCM against SLC per CPU, and whether each load is one home-node read
  • Dense all-five control rows and sparse all-five rows (one line per 4 KiB page) from the same four CPUs [run 3 (004)]: repeatability of run 2's rows, and the sparse-against-dense difference
  • Dense all-five rows from CPUs 2 and 8 on five boots: A (4 KiB pages), B (prefetchers off), C (OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations), D (hint and prefetchers off), E (L3 on); per-region TLB-counted rows from CPU 2 on the same boots [run 4 (005 to 008, 010)]: how much of the gap the OCM page size carries (C against A, D against B)
  • Dense all-five rows from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8 and 2 MiB SLC rows from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8 with the L3 on [run 6 boot F1 (011)]: whether the gap survives with the DSU L3 holding data

What the tests showed. Run 2: both rows count 1.00 refills per load at L1, L2 and L3 (0.998 to 1.001), so each load is one home-node read. The rows order the CPUs by their mean distance to the five home nodes: CPUs 2 and 6 (1.8 crosspoints) fastest, CPU 4 (2.6) next, CPU 8 (3.4) about 2 ns behind CPU 2 (2.19 ns on the OCM row, 1.87 ns on the SLC row). Run 3: the dense controls repeat run 2 within 0.17 ns (-0.166 to +0.009 ns). The sparse all-five rows read 0.45 to 1.16 ns above the dense ones. Run 4: with the OCM in 64 KiB translations the dense all-five row from CPU 2 falls from 26.01 ns (boot A) to 24.96 ns (boot C), and from 25.58 ns (boot B) to 24.96 ns (boot D), while the 2 MiB row stays at 23.89 to 24.18 ns. So the gap on CPU 2 falls from 1.92 ns (A) to 0.91 ns (C) and from 1.67 ns (B) to 1.07 ns (D). The page size carries about 0.6 to 1.0 ns of the gap (est., from the boot pairs, not from a TLB counter on the all-five row). About 0.9 to 1.1 ns remains on boots C and D and is not attributed. Run 6 boot F1 (L3 on): the gap stays, 1.82 ns on CPU 2, 1.10 on CPU 4, 1.06 on CPU 6 and 1.50 on CPU 8. No all-five row was ever run under the TLB counter set (the TLB-set rows are per region only), so the TLB share is an estimate from the boot pairs.

4.8 3 MiB fresh chain already above the SLC plateau; the 4 MiB row moves between runs; the 8 MiB fresh chain reads 7.6 to 7.7 ns below the flushed onepartly explained

The 3 and 4 MiB fresh chains read above an ideal 3.75 MiB SLC. The 8 MiB fresh chain reads 7.6 to 7.7 ns below flushed.

What looked wrong

  • Fresh chains (a pointer chain walked right after it is written, with no cache flush) of 512 KiB to 2 MiB read a flat 23.075 to 23.998 ns per load on run 1. [001 latency-dram-large.csv:6 to :26]
  • The 3 MiB chain read 25.449 ns per load. That is 1.47 ns above the 2 MiB row (23.980 ns). [001 latency-dram-large.csv:6 to :26]
  • The two 2 MiB passes on run 1 differ by only 0.14 ns. The 3 MiB step is about 10 times that repeat spread.
  • The 4 MiB chain read 29.760 ns per load on run 1. [001 latency-dram-large.csv:22, :30, :46]
  • That is 20.4 % of the way from the 2 MiB SLC row (23.980 ns) to the 32 MiB DRAM row (52.300 ns).
  • Yet 4 MiB is larger than the 3.75 MiB SLC (system level cache, the shared cache held at the mesh home nodes).
  • The 4 MiB row is the one latency row that moved by more than 1.7 % from run 1 to run 2, and by more than 1.44 % from run 1 to the control run. [002 README line 92, 003 README line 51]
  • Its bests on the runs are 29.760 ns per load (run 1), 28.704 (run 2), 28.399 (control run) and 28.270 (run 3). [latency-dram-large.csv of 001 to 011]
  • Its bests on the boots are 29.838 (boot A), 28.161 (boot B, prefetchers off), 29.216 (boot C), 28.234 (boot D), 28.321 (boot E) and 29.379 (boot F1). [latency-dram-large.csv of 001 to 011]
  • Boot B's 4 MiB row is 5.6 % faster than boot A's. [006 README line 47]
  • The 8 MiB fresh chain read 45.077 ns per load on run 3. The 8 MiB flushed chain (the same chain walked after a cache flush) read 52.738 ns per load on run 3. [004 latency-dram-large.csv:39, 004 latency-dram-flushed.csv:7]
  • The 32 MiB fresh chain read 52.185 ns on run 3. [004 latency-dram-large.csv:47]
  • The fresh 8 MiB walk is 7.66 ns per load faster than the flushed one on run 3. It is 7.63 ns faster on run 1 (45.086 vs 52.711 ns). [001 latency-dram-large.csv:38, 001 latency-dram-flushed.csv:27]
  • Two smaller observations. The 6 MiB chain reads 39.753 ns per load or more on all 16 passes with the L3 (the DSU cluster cache) off, runs 001 to 008. [006 latency-dram-large.csv:34]
  • CPU 6's 2 MiB SLC chase moved +2.56 % from run 2 to run 3 (24.050 to 24.665 ns per load). The control run's second pass also read 24.653 ns. [004 README line 96]
  • 33 of the 36 repeated latency rows agreed within 0.73 %. [004 README line 96]

Why it looked wrong

  • An ideal 3.75 MiB cache with the run 1 end points (23.980 ns per load in the SLC, 52.300 ns per load in DRAM) predicts 24.0 ns per load est. at 3 MiB, where the chain fits. [computed from 001 latency-dram-large.csv:22, :46]
  • At 4 MiB, 3.75/4 of the loads would hit. The prediction there is 25.8 ns per load est.
  • The measured 25.449 and 29.760 ns on run 1 are both higher. [computed from 001 latency-dram-large.csv:22, :46]
  • The transition is spread over 2 to 16 MiB instead of ending near 3.75 MiB.
  • Under an ideal-LRU model (LRU, least recently used: the cache evicts the line unused for longest), effective capacity = size x (1 - (lat - 23.980) / (52.300 - 23.980)).
  • The 3, 4, 6, 8 and 16 MiB points on run 1 then imply 2.84, 3.18, 2.64, 2.04 and 0.88 MiB est. of SLC, not one size. [recomputed from 001 latency-dram-large.csv:26, :30, :34, :38, :42]
  • 4 MiB sits just over the SLC size. Small changes in how much the SLC holds then move its latency (Jesse's reading). [003 README line 51]
  • The 5.6 % move at 4 MiB from boot A to boot B has no prefetcher cause in the files. Both boots read 0.0000 prefetch refills per load (the core counter of lines fetched by the hardware prefetcher). [006 README lines 7 and 47]
  • 8 MiB is more than twice the SLC. A fresh walk was therefore expected to read DRAM latency like the flushed walk.
  • The 7.6 to 7.7 ns per load gap means the fresh walk still gets some SLC service that the flush removes. This is a hypothesis. [004 latency-dram-large.csv:39, 004 latency-dram-flushed.csv:7]
  • The core counters read 1.00 L3 read refills per load on both rows and cannot show SLC hits. [004 latency-dram-large.csv:39, 004 latency-dram-flushed.csv:7]
