What the tests showed

  • Per-core 2 MiB chase on run 2: 24.382 ns per load (CPU 2), 24.636 ns (CPU 4), 24.050 ns (CPU 6), 26.255 ns (CPU 8). [002 latency-dram-large.csv:22, 002 latency-dram-slc-cpu4/6/8.csv:6]
  • The order follows each CPU's mean distance to the five home nodes: CPUs 6 and 2 at 1.8 crosspoints (mesh steps), CPU 4 at 2.6, CPU 8 at 3.4. [002 README line 65]
  • Jesse reads the 4 MiB drift as the size sitting just over the SLC's 3.75 MiB. [003 README line 51]
  • The control run (run 1 firmware with run 2 code) read 28.399 ns per load at 4 MiB. So the move from run 1 (29.760 ns) is not from the firmware alone. [003 latency-dram-large.csv:30]
  • On boot F1 (L3 on) both passes at 2, 6, 8 and 16 MiB lie below every pass of runs 2, 3 and boots A to E. The margins from the nearest earlier pass are 0.05, 0.47, 0.41 and 0.12 ns per load. [011 README line 143]
  • At 8 MiB, F1's best is 44.485 ns per load against 45.077 ns on run 3. [011 latency-dram-large.csv:39, 004 latency-dram-large.csv:39]
  • F1's 4 MiB best, 29.379 ns per load, lies inside the 28.161 to 29.838 ns span of the earlier bests. See the entry boot-e-large-chains-slower. [011 latency-dram-large.csv:31]
  • Run 1's flushed file carried 1, 2, 3 and 8 MiB rows at 52.716, 52.714, 52.713 and 52.711 ns per load. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • Flushed latency was flat at DRAM latency on run 1 at every size that ran. [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv, 001 README line 36]

Still open

The spread of the transition (set conflicts or non-LRU replacement) and the SLC service behind the 8 MiB gap were not measured further. The proposed flushed rows at 4 MiB and 16 MiB (expected 52 to 53 ns per load at any size) never ran. They would settle whether the 7.6 to 7.7 ns per load gap at 8 MiB is SLC service.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (membench-jibin-001, ran 2026-10-31 per its README; report verification dated 2026-11-02 in the session transcript, not verifiable from the primary files). The 8 MiB fresh-vs-flushed question: 2026-11-03 (peer session transcript; run 3 = membench-jibin-004 ran 2026-11-03 per its README). The 4 MiB prefetcher-off move: boot B (006) README, 'Against boot A'.

What looked wrong. Fresh chains of 512 KiB to 2 MiB read a flat 23.075 to 23.998 ns per load on run 1 [membench-jibin-001 latency-dram-large.csv:6 to :22]. The 3 MiB chain read 25.449 ns, 1.47 ns above the 2 MiB row [:26 vs :22]. The two 2 MiB passes differ by only 0.14 ns (23.980 and 24.119), so the 3 MiB step is about ten times the repeat spread. At 4 MiB the chain read 29.760 ns [:30]. That is 20 % of the way from the 2 MiB SLC row (23.980 ns) to the 32 MiB DRAM row (52.300 ns [:46]), although 4 MiB exceeds the 3.75 MiB SLC. The 4 MiB row is the one latency row that moved between runs 1 and 2 beyond 1.7 % and between run 1 and the control beyond 1.44 % [002 README line 92; 003 README line 51]. Its bests: 29.760 (run 1), 28.704 (run 2), 28.399 (control 003), 28.270 (run 3), 29.838 (boot A), 28.161 (boot B, prefetchers off), 29.216 (boot C), 28.234 (boot D), 28.321 (boot E), 29.379 (F1) ns per load. Boot B's 4 MiB row is 5.6 % faster than boot A's with no prefetch refill on either boot [006 README line 47]. The core's 8 MiB fresh chain reads 45.077 ns per load on run 3 [004 latency-dram-large.csv:39]. The 8 MiB flushed row on the same run reads 52.738 ns [004 latency-dram-flushed.csv:7] and the 32 MiB fresh row 52.185 ns [004 latency-dram-large.csv:47]. The fresh 8 MiB walk is 7.66 ns faster than the flushed one (7.63 ns on run 1: 45.086 vs 52.711). The 6 MiB chain reads 39.753 ns or more on every pass of every boot with the L3 off (16 passes over 001 to 008). CPU 6's 2 MiB SLC chase moved +2.56 % between runs 2 and 3 (24.050 to 24.665 ns; the control run's second pass also read 24.653) while 33 of the 36 repeated latency rows agreed within 0.73 % [004 README line 96].

Why it looked wrong. An ideal 3.75 MiB cache with the run 1 end points (23.980 ns in the SLC, 52.300 ns in DRAM) predicts 24.0 ns at 3 MiB (the chain fits) and 25.8 ns at 4 MiB (3.75/4 of the loads hit). The measured 25.449 and 29.760 ns are both higher. The transition is spread over 2 to 16 MiB. Under an ideal-LRU model (capacity = size x (1 - (lat - 23.980) / (52.300 - 23.980))), the 3, 4, 6, 8 and 16 MiB points imply 2.84, 3.18, 2.64, 2.04 and 0.88 MiB est. of effective SLC, not one size. 4 MiB sits just over the SLC size, so small changes in how much the SLC holds move its latency [003 README line 51, Jesse's reading]. 8 MiB is more than twice the SLC, so a fresh walk was expected to read DRAM latency like the flushed walk. The 7.7 ns gap means the fresh walk still gets some SLC service that the flush removes (hypothesis: the core counters read 1.00 L3 read refills per load on both rows and cannot show SLC hits). A 5.6 % move at 4 MiB with 0.0000 prefetch refills per load on both boots has no prefetcher cause in the files [006 README line 7 and line 47].

Tests added.

  • Report wording changed to 'consistent with Jesse's 3.75 MiB of SLC for DRAM (an RTL configuration figure); the sweep does not measure the size itself' [run 1 report (run1-report.html, SLC row of the cross-check table)]: none
  • 2 MiB SLC chase from CPUs 4, 6, 8 (latency-dram-slc-cpu4/6/8.csv) beside CPU 2's 2 MiB row, with the mesh PMU counting requests at the five home nodes [run 2 (002); repeated on control 003, run 3 (004) and F1 (011)]: SLC-hit latency per core by mesh distance
  • Proposed: flushed rows at 4 MiB and 16 MiB (should read 52 to 53 ns regardless of size) [not run. Every flushed file from run 2 on carries only the 8 MiB row. Run 1's flushed file did carry 1, 2 and 3 MiB rows: 52.716, 52.714, 52.713 ns [001 latency-dram-flushed.csv]]: that flushed latency is flat at DRAM latency above the SLC size, and that the 8 MiB fresh gap is SLC service
  • Same 512 KiB to 32 MiB fresh-chain command lines (run_asimov.sh of round three, byte for byte) with the DSU L3 on [run 6 boot F1 (011)]: whether the SLC and DRAM rows move with the L3 on

What the tests showed. Per-core 2 MiB chase on run 2: 24.382 (CPU 2), 24.636 (CPU 4), 24.050 (CPU 6), 26.255 (CPU 8) ns per load. The order follows each CPU's mean distance to the five home nodes: CPUs 6 and 2 at 1.8 crosspoints, CPU 4 at 2.6, CPU 8 at 3.4 [002 README line 65]. Jesse reads the 4 MiB drift as the size sitting just over the SLC's 3.75 MiB [003 README line 51]. The control run (run 1 firmware, run 2 code) read 28.399 ns at 4 MiB, so the move from run 1 is not from the firmware alone. On F1 both passes at 2, 6, 8 and 16 MiB lie below every pass of runs 2, 3 and boots A to E, by 0.05, 0.47, 0.41 and 0.12 ns from the nearest [011 README line 143; recomputed from the CSVs: F1 6 MiB 39.085 and 39.116 vs boot E's 39.584; 8 MiB 44.485 and 44.612 vs boot B's 45.023]. F1's 4 MiB best, 29.379 ns, lies inside the 28.161 to 29.838 ns span of the earlier bests (see boot-e-large-chains-slower). The smeared transition (set conflicts, non-LRU replacement) and the fresh 8 MiB chain's SLC service were not measured further. The proposed flushed 4 and 16 MiB rows never ran.

4.9 No L3 level: the 192 KiB chase read 14 ns with 42 % L2 hits, and the L3 looked slower than OCM (the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data)explained

L3-sized chases read 14 to 23 ns per load on runs 1 to 3. The L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data.

What looked wrong

  • On run 1 the 192 KiB pointer chase (a chain of dependent loads, one per cache line) read 14.072 ns per load [001 latency-dram-small.csv row 52].
  • On run 3 the 192 / 256 / 384 KiB chases read 14.045 / 19.333 / 22.729 ns per load [004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 53, 58, 63].
  • These values climb from the L2 level (6.090 ns per load at 128 KiB, run 3) [004 latency-dram-small.csv row 48].
  • They climb up to the SLC level (24.096 ns per load at 2 MiB, run 3), with no flat step between [004 latency-dram-large.csv row 23].
  • At 192 KiB on run 3 the best rep counted 0.5808 L2 refills and 0.4605 L3 read refills per load [004 latency-dram-small.csv row 50].
  • So 42 % of loads hit the L2, 46 % reached the mesh, and about 12 % (0.5808 minus 0.4605) were served by the L3.
  • On run 3 one core read a 256 KiB stream at 10.164 GB/s [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 52].
  • That is below the 14.817 to 16.619 GB/s of a 256 KiB OCM (on-chip memory on the mesh) region [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv row 7].
  • Jibin: 'L3 should be faster than OCM' [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md:202].
  • Bill: 'L3 is confusing. 42% L2 hit rate?' [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md:219].

Why it looked wrong

  • Each DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, the two-core cluster) has a 256 KiB L3 beside its 128 KiB L2 [004 README.md:34].
  • A 192 KiB chain fits inside the L3.
  • The chase was therefore expected to read at one flat time between the L2 level (6.090 ns per load) and the SLC level (24.096 ns per load).
  • Instead it read 14.045 ns per load, with 46 % of loads leaving the cluster.
  • The L3 sits inside the cluster and OCM sits across the mesh.
  • So a 256 KiB read served by the L3 was expected to exceed the 14.817 to 16.619 GB/s OCM read on run 3, not fall below it at 10.164 GB/s.
  • First hypothesis (plan section 10, 2026-11-04): part of the 256 KiB L3 was powered down, the DSU's HALF RAM operating mode [follow-up-run-plan.md:191].

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
L3 hit set: L2 hit, L3 read, L3 hit PMU eventsboot B, boot C, boot D, boot ECounts L2 read hits, L3 read accesses and L3 read hits per load on the 64 to 512 KiB rows, instead of inferring them from refills. The PMU events are 0x81C5 L2D_CACHE_HIT_RD, 0xA0 L3D_CACHE_RD and 0x81C6 L3D_CACHE_HIT_RD, added in commit 7921962. 0x2A L3D_CACHE_REFILL is not implemented on the C1-Nano. A nonzero L3 hit count would mean the L3 holds data. 0.0000 would mean it holds none [follow-up-run-plan.md:191, 006 README.md:36].
IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1 read around the hit-set row, plus BL31 printboot B, boot C, boot D, boot E, boot F1, boot F2Reads the cluster power-status register (L3 slice count and L3 RAM state: SFONLY, HALF_ON or FULL_ON) just before and just after the hit-set row. On boots B to E that row is the core row (log.txt lines 7 and 9). On F1 and F2 it is the CME row (log.txt lines 146/148 and 65/67). BL31 (the Arm trusted firmware) prints the state at every power-on of CPUs 2 to 9. 0x0 would mean snoop-filter-only. 0x70 would mean all slices with full L3 RAM [006 README.md:27, :67].
SCP source read: which clusters the stock firmware stages in full-L3 modeotherJesse read asimov_system_init_primary_core in mod_asimov_system.c (scp-v0.48.0, call at :703, staging added in commit 9ef7952 at lines 286-309). The aim was to find which clusters the stock SCP (System Control Processor firmware) stages in the full-L3 operating mode. A cluster missing from the staging would explain an empty L3 [006 README.md:28].
Boot E firmware: SCP stages full L3 for clusters 1 to 4boot E, boot F1Reruns the same chases and the hit set on SCP 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1 (commit 28663ab on e361a83). That firmware stages operating mode 7 (all slices, full L3 RAM) for clusters 1 to 4 (the clusters of CPUs 2 to 9) before the primary core powers on. A drop in the 192 to 384 KiB chase times with nonzero L3 hits would confirm that the firmware, not the L3, caused the outlier. F2 ran CME rows only [010 README.md:18-19].

What the tests showed

  • Boots B, C and D: the L3 read-hit counter read 0.0000 hits per load in all 21 rows of each boot, and every L3 access was a refill [006/007/008 latency-dram-small-l3.csv].
  • IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1 read 0x0 (one slice, L3 RAM snoop-filter-only) before and after the row on each boot [log.txt lines 7 and 9].
  • The stock SCP prints one staging line, 'Staged cluster 0 PPU PWPR=0x00070008' [006 README.md:28].
  • So only the cluster of CPUs 0 and 1 gets the full-L3 operating mode. Linux powers the other clusters on later in the reset operating mode 0.
  • So runs 1 to 3 and boots A to D measured cores whose L3 held no data. The 192 to 384 KiB rows were L2 hits mixed with reads from the SLC.
  • Boot E (new SCP): the register read 0x70 (all slices, FULL_ON) [010 log.txt lines 7 and 9].
  • L3 hits per load were 0.4651 / 0.7508 / 0.9236 at 192 / 256 / 384 KiB. The chases read 7.811 / 9.489 / 10.906 ns per load, against 14.045 / 19.333 / 22.729 ns on run 3 [010 latency-dram-small-l3.csv].
  • One L3 hit costs about 10.8 ns est. (boot E rows against boot C): 10.6 ns est. from the 256 KiB row and 11.0 ns est. from the 384 KiB row [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 4, gen_run4.py l3_hit_est].
  • The 192 KiB row gives 9.9 ns est. and is left out. Under half of its loads hit the L3.
  • Rows outside the L3 did not move: 6.091 vs 6.019 ns per load at 128 KiB (boot C vs boot E), and 24.096 / 24.053 / 24.177 ns per load at 2 MiB (run 3 / boot C / boot E) [004/007/010 latency-dram-large.csv, 010/007 latency-dram-small-l3.csv].
  • The 512 KiB row is partly held: 18.481 ns per load with 0.41 L3 hits per load on boot E, against 23.722 ns on boot C [004/007/010 latency-dram-large.csv, 010/007 latency-dram-small-l3.csv].
  • Boot F1 repeats boot E within 0.08 ns per load: 7.825 / 9.509 / 10.986 ns at 192 / 256 / 384 KiB [011 latency-dram-small.csv rows 53, 58, 63].
  • The 192 KiB row has the lowest L3 share. The L2 keeps more of a smaller chain (0.53 L2 hits per load on boot E).
  • So fewer loads reach the L3.

Still open

The register and the hit counter cover CPU 2's cluster only. So reading IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1 and the hit set on one core of each other cluster would settle the L3 state of those clusters [asimov-c1nano-perf.html line 206]. asimov-bench's 15.16 ns per load lower bound on an L3 hit is about twice boot E's 7.811 ns and boot F1's 7.825 ns at 192 KiB. This gap is not explained [010 README.md:108, 011 README.md:142].

4.10 100 % L1 misses on a 192 KiB chain with a 32 KiB L1 (Jibin's question), and the 32 KiB row as the L1 edgepartly explained

A 192 KiB chain missed the 32 KiB L1 on every load. The 32 KiB row itself read slower than the smaller rows.

What looked wrong

  • The run 3 core page listed 1.00 L1 refills per load for the 192 KiB repeated chase [asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.1].
  • The CSV behind it reads 0.9987 to 0.9989 [004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 50-52]. An L1 refill is a load that missed the L1. So 1.00 means every load missed.
  • Jibin asked how a 32 KB L1 can miss on every load. He also asked whether the chain step is larger than 32 KB [page comment 23, 2026-11-03 11:11] [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md lines 135-137].
  • The 32 KiB repeated row read 2.108 ns per load in run 3, with 0.0377 to 0.0433 L1 refills per load [004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
  • Run 1 read 2.112 ns per load on the same row [001 rows 24-27].
  • The 4 to 16 KiB rows read 2.002 to 2.007 ns per load. The 24 KiB row read 2.013 ns per load. The 32 KiB row sits above all of them [004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 8, 13, 18, 23].
  • In run 4 the 32 KiB row moved with the data prefetchers (hardware that fetches lines before a load asks for them). Boot A (prefetchers on) read 2.114 ns per load [005 latency-dram-small.csv row 28].
  • Boot B (prefetchers off) read 2.031 ns per load, 3.93 % faster [006 latency-dram-small.csv row 28] [006 README.md line 47].

Why it looked wrong

  • A 32 KiB cache (512 lines of 64 bytes) was expected to hold part of any chain. So some loads should have hit the L1, even on a 192 KiB chain.
  • The page did not say how the chain is ordered. It also did not say what the refill counter counts.
  • The 32 KiB row equals the L1 size: 512 chain lines in a 512-line cache.
  • It was expected to read with the 4 to 24 KiB rows (2.002 to 2.013 ns per load). Instead it read 2.108 ns per load, above them.
  • The 32 KiB row's 3.93 % move between boot A and boot B (2.114 ns to 2.031 ns per load) had no cause in any file.
  • The move was listed without a note [006 README.md line 47] [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 11.2].

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Definitions of repeat, fresh and flushed added to the core pageotherWording only, after run 3 (004). Page comment 24 asked for definitions of repeat, fresh and flushed. It also asked how the test code implements them [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md lines 139-141]. The core page now defines the three forms under 'Words used here' [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Words used here].
32 KiB and 192 KiB rows with prefetch refill countersboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EMeasures L1 refills per load on the 32 KiB row (the L1 edge), and the L1 prefetcher's share of them. Measures L1 refills per load on the 192 KiB row with the prefetchers on (A, C, E), off (B, D) and with the L3 on (E). A 192 KiB row that stays near 1.0 refills per load on every boot means the 100 % miss rate is the chain's construction. It is then not a prefetcher or measurement effect. Counters used: l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load, l2d_refill_hwprf_per_load, l2d_refill_l1dhwprf_per_load [005, 006, 007, 008, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28 and 50-53].

What the tests showed

  • The chain is one random cycle over all its lines. The test source builds it with Sattolo's algorithm, which yields a single cycle [latency.c lines 5-6] [transcript-peer.txt lines 1045-1054].
  • At 192 KiB the chain has 3,072 lines of 64 bytes, and the L1 holds 512 lines [004 latency-dram-small.csv header rows 24 and 49].
  • Each line is revisited only after 3,071 other loads. So every load misses the L1, whatever the step size.
  • The 100 % miss rate is the chain's construction, not a measurement defect.
  • The 192 KiB row reads 0.9986 to 0.9991 L1 refills per load on every boot A to E [005, 006, 007, 008, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 50-53].
  • This includes boot B with the prefetchers off (14.457 ns per load) and boot E with the L3 on (7.821 ns per load).
  • Run 3 read 14.045 ns per load on the same row [004 row 53].
  • The 32 KiB row repeats on every boot. With the prefetchers on (boots A, C, E) it reads 2.114, 2.117 and 2.121 ns per load [005, 007, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
  • On those boots it shows 0.0398 to 0.0447 L1 refills per load, 0.0078 to 0.0087 of them from the L1 prefetcher [005, 007, 010 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
  • With the prefetchers off (boots B, D) the 32 KiB row reads 2.031 and 2.036 ns per load [006, 008 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
  • On those boots it shows 0.0094 to 0.0112 L1 refills per load and 0.0000 prefetch refills [006, 008 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28].
  • The peer session's reading of the 32 KiB row is a hypothesis, not a measurement [transcript-peer.txt line 1054].
  • In that reading, the kernel's own lines and the chain compete for the L1. Then 0.04 refills per load marks the L1 edge [transcript-peer.txt line 1054].
  • The current core page labels the 32 KiB row 'L1 and L2' in its Reads-from column [asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.1].
  • At boot E that row reads 2.121 ns per load and 0.04 L1 refills per load [asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.1].

Still open

Why boot B's 32 KiB row is 3.93 % faster than boot A's (2.114 to 2.031 ns per load) is not explained in any file. The L1 refill drop from A to B (about 0.030 per load) is larger than the L1 prefetcher's own refills on A (0.008 to 0.009 per load). So the demand misses also dropped when the prefetcher went off. Hypothesis, not measured: prefetched lines evict chain lines at the L1 edge. No file measures this.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. The 32 KiB repeated row read 2.112 ns in run 1 (001) and 2.108 ns in run 3 (004). Jibin asked the 100 % L1 miss question as page comment 23 on 2026-11-03 11:11 (jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md lines 135-137) and asked for the repeat/fresh/flushed definitions as comment 24 at 12:04 (lines 139-141). The 32 KiB row's move between boots A and B appeared in Jesse's boot B README on 2026-11-05 (results/membench-jibin-006/README.md line 47).

What looked wrong. The run 3 core page listed 1.00 L1 refills per load on the 192 KiB repeated chase (the CSV reads 0.9987 to 0.9989 refills per load, membench-jibin-004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 50-52; the page rounds to 1.00). An L1 refill is a load that missed the L1, so 1.00 means 100 % misses. Jibin asked how a 32 KB L1 can miss on every load and whether the step size is larger than 32 KB (comment 23). The 32 KiB repeated row reads 2.108 ns with 0.0377 to 0.0433 L1 refills per load (membench-jibin-004 latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28), above the 2.002 to 2.007 ns of the 4 to 16 KiB rows and the 2.013 ns of the 24 KiB row (rows 8, 13, 18, 23), even though 32 KiB is the L1 size. In run 4, with the data prefetchers off, the 32 KiB row read 3.93 % faster (boot A 2.114 ns, boot B 2.031 ns; membench-jibin-005 and -006 latency-dram-small.csv row 28), with L1 refills 0.0398 to 0.0426 per load on A (0.0078 to 0.0087 of them made by the L1 prefetcher, column l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load) and 0.0094 to 0.0112 on B (prefetch refills 0.0000).

Why it looked wrong. A 32 KiB cache was expected to hold part of any chain, so some loads should hit. The page did not say how the chain is ordered or what the refill counter counts. Answer given by the peer session (transcript-peer.txt lines 1045-1054) and confirmed by the test source: the chain is one random cycle over all lines (latency.c lines 5-6, Sattolo's algorithm yields a single n-cycle). At 192 KiB the chain has 3,072 lines and the L1 holds 512 lines (the CSV headers '# size=196608 lines=3072' and '# size=32768 lines=512'). Each line is revisited only after 3,071 other loads, so every load misses the L1 whatever the step size. The 32 KiB row equals the L1 size: 512 chain lines in a 512-line cache. The peer's reading, a hypothesis and not a measurement: the kernel's own lines and the chain compete for the L1, so 0.04 refills per load is the L1 edge. Why boot B's 32 KiB row is 3.93 % faster than boot A's is not explained in the files. The L1 refill drop from A to B (about 0.030 per load) is larger than the L1 prefetcher's own refills on A (0.008 to 0.009 per load), so the demand misses also dropped when the prefetcher went off; no file explains this. Hypothesis, not measured: prefetched lines evict chain lines at the L1 edge.

Tests added.

  • None new for the miss rate; page comment 24 asked for definitions of repeat, fresh and flushed and how the test code implements them. The core page now defines them under 'Words used here' (Repeated: a random chain walked many times, so later walks hit whatever cache holds it. Fresh: a chain walked once. Flushed: every line was cleaned and invalidated from the caches with DC CIVAC first) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Words used here]. [page edit after run 3 (004)]: wording only
  • 32 KiB and 192 KiB repeated rows on boots A to E with the prefetch refill events (l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load, l2d_refill_hwprf_per_load, l2d_refill_l1dhwprf_per_load) and boots B and D with the data prefetchers off [run 4 boots A to E (005, 006, 007, 008, 010), latency-dram-small.csv rows 25-28 and 50-53]: L1 refills per load and the L1 prefetcher's share on the L1-edge row; L1 refills per load on the 192 KiB row with and without prefetchers and with the L3 on

What the tests showed. The 100 % miss rate is the chain's construction (a random cycle larger than the L1), not a measurement defect. The 192 KiB row reads 0.9986 to 0.9991 L1 refills per load on every boot A to E (latency-dram-small.csv rows 50-52 of 005, 006, 007, 008, 010), including boot B with the prefetchers off (14.457 ns) and boot E with the L3 on (7.821 ns). The 32 KiB row repeats on every boot: with the prefetchers on (A, C, E) 2.114, 2.117 and 2.121 ns with 0.0398 to 0.0447 L1 refills per load, of which 0.0078 to 0.0087 by the L1 prefetcher; with them off (B, D) 2.031 and 2.036 ns with 0.0094 to 0.0112 refills per load and 0.0000 prefetch refills (row 25-28 of each boot's latency-dram-small.csv). The 3.93 % move is listed in Jesse's boot B README (line 47, Against boot A) and in table 11.2 of the run 4 core page (asimov-c1nano-run4.html, '11.2 The core's chases with the prefetchers off': 32 KiB repeat 2.114 / 2.031 / -3.93 %) without a cause. The current core page labels the 32 KiB row 'L1 and L2' in its Reads-from column (asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.1, boot E 2.121 ns, 0.04 L1 refills).

4.11 One-core read beyond L2 stops at 9.2 GB/s from both SLC and DRAMpartly explained

One core reads 9.3 GB/s from the SLC and 9.2 GB/s from DRAM in run 3. The CME beside it reads 36.6 GB/s.

What looked wrong

  • One core reads 9.311 GB/s at 2 MiB (the SLC footprint, SLC = the system level cache) and 9.172 GB/s at 32 MiB (DRAM) in run 3. The same core reads 58.127 GB/s at 16 KiB (L1) in the same file [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]
  • Run 1 gave nearly the same rates: 9.306 GB/s at 2 MiB and 9.178 GB/s at 32 MiB [001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]
  • One core reads 14.971 to 16.623 GB/s from one OCM region (OCM = on-chip memory) in run 1 [001 bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows]
  • Regions 0 to 4 read 16.327, 16.623, 16.274, 15.295 and 14.971 GB/s [001 bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows]
  • The CME (the Arm C1-SME2 unit on the same DSU, DSU = the Arm DynamIQ cluster) reads 36.564 GB/s from DRAM at 32 MiB in run 3 [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]
  • The CME reads 36.899 GB/s at 2 MiB in run 3 [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]
  • Eight cores together read 67.756 GB/s at 2 MiB in run 3. That is 8.47 to 9.04 GB/s per thread. So the limit is per core, not a shared one [004 bandwidth-all8.csv, 2 MiB rows]
  • The CRB (the Arm Neoverse V3AE reference server) reads 30 GB/s from DRAM with one core. That figure is quoted in the message to Bill and is not in any results folder [message-to-bill.md, point 5 table]
  • Bill raised the Asimov rate as a defect on 2026-11-04 09:26 PST: "The read throughput from DRAM is too slow. I doubt that's reality. It's probably a software mechanism issue." [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, Bill 6]

Why it looked wrong

  • The rate is the same at two very different latencies. The 2 MiB chase (a pointer-chase latency test, one load at a time) reads 24.096 ns per load in run 3 [004 latency-dram-large.csv, best rows]
  • The 32 MiB chase reads 52.185 ns per load. So the memory itself is not the limit [004 latency-dram-large.csv, best rows]
  • Little's law (lines in flight = rate x latency / line size) gives about 3.5 lines in flight at 2 MiB (9.311 GB/s x 24.096 ns / 64 B = 3.51, est.) [derived from 004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv and latency-dram-large.csv]
  • It gives about 7.5 lines at 32 MiB (9.172 GB/s x 52.185 ns / 64 B = 7.48, est., or 7.56 with the flushed row's 52.738 ns) [derived from 004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, latency-dram-large.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv]
  • Bill judged 9.2 GB/s too slow to be real, against the CRB's 30 GB/s with one core [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, Bill 6 and message-to-bill.md, point 5 table]
  • Two candidate causes were named: the core's miss-handling capacity, or the software not keeping enough loads in flight (Bill's suggestion) [message-to-bill.md, point 6]
  • Hypothesis H7 (the plan's name for this guess): the plain ldp loop (ldp = the Arm load-pair instruction) keeps too few lines in flight [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10, Ask 2]
  • A streaming read is then limited by how far the hardware prefetcher runs ahead. A software prefetch hint or a second stream should raise the rate [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10, Ask 2]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
2 MiB one-core read under the mesh home-node counters (dram-read-2M-cpu2)run 2, run 3, boot F1Counts requests received per home node (counter hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all) during the read. It answers the plan's question of whether a DRAM buffer spreads over all 5 home nodes (about 40,000 requests per node expected if even, est.) [RUN2-PLAN.md, question table, line 105].
G7 read variants: plain loop, PRFM 4/8/16 ahead, two streamsboot B, boot C, boot D, boot EMeasures whether more lines in flight raise the one-core rate at 2 MiB (4 passes) and 32 MiB (2 passes), 3 reps. The hardware prefetcher is off (boots B and D) and on (boots C and E). A rise with PRFM (the Arm prefetch-hint instruction, PLDL1KEEP form) would support H7. The columns l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line and l2d_refill_l1dhwprf_per_line show whether the hardware prefetcher ran [006/007/008/010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv and follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10].
One-core DRAM read sweep with the L3 on (run 3's phase D rows)boot F1Repeats run 3's one-core read rows with the DSU L3 in full mode (boot E's firmware). A change from run 3's rates would show what the L3 mode does to the one-core read [011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv].

What the tests showed

  • In run 2 the 2 MiB read spread evenly over the five home nodes: 87,786, 87,780, 87,386, 87,730 and 88,013 requests (nodes 88, 160, 216, 288, 344) [002 cmn-counts.csv, dram-read-2M-cpu2 rows and 002 README.md line 72]
  • That is about twice the plan's estimate of 40,000 per node [002 README.md line 72]
  • Run 3 repeated it at 87,579 to 88,012 requests per node [004 cmn-counts.csv]
  • Boot B (prefetchers off): the plain loop reads 5.031 GB/s at 2 MiB and 2.377 GB/s at 32 MiB [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • PRFM 4 lines ahead reads 12.146 and 6.334 GB/s (2.41 and 2.66 times the plain loop). PRFM 8 ahead reads 10.878 and 5.705 GB/s [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • PRFM 16 ahead reads 9.475 and 4.919 GB/s. Two streams reads 5.033 and 2.370 GB/s (no change) [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • So the number of lines in flight sets the rate, and the hardware prefetcher supplies most of them. H7 is supported for the prefetcher-off case [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 11.4]
  • Boot D repeats boot B within 0.5 % (plain 5.007 and 2.377 GB/s, PRFM 4 ahead 12.145 and 6.336 GB/s) [008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • Boot C (prefetchers on, L3 off): the plain loop reads 9.294 GB/s at 2 MiB and 9.196 GB/s at 32 MiB, run 3's rate [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • PRFM 4 ahead adds 3.8 % at 2 MiB (9.651 GB/s) and 1.5 % at 32 MiB (9.339 GB/s) [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • Two streams reads 11.400 GB/s at 2 MiB (+22.7 %) and 8.681 GB/s at 32 MiB (-5.6 %) [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • The plain loop counts 0.992 to 0.999 L1 hardware-prefetch refills per line, so the prefetcher fetched nearly every line. The software hint adds little once the hardware prefetcher runs [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows and asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 12]
  • Boot E (prefetchers on, L3 on): the plain loop reads 24.945 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB, 2.68 and 2.67 times boot C, with the same refills per line [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • It spends 5.13 to 5.22 cycles per line against boot C's 13.78 to 13.93 cycles [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • Every variant is slower than the plain loop on boot E (PRFM 4 ahead 20.196 and 20.353 GB/s, two streams 17.982 and 18.911 GB/s) [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]
  • Boot F1 confirms the rise on run 3's own rows: 25.044 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.575 GB/s at 32 MiB (2.68 times run 3) [011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]
  • The home nodes received 85,518 to 85,777 requests each (0.975 times run 3) in a command 0.648 times as long. This rise is the read-stream-rise entry [011 cmn-counts.csv, dram-read-2M-cpu2 and 011 README.md]
  • With no prefetcher, one DRAM latency carries about two lines. The boot B plain loop takes 53.84 cycles per line at 32 MiB [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, cycles_per_line]
  • That is 26.88 ns at 2.003 GHz. 52.185 ns / 26.88 ns = 1.94 lines (est.) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 2.3]

Still open

The limiting unit (core miss handling, cluster, or prefetcher reach) is not named. No file on disk counts requests in flight [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 2.3]. The run 7 plan proposes the home nodes' read-queue occupancy event (PMU_HNF_POCQ_OCCUPANCY_EVENT) around the same reads on an L3-on and an L3-off boot. It also proposes the one-core read sweep on the prefetchers-off boots with the L3 on and off [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 14].

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (001), 2026-10-31: 9.306 GB/s at 2 MiB and 9.178 GB/s at 32 MiB [001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]. Raised as a defect by Bill on 2026-11-04 09:26 PST (comment "Bill 6" on asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html) [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, the Bill 6 heading].

What looked wrong. One core reads 9.311 GB/s at 2 MiB (the SLC footprint) and 9.172 GB/s at 32 MiB (DRAM) in run 3 [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]. The same core reads 58.127 GB/s at 16 KiB (L1) in the same file. It reads 15.0 to 16.6 GB/s from one OCM region in run 1 (regions 0 to 4: 16.327, 16.623, 16.274, 15.295, 14.971 GB/s) [001 bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, best rows]. The CME on the same DSU reads 36.564 GB/s from DRAM at 32 MiB and 36.899 GB/s at 2 MiB [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows]. Eight cores read 67.756 GB/s at 2 MiB, 8.47 to 9.04 GB/s per thread, so the limit is per core [004 bandwidth-all8.csv, 2 MiB rows]. The CRB (the Arm Neoverse V3AE reference server) reads 30 GB/s from DRAM with one core; that figure is quoted in the message to Bill and is not in the results folders [message-to-bill.md, the table in point 5]. Bill: "The read throughput from DRAM is too slow. I doubt that's reality. It's probably a software mechanism issue." [jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, Bill 6].

Why it looked wrong. The rate is the same at a 24.1 ns level and a 52.2 ns level (the 2 MiB chase reads 24.096 ns, the 32 MiB chase 52.185 ns) [004 latency-dram-large.csv, best rows], so the memory is not the limit. By Little's law the core holds about 3.5 lines in flight at 2 MiB (9.311 GB/s x 24.096 ns / 64 B = 3.51) and about 7.5 at 32 MiB (9.172 x 52.185 / 64 = 7.48; 7.56 with the flushed row's 52.738 ns) [derived from 004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv and latency-dram-large.csv / latency-dram-flushed.csv]. Two candidate causes were named: the core's miss-handling capacity, or the software not getting enough loads in flight (Bill's suggestion) [message-to-bill.md, point 6]. Hypothesis H7: the plain ldp loop keeps too few lines in flight, so a streaming read is limited by how far the hardware prefetcher runs ahead, and a software prefetch hint or a second stream raises it [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10 "Ask 2, the one-core read"].

Tests added.

  • 2 MiB one-core read under the mesh home-node counters (label dram-read-2M-cpu2) [run 2 (002), repeated in run 3 (004) and run 6 boot F1 (011)]: requests received per home node (hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all) during the read. The plan's stated question was whether a DRAM buffer spreads over all 5 home nodes, with about 40,000 requests per node expected if even (est.) [RUN2-PLAN.md, the question table, line 105].
  • G7 read variants: the plain loop, PRFM PLDL1KEEP 4, 8 and 16 lines ahead (read-pf4, read-pf8, read-pf16) and two streams (read-2s), at 2 MiB (4 passes) and 32 MiB (2 passes), 3 reps, with the core prefetch counter set (bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv) [run 4 boots B (006, commit 7921962, prefetchers off), C (007, b79dffa, prefetchers on, L3 off), D (008, ed6056a, prefetchers off, OCM 64 KiB hint), E (010, b79dffa, prefetchers on, L3 on). Boot A (005) has no such row. Commit cd1e6fd is the plan's reviewed commit, not a boot's [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 10].]: whether more lines in flight raise the rate, with the hardware prefetcher off (B, D) and on (C, E); the columns l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line and l2d_refill_l1dhwprf_per_line show whether the hardware prefetcher ran.
  • One-core DRAM read sweep with the L3 on (run 3's phase D rows) [run 6 boot F1 (011)]: the same one-core read rows with the DSU L3 in full mode (boot E's firmware) [011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv].

What the tests showed. Run 2: the 2 MiB read spread evenly over the five home nodes, 87,386 to 88,013 requests each (nodes 88, 160, 216, 288, 344: 87,786, 87,780, 87,386, 87,730, 88,013), about twice the plan's estimate of 40,000 [002 cmn-counts.csv, dram-read-2M-cpu2 rows; 002 README.md line 72]. Run 3 repeated it at 87,579 to 88,012 per node [004 cmn-counts.csv]. Boot B (prefetchers off): the plain loop reads 5.031 GB/s at 2 MiB and 2.377 GB/s at 32 MiB. PRFM 4 lines ahead reads 12.146 and 6.334 GB/s (2.41 and 2.66 times the plain loop). PRFM 8 ahead reads 10.878 and 5.705, PRFM 16 ahead 9.475 and 4.919, two streams 5.033 and 2.370 (no change) [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, best rows]. So the number of lines in flight sets the rate, and the hardware prefetcher supplies most of them (H7 supported for the prefetcher-off case) [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 11.4]. Boot D repeats B within 0.5 %: plain 5.007 and 2.377, PRFM 4 ahead 12.145 and 6.336 GB/s [008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. Boot C (prefetchers on, L3 off): the plain loop reads 9.294 and 9.196 GB/s, run 3's rate. PRFM 4 ahead adds 3.8 % at 2 MiB (9.651 GB/s) and 1.5 % at 32 MiB (9.339 GB/s). Two streams reads 11.400 GB/s at 2 MiB (+22.7 %) and 8.681 at 32 MiB (-5.6 %). The plain loop counts 0.992 to 0.999 L1 hardware-prefetch refills per line, so the prefetcher fetched nearly every line [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. So the software hint adds little once the hardware prefetcher runs [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 12]. Boot E (prefetchers on, L3 on): the plain loop reads 24.945 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.546 at 32 MiB, 2.68 and 2.67 times boot C with the same refills per line (5.13 to 5.22 cycles per line against C's 13.78 to 13.93). Every variant is slower than the plain loop on E (PRFM 4 ahead 20.196 and 20.353, two streams 17.982 and 18.911 GB/s) [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. Run 6 boot F1 confirms it on run 3's own rows: 25.044 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.575 at 32 MiB (2.68 times run 3), while the home nodes received 85,518 to 85,777 requests each (0.975 times run 3) in a command 0.648 times as long [011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv; 011 cmn-counts.csv dram-read-2M-cpu2; 011 README.md]. This is the read-stream-rise entry. With no prefetcher one DRAM latency carries about two lines: the boot B plain loop takes 53.84 cycles per line at 32 MiB, 26.88 ns at 2.003 GHz, and 52.185 / 26.88 = 1.94 lines [006 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv, cycles_per_line; asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 2.3 "What is known"]. What is not measured: no file on disk counts requests in flight, so the limiting unit (core miss handling, cluster, or prefetcher reach) is not named [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 2.3 "The test"]. The run 7 plan proposes the home nodes' read-queue occupancy event (PMU_HNF_POCQ_OCCUPANCY_EVENT) around the same reads on an L3-on and an L3-off boot, and the one-core read sweep on the prefetchers-off boots with the L3 on and off [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 14].

4.12 Eight writers no faster than four (88 GB/s), then multi-DSU writes jump 44 to 76 % with a firmware changeexplained

In run 1 eight DRAM writers were no faster than four (about 88 GB/s). A firmware change then lifted both 44 to 76 %.

What looked wrong

  • Run 1 (membench-jibin-001, 2026-10-31): four writers, one per DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, a two-core cluster) on CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8, wrote 88.8 GB/s at 2 MiB per writer and 86.8 GB/s at 16 MiB.
  • Eight writers (CPUs 2 to 9) wrote 88.3 GB/s and 86.7 GB/s. Doubling the writers added nothing [001 bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv, best rows].
  • One core alone writes 32.0 GB/s at 2 MiB and at 32 MiB in run 1.
  • So each of four writers got 21.6 to 22.4 GB/s, and each of eight writers got 10.8 to 11.2 GB/s, far below the one-core rate [001 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, README 003 'Writes on the two firmware sets'].
  • Run 2 (membench-jibin-002, 2026-11-02) used the same write kernel and the same RTL (the hardware design source, commit 0d9e214eb43b).
  • Four writers wrote 127.9 GB/s at 2 MiB (+44.1 %) and 128.0 GB/s at 16 MiB (+47.5 %).
  • Eight writers wrote 155.4 GB/s at 2 MiB (+76.1 %) and 151.7 GB/s at 16 MiB (+74.9 %) [002 bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv, best rows, README 002 lines 44 to 47].
  • Every other best row shared by run 1 and run 2 agreed within 3.6 % by README 002's count over 22 shared commands.
  • A recompute over the shared bandwidth best rows alone gives 1.80 % at most, at the pair's 48 KiB write [README 002 line 92].
  • The firmware had changed between the runs. SCP (System Control Processor firmware, the firmware that carries the mesh route overrides) went from 0.34.0 (release build) to 0.48.0-nopcie.1 (the box's rebuild with PCIe0 held, debug build).
  • TF-A (Trusted Firmware-A, the Arm boot firmware) went from 0.24.0 to 0.35.0, both debug builds [README 001 line 19, README 002 line 26, README 003 line 11].

Why it looked wrong

  • In run 1, four writers and eight writers reached the same 88.8 and 88.3 GB/s at 2 MiB [001 bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv].
  • One shared limit of about 87 to 89 GB/s therefore sat somewhere in the hemisphere (the half of the Asimov chip that the emulator ran, which holds the DSUs, the home nodes and the memory behind them).
  • Its place (DSU, mesh port, home node, or memory controller) was unknown.
  • In run 2 the same multi-core write rows moved 44 to 76 %. The one-core write stayed at 32.0 GB/s.
  • The read and copy rows of the same commands moved under 0.5 %. A write-only change that large contradicted a stable platform [README 002 line 49].
  • The write kernel and the RTL were unchanged between run 1 and run 2.
  • The change could come from the firmware or from the code changes between the runs. The two causes were not separable from runs 1 and 2 alone [README 003 'Result'].

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Writer placement rows at 16 MiB per writerrun 2, control run, run 3, boot F1Places two or four writers on chosen CPUs (2+3 in one DSU, 2+4 and 2+8 on two DSUs, 2+3+4+5 and 2+3+8+9 on two DSUs with two writers each, 2+4+6+8 on four DSUs). The aim is to find whether the write limit is per core, per DSU, per pair of DSUs, or hemisphere-wide. Files bandwidth-write-cpus*.csv, one pass, best of 2 repetitions.
Control run: run 2 binaries on run 1 firmwarecontrol runRuns run 2's binaries (latency 78b5b55a, bandwidth e850315a, cmncount bb0d30be), kernel, init, /dev/ocm module, and CPU layout on run 1's firmware (SCP 0.34.0 release, TF-A 0.24.0 debug). If the write rows return to run 1's values, the firmware caused the jump. If they stay at run 2's values, the code or kernel caused it. Run membench-jibin-003, 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-03.
Mesh PMU counts around each write rowrun 2, control runReads the CMN (Coherent Mesh Network, the on-chip interconnect) PMU (performance monitoring unit) counters hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all per home node, hns_mc_reqs_local_all, and hns_cache_miss_all with the cmncount tool. The aim is to see how write requests spread over the five home nodes under each firmware. File cmn-counts.csv.

What the tests showed

  • Control run (003): on run 1's firmware the four multi-core write rows returned to 88.8, 88.6, 86.8 and 86.7 GB/s. That is within 0.40 % of run 1.
  • The eight-writer 2 MiB row moved most, 88.254 to 88.605 GB/s.
  • So the firmware caused the change, not the code or the kernel [001 and 003 bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv, README 003 'Result'].
  • Placement rows read the same on both firmwares except where more than about 87 GB/s is needed over all four DSUs.
  • CPUs 2+3 (one DSU): 40.9 GB/s on both, a per-DSU limit. CPUs 2+4 and 2+8 (two DSUs): 64.0 GB/s on both, 32.0 GB/s each.
  • CPUs 2+3+4+5 and 2+3+8+9: 85.8 and 84.1 GB/s on both. CPUs 2+4+6+8 (four DSUs): 86.6 GB/s on the control run and 128.0 GB/s on run 2 [002 and 003 bandwidth-write-cpus*.csv, README 003 table].
  • Mesh counts on the control run's 2+4+6+8 row: home node 344 (the home of OCM4, crosspoint (5,3)) received 2,105,333 requests.
  • Each of the other four home nodes received 1,275,875 to 1,277,589 requests. Node 344 therefore saw about 829,000 extra.
  • On run 2's firmware all five home nodes read 1,276,581 to 1,278,473 requests [002 and 003 cmn-counts.csv, event hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all].
  • Memory-controller requests (5,621,097 on the control run against 5,625,931 on run 2) and SLC (system level cache) misses (5,604,936 against 5,608,583) did not rise.
  • README 003 reads the extra requests at node 344 as the same writes received more than once, as retries would be [002 and 003 cmn-counts.csv, README 003 'Mesh counts on the limited row'].
  • Likely cause named in README 003: SCP 0.48.0 adds 15 route overrides from the HN-S (the home node) to the SMS (the mesh node in front of the memory controller), vertical first with the same step count.
  • The other mesh change in SCP 0.48.0, a POCQ (point-of-coherence queue) class-3 cap for QoS (quality of service) levels 0 to 7, does not apply to the cores' QoS 14 traffic [README 002 line 26, README 003 line 40].
  • Later runs: run 3 (004, 2026-11-03) repeated run 2's four multi-core write rows within 0.32 % (127.919, 155.154, 127.981, 152.177 GB/s) and the six placement rows within 0.064 %.
  • The pair's 48 KiB write moved -2.29 % (60.457 to 59.070 GB/s). README 004 attributes that to the rebuilt bandwidth binary adding 7.7 to 8.0 ns per pass.
  • Boot F1 (011, 2026-11-06, the L3 on) repeated the six placement rows within 0.026 % of run 3.
  • F1's eight-writer 2 MiB row rose to 165.2 GB/s (+6.45 % over run 3's 155.2 GB/s), and its 16 MiB row to 153.0 GB/s from run 3's 152.2 GB/s.
  • The core page reads the eight-writer rows (151.7 to 165.2 GB/s across runs 2, 3 and F1) as a shared DRAM write ceiling that four writers at 128.0 GB/s do not reach. That reading is the page's interpretation, not a separate measurement [004 and 011 bandwidth-perdsu.csv, bandwidth-all8.csv, bandwidth-pair.csv and bandwidth-write-cpus*.csv, README 004 lines 8, 97, 98, asimov-c1nano-perf.html tables 4.4, 4.5, section 9].

Still open

The control run changed the whole firmware set at once. The exact component (the 15 route overrides, the rest of SCP 0.48.0, TF-A 0.35.0, or the debug build) is not isolated. A run with only the route overrides changed would settle that. The counter hns_pocq_retry_all (not yet run) would confirm that the about 829,000 extra requests at home node 344 on the old firmware are retries.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (membench-jibin-001), 2026-10-31: the data; first written as a limit in run 2's README (membench-jibin-002, 2026-11-02, 'round one's hemisphere write limit is gone'); control run membench-jibin-003 ran 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-03 (script 23:44 UTC to 00:59 UTC)

What looked wrong. Run 1: four writers (one per DSU, CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8) wrote 88.8 GB/s at 2 MiB each and 86.8 GB/s at 16 MiB each. Eight writers (CPUs 2 to 9) wrote 88.3 GB/s at 2 MiB and 86.7 GB/s at 16 MiB. One core alone writes 32.0 GB/s at 2 MiB and 32 MiB. So four writers got 21.6 to 22.4 GB/s each and eight writers 10.8 to 11.2 GB/s each, far below one core's rate [membench-jibin-001 bandwidth-perdsu.csv, bandwidth-all8.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, best rows; README 003 'Writes on the two firmware sets']. Run 2, same write kernel and same RTL (0d9e214eb43b): 127.9 GB/s with four writers (+44.1 %) and 155.4 GB/s with eight (+76.1 %) at 2 MiB; 128.0 (+47.5 %) and 151.7 (+74.9 %) at 16 MiB. Run 2's README says every other best row the two rounds shared agrees within 3.6 % (a recompute over the shared bandwidth best rows gives 1.80 % at most, the pair's 48 KiB write). The firmware had changed: SCP 0.34.0 (release) to 0.48.0-nopcie.1 (the box's rebuild with PCIe0 held, debug build), TF-A 0.24.0 to 0.35.0 (both debug) [README 001 line 19, README 002 lines 7, 9, 26, 44 to 47, 92].

Why it looked wrong. Doubling the writers from four to eight added nothing in run 1 (88.8 to 88.3 GB/s), so one shared limit of about 87 to 89 GB/s sat somewhere in the hemisphere. Its place (DSU, mesh port, home node, memory controller) was unknown. In run 2 the same write rows moved 44 to 76 % while the one-core write stayed at 32.0 GB/s and the read and copy rows of the same commands moved under 0.5 %. A change that large with no change to the write kernel or the RTL contradicted a stable platform, and could come from the firmware or from the code changes between the runs [README 002 line 49; README 003 'Result'].

Tests added.

  • Writer placement rows, 16 MiB per writer, one pass, best of 2 reps: CPUs 2+3 (one DSU), 2+4 and 2+8 (two DSUs), 2+3+4+5 and 2+3+8+9 (two DSUs, two writers each), 2+4+6+8 (four DSUs) [run 2 (002, 2026-11-02), control 003, run 3 (004, 2026-11-03), run 6 boot F1 (011, 2026-11-06); files bandwidth-write-cpus*.csv]: where the write limit sits: per core, per DSU, per pair of DSUs, or hemisphere-wide

  • Mesh PMU counts around each write row (cmncount: hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all per home node, hns_mc_reqs_local_all, hns_cache_miss_all) [run 2 (002) and control 003; file cmn-counts.csv]: how the write requests spread over the five home nodes under each firmware

What the tests showed. Control run: on run 1's firmware the four multi-core write rows returned to 88.8, 88.6, 86.8 and 86.7 GB/s, within 0.40 % of run 1 (the eight-writer 2 MiB row moved most, 88.254 to 88.605 GB/s). So the firmware caused the change, not the code or the kernel [README 003 'Result'; bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv of 001 and 003]. Likely cause named in README 003: the new SCP's route overrides from the home nodes to the memory controllers (README 002 counts 15 HN-S-to-SMS route overrides, vertical first, same step count). The other mesh change, a POCQ class-3 cap for QoS 0 to 7, does not apply to the cores' QoS 14 traffic. The control changed the whole firmware set at once, so the exact component (the overrides, the rest of SCP 0.48.0, TF-A 0.35.0, or the debug build) is not isolated [README 003 line 40]. Placement rows: two writers in one DSU (CPUs 2+3) get 40.9 GB/s on both firmwares (per-DSU limit, not firmware). Two writers on two DSUs (2+4, 2+8) get 64.0 GB/s on both firmwares, 32.0 each. Two DSUs with two writers each (2+3+4+5, 2+3+8+9) get 85.8 and 84.1 GB/s on both. Only the placements that need more than about 87 GB/s over all four DSUs differ: 2+4+6+8 reads 86.6 GB/s on the old firmware and 128.0 GB/s on the new, and the 4- and 8-thread rows likewise [README 003 table; bandwidth-write-cpus*.csv of 002 and 003]. Mesh counts on the control's 2+4+6+8 row: home node 344 (OCM4's home, crosspoint (5,3)) received 2,105,333 requests against 1,275,875 to 1,277,589 at each of the other four nodes, about 829,000 extra. On run 2's firmware all five read 1,276,581 to 1,278,473. Memory-controller requests (5,621,097 against 5,625,931) and misses (5,604,936 against 5,608,583) did not rise, so README 003 reads the extra requests as the same writes received more than once, as retries would be. The counter hns_pocq_retry_all would confirm this and was not run [cmn-counts.csv of 003 and 002; README 003 'Mesh counts on the limited row']. Later runs: run 3 (004) repeated run 2's four multi-core write rows within 0.32 % (127.919, 155.154, 127.981, 152.177 GB/s) and the six placement rows within 0.064 %; the only write row that moved more was the pair's 48 KiB write, -2.29 % (60.457 to 59.070 GB/s), which README 004 attributes to the rebuilt bandwidth binary adding 7.7 to 8.0 ns per pass. Boot F1 (011, the L3 on) repeated the six placement rows within 0.026 % of run 3 (within 0.09 % of run 2), so the L3 does not change a write stream. F1's eight-writer 2 MiB row rose to 165.2 GB/s (+6.45 % over run 3's 155.2), its 16 MiB row to 153.0 (+0.79 %). The core page reads the eight-writer rows (151.7 to 165.2 GB/s across runs 2, 3 and F1) as a shared DRAM write ceiling that four writers at 128.0 GB/s do not reach; that reading is the page's interpretation, not a separate measurement [asimov-c1nano-perf.html tables 4.4, 4.5, section 9; README 004 lines 8, 97, 98].

4.13 Two writers in one DSU get 40.9 GB/s, not 64.0; the pair's 160 KiB write rose 23 % on F1partly explained

Two cores of one DSU (cluster) write 40.9 GB/s together, not 64.0 GB/s. Their 160 KiB write rose 23 % with the L3 on.

What looked wrong

  • CPUs 2 and 3 share one DSU (a cluster of two cores). In run 2 each wrote 16 MiB. Together they reached 40.922 GB/s (20.457 to 21.737 GB/s per writer). [002 bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv rows 4 to 6]
  • CPUs 2 and 4 sit on two different DSUs. Writing 16 MiB each in run 2, they reached 63.984 GB/s (31.982 to 31.993 GB/s per writer). [002 bandwidth-write-cpus2-4.csv rows 4 to 6]
  • One core alone writes 31.997 GB/s at 32 MiB in run 1 (31.996 GB/s in run 3). So two cores of one DSU lose 36 % of two one-core rates. [001 and 004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 86]
  • The same pair writing 160 KiB each reached 47.029 GB/s in run 1 and 47.241 GB/s in run 3 (23.620 to 24.801 GB/s per core). [001 and 004 bandwidth-pair.csv rows 38 to 41]
  • 47.241 GB/s is 74 % of two one-core 256 KiB writes (2 x 31.869 GB/s in run 3), the nearest one-core size. [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 56]
  • On boot F1 (the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 on) the pair's 160 KiB write rose to 58.250 GB/s, +23.3 % over run 3. [011 bandwidth-pair.csv row 41]
  • Every write row of 2 MiB and above repeated run 3 within 6.4 %. The largest move was all eight cores at 2 MiB each, 155.154 to 165.154 GB/s. [004 and 011 bandwidth-all8.csv row 11]

Why it looked wrong

  • Cores 2 and 3 share an L2 (the 128 KiB cache of the cluster), an L3 (the 256 KiB cache of the cluster), a CME (a unit of the cluster that writes memory on its own) and one mesh port (the cluster's one link to the mesh). [004 README.md line 32 and 011 README.md line 348]
  • Which shared part limits two writers was unknown.
  • Run 1's hemisphere write limit (86.8 GB/s at 16 MiB per writer) was measured with writers on all four DSUs. A per-DSU limit of 41 GB/s was a new, smaller limit. [RUN2-PLAN.md line 108]
  • For the 160 KiB pair the two buffers total 320 KiB. That is more than the L2 (128 KiB) and more than the L3 (256 KiB).
  • With the L3 off, the lines beyond the L2 go across the mesh to the SLC (the system level cache).
  • Boot E (an earlier L3-on boot) ran no multi-core row. So no second L3-on observation of the pair exists.
  • The pages give no pointer for why the L3 mode moved this one write row by 23 %. [011 README.md line 145]

Tests added to clarify it

A pair under 2 x 32 GB/s shows a per-DSU path [RUN2-PLAN.md line 108].

A CME rate above 40.9 GB/s would put the two-core limit on the cores' side if the CME's stores leave through the same port [004 README.md line 85].

What the tests showed

  • The per-DSU write limit does not depend on the firmware.
  • The CPUs 2+3 row reads 40.922 GB/s on run 2 (new firmware), 40.939 GB/s on the control run (old firmware) and 40.940 GB/s on run 3. [002, 003 and 004 bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv row 6 and 003 README.md line 38]
  • On run 3 one CME writes 32 MiB at 61.971 GB/s through CPU 2 and 3's cluster. That is 1.51 times the two cores' 40.940 GB/s. [004 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 116]
  • Jesse's reading (an inference, not a measurement): if the CME's stores leave through the same cluster port, the two-core limit is on the cores' side, not the port's. [004 README.md line 85]
  • The CME page keeps this as a hypothesis. [asimov-cme-perf.html 'Writes beside the cluster's two cores']
  • With the L3 on (boot F1) the same CME write reads 40.445 GB/s by the bracket (40.459 GB/s in span). That is 0.99 times the pair's 40.949 GB/s on the same boot. [011 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 116 and 011 bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv row 6]
  • Boot F2 reads 40.357 GB/s. So with the L3 on the CME no longer exceeds the pair. [012 cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 116]
  • The two pages disagree on the pair's shared path. asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 9 says 'For the pair it is the DSU's one mesh port'. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 9]
  • asimov-cme-perf.html and Jesse's run 3 README put the limit on the cores' side. Neither page resolves it. [004 README.md line 85]
  • The pair's 160 KiB write rose 1.233 times on F1 (58.250 GB/s against 47.241 GB/s on run 3). Its 48 KiB write rose 1.049 times.
  • The placement rows and the one-core writes held within 0.3 %. [011 README.md lines 113 and 145 and asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.4]

Still open

Two things are open. One is which shared part of the DSU limits two writers to 40.9 GB/s (the pages name the mesh port and the cores' side). The other is why the L3 on moved the pair's 160 KiB write by 23 %. The two proposed tests (a two-core write with one core in streaming mode, and 16 MiB readers on CPUs 2+3 against 2+4) plus a second L3-on boot of the pair rows would settle them.

4.14 The counted 2 MiB read puts 3.35 requests per line and pass on the home nodes, about twice the 40,000-per-node estimate; the dense all-five OCM chain loads the five home nodes unevenly (16 % spread)open

The 2 MiB read put 2.2 times the estimated requests on each home node, and the dense OCM chain loads the five nodes unevenly.

What looked wrong

  • Run 2 (membench-jibin-002, run on 2026-11-02) put the counted 2 MiB read under the CMN counters. Each of the five home nodes received 87,386 to 88,013 requests (hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all). [002 cmn-counts.csv rows dram-read-2M-cpu2, run_asimov.sh:151]
  • The five nodes sum to 438,695 requests. That is 3.35 requests per line and timed pass (438,695 / (4 x 32,768)), or 13.4 requests per line over the whole command (438,695 / 32,768). [recomputed from 002 cmn-counts.csv]
  • The plan estimated about 40,000 requests per node (200,000 in all, est.) for an even spread of the buffer. [README.md:413, RUN2-PLAN.md:105]
  • The measured sum is 2.2 times that (438,695 / 200,000). Jesse's README calls it about twice his estimate. [002 README.md:72]
  • The dense all-five chain put 153,501 / 154,463 / 145,606 / 138,988 / 129,998 requests on nodes 88 / 160 / 216 / 288 / 344 from CPU 2. [002 cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-cpu2]
  • The spread from the highest node to the lowest is 15.8 % ((154,463 - 129,998) / 154,463). [002 cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-cpu2]
  • The order is the same from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8: node 160 (OCM1) most, then 88 (OCM0), 216 (OCM2), 288 (OCM3), and 344 (OCM4) least. [002 cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-cpu4/6/8]
  • The spreads over the four CPUs are 14.6 % to 15.8 %. The lowest count is 129,929 (CPU 6, node 344). [002 cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-cpu4/6/8]

Why it looked wrong

  • The estimate assumed about one home-node request per line touch. One rep touches every line 6 times (fill, warm-up pass, 4 timed passes): 196,608 touches. [bandwidth.c:385, 406, 416]
  • That is close to the estimate's 200,000 (5 x 40,000, est., derived here). [README.md:413]
  • At 13.4 requests per line over the command, each line touch caused about two home-node requests, not one. [002 cmn-counts.csv rows dram-read-2M-cpu2]
  • The same row counted 213,249 hns_mc_reqs_local_all (6.5 per line) and 364,449 hns_cache_miss_all (11.1 per line). [002 cmn-counts.csv rows dram-read-2M-cpu2, 002 README.md:83]
  • The counters span the whole command, from before exec to after exit: program load, buffer fill, chain builds, warm-up, flushes and timed passes. [README.md:409-410, RUN2-PLAN.md section 2.2]
  • They cannot separate the timed passes from the rest. [README.md:409-410, RUN2-PLAN.md section 2.2]
  • For the all-five chain, the five regions are equal in size (256 KiB each) and each sits in its own home node. So an even count per node was expected. [RUN2-PLAN.md section 2.2]

Tests added to clarify it

What the tests showed

  • The 2 MiB read count repeats on three boots: run 2 87,386 to 88,013, control run 87,683 to 88,008, run 3 87,579 to 88,012 requests per node. [cmn-counts.csv of 002, 003, 004]
  • Each is about 3.35 per line and timed pass. So neither the firmware nor the rebuilt program changes it. [004 README.md:130]
  • Boot F1 (L3 on) put 85,518 to 85,777 requests per node (sum 427,991, 0.975 times run 3, 3.27 per line and timed pass) in 0.648 times run 3's command lifetime. [011 bootF1/cmn-counts.csv rows dram-read-2M-cpu2, 011 README.md:144]
  • So the L3 in full mode did not take these reads off the mesh. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2.3]
  • The dense all-five order (160 > 88 > 216 > 288 > 344) repeats in run 3 within -2.3 % to +1.4 % per node: 149,929 / 151,125 / 142,596 / 136,285 / 129,453 requests, spread 14.3 %. [004 cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-dense-cpu2, 004 README.md:118]
  • On boot F1 the dense row's spread grew to 18.3 % from CPU 2 (140,506 / 146,791 / 139,517 / 134,499 / 119,924 requests). [011 bootF1/cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-dense-cpu2]
  • Nodes 88 and 216 swapped order (160 > 216 > 88 > 288 > 344). Node 344 stays lowest. [011 bootF1/cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-dense-cpu2]
  • The sparse all-five rows put 0.40 to 0.42 of the dense count on each node (run 3: 53,293 / 53,041 / 52,049 / 51,790 / 50,097 requests, spread 6.0 %). [cmn-counts.csv of 004 and 011]
  • The spread is 6 to 7 % in run 3 and 7 to 10 % on boot F1, in the same direction as the dense rows. [cmn-counts.csv of 004 and 011]
  • A related note from the control run: the 2+4+6+8 write row put about 829,000 extra requests on node 344 on the old firmware, with no extra memory requests or misses. [003 README.md:44-45]
  • Jesse's README names hns_pocq_retry_all per node as the event that would show retries. [003 README.md:44-45]

Still open

No explanation of the two-requests-per-touch ratio or of the per-node order has been reached. Run 7 phase H1 would show the per-node count when the timed passes take most of the counted lifetime. Only a counter window over the timed passes alone would settle the ratio. cmncount lacks such a window.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 2 (membench-jibin-002), run on 2026-11-02 (README 002, 'Reading the numbers'); analysed 2026-11-03

What looked wrong. The counted 2 MiB read (bandwidth read kernel, CPU 2, 4 timed passes over 32,768 lines of 64 bytes; run_asimov.sh:151) put 87,386 to 88,013 hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all requests on each of the five home nodes [membench-jibin-002 cmn-counts.csv, rows dram-read-2M-cpu2]. The five nodes sum to 438,695 requests. That is 3.35 requests per line and timed pass (438,695 / (4 x 32,768)). The plan's estimate was about 40,000 requests per node if the buffer spreads evenly [README.md:413; RUN2-PLAN.md:105], so the measured count is about 2.2 times the estimate. Jesse's README states it as 'about twice his estimate of 40,000' [membench-jibin-002 README.md:72]. The dense all-five OCM chain rows (1.25 MiB over five 256 KiB regions, 20,480 lines, '--fresh 3 --flush') put 153,501 / 154,463 / 145,606 / 138,988 / 129,998 requests on nodes 88 / 160 / 216 / 288 / 344 from CPU 2 [membench-jibin-002 cmn-counts.csv, rows ocm-all5-cpu2]. The spread from the highest to the lowest node is 15.8 % ((154,463 - 129,998) / 154,463). The ordering is the same on CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8: node 160 (OCM1) most, then 88 (OCM0), 216 (OCM2), 288 (OCM3), and 344 (OCM4) least. The node-to-region mapping comes from the per-region rows, where each region's own node reads 111,468 to 123,460 against 9,042 to 10,576 on the other four [membench-jibin-002 README.md:70].

Why it looked wrong. The estimate assumed about one home-node request per line touch. One rep of the bandwidth read command touches every line six times: one fill (fill_buf, bandwidth.c:385), one warm-up pass (bandwidth.c:406), then the 4 timed passes (bandwidth.c:416). 6 x 32,768 = 196,608 touches, which is about 200,000 = 5 x 40,000 (est., derived here; README.md:413 does not show its arithmetic). The measured 438,695 is 13.4 requests per line over the whole command. So each line touch caused about two requests at the home node, not one. The counters span the whole command from before exec to after exit: program load, buffer fill, chain builds, warm-up, flushes and timed passes [README.md:409-410; RUN2-PLAN.md section 2.2 'Counters around the whole process']. They cannot separate the timed passes from the rest. The same row counted 213,249 hns_mc_reqs_local_all (requests the home nodes sent on to memory, 6.5 per line) and 364,449 hns_cache_miss_all (SLC misses, 11.1 per line) [membench-jibin-002 cmn-counts.csv]. hns_cache_miss_all counts every qualified lookup that misses, fills and flushes included [membench-jibin-002 README.md:83]. For the all-five chain, the five regions are equal in size (256 KiB each) and each sits in its own home node, so an even count per node was expected. The dense chain command builds three chains over the same lines, walks chain 0 twice untimed, flushes, and times chains 1 and 2 once each [RUN2-PLAN.md section 2.2]. The run 3 dense control repeated run 2's all-five counts node for node within -2.3 % to +1.4 % [membench-jibin-004 README.md:118], so the uneven spread is repeatable, not noise.

Tests added.

  • Run 3 (membench-jibin-004): the same counted 2 MiB read row repeated [run 3, membench-jibin-004, cmn-counts.csv rows dram-read-2M-cpu2]: whether the per-node count repeats with the newer firmware and the rebuilt bandwidth program; 87,579 to 88,012 per node, sum 438,961, 3.35 per line and pass
  • Control run (membench-jibin-003, run 1's firmware): the same counted 2 MiB read row [control run, membench-jibin-003, cmn-counts.csv rows dram-read-2M-cpu2]: whether the firmware changes the count; 87,683 to 88,008 per node, sum 439,150, 3.35 per line and pass
  • Run 3: dense all-five chain kept as a control beside the new sparse all-five chain (ocm-all5-dense-cpuN and ocm-all5-cpuN, run_asimov.sh:136-137) [run 3, membench-jibin-004, cmn-counts.csv rows ocm-all5-dense-cpu2 and ocm-all5-cpu2]: whether the uneven per-node count repeats (dense: 149,929 / 151,125 / 142,596 / 136,285 / 129,453, same ordering, 14.3 % spread) and how the sparse chain (320 loads per pass, 7 passes) loads the nodes (53,293 / 53,041 / 52,049 / 51,790 / 50,097, 6.0 % spread, 0.40 to 0.42 times the dense count per node)
  • Run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, L3 on): the counted 2 MiB read row repeated [run 6, membench-jibin-011, results/bootF1/cmn-counts.csv rows dram-read-2M-cpu2]: whether the L3 in full mode takes the read off the mesh; 85,518 to 85,777 per node, sum 427,991, 0.975 times run 3's sum, 3.27 per line and pass, while the command lived 0.648 times as long [membench-jibin-011 README.md:144; asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2.3]
  • Run 7 plan, phase H1 (run_l3.sh:94-98, follow-up-run-plan.md section 14): the 2 MiB read with 64 passes and the 32 MiB read with 8 passes, 3 reps, under the request set (cmn) and under a queue set (cmnq: hns_qos_pocq_occupancy_read per node plus dtc_cycles) [not run as of 2026-11-08 (no results folder after 012; requested in message-to-jesse-round6.md)]: requests per node when the timed passes take most of the counted lifetime, and the mean number of active read entries in each home node's queue over the whole command; the events still cannot select the timed passes or this core alone [follow-up-run-plan.md section 14, 'Words used here']
  • A per-phase request count (timed passes alone) [not run; no such counter window exists in cmncount]: requests during the timed passes alone (the plan's section 14 says claims about the timed passes alone need a measurement window and an event that identify them)

What the tests showed. The 2 MiB read count repeats on three boots: run 2 87,386 to 88,013, the control run 87,683 to 88,008, run 3 87,579 to 88,012 per node (each about 3.35 requests per line and timed pass) [cmn-counts.csv of 002, 003, 004]. So neither the firmware nor the rebuilt program changes it. Boot F1 (L3 on) put 85,518 to 85,777 per node, 0.975 times run 3, so the L3 in full mode did not take these reads off the mesh [membench-jibin-011 README.md:144]. The dense all-five chain's uneven ordering (160 > 88 > 216 > 288 > 344) repeats in run 3 node for node within -2.3 % to +1.4 % [membench-jibin-004 README.md:118]. On boot F1 the dense row's spread grew to 18.3 % from CPU 2 (140,506 / 146,791 / 139,517 / 134,499 / 119,924) and the order of nodes 88 and 216 swapped (160 > 216 > 88 > 288 > 344); node 344 stays lowest [membench-jibin-011 bootF1/cmn-counts.csv]. The sparse all-five rows put 0.40 to 0.42 of the dense count on each node with a 6 to 7 % spread in run 3 and 7 to 10 % on F1, in the same direction [cmn-counts.csv of 004 and 011]. No explanation of the two-requests-per-touch ratio or of the per-node ordering has been reached. The claim that a page text was corrected to '3.3 per line and pass' is not in the primary files: none of the four generated pages carries that phrase. Related note from the control run: the 2+4+6+8 write row put about 829,000 extra requests on node 344 on the old firmware with no extra memory requests or misses, and Jesse's README names hns_pocq_retry_all per node as the event that would show retries [membench-jibin-003 README.md:44-45].
