4.15 Which crosspoint holds CPU 6's and CPU 8's mesh ports: the per-region OCM pattern alone could not tell them apartexplained

The fastest-region rule placed CPU 4's mesh port but could not tell whether CPU 6 and CPU 8 had swapped ports.

What looked wrong

  • Run 2 measured each CPU's load latency from each of the five OCM regions. Each row is the best of two fresh-chain passes. [002 README:64, latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]
  • Averages by mesh distance, run 2, at 1 crosspoint: 19.64 ns per load (8 rows, 18.46 to 21.36 ns).
  • At 3 crosspoints: 21.82 ns per load (10 rows, 20.49 to 23.44 ns).
  • At 5 crosspoints: 24.58 ns per load (2 rows, 24.48 to 24.68 ns).
  • That is about 1.1 to 1.4 ns per load for each extra crosspoint. Each CPU's fastest region is 1 crosspoint away. This rule places CPU 4's port at crosspoint (3,2).
  • The rule does not place CPUs 6 and 8.
  • With the ports swapped (CPU 6 at (5,2), CPU 8 at (4,3)), CPU 6's distances to OCM0 to OCM4 would be 5, 5, 3, 3, 1 crosspoints.
  • Under the same swap, CPU 8's distances would be 3, 3, 1, 1, 1 crosspoints.
  • OCM4 stays the fastest region for both CPUs under the swap. So the fastest-region rule cannot tell the two assignments apart. [recomputed from the run 2 region CSVs]

Why it looked wrong

  • The platform facts put the DSU mesh ports of CPUs 6-7 and 8-9 (node ids 280 and 336) at crosspoints (4,3) and (5,2). [002 README:31]
  • They put the OCM0 to OCM4 home nodes (node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344) at (1,3), (2,4), (3,3), (4,4), (5,3). [002 README:31]
  • The source is Jesse's reading of the RTL mesh file cmns3_12_1.yml, lines 648 to 720. [HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:19]
  • That reading gives DSU ports at crosspoints 12, 23, 32, 43, 52 and home nodes at 13, 24, 33, 44, 53, written as two-digit (x,y). [HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:19]
  • Only CPU 2's placement had been checked by measurement (round one's qualification boot).
  • The two candidate assignments for CPUs 6 and 8 give the same fastest region for each CPU. Every later distance fit (step counts per cell) depends on this assignment.
  • The per-region rows are rough. Two passes differ by up to 3.4 ns per load. [002 README:67]
  • The rows count 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load (some lines arrive before their load). [002 README:67]
  • That spread is the same size as the CPU 8 minus CPU 6 gap used to tell the ports apart.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Per-region and all-five OCM latency rows from CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8run 2, run 3CPU 8 against CPU 6 from each region (ns per load, best pass), and the all-five row order against each CPU's mean distance to the five home nodes. A slower CPU 8 from the far regions and an order by mean distance confirm the README's coordinates. A faster CPU 8 means the ports are swapped. Run 3 used sparse chains, best of 7 passes of 64 loads per region. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv, latency-ocm-all5-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]
G6 route rows with crosspoint data-flit counters at both endsboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EOne 20-cell set (4 CPUs x 5 regions) reads the counters mxp_{e,w,n,s}_dat_txflit_valid (outgoing data flits per direction) at the DSU's crosspoint (node ids 152, 208, 280, 336) and at the home node's crosspoint (node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344) over the whole command, data channel only. The best ns per load of each cell feeds a fit of latency against X and Y step counts. A low fit residual and X-first dominant directions in every cell mean the coordinates are right. [cmn-counts.csv labels route-ocm{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}, latency-ocm-region{0..4}-route-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]

What the tests showed

  • Run 2: CPU 8 reads slower than CPU 6 from OCM0 to OCM3 by +1.24, +3.20, +1.14 and +2.31 ns per load. [002 README:61-64, latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv]
  • From OCM4 the two are level (18.89 against 18.96 ns per load, 0.07 ns apart). [002 README:61-64, latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv]
  • Run 2 all-five rows follow mean distance to the five home nodes. [002 README:65, latency-ocm-all5-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]
  • CPU 6 (1.8 crosspoints) 25.37 ns per load, CPU 2 (1.8) 25.51 ns, CPU 4 (2.6) 26.11 ns, CPU 8 (3.4) 27.70 ns, 2.19 ns behind CPU 2. [002 README:65, latency-ocm-all5-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]
  • A swap would make CPU 8 the nearer CPU. So CPUs 6-7 sit at (4,3) and CPUs 8-9 at (5,2).
  • Run 3 (sparse chains) repeats the order by distance: 21.58 ns per load at 1 crosspoint, 24.25 ns at 3, 27.73 ns at 5. [004 README:109, recomputed from latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv]
  • Within each CPU every nearer region's best is below every farther one's. [004 README:109, recomputed from latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv]
  • CPU 8 minus CPU 6 is +0.48, +4.56, +2.97, +4.03 ns per load from OCM0 to OCM3 and -1.84 ns per load from OCM4. [004 README:109, recomputed from latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv]
  • Run 4 boot B (prefetchers off) fits the 20 route cells as 20.75 ns + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step, 0.09 ns rms, with the README's coordinates. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 4, latency-ocm-region*-route-cpu*.csv]
  • Boot D (prefetchers off) repeats it: 20.63 ns + 2.00 ns per X step + 0.98 ns per Y step, 0.13 ns rms. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 4, latency-ocm-region*-route-cpu*.csv]
  • With prefetchers on the residual is 0.90 ns rms (boot A) and 0.80 ns rms (boot C). On boot E the fit is not usable (2.05 ns rms). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 4, latency-ocm-region*-route-cpu*.csv]
  • Recomputed here: with CPU 6 and CPU 8 swapped, the same boot B and boot D rows fit at 1.61 and 1.62 ns rms. The Y slope turns negative (-0.18 and -0.17 ns per Y step). [recomputed from the boot B and boot D route CSVs]
  • So the measured assignment is the only one the step model fits. [recomputed from the boot B and boot D route CSVs]
  • G6 counters: the direction with the most outgoing data flits is the X-first direction toward the other end, on boots A to E. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6, asimov-c1nano-perf.html route-counter paragraph, cmn-counts.csv]
  • That holds in 20 of 20 cells at the DSU's crosspoint and 20 of 20 at the home node's crosspoint. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6, asimov-c1nano-perf.html route-counter paragraph, cmn-counts.csv]
  • That direction carries at least 75 % of the four directions' flits on boots A to D and at least 61 % on boot E. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6, asimov-c1nano-perf.html route-counter paragraph, cmn-counts.csv]
  • Recomputed here: with swapped coordinates only 16 of 20 cells at each end match X-first on boots A and B. So the data-flit directions also reject the swap. [cmn-counts.csv]

Still open

The G6 counters count the data channel only. They do not identify the read-request route or the response's last link. So the X and Y step counts per cell remain coordinate assumptions. Counting the read-request channel at the same two crosspoints would settle the full route.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 2 (membench-jibin-002), README dated 2026-11-02

What looked wrong. Run 2 measured each CPU's load latency from each of the five OCM regions (best of two fresh-chain passes). Sorted by mesh distance, the per-region rows average 19.64 ns per load at 1 crosspoint (8 rows, 18.46 to 21.36), 21.82 ns at 3 (10 rows, 20.49 to 23.44) and 24.58 ns at 5 (2 rows, 24.48 to 24.68) [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:64, recomputed from results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]. That is about 1.1 to 1.4 ns per extra crosspoint. Each CPU's fastest region is one at 1 crosspoint. This places CPU 4's port at (3,2). It does not place CPUs 6 and 8: with the two ports swapped, (5,2) for CPU 6 and (4,3) for CPU 8, each CPU's fastest region is still OCM4 (recomputed here from the same CSVs: under the swap CPU 6's distances would be 5,5,3,3,1 and CPU 8's 3,3,1,1,1, and OCM4 stays the fastest region for both).

Why it looked wrong. The platform facts put the mesh ports of the clusters of CPUs 6-7 and 8-9 (node ids 280 and 336) at crosspoints (4,3) and (5,2), and the OCM0-4 home nodes (node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344) at (1,3), (2,4), (3,3), (4,4), (5,3) [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:31]. The source of those coordinates is Jesse's reading of the RTL mesh file cmns3_12_1.yml lines 648 to 720: DSU ports at crosspoints 12, 23, 32, 43, 52 and home nodes at 13, 24, 33, 44, 53, written as two-digit (x,y) [HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:19]. Only CPU 2's placement had been checked by measurement (round one's qualification boot). The two candidate assignments for CPUs 6 and 8 give the same fastest region for each CPU. So the fastest-region rule by itself does not say which cluster sits where. Every later distance fit (step counts per cell) depends on this assignment. The per-region rows are also rough: their two passes differ by up to 3.4 ns, and they count 1.11 to 1.45 L2 refills per load, so some lines reach the cluster before their load [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:67]. That spread is the same size as the CPU 8 minus CPU 6 gap used to tell the ports apart.

Tests added.

  • Per-region and all-five OCM latency rows from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8, compared region by region and by mean distance [run 2 (membench-jibin-002); repeated in run 3 (membench-jibin-004) with sparse chains (best of 7 passes of 64 loads per region)]: CPU 8 against CPU 6 from each region (ns per load, best pass) and the all-five row order against each CPU's mean distance to the five home nodes [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv, latency-ocm-all5-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]
  • G6 route rows (one 20-cell set: 4 CPUs x 5 regions) with crosspoint counters mxp_{e,w,n,s}_dat_txflit_valid at the DSU's crosspoint (node ids 152, 208, 280, 336) and at the home node's crosspoint (node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344) [run 4 boots A to D (membench-jibin-005 to 008) and boot E (membench-jibin-010)]: the outgoing data-flit direction at each end of each route, over the whole command (data channel only; the read-request channel is not counted) [cmn-counts.csv, labels route-ocm{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}]; and the best ns per load of each route cell for a fit of latency against X and Y step counts [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-route-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]

What the tests showed. Run 2: CPU 8 reads slower than CPU 6 from OCM0 to OCM3 by +1.24, +3.20, +1.14 and +2.31 ns per load, and level from OCM4 (18.89 against 18.96 ns, a difference of 0.07 ns) [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:61-64; recomputed from the region CSVs]. The all-five rows order the CPUs by their mean distance to the five home nodes: CPU 6 and CPU 2 (mean 1.8 crosspoints) read 25.37 and 25.51 ns, CPU 4 (2.6) 26.11 ns, CPU 8 (3.4) 27.70 ns, 2.19 ns behind CPU 2 [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:65; latency-ocm-all5-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv]. Under the swapped assignment CPU 8 would be the nearer CPU, so the data put CPUs 6-7 at (4,3) and CPUs 8-9 at (5,2). Run 3 repeats the order by distance: 21.58 ns at 1 crosspoint, 24.25 at 3, 27.73 at 5 (sparse chains), and within each CPU every nearer region's best is below every farther one's [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md:109]. In run 3 CPU 8 minus CPU 6 is +0.48, +4.56, +2.97, +4.03 ns from OCM0 to OCM3 and -1.84 ns from OCM4 (recomputed from results/membench-jibin-004/results/*/latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{6,8}.csv). Run 4 boot B (prefetchers off) fits the 20 route cells as 20.75 ns + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step with 0.09 ns rms, using these coordinates; boot D repeats it (20.63 + 2.00 per X + 0.98 per Y, 0.13 ns rms); with prefetchers on the residual is 0.90 ns on boot A and 0.80 ns on boot C, and on boot E the fit is not usable (2.05 ns rms) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 4 text 'With the prefetchers off (boot B) the 20 route cells fit...'; all five refits recomputed from latency-ocm-region*-route-cpu*.csv]. Recomputed here: with CPU 6 and CPU 8 swapped, the same boot B and boot D rows fit at 1.61 and 1.62 ns rms with a negative Y slope (-0.18 ns per Y step), so the measured assignment is the only one the step model fits. The G6 counters show the direction with the most outgoing data flits is the X-first direction toward the other end in 20 of 20 cells at the DSU's crosspoint and 20 of 20 at the home node's, on boots A, B, C, D and E; the dominant direction carries at least 75 % of the four directions' flits on boots A to D and at least 61 % on E [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6 text; asimov-c1nano-perf.html section on route counters; recomputed from each boot's cmn-counts.csv]. Recomputed here: under the swapped coordinates only 16 of 20 cells at each end match X-first on boots A and B, so the data-flit directions also reject the swap. These events count the data channel only. They do not identify the read-request route or the response's last link, so the X and Y step counts per cell stay coordinate assumptions.

Highlighted: mesh, DSU, home-node, OCM.

4.16 The kernel's mesh map prints logical ids, not node ids: HN-S #0 to #4 are OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1, OCM3explained

The kernel's mesh map labels home nodes by logical id. HN-S #0 to #4 are OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1, OCM3, not OCM0 to OCM4.

What looked wrong

  • The mesh map in sysinfo.txt (the system-information dump collected on each run) prints crosspoint numbers XP #0 to #35 and each node's logical id within its type. It does not print node ids [002 sysinfo.txt:489-560].
  • The five HN-S cells (HN-S: a home node, the mesh unit that owns one OCM region) print #0 at crosspoint (1,3), #1 at (3,3), #2 at (5,3), #3 at (2,4), #4 at (4,4) [002 sysinfo.txt:505-536].
  • A node id decodes to a crosspoint as X = bits 8:6 and Y = bits 5:3. Node 88 is (1,3), 160 is (2,4), 216 is (3,3), 288 is (4,4), 344 is (5,3) [gen_hierarchy.py:51].
  • So HN-S #0 to #4 are nodes 88, 216, 344, 160, 288, that is OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1, OCM3.
  • A reader who matches HN-S #n to OCMn places three of the five home nodes wrongly [002 README.md:80].
  • Before run 2, the node ids 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 came only from the address map.
  • No perf_event_open (the Linux system call that opens a hardware counter) with bynodeid had been tried on the image [RUN2-PLAN.md:337-341, HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:33].

Why it looked wrong

  • Every per-region latency claim and every mesh-distance claim depends on which home node owns each OCM region [002 README.md:31]. The expected reading was that HN-S #n in the map is OCMn.
  • The map looks like a node-id list but is a logical-id list. Under the HN-S #n = OCMn reading, three of the five rows (#1, #2, #3) point to the wrong OCM region.
  • Jesse's README states that the kernel's arm-cmn driver (the Linux driver for the mesh counters) places the HN-S filter fields one bit off this RTL's (the chip design source) [002 README.md:82].
  • If that offset reached the events used, per-node counts could go to the wrong node.
  • A wrong node id would not count the wrong node silently. The driver rejects it, and the line reads unavailable (Invalid argument) [RUN2-PLAN.md:339-341, 002 README.md:81].

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Per-region OCM rows under cmncount, one home-node counter per node idrun 2, run 3, boot F1cmncount (the harness's counter reader) opens hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all (requests received at a home node) once per node id for 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 [cmncount.c:11,141-142]. It wraps each per-region latency row (one region at a time, 256 KiB), each per-region OCM read row and a 4 KiB control chase per core [run_asimov.sh:126,134-136,154-156, 002 log.txt:10,19,28,37]. The region's own node must exceed every other node. The other nodes must sit near the control row's background count.
sysinfo collection of the kernel's CMN mesh maprun 2, control run, run 3, boot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E, boot F1From run 2 onward run_asimov.sh greps the kernel config for DEBUG_FS. It reads the arm_cmn_0 type, cpumask and event count (type=8 cpumask=0 events=280 in run 2). It mounts debugfs (the kernel's debug file system) and cats /sys/kernel/debug/arm-cmn/map* [run_asimov.sh:64-98, 002 sysinfo.txt:146-149,202,489-560]. The HN-S and RN-F cells (RN-F: a requester node) can then be compared with the RTL crosspoints and the address-map node ids.
gen_hierarchy.py asserts each node-id crosspoint has an HN-S cellboot E, boot F1, boot F2On every page build from run 4 boot E onward, gen_hierarchy.py (the page generator) decodes each node id to (x, y). It asserts the map text has an HN-S cell at that crosspoint. A disagreement between the decoding and the map would fail the build [gen_hierarchy.py:61-73, asimov-c1nano-perf.html mesh-grid section].

What the tests showed

  • Run 2: in each of the 20 per-region latency rows the region's own home node received 111,468 to 123,460 requests, against 9,042 to 10,576 requests at each other node [002 cmn-counts.csv ocm-region0..4-cpu2/4/6/8].
  • Run 2: the 5 OCM read rows put 71,550 to 76,496 requests at the own node against 9,485 to 9,909 at the others [002 cmn-counts.csv ocm-read-region0..4].
  • Run 2: the control rows gave 8,372 to 10,859 requests per node [002 cmn-counts.csv control-cpu2/4/6/8]. All 25 rows pass own node > every other node.
  • Run 3: core latency rows 47,972 to 57,204 requests at the own node against 8,566 to 10,516 at the others [004 cmn-counts.csv ocm-region0..4-cpu2/4/6/8].
  • Run 3: CME (the streaming unit attached to each core cluster) latency rows 47,463 to 51,153 against 8,877 to 9,290 [004 cmn-counts.csv cme-ocm-region0..4-cpu2].
  • Run 3: core read rows 71,687 to 76,534 requests against 9,368 to 9,912 [004 cmn-counts.csv ocm-read-region0..4]. CME read rows 108,075 to 109,528 against 9,431 to 10,386 [004 cmn-counts.csv cme-ocm-read-region0..4].
  • Run 3: controls 8,337 to 10,657 per node [004 cmn-counts.csv control-cpu2/4/6/8]. All 35 rows pass.
  • Boot F1: core latency rows 43,950 to 49,577 requests against 7,293 to 10,855. CME latency rows 45,087 to 48,065 against 7,915 to 8,877 [011 bootF1/cmn-counts.csv].
  • Boot F1: core read rows 66,434 to 69,389 against 8,378 to 8,861. Controls 7,348 to 10,118 per node. All rows pass [011 bootF1/cmn-counts.csv].
  • So nodes 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 are OCM0 to OCM4. The map's HN-S #0, #1, #2, #3, #4 are nodes 88, 216, 344, 160, 288.
  • Run 3's README confirms the kernel and cmncount were unchanged. The run 2 map reading therefore still held in run 3 [004 README.md:129].

Still open

Jesse's README states that the one-bit HN-S filter offset does not affect the _all events used. The primary files hold no RTL register map to re-check it [002 README.md:82, 004 README.md:129]. A comparison of the arm-cmn driver's HN-S filter field layout against this RTL's register map would settle it.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 2 (membench-jibin-002) sysinfo.txt, run date 2026-11-02 [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:3,78]. Before run 2 the node ids were an open item: RUN2-PLAN.md section 6 (lines 337 to 341) says 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 come from the address map and no perf_event_open with bynodeid had been tried on the image; HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md:33 asks the same question.

What looked wrong. The mesh map in sysinfo.txt prints crosspoint numbers (XP #0 to #35) and each node's logical id within its type, not node ids [results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/sysinfo.txt:489-560]. The five HN-S cells read #0 at crosspoint (1,3), #1 at (3,3), #2 at (5,3), #3 at (2,4), #4 at (4,4). The node ids decode to crosspoints as X = bits 8:6 and Y = bits 5:3 [gen_hierarchy.py:51]: 88 is (1,3), 160 is (2,4), 216 is (3,3), 288 is (4,4), 344 is (5,3). So HN-S #0 to #4 are nodes 88, 216, 344, 160 and 288, that is OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1 and OCM3 [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:80]. A reader who matches HN-S #n to OCMn places three of the five home nodes wrongly. Jesse's README also states that the kernel's arm-cmn driver places the HN-S filter fields one bit off this RTL's [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:82]; that statement is Jesse's and is not re-checked here. Before run 2, which home node held each OCM region was unverified on the emulator: the node ids came from the address map, and no perf_event_open with bynodeid had been tried [RUN2-PLAN.md:337-341].

Why it looked wrong. Every per-region latency claim and every mesh-distance claim depends on which home node owns each region (run 2 README, Mesh placement, line 31). A map that looks like a node-id list but is a logical-id list is a trap for any reader. The filter-field offset, if it reached the events used, could have mis-attributed per-node counts. A wrong node id would not count the wrong node silently: the driver rejects it, and the line reads unavailable (Invalid argument) [RUN2-PLAN.md:339-341; results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:81].

Tests added.

  • Per-region latency rows (one region at a time, 256 KiB) and per-region OCM read rows under cmncount, which opens hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all once per node id (bynodeid=1, nodeid=id) for nodes 88, 160, 216, 288, 344 [cmncount.c:11,141-142; run_asimov.sh:134-136,154-156]. Plus a 4 KiB control chase per core on 4 KiB pages (latency --no-thp --sizes 4K --loads 8K --reps 1) for the background count [run_asimov.sh:126; results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/log.txt:10,19,28,37].   • sysinfo collection: kernel config grep for DEBUG_FS, the arm_cmn_0 type, cpumask and event count, a debugfs mount, and cat of /sys/kernel/debug/arm-cmn/map* [run 2 (002) onward; run_asimov.sh lines 64 to 98 (config grep line 78, cpumask line 86, mesh map lines 94 to 96). Results: sysinfo.txt lines 146 to 149 (CONFIG_DEBUG_FS=y, CONFIG_DEBUG_FS_ALLOW_ALL=y), line 202 (type=8 cpumask=0 events=280), lines 489 to 560 (the map)]: the mesh map's HN-S and RN-F cells, to compare with the RTL crosspoints and the address-map node ids
  • Script check in the page generator: gen_hierarchy.py decodes each node id to (x, y) and asserts that the map text has an HN-S cell at that crosspoint [gen_hierarchy.py:61-73]; the core page says the crosspoints were checked against the map text [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section with the mesh grid] [every page build from run 4 boot E onward (asimov-c1nano-perf.html)]: that the node-id decoding and the map text agree on the five home-node crosspoints

What the tests showed. Run 2 (membench-jibin-002, cmn-counts.csv, hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all): in each of the 20 per-region latency rows (ocm-region0..4-cpu2/4/6/8) the region's own home node received 111,468 to 123,460 requests, against 9,042 to 10,576 at each other node. The five OCM read rows (ocm-read-region0..4) showed 71,550 to 76,496 against 9,485 to 9,909. The control rows (control-cpu2/4/6/8) put 8,372 to 10,859 requests on each node. All 25 rows pass own > every other node. Run 3 (membench-jibin-004, cmn-counts.csv): core per-region latency rows 47,972 to 57,204 against 8,566 to 10,516; CME per-region rows (cme-ocm-region0..4-cpu2) 47,463 to 51,153 against 8,877 to 9,290; core read rows 71,687 to 76,534 against 9,368 to 9,912; CME read rows 108,075 to 109,528 against 9,431 to 10,386; controls 8,337 to 10,657. All 35 rows pass. Run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011/results/bootF1/cmn-counts.csv): core per-region rows 43,950 to 49,577 against 7,293 to 10,855; CME per-region rows 45,087 to 48,065 against 7,915 to 8,877; core read rows 66,434 to 69,389 against 8,378 to 8,861; controls 7,348 to 10,118. All rows pass. So 88, 160, 216, 288 and 344 are OCM0 to OCM4, and the map's logical ids must be translated (HN-S #0, #1, #2, #3, #4 = nodes 88, 216, 344, 160, 288). Jesse's README states the one-bit filter offset does not affect the _all events used [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:82; results/membench-jibin-004/README.md:129]; that is his statement and the primary files here cannot re-check it. Highlighted: kernel-os, mesh, home-node, harness, OCM.

4.17 Home node 344 took 65 % more requests than the others on the old-firmware four-writer rowopen

On the old firmware, home node 344 took 2,105,333 write requests while the other four home nodes took 1,275,875 to 1,277,589 each.

What looked wrong

  • The control run (membench-jibin-003) used the old firmware, SCP 0.34.0 / TF-A 0.24.0, with results dated 2026-11-03.
  • It repeated the write row with one writer per cluster (CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8, 16 MiB each) under the mesh counters. [003 README.md lines 1-7 and 44]
  • Home node 344 (the home node of OCM4, at mesh crosspoint (5,3)) received 2,105,333 requests in that row.
  • The other four home nodes (88, 160, 216, 288) received 1,277,589, 1,276,133, 1,276,022 and 1,275,875 requests. [003 cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8, event hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all]
  • Node 344 took 828,928 requests more than the mean of the other four (1,276,405 requests). That is 1.65 times as many, or 65 % more. [recomputed with python3 -I from 003 cmn-counts.csv]
  • The downstream counters did not rise with it. Memory-controller requests (hns_mc_reqs_local_all) were 5,621,097 in the control run against 5,625,931 in run 2.
  • SLC misses (hns_cache_miss_all) were 5,604,936 against 5,608,583. [003 and 002 cmn-counts.csv, same label]
  • On run 2's new firmware (SCP 0.48.0 / TF-A 0.35.0) the same row spread evenly: 1,276,581 to 1,278,473 requests per node, a 0.15 % spread. [002 cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8]
  • Run 1 (membench-jibin-001) had no such row. So the control run is the first time this row ran on the old firmware.

Why it looked wrong

  • DRAM writes interleave over the five home nodes. Each node should see about one fifth of the requests.
  • Every other write row in both runs spreads within 0.19 % across the five nodes (largest: write-cpus2-8 in run 2). [recomputed from 002 and 003 cmn-counts.csv, labels write-cpus2-3, 2-4, 2-8, 2-3-4-5, 2-3-8-9]
  • One node took 65 % more requests with no extra memory-controller requests and no extra SLC misses. That pattern means the same writes arrived at home node 344 more than once.
  • Retried requests would do that. Jesse's README states this hypothesis and names the counter to test it. [003 README.md line 45]
  • This row hit the old firmware's shared write limit, which the README gives as about 87 to 89 GB/s. [003 README.md, Writes on the two firmware sets]
  • It measured 86.598 GB/s on the old firmware against 127.971 GB/s on the new (GB = 1e9 bytes, best of 2 reps, 4 writers x 16 MiB). [bandwidth-write-cpus2-4-6-8.csv, rep best, in 003 and 002]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
hns_pocq_retry_all count per home nodenot runCounts retried requests at each home node. A count near 828,928 at node 344 alone would confirm the excess was retries. A count near zero would reject that.
Same four-writer row re-run under request counters on new firmwarerun 3, boot F1Measures the per-node request spread on the new firmware. An even spread would tie the excess to the old firmware. An uneven one would not.

What the tests showed

  • The retry counter was never run. The retry hypothesis is untested. The proposal is written in three places. [003 README.md line 45, RUN2-PLAN.md line 514, gen_hierarchy.py line 555]
  • The cmn-counts.csv files of run 3 (membench-jibin-004), boot F1 (011) and boot F2 (012) hold only hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all, hns_mc_reqs_local_all and hns_cache_miss_all.
  • Boots A to E (005 to 010) count crosspoint flit events only. hns_pocq_retry_all appears only in the PMU (performance monitoring unit) event lists of sysinfo.txt.
  • The same row ran again on the new firmware in run 3 and boot F1.
  • Run 3 spread 1,276,209 to 1,278,369 requests per node (0.17 % spread). Boot F1 spread 1,269,640 to 1,272,137 requests per node (0.20 % spread). [004 cmn-counts.csv and 011 bootF1/cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8]
  • So the excess appeared only on the old firmware. No run after the control run used the old firmware.
  • The counter check passed for the control run. enabled_ns equals running_ns on every row, 11,545,392 to 11,551,734 ns for this label. [003 cmn-counts.csv]
  • The claim that Jesse's Slack message reported the same 829 thousand extra requests is not in the primary files (CSVs, READMEs, generated pages).
  • The four generated pages (asimov-c1nano-perf.html, asimov-cme-perf.html, asimov-c1nano-run4.html, asimov-cme-run4.html) do not mention this outlier.
  • Only asimov-memory-hierarchy.html (gen_hierarchy.py, section 9 and its open-items list) covers it.

Still open

The retry hypothesis is untested. Counting hns_pocq_retry_all per home node on the old firmware (SCP 0.34.0 / TF-A 0.24.0) for row write-cpus2-4-6-8 would settle whether the 828,928 extra requests at node 344 were retries.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. control run (membench-jibin-003, run 2's code on run 1's firmware SCP 0.34.0 / TF-A 0.24.0), results dated 2026-11-03 [results/membench-jibin-003/README.md, lines 1-7 and 44]

What looked wrong. The control run repeated run 2's writer-placement row with one writer per cluster (CPUs 2+4+6+8, 16 MiB per writer) under the mesh counters. Node 344 (OCM4's home node, crosspoint (5,3)) received 2,105,333 requests. Each of the other four home nodes received 1,275,875 to 1,277,589 requests. That is 828,928 extra requests over the mean of the other four (1,276,405), or 1.65 times as many [results/membench-jibin-003/results/19700101T000000Z/cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8, event hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all]. The memory-controller requests (hns_mc_reqs_local_all) read 5,621,097 against 5,625,931 on run 2's firmware. The SLC misses (hns_cache_miss_all) read 5,604,936 against 5,608,583 [cmn-counts.csv of membench-jibin-003 and membench-jibin-002, same label]. On run 2's firmware (SCP 0.48.0 / TF-A 0.35.0) the same row spread evenly: 1,276,581 to 1,278,473 requests per node, a 0.15 % spread [results/membench-jibin-002/results/19700101T000000Z/cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8]. Run 1 (membench-jibin-001) had no such row, so the control run is the first place this row ran on the old firmware.

Why it looked wrong. DRAM writes interleave over the five home nodes. Every other write row in both runs spreads within 0.19 % across the five nodes (recomputed from cmn-counts.csv, labels write-cpus2-3, 2-4, 2-8, 2-3-4-5, 2-3-8-9, both runs). One node taking 65 % more requests with no extra memory-controller requests and no extra SLC misses means the same writes arrived at the home node more than once. Retried requests would do that. Jesse's README states this as the hypothesis and names the counter that would test it [results/membench-jibin-003/README.md, line 45]. This row is one of the rows that hit the old firmware's shared write limit: 86.598 GB/s best on the old firmware against 127.971 GB/s on the new [bandwidth-write-cpus2-4-6-8.csv, rep best, in membench-jibin-003 and membench-jibin-002]. The README gives the old-firmware limit as about 87-89 GB/s [results/membench-jibin-003/README.md, Writes on the two firmware sets].

Tests added.

  • hns_pocq_retry_all per home node (proposed, not run) [Not run. Proposed in results/membench-jibin-003/README.md line 45, RUN2-PLAN.md line 514 and gen_hierarchy.py line 555 ("Test: count hns_pocq_retry_all per node in run 3"). The cmn-counts.csv files of run 3 (membench-jibin-004), boot F1 (011) and boot F2 (012) count only hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all, hns_mc_reqs_local_all and hns_cache_miss_all. Boots A to E (005 to 010) count crosspoint flit events only. hns_pocq_retry_all appears only in the PMU event lists of sysinfo.txt.]: whether the 828,928 extra requests at node 344 are retries of the same writes

What the tests showed. The retry counter was never run, so the hypothesis is untested. The same four-writer row ran again on the new firmware under the request counters in run 3 and boot F1. It spread evenly both times: 1,276,209 to 1,278,369 requests per node (0.17 % spread) in run 3 [results/membench-jibin-004/results/19700101T000000Z/cmn-counts.csv, label write-cpus2-4-6-8] and 1,269,640 to 1,272,137 (0.20 % spread) in boot F1 [results/membench-jibin-011/results/bootF1/cmn-counts.csv, same label]. So the excess appeared only on the old firmware. No run after the control run used the old firmware. The claim that Jesse's own Slack message reported the same 829 thousand extra requests is not in the primary files (CSVs, READMEs, generated pages). The four generated pages (asimov-c1nano-perf.html, asimov-cme-perf.html, asimov-c1nano-run4.html, asimov-cme-run4.html) do not mention this outlier. It is covered in gen_hierarchy.py (asimov-memory-hierarchy.html, section 9 and its open-items list).

4.18 OCM cells at the same mesh distance differ by up to 18 % and do not repeat run to run (H5)explained

OCM cells at one mesh distance spread 14 to 18 % in latency. A cell's rank did not repeat across runs 2 and 3.

What looked wrong

  • The OCM latency test has 20 cells: CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8, each loading from OCM0 to OCM4.
  • Each cell has an assumed mesh distance of 1, 3 or 5 crosspoints (|dx| + |dy| between the DSU's crosspoint and the home node's crosspoint).
  • Run 3 (004, 2026-11-03) sparse chain bests at 1 crosspoint: 20.14 to 22.97 ns per load (8 cells, 14.0 % spread).
  • At 3 crosspoints: 22.39 to 26.52 ns (10 cells, 18.4 % spread). At 5: 27.00 to 28.45 ns (2 cells).
  • Spread is max minus min over min. [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 004, best rows and asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.2, third sub-table]
  • Run 2 (002, 2026-11-02) dense chain bests at 1 crosspoint: 18.46 to 21.36 ns per load (15.7 % spread).
  • At 3 crosspoints: 20.49 to 23.44 ns (14.4 % spread). At 5: 24.48 to 24.68 ns. [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 002]
  • The run 2 README said the per-region rows 'would fit CPUs 6 and 8 either way round'. [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:64]
  • The 20 cells correlate 0.81 between runs 2 and 3, distance effect included.
  • After removing each run's mean at each distance, the residuals correlate only 0.22.
  • A fit on the step count alone (ns = a + b (|dx| + |dy|)) leaves 0.88 ns rms (run 2) and 1.06 ns rms (run 3), R² 0.75 and 0.76. [codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md:913 and follow-up-run-plan.md:28 and asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.7]
  • On boot A (005) the same ten-cell dense chain (CPUs 2 and 8) ran once without counters (G2) and once under the crosspoint counters (G6).
  • The two differed by -0.63 to +3.44 ns per load (largest: CPU 8 to OCM1, 23.68 against 27.11 ns). [latency-ocm-region<r>-dense-cpu<c>.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 005 and asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6]
  • The G6 data-flit sums per cell also moved 1.062 to 1.346 times between boots C and D (up to 35 %). [results/membench-jibin-007/README.md:85,109]

Why it looked wrong

  • Expectation: a load's latency is a base cost plus a fixed cost per crosspoint step. Under that model, cells at the same distance should agree within repeat noise.
  • They spread 14 to 18 % instead (runs 2 and 3).
  • Expectation: a cell's rank inside its distance group should repeat from run to run. The within-distance residuals correlated only 0.22 between run 2 and run 3. So neither expectation held.
  • Hypothesis H5 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 5): an X step costs more than a Y step.
  • The first X/Y fits gave X 1.33 ns and Y 0.76 ns per step on run 2's dense bests. On run 3's sparse bests they gave X 1.66 ns and Y 0.92 ns.
  • R² was 0.79 and 0.80, with 0.80 and 0.96 ns rms left. [follow-up-run-plan.md:28 and asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.7]
  • The X and Y step counts were assumptions taken from mesh coordinates. No counter had measured the route. [follow-up-run-plan.md:122]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
G6 route rows: 20 cells under mesh crosspoint countersboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EEach cell's dense chain runs again under 8 data-flit counters (mxp_{e,w,n,s}_dat_txflit_valid, no multiplexing) on the DSU's crosspoint and on the home node's crosspoint. This gives the outgoing data-flit direction at each end over the whole command (which way the response leaves each crosspoint). It also gives a best-of-2 latency per cell. [latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv and cmn-counts.csv labels route-ocm<r>-cpu<c> of 005 to 010 and follow-up-run-plan.md:82,122]
Route rows with the data prefetchers offboot B, boot DThe same 20-cell fit to the assumed step counts without prefetch fills. The L2 prefetcher made 0.35 refills per load on boot A's route rows, and boot D also maps OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations. A small rms would mean the within-distance spread came from the prefetchers. [results/membench-jibin-006/README.md:49]
Same-cell repeat inside one boot: G2 dense rows beside G6 route rowsboot AHow much one cell's best moves between two processes of one boot. This compares the G2 row without counters against the G6 row of the same command under counters (CPUs 2 and 8, boot A onward). A difference above the repeat noise means a cell's value is not stable inside one boot. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6, last two columns]

What the tests showed

  • Boot A (005): the direction with the most outgoing data flits is the X-first direction at the DSU's crosspoint in 20 of 20 cells, and at the node's crosspoint in 20 of 20 cells. [cmn-counts.csv of 005]
  • The fit over the 20 route cells is 18.70 ns + 1.52 ns per X step + 0.88 ns per Y step, 0.90 ns rms. The X minus Y difference (0.64 ns) is below the residual.
  • H5 was 'not supported' on boot A. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html tables 3.6 and 3.7, sections 8 and 10]
  • Boot B (006, prefetchers off): 20.75 ns + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step, 0.09 ns rms. [latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 006]
  • The cells now order by distance: 21.70 to 22.89 ns at 1 crosspoint, 24.55 to 26.88 ns at 3, 28.54 to 29.80 ns at 5.
  • H5 is 'supported' on boot B. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.5 and asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.2, fourth sub-table]
  • Boot D (008, prefetchers off): 20.63 ns + 2.00 ns per X step + 0.98 ns per Y step, 0.13 ns rms. This repeats boot B. [latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 008 and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.2]
  • Boot C (007, prefetchers on): 18.43 ns + 1.36 ns per X step + 0.66 ns per Y step, 0.80 ns rms. This matches boot A.
  • So most of the within-distance spread of runs 2, 3 and boot A came from the prefetchers. [latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 007 and asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 6 'Distance']
  • Boot E (010, L3 on): 15.75 ns + 1.43 ns per X step - 0.34 ns per Y step, 2.05 ns rms. This fit is not usable. Part of each route row's loads are L3 hits. [latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 010 and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 14.4]
  • Limits: the X and Y costs rest on assumed step counts. |dy| is 0 or 1 in every cell, so the Y coefficient rests on 10 cells.
  • The G6 counts span the whole command (chain build, flushes, unmap). With cont=1 each unmap adds four broadcast TLB invalidates per region.
  • So the counts do not isolate one variable. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 8 and results/membench-jibin-007/README.md:85,174]

Still open

The request channel (mxp_<dir>_req_txflit_valid) was never counted. So the request route and the response's last link stay assumptions. Route rows with the request-channel counters on both crosspoints, with the prefetchers off, would settle the step counts. [codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md:1057 and follow-up-run-plan.md:122]

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. Run 2 (002, 2026-11-02): Jesse's README noted that the per-region rows place CPU 4's port but 'would fit CPUs 6 and 8 either way round' [results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:64]. The per-cell spread at one crosspoint count was raised on 2026-11-03 in follow-up-run-plan.md section 1 (written 2026-11-03) from the run 2 dense and run 3 (004, 2026-11-03) sparse per-region bests [follow-up-run-plan.md:5,28].

What looked wrong. Each of the 20 CPU-to-region cells (CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8 by OCM0 to OCM4) has an assumed mesh distance of 1, 3 or 5 crosspoints (|dx| + |dy| between the DSU's and the home node's crosspoints). Cells at the same distance spread 14 to 18 % in both runs. Run 3 sparse bests: 20.14 to 22.97 ns at 1 crosspoint (8 cells, 14.0 % spread), 22.39 to 26.52 ns at 3 (10 cells, 18.4 %), 27.00 to 28.45 ns at 5 (2 cells) [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 004, best rows; asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.2, third sub-table]. Run 2 dense bests: 18.46 to 21.36 ns at 1 (15.7 %), 20.49 to 23.44 ns at 3 (14.4 %), 24.48 to 24.68 ns at 5 [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 002; results/membench-jibin-002/README.md:64]. The 20 cells correlate 0.81 between runs 2 and 3, but that includes the distance effect. After removing each run's mean at each distance, the remaining cell differences correlate only 0.22 [codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md:913; recomputed 0.812 and 0.217]. A fit on the step count alone (ns = a + b (|dx| + |dy|)) explains 75 to 76 % of the variance (R² 0.75 run 2, 0.76 run 3) and leaves 0.88 ns rms (run 2) and 1.06 ns rms (run 3); splitting X and Y steps leaves 0.80 and 0.96 ns rms [follow-up-run-plan.md:28; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.7; recomputed]. On boot A (005) the same dense chain of ten cells, run once without counters (G2) and once under the crosspoint counters (G6), differed by -0.63 to +3.44 ns (CPU 8 to OCM1: 23.68 against 27.11 ns) [latency-ocm-region<r>-dense-cpu<c>.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv of 005; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6]. The G6 mesh data-flit sums per cell also moved between boots: 1.062 to 1.346 times between boots C and D (up to 35 %), 0.940 to 1.101 C against A, 0.961 to 1.084 D against B [results/membench-jibin-007/README.md:85,109; results/membench-jibin-008/README.md:10; cmn-counts.csv of 005 to 008, recomputed], and 0.360 to 0.731 E against A [results/membench-jibin-010/README.md:155].

Why it looked wrong. If a load's latency were a base plus a fixed cost per crosspoint step, cells at the same distance would agree within repeat noise. A cell's rank among its distance group would also repeat from run to run. Neither held. Hypothesis H5 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 5): an X step costs more than a Y step. The first fits gave X 1.33 and Y 0.76 ns per step on run 2's dense bests, and X 1.66 and Y 0.92 ns on run 3's sparse bests (R² 0.79 and 0.80) [follow-up-run-plan.md:28; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.7]. But the X and Y step counts are coordinate assumptions: no counter had measured the route [follow-up-run-plan.md:122].

Tests added.

  • G6 route rows: the dense chase of each of the 20 cells run again under the mesh crosspoint counters mxp_{e,w,n,s}_dat_txflit_valid on the DSU's crosspoint and on the home node's crosspoint (8 counters, no multiplexing) [run 4 boot A (005), repeated on boots B (006), C (007), D (008) and E (010)]: the outgoing data-flit direction at each end over the whole command, plus a best-of-2 latency per cell [latency-ocm-region<r>-route-cpu<c>.csv, cmn-counts.csv labels route-ocm<r>-cpu<c>]. It does not count the request channel (mxp_<dir>_req_txflit_valid), so the request route and the response's last link stay unmeasured and the step counts stay assumptions [follow-up-run-plan.md:82,122; codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md:1057]
  • Route rows with the data prefetchers off [run 4 boot B (006, prefetchers off) and boot D (008, prefetchers off, OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations)]: the same 20-cell fit to the assumed step counts without prefetch fills; the L2 prefetcher made 0.35 refills per load on boot A's route rows [results/membench-jibin-006/README.md:49]
  • Same-cell repeat inside one boot: G2 dense rows (CPUs 2 and 8, no counters) beside the G6 route rows (the same command under counters) [run 4 boot A (005) onward]: how much one cell's best moves between two processes of one boot [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6, last two columns]

What the tests showed. Boot A (005): both ends send X-first in 20 of 20 cells (the direction with the most outgoing data flits at the DSU's crosspoint is the X-first direction toward the node in 20 of 20, and at the node's crosspoint in 20 of 20) [cmn-counts.csv of 005; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.6 and section 8; recomputed]. The fit over the 20 route cells is 18.70 + 1.52 ns per X step + 0.88 ns per Y step, 0.90 ns rms; the difference (+0.64 ns) does not exceed the residual, so H5 was 'not supported' on A [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.7 and section 10; recomputed]. Boot B (006, prefetchers off): 20.75 + 1.99 ns per X step + 0.95 ns per Y step, 0.09 ns rms; the cells now order by distance (21.70 to 22.89 ns at 1 crosspoint, 24.55 to 26.88 at 3, 28.54 to 29.80 at 5) and H5 is 'supported' [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.5; asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.2 fourth sub-table; recomputed]. Boot D (008, prefetchers off): 20.63 + 2.00 x + 0.98 y, 0.13 ns rms, repeats B [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.2; recomputed]. Boot C (007, prefetchers on): 18.43 + 1.36 x + 0.66 y, 0.80 ns rms, like A [recomputed; asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 6 'Distance']. So most of the within-distance spread of runs 2, 3 and boot A was the prefetchers' [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 6]. Boot E (010, L3 on): 15.75 + 1.43 x - 0.34 y, 2.05 ns rms, not usable, since part of each route row's loads are L3 hits [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 14.4; recomputed]. The X and Y costs rest on assumed step counts (|dy| is 0 or 1 in every cell, so the Y coefficient rests on 10 cells), and the G6 counts span the whole command (chain build, flushes, unmap; with cont=1 each unmap adds four broadcast TLB invalidates per region), so they do not isolate one variable [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 8; results/membench-jibin-007/README.md:85,174].

Highlighted: mesh, home-node, OCM, L2-prefetcher, L1-prefetcher.

4.19 Sparse OCM chains read 2 to 4 ns above dense; vary chains faster than sparse (H2, H3, H4)partly explained

Sparse OCM chains read 2 to 4 ns per load above dense chains. A hashed-offset chain was faster than the sparse one.

What looked wrong

  • A sparse chain loads one cache line per 4 KiB page: 64 loads per pass over a 256 KiB region of OCM (on-chip memory, mapped into a process through the /dev/ocm device file).
  • A dense chain loads every line: 4,096 loads per pass. [latency-ocm-region0-cpu2.csv of 004, header lines=64 sparse=1]
  • On run 3 (result set membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03) the sparse rows read 2.31 ns per load above run 2's dense rows (membench-jibin-002), mean of 20 cells.
  • The range was -0.47 to +4.55 ns per load. Sparse was higher in 18 of 20 cells. [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 004 and 002, README 004 lines 3 and 9]
  • On run 4 boot A (membench-jibin-005) the sparse rows read 3.73 to 4.33 ns per load above dense on CPU 2.
  • On CPU 8 they read 1.79 to 3.56 ns per load above dense. [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv and -dense-cpu<c>.csv of 005, run-4 page section 6]
  • On boot A the vary chain (a sparse chain with a hashed line offset per page, 64 loads per pass) was faster than the sparse chain in 10 of 10 cells on CPUs 2 and 8.
  • By the median of the passes it was faster by 1.72 to 6.75 ns per load (mean 3.49 ns). By best pass it was faster by 1.86 to 7.14 ns per load.
  • It drew prefetches at a similar rate: 1.15 to 1.73 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2, against 1.81 to 2.22 for the sparse chain. [timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-vary-cpu<c>.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 005, run-4 page section 6 and table 3.4]
  • The dense rows' L1 TLB refills (the L1 data TLB is the core's first address-translation cache, and a refill is one miss) differed by a factor of 27 between regions on boot A.
  • They ranged from 0.005 to 0.136 refills per load, or 21 to 559 refills per pass of 4,096 loads. [l1d_tlb_refill_per_load of latency-ocm-region<r>-dense-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005, run-4 page table 3.5]

Why it looked wrong

  • Both chain shapes read the same region over the same path through the mesh (the on-chip interconnect). So a difference of 2 to 4 ns per load (boot A) needs a cause inside the core.
  • Jibin expected a much larger gap. A dense chain should hit the caches on most loads. A sparse chain should miss on every load.
  • So dense should have fewer refills than sparse. The gap should then be far above 2 to 4 ns per load.
  • This expectation is in the session transcript only, not in a result file.
  • Three hypotheses were written down. H2: the prefetcher reacts to the fixed line offset of the sparse chain.
  • H3: each sparse load takes one L1 TLB miss. Each load is on a new page.
  • H4: the 4 KiB page size is what separates the two shapes. [run-4 page section 10]
  • The factor-27 TLB difference between the dense regions came from mapping alignment. The kernel places each /dev/ocm mapping per process.
  • Each command on each boot is its own placement draw. On boot A the user-to-physical offset (va - pa) was a multiple of 64 KiB on 5 of 110 mappings.
  • The one dense row with a 64 KiB-aligned mapping (OCM4) refilled the L1 TLB 21 times per pass.
  • The four dense rows with 4 KiB-only mappings refilled 42 to 559 times per pass. [README 005 line 27, README 007 lines 58 and 124, run-4 page table 3.5]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Vary chains (hashed line offset per page) under the prefetch countersboot AMeasures prefetch refills per load (event 0x81BD) and time for the vary chain against the sparse chain on CPUs 2 and 8. A lower prefetch rate on the vary chain would support H2 (the prefetcher reacts to the fixed line offset). [latency-ocm-region<r>-vary-cpu<c>.csv of 005]
TLB counter set on 15 OCM rows and a DRAM stimulusboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EMeasures L1 data TLB refills (event 0x05), L2 data TLB refills (0x2D) and table walks (0x34) per load on CPU 2 for each chain shape (dense, sparse, vary) in 5 regions plus a 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB DRAM pages. About one L1 TLB refill per sparse load with matching walks would support H3. [latency-ocm-region<r>-{dense-,vary-,}tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005 to 010]
Boot B: data prefetchers off through a TF-A hookboot BMeasures the sparse-minus-dense gap, the vary advantage and the walk count on 4 KiB pages with the prefetchers off (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1, TF-A being the Arm boot firmware). A vary advantage that disappears, or a walk count that falls to zero, shows the prefetchers caused it on boot A. [membench-jibin-006]
Boots C and D: 64 KiB OCM translations, prefetchers on and offboot C, boot DMeasures L1 TLB refills per pass and the sparse-minus-dense gap with /dev/ocm loaded with cont=1. With cont=1 each mapping sits at a user address congruent to its physical address modulo 64 KiB. Its four 64 KiB blocks carry the contiguous bit. So the TLB holds 64 KiB translations. A gap that closes would support H4. D against B shows the hint alone. C against D shows the prefetchers with the hint on both. [membench-jibin-007 commit b79dffa, 008 commit ed6056a, README 007 line 33, README 008 line 38]
Walk rows on the sparse chains and the DRAM stimulusboot C, boot D, boot EMeasures table walks (0x34), block walks (0x8188) and page walks (0x818A) per load on the five sparse chains and the 32 MiB stimulus. A count of zero with the prefetchers off (boot D) shows the walks on the sparse chains belong to the prefetchers' requests. [latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv of 007, 008, 010]

What the tests showed

  • H2 not supported. On boot A the vary chain drew prefetches like the sparse chain: 1.15 to 1.73 against 1.81 to 2.22 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2.
  • On boot B (prefetchers off) vary minus sparse by median was -0.91 to +0.09 ns per load. Vary was faster in only 6 of 10 cells.
  • On boot A it was -6.75 to -1.72 ns per load, faster in 10 of 10 cells. So boot A's vary advantage came from the prefetcher.
  • Why the prefetcher's fills helped the vary chain more is a hypothesis without a test. [run-4 page table 3.4 and sections 6 and 11.5, timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-{vary-,}cpu<c>.csv of 005 and 006]
  • H3 not supported. On boot A a sparse load took 0.672 to 0.723 L1 TLB refills, 0.000 L2 TLB refills and 0.266 to 1.243 table walks (means over the timed passes).
  • With the prefetchers off, the walks read 0.000 per load on every sparse row on boot B, and 0.000 in all 35 passes on boot D.
  • With the prefetchers on, they read 0.27 to 1.24 walks per sparse load on boot A, 0.41 to 0.75 on boot C and 0.56 to 1.62 on boot E.
  • So the walks were translations for the prefetchers' requests, not for the chain's loads. [dtlb_walk_per_load of latency-ocm-region<r>-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005 to 010, run-4 page table 3.5 and section 13.3]
  • H4 supported in part. With 64 KiB translations (boots C and D) the L1 TLB refills per pass fell to 11 to 15 on every chain.
  • On boot A they were 21 to 559 per pass, and on boot B 25 to 599 per pass. [run-4 page table 13.1, TLB-set files of 005 to 008]
  • The sparse-minus-dense gap on CPU 2 (mean of the five regions, best passes) went from 4.01 ns per load (boot A) to 2.76 ns (boot C) with the prefetchers on.
  • With the prefetchers off it went from 1.77 ns per load (boot B) to 1.24 ns (boot D). It narrowed in 4 of 5 regions on each pair.
  • On boot E (L3 on, 4 KiB pages) the gap was 2.77 ns per load. The narrowing was on CPU 2 only.
  • CPU 8's gap widened from 2.468 ns per load (boot A) to 2.749 ns (boot C) by best pass. [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu2.csv and -dense-cpu2.csv of 005 to 008 and 010, run-4 page section 13.2, asimov-c1nano-perf.html OCM section, README 007 line 56]
  • Over the 69 core OCM rows, the hint alone (boot D against B) gave a geometric mean ratio of 0.985 (62 of 69 rows faster, about 1.5 %).
  • The hint with the prefetchers on (C against A) gave 0.977 (43 of 69 rows faster). The prefetchers with the hint on both (C against D) gave 0.861 (66 of 69 rows faster on C).
  • A ratio below 1 means faster on the first boot. So the prefetchers made these rows about 14 % faster, even though they widened the sparse-dense gap.
  • The hint changed them by about 1.5 %. [best rows of the 69 core OCM files of 005 to 008, run-4 page table 13.2]
  • Jesse's reading: the numbers at this spread do not decide H4. The same chain's best pass differed by up to 23.6 % between two processes of one boot (boot C), more than the mean changes.
  • No sparse or vary TLB-set row had a 64 KiB-aligned mapping on boot A or B.
  • So A against C and B against D cannot split the fall in TLB refills, or the latency change, between the contiguous bit and the 64 KiB placement. [README 007 lines 11 and 58, README 008 line 60]

Still open

On boot D (64 KiB translations, prefetchers off) the gap is still 0.80 to 1.75 ns per load per region (mean 1.24 ns). So the page size is part of what separates the two shapes, not all of it [run-4 page section 13.2]. Still unmeasured: a boot where the sparse and vary TLB-set rows get 64 KiB-aligned mappings, to split the fall in TLB refills between the contiguous bit and the placement. Also unmeasured: why the prefetcher's fills helped the vary chain more than the sparse one.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 (membench-jibin-004), run date 2026-11-03 UTC [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 3]; Jibin's question 2026-11-03 15:52 is from the session transcript only (not in the primary files)

What looked wrong. A sparse chain touches one line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads per pass of a 256 KiB region [latency-ocm-region0-cpu2.csv of 004, header: lines=64 sparse=1]. A dense chain touches every line, 4,096 loads per pass. On run 3 the sparse rows read 2.31 ns per load above run 2's dense rows on average over the 20 CPU-by-region cells (range -0.47 to +4.55 ns, higher in 18 of 20 cells) [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 004 and 002; README 004 line 9 says 2.3 ns]. On run 4 boot A the sparse rows read 3.73 to 4.33 ns above dense on CPU 2 and 1.79 to 3.56 ns on CPU 8 [best rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv and -dense-cpu<c>.csv of 005; asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 6]. Jibin expected the opposite (transcript only, not in the primary files): dense should hit more, sparse should miss every load, so the gap should be much larger, and dense should have fewer refills than sparse. On boot A the vary chain (a hashed line offset per page) was faster than the sparse chain in 10 of 10 cells, by 1.72 to 6.75 ns by the median of the passes (mean 3.49 ns; by best pass 1.86 to 7.14 ns) [timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-vary-cpu<c>.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu<c>.csv of 005, CPUs 2 and 8; run-4 page section 6], although it drew prefetches at a similar rate (1.15 to 1.73 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2 against the sparse chain's 1.81 to 2.22) [run-4 page table 3.4]. The dense rows' L1 TLB refills differed by a factor of 27 between regions: 0.005 to 0.136 per load, 21 to 559 per pass of 4,096 loads [l1d_tlb_refill_per_load of latency-ocm-region<r>-dense-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005; run-4 page table 3.5].

Why it looked wrong. Both chain shapes read the same region over the same mesh path, so a 2 to 4 ns difference per load needs a cause inside the core. Three hypotheses were written down [run-4 page section 10]: H2, the fixed line offset of the sparse chain is what the prefetcher reacts to; H3, each sparse load takes one L1 TLB miss (one page per load); H4, the 4 KiB page size is what separates the two shapes. The TLB difference between the dense regions came from the per-command mapping alignment: the kernel places each /dev/ocm mapping per process, and on boot A the user-to-physical offset (va - pa) was a multiple of 64 KiB on only 5 of the 110 mappings, of 32 KiB on 8 and of 16 KiB on 23 [README 005 line 27; run-4 page table 3.5 second table: 5 at 64 KiB, 3 at 32 KiB only, 15 at 16 KiB only, 87 at 4 KiB only]. Each command on each boot is its own placement draw [README 007 line 124]. The one dense row whose mapping was 64 KiB aligned (OCM4) refilled the L1 TLB 21 times per pass; the four with 4 KiB-only mappings refilled 42 to 559 times [README 007 line 58; run-4 page table 3.5].

Tests added.

  • --sparse-vary chains (a hashed line offset per page, 64 loads per pass), CPUs 2 and 8, under the prefetch counter set [run 4 boot A (membench-jibin-005), files latency-ocm-region<r>-vary-cpu<c>.csv]: H2: whether the prefetcher reacts to the fixed line offset (prefetch refills 0x81BD per load, vary against sparse) and whether the vary chain's time differs
  • TLB counter set (0x05 L1 data TLB refills, 0x2D L2 data TLB refills, 0x34 table walks) on CPU 2's 15 OCM rows (5 regions by dense, sparse, vary) and on a 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB DRAM pages as the stimulus [run 4 boot A (005), files latency-ocm-region<r>-{dense-,vary-,}tlb-cpu2.csv, latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv; repeated on boots B to E]: H3: TLB refills and walks per load on each chain shape
  • Boot B: data prefetchers off through a TF-A hook (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1), 4 KiB pages [run 4 boot B (006)]: the sparse-minus-dense gap and the vary advantage with no prefetch; whether the walks of boot A were the prefetchers'
  • Boots C and D: /dev/ocm loaded with cont=1, so each OCM mapping sits at a user address congruent to its physical address modulo 64 KiB and its four 64 KiB blocks carry the contiguous bit (64 KiB translations); prefetchers on (C) and off (D) [run 4 boots C (007, commit b79dffa) and D (008, commit ed6056a)]: H4: L1 TLB refills per pass and the sparse-minus-dense gap with larger translations; D against B is the hint alone, C against D the prefetchers with the hint on both [README 007 line 33, README 008 line 38]
  • Walk rows (0x34, 0x8188 block walks, 0x818A page walks) on the five sparse chains and the 32 MiB stimulus [run 4 boots C (007), D (008), E (010), files latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv]: what kind of walk 0x34 counts on the sparse chains with the prefetchers on

What the tests showed. H2 not supported. The vary chain draws prefetches like the sparse chain (1.15 to 1.73 against 1.81 to 2.22 prefetch refills per load on CPU 2) [run-4 page table 3.4 and section 6]. On boot B, prefetchers off, the vary chain is faster than the sparse one by median in only 6 of 10 cells, by -0.91 to +0.09 ns (boot A: 10 of 10, -6.75 to -1.72 ns) [timed rows of latency-ocm-region<r>-{vary-,}cpu<c>.csv of 006 and 005; run-4 page section 11.5]. So boot A's vary advantage came from the prefetcher. Why its fills helped the vary chain more is a hypothesis without a test. H3 not supported. A sparse load on boot A takes 0.672 to 0.723 L1 TLB refills, 0.000 L2 TLB refills and 0.266 to 1.243 table walks (means over the timed passes) [latency-ocm-region<r>-tlb-cpu2.csv of 005; run-4 page table 3.5]. On boot B the walks read 0.000 per load on every sparse row, and on boot D 0.000 in all 35 passes, while boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) count 0.27 to 1.24, 0.41 to 0.75 and 0.56 to 1.62 walks per sparse load [dtlb_walk_per_load of the TLB-set files of 005 to 010; run-4 page section 13.3]. So the walks were translations for the prefetchers' requests, not the chain's. H4 supported in part. With the 64 KiB translations the L1 TLB refills per pass fell to 11 to 15 on every chain (boots C and D), from 21 to 559 on boot A and 25 to 599 on boot B [run-4 page table 13.1; recomputed from the TLB-set files of 005 to 008]. The sparse-minus-dense gap on CPU 2 (mean of the five regions, best passes) went from 4.01 ns (A) to 2.76 ns (C) with the prefetchers on, and from 1.77 ns (B) to 1.24 ns (D) with them off; it narrowed in 4 of 5 regions on each pair [latency-ocm-region<r>-cpu2.csv and -dense-cpu2.csv of 005 to 008; run-4 page section 13.2]. On boot E (L3 on, 4 KiB pages) the gap is 2.77 ns [same files of 010; asimov-c1nano-perf.html, OCM section]. The narrowing is on CPU 2 only: CPU 8's gap widened from 2.468 ns (A) to 2.749 ns (C) by best pass [README 007 line 56]. Over the 69 core OCM rows the hint alone (D against B) gives a geometric mean ratio of 0.985 (62 of 69 rows faster, about 1.5 %), the hint with the prefetchers on (C against A) 0.977 (43 of 69), and the prefetchers with the hint on both (C against D) 0.861 (66 of 69 rows faster on C) [best rows of the 69 core OCM files of 005 to 008; run-4 page table 13.2]. So the prefetchers make these rows about 14 % faster even though they widen the sparse-dense gap, and the hint changes them by about 1.5 %. Jesse's reading: the numbers at this spread do not decide H4 [README 007 line 11]. No sparse or vary TLB-set row had a 64 KiB-aligned mapping on A or B, so A against C and B against D cannot split the fall in TLB refills, or the latency change, between the contiguous bit and the 64 KiB placement [README 007 line 58; README 008 line 60]. The same chain's best differs by up to 23.6 % between two processes of one boot, more than the mean changes [README 007 line 11]. What remains open: on boot D (hint, prefetchers off) the gap is still 0.80 to 1.75 ns per region (mean 1.24 ns), so the page size is part of what separates the two shapes, not all of it [run-4 page section 13.2].

4.20 OCM rows with the prefetchers on are noisy: the passes of one row spread up to 68 %, and the same chain differs up to 23.6 % between two processes of one bootpartly explained

With the prefetchers on, one OCM row's passes spread up to 68 % and two processes of one boot differ up to 23.6 %.

What looked wrong

  • Run 2 (membench-jibin-002, 2026-11-02): the two passes of one per-region OCM row differ by up to 3.444 ns per load. The widest is region 3 from CPU 4: 23.938 and 20.494 ns per load. [002 latency-ocm-region3-cpu4.csv]
  • In 19 of the 20 rows the faster pass counted fewer L3 read refills per load. [002 README line 66]
  • Run 3 (004, 2026-11-03): the 7 passes of one sparse row spread 5.16 to 14.55 ns per load across the 20 rows (22 % to 68 %). [004 README line 110]
  • The widest is CPU 2 to OCM1: 21.359 to 35.906 ns per load, 68.1 %. [004 latency-ocm-region1-cpu2.csv]
  • Boot A (005, 2026-11-04) ran on run 3's platform. Both controls repeated run 3 within 0.5 % (4 KiB chase 2.002 ns per load, CME round trip 21.004 to 21.005 ns). [005 README line 8]
  • Yet 12 of the 70 best rows the two share moved by more than 3 % (8 core OCM rows, 3 CME rows, 1 DRAM 4 MiB chain at +5.55 %). [005 README line 8, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 3.9]
  • The largest is CPU 2 to OCM3: 26.391 ns per load on boot A against 23.719 ns on run 3, +11.27 %. [latency-ocm-region3-cpu2.csv of 005 and 004]
  • One CME row moved too: the 32 KiB repeated chain read 42.156 ns per load on boot A against 39.721 ns on run 3, +6.13 %. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005 and 004, asimov-cme-run4.html section 3.3]
  • Boot C (007) against boot A: two vary chains with the TLB set moved in opposite directions. Region 0 read 13.734 ns per load on C against 19.906 ns on A (0.690 times, -31 %). [latency-ocm-region0-vary-tlb-cpu2.csv of 007 and 005]
  • Region 2 read 21.531 ns per load on C against 17.047 ns on A (1.263 times, +26 %). [latency-ocm-region2-vary-tlb-cpu2.csv of 007 and 005]
  • Each time the faster boot's best pass counted fewer L3 read refills per load (region 0: 0.3125 on C against 0.6719 on A, region 2: 0.7969 on C against 0.4688 on A). [007 README line 53]
  • With the prefetchers on, the same chain's best differs between two processes of one boot by up to 23.6 % on the vary chains of boot C, and 22.9 % on boot A. [007 README line 52]
  • With the prefetchers off on boot D (008), three processes of region 2's sparse chain differ by at most 3.0 % (24.328, 23.703 and 23.609 ns per load). [008 README line 38]

Why it looked wrong

  • Expectation: a chain walked again over the same lines should take the same time pass after pass. The dense rows meet this.
  • The dense all-five control on run 3 repeats run 2 within 0.17 ns per load. [004 README line 110]
  • The per-region rows do not meet it. On run 3 the slow passes carry more L2 refills (correlation +0.84 within rows) and fewer L3 read refills (correlation -0.31). [004 README line 111]
  • So the spread follows what the prefetchers fetch, not the chain's own loads. [004 README line 111]
  • Each benchmark command is a new process with its own physical page placement. So a ratio taken from one row between two boots says little by itself. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, page placement section]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Median beside best on every OCM cell, pass time against refill countsboot APrints the median of the passes beside the best on every OCM cell. Correlates each pass's time with the prefetch refills (event 0x81BD), the L2 refills (event 0x17) and the L3 read refills (event 0xA2). A high correlation would mean the pass time follows how many lines the prefetcher fetched. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 3.3 and the pass-to-pass paragraph]
Prefetchers off as the quiet comparison, groups compared by geometric meanboot B, boot DMeasures the pass spread and the process-to-process spread with the data prefetchers off. Compares groups of rows by geometric mean instead of single rows. A much smaller spread would mean the prefetchers cause most of it.
Every CME OCM pass timed inside its own streaming spanboot F1, boot F2Times each CME OCM pass inside its own streaming span (the ns_per_load_span column). A spread inside the span would be the prefetcher's. A spread outside it would be call cost or a wake-up.

What the tests showed

  • Boot A: a pass's time correlates only weakly with its counts: +0.19 with the prefetch refills (0x81BD), +0.33 with the L2 refills and +0.30 with the L3 read refills. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html pass-to-pass paragraph]
  • Run 3's sparse rows had shown +0.84 with the L2 refills. So the count alone does not explain the spread. [004 README line 111]
  • Largest spread of one row's passes, by boot. Boot A: 12.218 ns per load (region 4 from CPU 8, 21.813 to 34.031 ns). [latency-ocm-region4-cpu8.csv of 005]
  • Boot C: 14.422 ns (region 3 TLB-set row from CPU 2) and 17.812 ns on a walk row (region 0 from CPU 2). [latency-ocm-region3-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-region0-walk-cpu2.csv of 007]
  • Boot E: 11.172 ns (region 0 vary row from CPU 8). [latency-ocm-region0-vary-cpu8.csv of 010]
  • Boot B: 1.437 ns (region 1 from CPU 2). Boot D: 1.640 ns (region 2 from CPU 8). [latency-ocm-region1-cpu2.csv of 006, latency-ocm-region2-cpu8.csv of 008]
  • With the prefetchers off (B, D) the spread is about a tenth of the spread with them on.
  • Run 6 boot F1 (011): the CME OCM passes carry a steady 286 to 292 ns per pass outside the span. The pass-to-pass spread of 3.1 to 8.7 ns per load (5.2 to 22.5 % of the row) sits inside the span. [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011]
  • Boot F2 (012, prefetchers off): the spread falls to 0.2 to 0.7 ns per load (0.2 to 1.3 % of the row). [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 012, 012 README line 141]
  • So the spread is the prefetchers' plus page placement, not a wake-up outside the span. [asimov-cme-perf.html CME wake-up item]
  • Run 6 boot F1: the core's sparse OCM rows still spread up to 59.7 % between passes (region 0 from CPU 6, 19.328 to 30.875 ns per load). [011 latency-ocm-region0-cpu6.csv]
  • The number quoted for OCM is the dense all-five row from CPU 2 (20,480 loads, one L3 read refill per load). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 1]
  • It read 26.009 ns per load on boot A, 24.959 ns on boot C, 26.082 ns on boot E. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 005, 007 and 010]

Still open

Two things are still open: which lines the prefetchers brought in, and why one process places its pages faster than another. [007 README line 53] A per-pass record of the lines the prefetchers fetched, matched to each process's physical page placement, would settle both.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 2 (002, 2026-11-02): two passes of a per-region row differ by up to 3.444 ns; run 3 (004, 2026-11-03): one row's 7 passes spread 68.1 %; boot A (005, 2026-11-04) against run 3: 12 of 70 shared rows moved more than 3 %

What looked wrong. In run 2 the two passes of a per-region OCM row differ by up to 3.444 ns per load (region 3 from CPU 4: 23.938 and 20.494 ns) [membench-jibin-002 latency-ocm-region3-cpu4.csv; README line 66]. In 19 of the 20 rows the faster pass is the one with fewer L3 read refills per load (in the 20th the two counts differ by 0.001) [002 README line 66; recomputed from the 20 CSVs]. In run 3 the 7 passes of one sparse row spread 5.16 to 14.55 ns per load (22 % to 68 %). The widest is CPU 2 to OCM1: 21.359 to 35.906 ns, 68.1 % [membench-jibin-004 latency-ocm-region1-cpu2.csv; README line 110]. Boot A ran on run 3's platform, and both controls repeated run 3 within 0.5 % (4 KiB chase 2.002 ns, CME round trip 21.004 to 21.005 ns) [005 README line 8]. Yet 12 of the 70 best rows the two share moved by more than 3 %. The largest is CPU 2 to OCM3: 26.391 ns on boot A against 23.719 ns on run 3, +11.27 % [latency-ocm-region3-cpu2.csv of 005 and 004; asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 3.9]. Of the 12, 8 are core OCM rows, 3 are CME rows and 1 is the 4 MiB DRAM chain (+5.55 %) [recomputed from the best rows of 005 and 004]. On boot C two vary chains with the TLB set moved in opposite directions against boot A: region 0 read 13.734 against 19.906 ns (0.690 times, -31 %), region 2 read 21.531 against 17.047 ns (1.263 times, +26 %) [latency-ocm-region0-vary-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-region2-vary-tlb-cpu2.csv of 007 and 005; 007 README line 53]. The faster boot's best pass counted fewer L3 read refills per load each time (region 0: 0.3125 on C against 0.6719 on A; region 2: 0.7969 on C against 0.4688 on A) [same CSVs]. The same chain's best differs between two processes of one boot by up to 23.6 % on the vary chains of boot C (22.9 % on boot A) with the prefetchers on [007 README line 52], and by at most 3.0 % on boot D with them off (region 2's sparse chain: 24.328, 23.703 and 23.609 ns in three processes) [008 README line 38]. One CME row moved too: the 32 KiB repeated chain read 42.156 ns on boot A against 39.721 ns on run 3, +6.13 % [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005 and 004; asimov-cme-run4.html section 3.3].

Why it looked wrong. A chain walked again over the same lines should take the same time pass after pass. On the dense rows it does: the dense all-five control repeats run 2 within 0.17 ns [004 README line 110]. On the per-region rows it does not. The slow passes carry more L2 refills (correlation +0.84 within rows on run 3) and fewer L3 read refills (-0.31) [004 README line 111]. So the spread tracks what the prefetchers fetch, not the chain's own loads. Each command is also a new process with its own physical page placement [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section on page placement]. A ratio taken from one row between two boots therefore says little by itself.

Tests added.

  • Median of the passes printed beside the best on every OCM cell; pass-time correlation with the prefetch refills (0x81BD), the L2 refills (0x17) and the L3 read refills (0xA2) [run 4 boot A (005); asimov-c1nano-run4.html sections 3.3 and the pass-to-pass paragraph]: whether a pass's time follows how many lines the prefetcher fetched
  • Boots B and D with the data prefetchers off as the quiet comparison; groups of rows compared by geometric mean instead of single rows [run 4 boots B (006) and D (008)]: the pass spread and the process-to-process spread without the prefetchers
  • Every CME OCM pass timed inside its own streaming span (ns_per_load_span column) [run 6 boots F1 (011) and F2 (012)]: whether the spread sits inside the span (the prefetcher's) or outside it (call cost or a wake-up)

What the tests showed. On boot A a pass's time correlates only weakly with its counts: +0.19 with the prefetch refills (0x81BD), +0.33 with the L2 refills and +0.30 with the L3 read refills [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, pass-to-pass paragraph]. Run 3's sparse rows showed +0.84 with the L2 refills [004 README line 111]. So the count alone does not explain the spread. The largest spread of one row's passes, by boot: A 12.218 ns (latency-ocm-region4-cpu8.csv, 21.813 to 34.031 ns), C 14.422 ns (latency-ocm-region3-tlb-cpu2.csv) and 17.812 ns on a walk row (latency-ocm-region0-walk-cpu2.csv), E 11.172 ns (latency-ocm-region0-vary-cpu8.csv), B 1.437 ns (latency-ocm-region1-cpu2.csv), D 1.640 ns (latency-ocm-region2-cpu8.csv) [recomputed from 005 to 008 and 010; READMEs 006 line 36, 007 line 52, 008 line 38, 010 line 152]. With the prefetchers off (B, D) the spread is about a tenth of what it is with them on. On run 6 the CME OCM passes carry a steady 286 to 292 ns per pass outside the span on F1. The pass-to-pass spread of 3.1 to 8.7 ns per load sits inside the span. On F2 (prefetchers off) the spread falls to 0.2 to 0.7 ns per load (0.2 to 1.3 % of the row, against 5.2 to 22.5 % on F1) [cme-latency-ocm-region*.csv of 011 and 012; 012 README line 141; asimov-cme-perf.html, CME wake-up item]. So the spread is the prefetchers' plus page placement, not a wake-up outside the span. On run 6 F1 the core's sparse rows still spread up to 59.7 % between passes (latency-ocm-region0-cpu6.csv, 19.328 to 30.875 ns) [recomputed from 011]. The number used for OCM is the dense all-five row (20,480 loads, one L3 read refill per load): 26.009 ns on boot A, 24.959 ns on boot C, 26.082 ns on boot E [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 005, 007 and 010; asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 1]. Still open: which lines the prefetchers brought in, and why one process places faster than another [007 README line 53].
