4.21 Run 3's one-core write rows cost 7.7 to 8.0 ns more per pass than run 2's (H6)partly explained

Run 3's one-core write rows cost 7.7 to 8.0 ns more per pass than run 2's. The fixed cost was traced to run 3's program.

What looked wrong

  • In run 3 (results folder 004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC) the one-core write rows at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB cost more per pass than in run 2 (folder 002). The extra was 8.0, 8.0, 7.9 and 7.7 ns per pass. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 002, write 'best' rows]
  • At 16 KiB run 3 wrote at 30.127 GB/s. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 001, 002, 003, 004]
  • That is 1.48 % below run 1 (001), run 2 (002) and the control run (003) at 30.578, 30.579 and 30.579 GB/s. [004 README.md, Bandwidth]
  • 8.0 ns is 16.0 cycles at 2.003 GHz (derived). The offset was the same at every size.
  • So it is a fixed cost per pass, not a change in rate. The timed loop (the assembly write kernel) was the same in both runs. [004 README.md, Bandwidth]
  • At 16 KiB the reads got faster at the same time: 58.127 GB/s in run 3 against 57.529 GB/s in run 2 (+1.04 %). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 002, read 'best' rows]
  • In the 16 KiB two-core pair the faster writer slowed by about 4 ns per pass, not 8 ns. [004 README.md, Bandwidth]

Why it looked wrong

  • The same assembly kernel on the same platform should repeat within a fraction of a percent. The other bandwidth rows did: every bandwidth row of run 3 was within 2.3 % of run 2. [004 README.md, line 8]
  • Run 3's bandwidth.c (the bandwidth test's C source, commit ba834c0) had gained a CME switch (code that selects the CME, the cluster's matrix unit) in its pass loop. [004 README.md, Bandwidth]
  • Jesse's disassembly check before the run was queued put that switch at 4 to 15 cycles per pass (est.). The measured 16 cycles is at the top of that range. [004 README.md, Bandwidth]
  • Run 3 was also a different binary on a different day. So the two runs alone could not separate a program cost from a platform drift.
  • The firmware was not a candidate. Run 3 ran on run 2's image copy, firmware (SCP 0.48.0-nopcie.1, TF-A 0.35.0), kernel and OCM module. [004 README.md, Platform facts]
  • The firmware change was between run 1 and run 2. The control run (003) was for that question. [002 README.md, lines 7 and 10]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
G5: both bandwidth programs side by side on one bootboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot ERun 2's bandwidth program (commit 8ae533c, binary bandwidth_r2) and run 3's (commit ba834c0) run the one-core write kernel at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB on the same boot. They use run 3's pass counts (256, 128, 64, 32), 3 repetitions, CPU 2. H6 is supported if run 2's program reads run 2's numbers and run 3's program reads run 3's numbers on that one boot [follow-up-run-plan.md, H6]. On boot A (005) the run 3 side was the binary named 'bandwidth', which has run 3's machine code (objdump -d identical, objdump being the tool that prints a binary's machine code) [005 README.md, Build]. On boots B to E the run 3 side was 'bandwidth_r3', ba834c0's bandwidth.c kept verbatim. That binary is also run 3's machine code by objdump [006 README.md, Build and 007 README.md, Against boot A]. Files: bandwidth-write-small.csv (run 3's program) and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv (run 2's).

What the tests showed

  • Boot A (005): run 3's program was 11.2, 7.1, 7.4 and 6.7 ns per pass slower than run 2's at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB. [bandwidth-write-small.csv and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv of 005]
  • The GB/s pairs (run 3's program, then run 2's) were 30.210 and 30.847, 31.375 and 31.517, 31.674 and 31.750, 31.875 and 31.901. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.8]
  • On boot A each program read its own run's numbers back, within 0.28 % and 0.88 %. So the per-pass cost belongs to the program, not the platform. H6 is supported. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 9]
  • The C1-Nano (the core under test) is an in-order core. So work at each pass boundary shows as a fixed per-pass cost. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 7]
  • A straight-line fit t_pass = fixed + bytes / rate over the four boot A rows gives a fixed cost of 30.4 ns per pass for run 3's program and 21.0 ns per pass for run 2's. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • Both are at 32.0 GB/s (est., least squares over four points). [verifier recompute 30.4 and 21.0 ns at 31.99 and 31.98 GB/s]
  • Boots B to E repeat the offset at 48, 96 and 256 KiB. Run 3's program was slower by 7.3, 8.3, 8.3 ns per pass on boot B (006) and 7.9, 9.0, 8.3 ns on boot C (007). [bandwidth-write-small.csv and -r2prog.csv of 006, 007, verifier recompute]
  • It was slower by 7.3, 8.0, 7.0 ns per pass on boot D (008) and 7.9, 7.4, 7.7 ns on boot E (010). [bandwidth-write-small.csv and -r2prog.csv of 008, 010, verifier recompute]
  • The 16 KiB row varies by boot. Run 3's program was 11.2 ns (boot A), 3.1 ns (boot B) and 11.4 ns (boot D) per pass slower. It was 0.9 ns (boot C) and 0.8 ns (boot E) per pass faster.
  • The run 4 page attributes the boot C and E change to the b79dffa build. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html sections 11.5 and 13.2]
  • Jesse's READMEs say otherwise. On C and E the G5 rows ran bandwidth_r3, which is run 3's machine code by objdump. So the two G5 binaries were the same machine code on all five boots. [007 README.md, Against boot A and 006 README.md, Build]
  • The 'not byte for byte' note in the boot C README is about the default bandwidth binary used by G7 and G8, not bandwidth_r3. [007 README.md, The G8 rows]
  • On the CRB (a board with an out-of-order V3AE core) the plan notes 89.0 GB/s with run 3's program and 89.3 GB/s with run 2's at 16 KiB. So that core shows no per-pass difference. This is a plan note, not a primary results file. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 9, G5]
  • The crb-validation folder holds only one program's 16 KiB write, 89.286 GB/s from the 2026-10-31 build, before run 3's. [crb-validation/20261031T073509Z/bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]

Still open

Why the 16 KiB row shows no difference on boots C and E (0.9 and 0.8 ns per pass faster), and only 3.1 ns per pass on boot B, is Insufficient data in the primary files. A per-pass cycle count from the PMU (the core's performance monitor counters) on the two binaries at 16 KiB would settle it.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 (004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC) against run 2 (002); isolated on run 4 boot A (005, ran 2026-11-04 UTC)

What looked wrong. The one-core write rows at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB took 8.0, 8.0, 7.9 and 7.7 ns more per pass in run 3 than in run 2 [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 002, write 'best' rows; ns per pass = bytes_per_thread / (aggregate_GBps x 1e9)]. At 16 KiB run 3 read 30.127 GB/s where run 1, run 2 and the control read 30.578, 30.579 and 30.579 GB/s (-1.48 %) [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 001, 002, 003, 004; 004 README.md, Bandwidth]. 8.0 ns is 16.0 cycles at 2.003 GHz (derived). The offset was the same at every size, so it is a fixed cost per pass, not a rate change. The timed loop (the assembly write kernel) was the same in both runs. The 16 KiB reads got faster at the same time: 58.127 GB/s in run 3 against 57.529 in run 2 (+1.04 %) [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 002, read 'best' rows]. In the 16 KiB two-core pair the faster writer slowed by about 4 ns per pass, not 8 ns [004 README.md, Bandwidth].

Why it looked wrong. The same assembly kernel on the same platform should repeat within a fraction of a percent, and the other bandwidth rows did (every bandwidth row within 2.3 %) [004 README.md, line 8]. Run 3's bandwidth.c (commit ba834c0) had gained a CME switch in its pass loop. Jesse's pre-queue check of the disassembly estimated that switch at 4 to 15 cycles per pass. The measured 16 cycles sits at the top of that range [004 README.md, Bandwidth]. But run 3 was also a different binary on a different day, so a program cost and a platform drift could not be told apart from the two runs alone. The firmware was not a candidate: run 3 ran on run 2's image copy, firmware (SCP 0.48.0-nopcie.1, TF-A 0.35.0), kernel and OCM module [004 README.md, Platform facts]. The firmware change was between run 1 and run 2, and the control run (003) was for that question [002 README.md, lines 7 and 10].

Tests added.

  • G5: run 2's bandwidth program (commit 8ae533c, binary bandwidth_r2) and run 3's (commit ba834c0) run side by side on one boot: the one-core write kernel at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB with run 3's pass counts (256, 128, 64, 32), 3 reps, CPU 2. On boot A the run 3 side was the binary named 'bandwidth', which has run 3's machine code (objdump -d identical) [005 README.md, Build]. On boots B to E the run 3 side was 'bandwidth_r3', ba834c0's bandwidth.c kept verbatim, also run 3's machine code by objdump [006 README.md, Build; 007 README.md, Against boot A]. Files: bandwidth-write-small.csv (run 3's program) and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv (run 2's). [run 4 boots A to E (005, 006, 007, 008, 010)]: time per pass of each program on the same platform; H6 is supported if run 2's program reads run 2's numbers and run 3's reads run 3's on one boot [follow-up-run-plan.md, H6]

What the tests showed. Boot A (005): run 3's program is 11.2, 7.1, 7.4 and 6.7 ns per pass slower than run 2's at 16, 48, 96 and 256 KiB (30.210 vs 30.847, 31.375 vs 31.517, 31.674 vs 31.750, 31.875 vs 31.901 GB/s) [bandwidth-write-small.csv and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv of 005; asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.8]. Both programs read their own run's numbers back within 0.28 % and 0.88 % [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 9]. So the per-pass cost is the program's, not the platform's. H6 supported. A straight line t_pass = fixed + bytes / rate over the four boot A rows gives a fixed cost of 30.4 ns per pass for run 3's program and 21.0 ns for run 2's, both at 32.0 GB/s (est., least squares over four points) [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 12, The arithmetic; verifier recompute 30.4 and 21.0 ns, 31.99 and 31.98 GB/s]. The other boots repeat it at 48 to 256 KiB: B (006) 7.3, 8.3, 8.3 ns; C (007) 7.9, 9.0, 8.3 ns; D (008) 7.3, 8.0, 7.0 ns; E (010) 7.9, 7.4, 7.7 ns (verifier recompute from the same two files on each boot). The 16 KiB row varies by boot: A 11.2, B 3.1, D 11.4 ns slower, but C -0.9 and E -0.8 ns (run 3's program slightly faster) [asimov-c1nano-run4.html sections 11.5 and 13.2]. The run4 page attributes the C and E 16 KiB change to the b79dffa build. Jesse's READMEs say otherwise: on C and E the G5 rows ran bandwidth_r3, which is run 3's machine code by objdump, so the two G5 binaries were the same machine code on all five boots [007 README.md, Against boot A; 006 README.md, Build]. The 'not byte for byte' note in the boot C README is about the default bandwidth binary used by G7 and G8, not bandwidth_r3 [007 README.md, The G8 rows]. Why the 16 KiB row shows no difference on C and E, and only 3.1 ns on B, is Insufficient data in the primary files. A per-pass cycle count from the PMU on the two binaries at 16 KiB would resolve it. On the CRB (an out-of-order V3AE core) the plan notes 89.0 GB/s with run 3's program and 89.3 GB/s with run 2's at 16 KiB, so that core shows no per-pass difference [follow-up-run-plan.md, section 9, G5; a plan note, not a primary results file]. The crb-validation folder holds one program's 16 KiB write at 89.286 GB/s (2026-10-31 build, before run 3's) [crb-validation/20261031T073509Z/bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]. The run 6 pages generalise the finding: the C1-Nano is an in-order core, so work at each pass boundary shows as a fixed per-pass cost [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, section 7].

4.22 One-core L1 read at 58 GB/s, 91 % of the 64 GB/s read path; small writes below the 32 GB/s write pathpartly explained

One core read L1 at 58 GB/s against a 64 GB/s read path. The pages attribute the gap to the test program's per-pass cost.

What looked wrong

  • One core read a 16 KiB buffer at 58.127 GB/s in run 3 (membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03). The buffer sits in L1 (the level-1 cache of one core). [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 7, best of 3 reps]
  • The C1-Nano (the Arm core under test) has a dual 128-bit read path, 32 B per cycle. At the 2.003 GHz core clock that is 64.1 GB/s. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • The run 3 row is 90.7 % of that limit. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • One 16 KiB pass in run 3 took 281.9 ns (564.6 cycles at 2.003 GHz). The ideal is 512 cycles. The pass is 52 cycles over. [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv row 7]
  • On the CRB (the Arm reference server, Neoverse V3AE cores at 2.8 GHz) the validation program's single-call read of 32 KiB ran 692 cycles against 683 ideal. [crb/data-all.json asm[0] and follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • That is 98.7 % of its 48 B per cycle path, 132.67 GB/s. [crb/data-all.json asm[0] and follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • Writes in run 3 reached the 128-bit write path (32.0 GB/s) only from 2 MiB up. [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv rows 11, 26, 41, 56, 71, 86]
  • The rows read 30.127 (16 KiB), 31.345 (48 KiB), 31.664 (96 KiB), 31.869 (256 KiB), 31.982 (2 MiB) and 31.996 GB/s (32 MiB). [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv rows 11, 26, 41, 56, 71, 86]

Why it looked wrong

  • A loop over a buffer that sits in L1 needs no cache refills. It should run at the limit of the load pipes, 64.1 GB/s at 2.003 GHz.
  • Bill wrote on 2026-11-04 that 58 GB/s from L1 is "WAY too slow". [edit-jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md:229-231]
  • Suspected cause (hypothesis H8, follow-up-run-plan.md section 12): a fixed cost at every pass boundary.
  • The boundary holds the loop exit, the return, the save and restore of vector registers d8 to d15, the C loop's step, and the next call.
  • The C1-Nano is an in-order core (it cannot start later instructions before earlier ones finish).
  • It cannot overlap that boundary cost with the next pass's loads. The cost weighs most on short passes. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • Run 3 measured only one size inside L1 (16 KiB). One size cannot separate a per-pass cost from the L1 rate.
  • Jibin asked on 2026-11-03 for a note that the test code's per-pass overhead keeps the small write rows below the write path. [edit-jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md, comments before 76]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
G8 rows: L1 reads and writes, two forms, 4 to 24 KiBboot C, boot EThe fixed cost per pass of each form, and the L1 rate with that cost removed. Both come from a fit t_pass = a + bytes / rate through the four best of 5 reps at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB (1,024, 512, 256 and 176 passes) on CPU 2. The looped form makes one kernel call per pass (bandwidth-l1-passes.csv). The single-call form runs all passes of a rep inside one assembly call (bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv). The fit counts only when the largest residual is under 2 % of the smallest pass time. One L1 rate near 64.1 GB/s from both forms would mean the per-pass cost explains the 58 GB/s row.
CRB check of the two forms on the V3AE, read onlyotherThe same two forms at 4 to 24 KiB, 21 reps, 16 MiB per rep, on CPUs 3 and 60 of the CRB (2026-11-04 evening, files under ~/workspace/ai-runs/run5c-crb-sample). The test shows whether the method gives one L1 rate from both forms on an out-of-order core with a known answer of 48 B per cycle. Agreement between the forms would mean the method is sound.

What the tests showed

  • CRB (V3AE): the looped fit is 4.2 ns per pass + bytes / 134.2 GB/s on CPU 3 and 134.3 GB/s on CPU 60 (residuals 0.5 % and 0.4 %, rule met). [run5c-crb-sample bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu3 and cpu60 files via l1_reader.py]
  • The single-call rows read 134.2 to 134.4 GB/s at every size, 1.33 cycles per line = 48 B per cycle. [run5c-crb-sample bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu3 and cpu60 files via l1_reader.py]
  • Both forms give the same L1 rate. So the method works.
  • The V3AE's looped per-pass cost of 4.2 ns is 12 cycles at 2.8 GHz. [run5c-crb-sample bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu3 and cpu60 files via l1_reader.py]
  • C1-Nano single-call reads at 4 / 8 / 16 / 24 KiB: 53.096 / 57.890 / 60.331 / 60.586 GB/s on boot E and 53.103 / 57.898 / 60.249 / 59.812 GB/s on boot C. [bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv rows 9, 27, 45, 63 of 007 and 010]
  • Looped reads: 40.910 / 50.426 / 56.004 / 57.258 GB/s on boot E and 46.180 / 50.234 / 56.586 / 57.962 GB/s on boot C. [bandwidth-l1-passes.csv rows 9, 27, 45, 63 of 007 and 010]
  • The single-call 16 and 24 KiB rows (59.8 to 60.6 GB/s) are 93 to 95 % of 64.1 GB/s. [bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and bandwidth-l1-passes.csv rows 9, 27, 45, 63 of 007 and 010]
  • The bytes added between the 8 KiB and 16 KiB rows move at 64.8 GB/s (boot C looped), 62.8 GB/s (C single-call), 63.0 GB/s (E looped) and 63.0 GB/s (E single-call). [8,192 B divided by the 16 KiB minus 8 KiB best-rep pass times, l1_reader.py]
  • That is the read path's rate on every form and boot. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html (the run 4 page) table 15b]
  • Write fits pass the 2 % rule on both boots and forms. Rates: 31.9 GB/s (C looped), 32.0 GB/s (C single-call), 32.0 GB/s (E looped), 32.1 GB/s (E single-call). [l1_reader.py fits of the G8 files of 007 and 010]
  • Fixed cost per pass: 23.7 ns (C) and 25.7 ns (E) looped, 9.1 ns (C) and 14.0 ns (E) single-call. [l1_reader.py fits of the G8 files of 007 and 010]
  • Residuals 1.9 %, 0.0 %, 0.3 %, 0.7 % in the same order. [l1_reader.py fits of the G8 files of 007 and 010]
  • Read fits fail the rule: residuals 5.4 % (C looped), 4.4 % (C single-call), 2.9 % (E looped), 2.1 % (E single-call). [l1_reader.py]
  • The failed fits would give 25.5 / 8.7 ns per pass (C looped / single-call) and 32.0 / 10.5 ns (E) with rates 61.4 to 62.4 GB/s. The pages do not quote them. [l1_reader.py]
  • The core page (asimov-c1nano-perf.html) instead takes the 8 KiB pass time minus 8,192 B at the 8-to-16 KiB rate. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 7.1]
  • That gives 11.5 ns est. per pass single-call on boot E (141.5 ns minus 130.1 ns) and 11.0 ns est. on boot C. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 7.1]
  • Looped, it gives 32.4 ns est. (E) and 36.6 ns est. (C). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 7.1]
  • The run 4 page's table 15b gives each read row's time above the 64 GB/s ideal as 13 to 27 ns per pass single-call and 25 to 45 ns looped. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 15b]
  • Conclusion on the pages: the shortfall is the program's per-pass cost on an in-order core, not the L1's rate. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 7]
  • The C1-Nano TRM (Technical Reference Manual) r0p2, document 107753_0002_06_en, section 1.1 lists an in-order pipeline. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 7]
  • The V3AE is out of order and overlaps the boundary. The TRM quote was not checked at source in this check.

Still open

Three items stay open. First, who owns the per-pass cost left in the single-call form (9 to 14 ns per pass on the write fits of boots C and E, 11.5 ns est. on the boot E read passes). Second, why the C1-Nano's looped read cost (32.4 ns est., boot E) is about 8 times (est.) the V3AE's 4.2 ns when the clock ratio is 1.4 (2.8 GHz / 2.003 GHz). The looped write fits (23.7 to 25.7 ns) are 5.6 to 6.1 times. Third, why boot E's 4 KiB looped read (40.910 GB/s, rep spread 0.2 %) is 0.886 times boot C's (46.180 GB/s, rep spread 0.5 %). The other 15 G8 rows are 0.972 to 1.013 times C's. Insufficient data: the record names no measurement that would settle these three items.

C1-Nano, boot C: single-call reads 53.103 / 57.898 / 60.249 / 59.812 GB/s at 4 / 8 / 16 / 24 KiB; looped reads 46.180 / 50.234 / 56.586 / 57.962. Boot E: single-call 53.096 / 57.890 / 60.331 / 60.586; looped 40.910 / 50.426 / 56.004 / 57.258. The single-call 16 and 24 KiB rows (59.8 to 60.6 GB/s) are 93 to 95 % of 64.1 GB/s. The bytes added between the 8 and 16 KiB rows move at 64.8 (C looped), 62.8 (C single-call), 63.0 (E looped) and 63.0 (E single-call) GB/s: the read path's rate on every form and boot. Write fits pass the 2 % rule on both boots and forms: rate 31.9 (C looped), 32.0 (C single-call), 32.0 (E looped), 32.1 (E single-call) GB/s; fixed cost 23.7 (C) and 25.7 (E) ns per pass looped, 9.1 (C) and 14.0 (E) ns single-call; residuals 1.9 %, 0.0 %, 0.3 %, 0.7 %. Read fits fail the rule: residuals 5.4 % (C looped), 4.4 % (C single-call), 2.9 % (E looped), 2.1 % (E single-call). The failed four-point fits would give 25.5 / 8.7 ns (C looped / single-call) and 32.0 / 10.5 ns (E), with rates 61.4 to 62.4 GB/s, but the pages do not quote them. The core page's estimate instead takes the 8 KiB pass time minus 8,192 B at the 8-to-16 KiB rate: 11.5 ns est. per pass single-call on boot E (141.5 ns minus 130.1 ns); the same method gives 11.0 ns est. on boot C, and 32.4 ns est. (E) and 36.6 ns est. (C) looped. The run 4 page's table 15b gives each read row's time above the 64 GB/s ideal: 13 to 27 ns per pass single-call, 25 to 45 ns looped. Conclusion on the pages: the shortfall is the program's per-pass cost on an in-order core, not the L1's rate. The C1-Nano TRM r0p2 (document 107753_0002_06_en) section 1.1 lists an in-order pipeline; the V3AE is out of order and overlaps the boundary. Open: (1) who owns the per-pass cost that remains in the single-call form, 9 to 14 ns on the write fits and 11.5 ns est. on the read passes; (2) why the C1-Nano's looped read cost (32.4 ns est. on boot E) is about 8 times (est.) the V3AE's 4.2 ns against a clock ratio of 1.4 (2.8 / 2.003); the looped write fits (23.7 to 25.7 ns) are 5.6 to 6.1 times; (3) boot E's 4 KiB looped read reads 40.910 GB/s against boot C's 46.180, with rep spreads of 0.2 % and 0.5 %, while the other 15 G8 rows read 0.972 to 1.013 times C's.

4.23 CRB: single-call L1 read form has slow reps at 16 and 24 KiB (134 to 106 GB/s)open

On the CRB, the single-call L1 read form fell from 134 GB/s at 4 KiB to 106 GB/s at 24 KiB, below the looped form.

What looked wrong

  • 3-rep sample on the CRB (the Arm reference server, Neoverse V3AE cores at 2.8 GHz), CPU 3, 2026-11-04 evening.
  • The single-call read form (--asm-passes) read 134.2 / 134.3 / 120.5 / 106.1 GB/s best of 3 at 4 / 8 / 16 / 24 KiB. The rate fell as the buffer grew. [bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv lines 6, 19, 34, 47]
  • The looped form (one kernel call per pass) read 116.6 / 125.7 / 129.6 / 127.0 GB/s best of 3 at the same sizes. So at 16 and 24 KiB the single-call form read below the looped form. [bandwidth-l1-passes.csv lines 5, 20, 34, 47, 48]
  • The looped sample also has one slow rep at 24 KiB, 106.1 GB/s. [bandwidth-l1-passes.csv lines 5, 20, 34, 47, 48]
  • With 21 reps the best single-call rep reaches 134.2 to 134.4 GB/s at every size on CPU 3 and CPU 60. That is the three-pipe limit (48 B per cycle at 2.8 GHz). [read21 cpu3 and cpu60 asmpasses CSVs]
  • The looped best reps are 117.8 / 126.0 / 129.7 / 131.3 GB/s (CPU 3) and 117.8 / 126.0 / 129.8 / 131.3 GB/s (CPU 60). [read21 cpu3 and cpu60 passes CSVs]
  • At 16 KiB only 4 of 21 single-call reps on CPU 3 and 7 of 21 on CPU 60 are fast (within 2 % of the best rep). The looped form has 13 and 18 of 21 fast reps. [the four read21 CSVs, 16 KiB blocks]
  • At 24 KiB the single-call form has 10 of 21 fast reps on both CPUs. The looped form has 14 and 12 of 21. [the four read21 CSVs, 24 KiB blocks]
  • L1 refills (lines fetched into L1 from outside it) are at most 0.0008 per line in every 21-rep rep, fast or slow, and at most 0.0024 per line in the 3-rep sample. [bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu60-asmpasses.csv 24 KiB block, bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv line 46]
  • So the rows stayed in L1 in every rep.

Why it looked wrong

  • An L1-resident row should read at the same rate in every rep.
  • In the 3-rep sample the best single-call rate fell from 134.2 GB/s at 4 KiB to 106.1 GB/s at 24 KiB. Refills stayed at most 0.0024 per line.
  • The single-call form removes the per-pass call, return and register save.
  • On the V3AE that per-pass cost is 4.2 ns (12 cycles at 2.8 GHz, fit through the best looped reps, residual 0.4 to 0.5 %). [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • So the single-call form should never read slower than the looped form. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • The refill counters give how often a refill happened, not the time spent on it. So the cause of a slow rep is Insufficient data. [codex R26, 2026-11-04]
  • The CRB core is not isolated. A slow rep on either form may therefore be an interrupt or another core's work. [codex R26, 2026-11-04]
  • Hypothesis H9 (from the V3AE only): the single-call form shows a slow state of the core more often than the looped form at the two larger sizes. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]
  • No primary file names a branch-predictor cause. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 12]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures

Also measures whether a 16 or 24 KiB single-call row costs more cycles per line than the 4 and 8 KiB rows. (Run 5c, membench-jibin-007 boot C and membench-jibin-010 boot E, 2026-11-05, read with the l1_reader.py spread check and slow-state check defined under terms.)

What the tests showed

  • On the CRB only CPU 60 is bimodal (its slow reps sit in one group).
  • Ten of its slow 16 KiB single-call reps read 118.7 to 120.8 GB/s. The median over all 21 reps is 129.2 GB/s. [bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu60-asmpasses.csv lines 54 to 74]
  • CPU 3's slow 16 KiB single-call reps spread evenly from 106.6 to 131.3 GB/s, with a median of 120.8 GB/s. [bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu3-asmpasses.csv lines 54 to 74]
  • The slowest CPU 3 rep (106.6 GB/s, rep 6) counts 0.0001 L1 refills per line. The fastest (134.3 GB/s, rep 0) counts 0.0002. [bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu3-asmpasses.csv lines 60 and 54]
  • So the refill count does not separate slow from fast reps.
  • On the C1-Nano the slow-state check flagged no single-call row on boots C or E. [l1_reader.py on bootC and bootE bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv]
  • Their best reps at 16 and 24 KiB cost 7.4 to 8.2 % fewer cycles per line on read than the 4 and 8 KiB mean (2.12 to 2.14 against 2.31). [l1_reader.py on bootC and bootE bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv]
  • On write they cost 3.3 to 5.8 % fewer. [l1_reader.py on bootC and bootE bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv]
  • The spread check did find slow single-call read reps on the isolated C1-Nano.
  • Boot C rep 1 at 4 KiB read 47.8 GB/s against a best of 53.1 GB/s (spread 9.9 % of best). Its 8, 16 and 24 KiB rows spread 2.8, 2.9 and 3.3 %. [membench-jibin-007 bootC bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv line 5]
  • Boot E rep 1 at 8 KiB read 54.8 GB/s against 57.9 GB/s (spread 5.4 %). Its other rows spread 0.2 to 1.7 %. [membench-jibin-010 bootE bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv line 23]
  • The looped-form read rows spread only 0.1 to 1.8 % on both boots. [bootC and bootE bandwidth-l1-passes.csv]
  • The run 4 page does not report these spreads. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 15]

Still open

The cause of the slow reps on either machine stays open. The refill counters cannot settle it. They count refills, not time spent. A measurement that would settle it is a per-rep count of stall cycles or interrupts on an isolated CRB core, run for both forms at 16 and 24 KiB.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. CRB (the Arm reference server, Neoverse V3AE cores, 2.8 GHz) 3-rep sample on CPU 3 (not isolated), 2026-11-04 evening; 21-rep check on CPUs 3 and 60 the same evening (files dated 2026-11-04 17:52 and 17:56). Written up in follow-up-run-plan.md section 12, 'CRB check of the two forms'.

What looked wrong. In a 3-rep CRB sample the single-call read form (--asm-passes, all passes of a rep inside one assembly call) read 134.2 / 134.3 / 120.5 / 106.1 GB/s best at 4 / 8 / 16 / 24 KiB. The rate fell with size. The looped form (one kernel call per pass) read 116.6 / 125.7 / 129.6 / 127.0 GB/s best at the same sizes, so at 16 and 24 KiB the single-call form read below the looped form. With 21 reps the best reps of the single-call form reach 134.2 to 134.4 GB/s at every size (the three-pipe limit, 48 B per cycle at 2.8 GHz). But at 16 KiB only 4 of 21 reps on CPU 3 and 7 of 21 on CPU 60 are fast (within 2 % of the best); the looped form has 13 and 18 of 21 fast reps. At 24 KiB the single-call form has 10 of 21 fast reps on both CPUs, the looped form 14 and 12 of 21. L1 refills are at most 0.0008 per line in every 21-rep rep, fast or slow, and at most 0.0024 per line in the 3-rep sample.

Why it looked wrong. An L1-resident row should read the same rate in every rep. The form that removes the per-pass call, return and register save should never read slower than the looped form. The refill counters give the incidence of refills, not the time spent on them, so the cause of a slow rep is Insufficient data (codex R26, 2026-11-04). The CRB core is not isolated, so a slow rep on either form may be an interrupt or another core's work. Hypothesis H9 (from the V3AE only): the single-call form shows a slow state of the core more often than the looped form at the two larger sizes. The branch-predictor idea in the original entry is not in the primary files.

Tests added.

  • 21-rep re-measurement on CPUs 3 and 60, read only, both forms, 16 MiB per rep [CRB, 2026-11-04 evening (bandwidth-l1-read21-cpu{3,60}-{passes,asmpasses}.csv under /home/jhan/workspace/ai-runs/run5c-crb-sample/)]: whether the slow reps are bimodal or spread, and whether the best rep of each form reaches the same L1 rate
  • G8 rows (run 5c): reps raised from 3 to 5, plus two reading checks in l1_reader.py: a spread check (rep spread as a share of the best rep, compared with the looped row at the same size) and a slow-state check (best rep's cycles per line at 16 and 24 KiB more than 2 % above the 4 and 8 KiB mean = slow-state row) [run 5c on the C1-Nano, boot C (membench-jibin-007) and boot E (membench-jibin-010), 2026-11-05, isolated CPU 2]: whether the slow reps appear on the isolated C1-Nano CPU 2, and whether a 16 or 24 KiB single-call row reads more cycles per line than the small rows

What the tests showed. On the CRB, bimodal fits CPU 60 only: ten of its slow 16 KiB single-call reps sit at 118.7 to 120.8 GB/s (median 129.2 GB/s). CPU 3's slow reps spread evenly from 106.6 to 131.3 GB/s (median 120.8 GB/s). The slowest rep (106.6 GB/s, rep 6) counts 0.0001 L1 refills per line against 0.0002 in the fastest (134.3 GB/s, rep 0), so the refill count does not separate slow from fast. On the C1-Nano boots C and E the slow-state check cleared every single-call row: the best reps at 16 and 24 KiB run 7.4 to 8.2 % fewer cycles per line than the 4 and 8 KiB mean on read (2.12 to 2.14 against 2.31) and 3.3 to 5.8 % fewer on write. The spread check did find slow reps on the C1-Nano single-call read rows: boot C rep 1 at 4 KiB read 47.8 GB/s against a best of 53.1 (spread 9.9 % of best) and the 8, 16 and 24 KiB rows spread 2.8, 2.9 and 3.3 %; boot E rep 1 at 8 KiB read 54.8 GB/s against 57.9 (spread 5.4 %), its other rows 0.2 to 1.7 %. The looped-form read rows spread 0.1 to 1.8 % on both boots. The run 4 page does not report these spreads. The cause of the slow reps on either machine stays open.

4.24 Four readers keep 93 % of the one-core rate while four writers keep 100 %; eight readers share a ceilingpartly explained

Four readers kept 93 % of one core's rate while four writers kept 100 %. Eight readers on boot F1 kept 55 %.

What looked wrong

  • Run 3 (the L3 off): four readers on CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8 read 34.6 GB/s together at 2 MiB each, 3.72x one core (93 % per core). [004 bandwidth-perdsu.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • At 16 MiB each, the same four readers read 34.0 GB/s, 3.70x the one-core 32 MiB row (93 %). [004 bandwidth-perdsu.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • Four writers on the same CPUs wrote 127.9 GB/s at 2 MiB each and 128.0 GB/s at 16 MiB each, 4.00x one core (100 % per core). [004 bandwidth-perdsu.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • Eight readers (CPUs 2 to 9) kept 91 % per core at both sizes, 67.8 GB/s at 2 MiB each and 66.7 GB/s at 16 MiB each. [004 bandwidth-all8.csv]
  • Eight writers kept 61 % at 2 MiB (155.2 GB/s) and 59 % at 16 MiB (152.2 GB/s). [004 bandwidth-all8.csv]
  • Boot F1 (the L3 on): four readers at 16 MiB each read 24.5 to 24.6 GB/s per thread, 99.8 to 100.1 % of F1's one-core 32 MiB row (24.6 GB/s). [011 bandwidth-perdsu.csv rep 0, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • Boot F1: eight readers at 16 MiB each read 107.6 GB/s together, 13.4 GB/s each, 55 % of the one-core rate. [011 bandwidth-all8.csv]
  • Boot F1: at 2 MiB each, the eight readers read 108.7 GB/s together, 13.6 GB/s each, 54 %. [011 bandwidth-all8.csv]

Why it looked wrong

  • Expectation: if the read and write paths were independent of each other and of the thread count, reads and writes would scale alike.
  • They did not. On run 3 four writers kept 100 % per core and four readers 93 %.
  • The aggregate rate (total bytes of all threads divided by the slowest thread's time) is set by the slowest thread. So one slow thread lowers the whole row.
  • Best rep on run 3: the four writers wrote 31.980 to 31.982 GB/s each, equal to one core alone (31.98 GB/s). [004 bandwidth-perdsu.csv rep 2, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • Best rep on run 3: the four readers read 8.65 to 9.26 GB/s each against 9.31 GB/s alone. The slowest reader kept 93 % and the fastest 99.4 %. [004 bandwidth-perdsu.csv rep 2, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • Boot F1: the analysis page reads the eight-reader rows two ways.
  • Section 9 reads them as one shared chip ceiling of about 109 GB/s (the 2 MiB row, 108.7 GB/s). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 9]
  • Section 2.3 reads them as a per-cluster cap of about 27 GB/s est. (107.6 GB/s over four clusters), near one reader's rate. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2.3]

What the tests showed

  • Run 3: the four-reader loss is the slowest thread. The readers spread 8.653 to 9.257 GB/s each (7 %). [004 bandwidth-perdsu.csv rep 2]

  • Run 3: the aggregate doubled, 34.6 to 67.8 GB/s at 2 MiB each. So the spread is a per-core property, not interference. [004 bandwidth-all8.csv rep 2]
  • Hypothesis on the page, not measured: the slowest reader is CPU 8, the core farthest from the home nodes. Its 2 MiB chase is 26.1 ns against 24.1 ns on CPU 2. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.4 note]
  • The program does not record which thread was slowest. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.4 note]

  • Two writers in one DSU (CPUs 2+3, the pair) at 160 KiB shared the DSU's one mesh port: 47.2 GB/s on run 3, 74 % per core of one core at 256 KiB. [004 bandwidth-pair.csv]

  • Boot F1: eight readers lost 45 % per core (55 % kept at 16 MiB each). [011 bandwidth-all8.csv]

Still open

Whether the F1 eight-reader loss is a per-cluster cap of about 27 GB/s est. or a chip-wide ceiling of about 109 GB/s is open. The rows on disk cannot tell the two apart (every row with two cores per cluster also runs all eight cores). The pair's 160 KiB read on F1 (33.7 GB/s, inside the L2 and L3 footprints) cannot tell them apart either. Two readers at 16 MiB each on CPUs 2+3 and on CPUs 2+4 would settle it. Boot F2 (membench-jibin-012, which ran only the run_cme.sh script) has no bandwidth-pair, bandwidth-perdsu or bandwidth-all8 file.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 (membench-jibin-004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC per its README); the eight-reader question on run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, ran 2026-11-06 UTC per its README). The dates 2026-11-04 (Jibin's question) and 2026-11-08 (eight-reader question) come from the session transcripts, not from the primary files.

What looked wrong. On run 3 (the L3 off) four readers on CPUs 2, 4, 6, 8 read 34.6 GB/s together at 2 MiB each, 3.72x one core (93 % per core), and 34.0 GB/s at 16 MiB each, 3.70x the one-core 32 MiB row (93 % per core). Four writers on the same CPUs write 127.9 and 128.0 GB/s, 4.00x one core (100 % per core). Eight readers (CPUs 2 to 9) keep 91 % per core at both sizes (67.8 and 66.7 GB/s). Eight writers keep only 61 % at 2 MiB (155.2 GB/s) and 59 % at 16 MiB (152.2 GB/s). On boot F1 (the L3 on) four readers at 16 MiB each read 24.5 to 24.6 GB/s per thread, 99.8 to 100.1 % of F1's one-core 32 MiB row (24.6 GB/s). Eight readers at 16 MiB each read 107.6 GB/s together, 13.4 GB/s each, 55 % of the one-core rate; at 2 MiB each 108.7 GB/s together, 13.6 each, 54 %.

Why it looked wrong. If the read and write paths were independent of each other and of the thread count, reads and writes would scale alike. They do not. The aggregate is total bytes over the slowest thread's time, so one slow thread lowers the whole row. Per thread on run 3 (best rep): the four writers write 31.980 to 31.982 GB/s each, the same as one core alone (31.98 GB/s), so no writer lost anything. The four readers read 8.65 to 9.26 GB/s each against 9.31 GB/s for one core alone: the fastest reader kept 99.4 % and the slowest 93 %. The 2 MiB chase (one dependent load at a time) from CPUs 2 / 4 / 6 / 8 reads 24.1 / 24.6 / 24.7 / 26.1 ns per load, an 8 % spread that matches the 7 % spread in read rate (9.257 over 8.653). With eight readers the per-thread range is 8.47 to 9.04 GB/s, nearly the same as with four, and the aggregate doubles, so on run 3 the spread is a per-core property and not interference. On F1 the eight-reader rows read differently in two sections of the same page: section 9 reads them as one shared chip ceiling of about 109 GB/s (the 2 MiB row, 108.7 GB/s); section 2.3 reads them as a per-cluster cap of about 27 GB/s est. (107.6 GB/s over four clusters), near one reader's rate. The rows on disk cannot tell the two apart. Every row with two cores per cluster also has all eight cores running.

Verification: verified; 8 corrections applied by the verifier.

Highlighted: mesh, home-node, DSU, DRAM, core.

4.25 SLC and OCM share one home-node array, yet one core reads OCM 1.6 to 1.7x faster than SLC-served data, writes it at 0.63x of its DRAM write, and the per-region OCM chase reads 3.5 to 3.8 ns below the SLC chase; through the CME the OCM read is 0.62 to 0.64x its DRAM rateopen

One core reads OCM 1.6 to 1.7 times faster than SLC-served data. Both sit in the same home-node array.

What looked wrong

  • Run 3 (004, the L3 off), CPU 2: one core reads one OCM region at 16.219, 16.619, 16.320, 15.323 and 14.817 GB/s for OCM0 to OCM4. All five together read at 15.974 GB/s. [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv of 004, best rows]
  • OCM3 and OCM4, three crosspoints away, read lowest. [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv of 004, best rows]
  • Run 3, same core: a DRAM-address buffer that the SLC holds reads at 10.164 GB/s (256 KiB) and 9.311 GB/s (2 MiB). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, best rows]
  • The OCM read over the SLC-served read is 1.57 to 1.72 for all five regions. Per region it is 1.46 to 1.79 (derived). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, best rows, and 004 README line 84]
  • Run 3: one core writes all five OCM regions at 20.326 GB/s. [bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 004]
  • The same core writes DRAM addresses at 31.982 GB/s (2 MiB) and 31.996 GB/s (32 MiB). The OCM write is 0.64 of the DRAM-address write. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]
  • Run 2 (002) dense chase from CPU 2: 19.770, 18.456, 21.355, 21.535 and 22.001 ns per load for OCM0 to OCM4 (mean 20.62 ns). [latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv of 002]
  • A 2 MiB SLC-resident chain reads 24.382 ns (run 2) and 24.096 ns (run 3). That is 3.8 ns and 3.5 ns slower. [latency-dram-large.csv of 002 line 22 and of 004 line 23]
  • Run 3, through the CME: OCM reads at 23.178 to 23.352 GB/s per region (23.160 GB/s all five) against 36.564 to 37.218 GB/s from a warm DRAM buffer (32 MiB to 256 KiB). [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]
  • The ratio is 0.62 to 0.64, the reverse of the core. [004 README line 84]
  • The five region bests lie within 0.75 % of each other. The CME's reps spread 1.5 % to 7.9 %, the core's 0.2 % to 1.3 %. [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]

Why it looked wrong

  • Each home node (HN-S) holds one 1 MiB array in 16 ways: 4 locked as its 256 KiB OCM, the rest 768 KiB of SLC (derived from 3.75 MiB over five nodes). [004 README line 34]
  • An SLC hit and an OCM read use the same array and the same mesh trip. They should cost and stream about the same. Instead the OCM read is 1.6 to 1.7 times faster.
  • The method differs. The OCM rows are one pass after a flush, over 4 KiB pages. The DRAM-address rows are 4 to 32 warm passes over 2 MiB huge pages. [CSV headers of 004 and 004 README lines 84 and 129]
  • Jesse's reading: the data do not say which of the two differences costs the CME. [004 README lines 84 and 129]
  • The chase comparison is not clean. The per-region OCM rows count 0.77 to 0.94 L3 read refills per load. [002 README lines 65 and 66]
  • Some lines therefore arrive before their load. The row then understates a single read.
  • The all-five OCM chase (1.25 MiB, 1.00 refills per load) reads 1.1 to 1.5 ns above the 2 MiB SLC chase on every CPU. [002 README lines 65 and 66, and 004 README line 104]
  • Run 3 sparse per-region bests from CPU 2, 21.359 to 25.781 ns, straddle the SLC row's 24.096 ns. [004 README line 104]
  • Three hypotheses were recorded (peer transcript, not in the primary files).
  • First: part of the 2 MiB chain misses the SLC (one miss in ten at 52 ns adds about 3 ns est.).
  • Second: the SLC hit path at the node is longer than the locked-way path (no counter separates them).
  • Third: the /dev/ocm mapping attributes cap the OCM stores.

What the tests showed

  • Run 3: the CME writes OCM at 19.795 GB/s, close to the core's 20.326 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 004]
  • The CME writes DRAM addresses at 61.971 to 63.865 GB/s. So the OCM write cap is not the core's store path alone. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]
  • Boot F1 (011, the L3 on): the core's OCM read rose to 20.143, 20.042, 19.883, 20.086 and 20.128 GB/s for OCM0 to OCM4, all within 1.3 %. [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011]
  • The all-five read rose to 19.822 GB/s. The distance dependence disappeared. [bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv of 011]
  • Boot F1: the SLC-served read rose to 26.297 GB/s (256 KiB), 25.044 GB/s (2 MiB) and 24.575 GB/s (32 MiB), overtaking the OCM read. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]
  • The OCM reads rose 1.21 to 1.36 times from run 3. The DRAM-address reads rose 2.6 to 2.7 times. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]
  • So the run 3 ratio of 1.6 to 1.7 belongs partly to the read-stream item (read-stream-rise-l3-on). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 10]
  • Boot F1: the core's OCM write stayed at 20.326 GB/s. [bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011]
  • The CME's OCM write rose to 30.659 GB/s (1.55 times run 3). The CME's DRAM-address writes fell to 40.445 to 52.530 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]
  • Boot F1: the CME's OCM read rose to 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s per region and 34.356 GB/s over all five, 1.45 to 1.71 times run 3. [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv of 011]
  • The CME's OCM reps spread up to 19.5 %. [011 README line 206]
  • Boot F1: against the CME's same-size warm 256 KiB DRAM row (41.562 GB/s) every region still reads lower (0.81 to 0.96). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]
  • Against its 32 MiB row (36.583 GB/s) only OCM0 (33.638 GB/s) and the all-five (34.356 GB/s) read lower. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]

Still open

Insufficient data on three points. First: why one core writes OCM at 20.3 GB/s instead of 32.0 GB/s on every run (run 2 20.433, run 3 20.326, F1 20.326 GB/s). Second: why the per-region OCM chase reads 3.5 to 3.8 ns below the SLC chase while the all-five OCM chase reads 1.1 to 1.5 ns above it. Third: why the CME's OCM read sits below its same-size DRAM read. The two proposed method-swap rows (a flush-before one-pass DRAM read, and a 32-pass warm OCM read) would separate the page-size and flush-against-warm differences. They did not run.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 1 (001): OCM1 read 16.623 GB/s against 9.306 GB/s from a 2 MiB SLC-resident buffer [bandwidth-ocm-region1.csv and bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 001, best rows]; the OCM streaming write of 20.3 to 20.4 GB/s against 32.0 GB/s first in the run 2 README [membench-jibin-002 README line 86]; the CME reversal in the run 3 README (004) line 84, 2026-11-03; raised by Jibin on the run 3 page 2026-11-04 02:01 and 02:12 (peer transcript; not in the primary files)

What looked wrong. Each home node (HN-S) holds one 1 MiB array in 16 ways. The firmware locks 4 ways of each node as its 256 KiB OCM region, so 3.75 MiB of SLC is left over five nodes [004 README line 34]. That is 768 KiB (12 ways) of SLC per node (derived from the 3.75 MiB; the README does not state 12 ways). On run 3 (004, the L3 off), from CPU 2: - Read stream from one OCM region: 16.219, 16.619, 16.320, 15.323 and 14.817 GB/s for OCM0 to OCM4 (16.0 over all five) [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv of 004, best rows]. The two regions three crosspoints away (OCM3, OCM4) read lowest. - Read stream from a DRAM-address buffer that the SLC holds: 9.311 GB/s at 2 MiB and 10.164 GB/s at 256 KiB [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, best rows]. - The OCM read over the DRAM-address read: 1.57 to 1.72 (the all-five 15.974 over 10.164 and over 9.311; per region the range is 1.46 to 1.79; derived) [004 README line 84 quotes 1.57 to 1.72]. - Write stream to all five OCM regions: 20.326 GB/s; write to DRAM addresses: 31.982 GB/s at 2 MiB and 31.996 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-ocm-write.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. So the OCM write is 0.64 times the DRAM-address write. - Chase (one dependent load after another) of one OCM region, run 2 dense rows from CPU 2: 19.770, 18.456, 21.355, 21.535 and 22.001 ns per load (mean 20.62) [latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv of 002, best rows]. Chase of a 2 MiB chain over the same five nodes (SLC-resident): 24.382 ns on run 2 and 24.096 ns on run 3 [latency-dram-large.csv of 002 line 22 and of 004 line 23]. The gap is 3.8 ns within run 2, 3.5 ns against run 3's SLC row. - Through the CME (the cluster's streaming unit): OCM read 23.178 to 23.352 GB/s per region (23.160 over all five) against the CME's warm DRAM-buffer read of 36.564 to 37.218 GB/s (32 MiB to 256 KiB) [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. That is 0.62 to 0.64 (the all-five over the 256 KiB row: 0.622), the reverse of the core's 1.57 to 1.72 [004 README line 84]. - The CME's five region bests lie within 0.75 % of each other (no distance step); its OCM read reps spread 1.5 % (all five) to 7.9 % (OCM3) against the core's 0.2 % (all five) to 1.3 % (OCM1) (recomputed from the rep rows of the same files).

Why it looked wrong. An SLC hit and an OCM read use the same array and the same mesh trip, so they should cost about the same at the node and stream at about the same rate. Instead the OCM read stream is 1.6 to 1.7 times faster than the SLC-served stream, the OCM write is 0.64 times the DRAM-address write, and the two chases differ by 3.5 to 3.8 ns in the OCM's favour. Things that differ besides the memory: - Method. The OCM rows are one pass after a flush, over 4 KiB pages. The DRAM-address rows are 4 to 32 warm passes over 2 MiB huge pages [CSV headers of 004: passes=1 flush_before=1 for OCM, passes=4 to 32 flush_before=0 for DRAM; 004 README line 129]. - The node's service path: locked ways against a hashed SLC lookup (hypothesis; no counter separates them). - The chase comparison is not clean. The per-region OCM rows count 0.77 to 0.94 L3 read refills per load, so some lines arrive before their load and the row understates a single read [002 README line 66]. The all-five OCM chase (1.25 MiB, 1.00 refills per load) reads 1.1 to 1.5 ns ABOVE the 2 MiB SLC chase on every CPU [002 README line 65]. On run 3 the sparse per-region bests from CPU 2 read 21.359 to 25.781 ns, around the SLC row's 24.096 [004 README line 104]. Three hypotheses were recorded (peer transcript; not in the primary files): part of the 2 MiB chain misses the SLC (one miss in ten at 52 ns adds about 3 ns est.); a longer SLC hit path at the node; the /dev/ocm mapping attributes cap the OCM stores. Jesse's reading: the OCM and DRAM rows differ in page size and in flushed-one-pass against warm passes, so the data do not say which of them costs the CME [004 README line 84].

Tests added.

  • Proposed (about 10 ms est. chip time): a 256 KiB DRAM-address read with the OCM method (flush before, one pass) and an OCM region read with the DRAM method (32 warm passes) [not run (run 4 had no bandwidth rows by design [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, Rows dropped]); source: peer transcript, not in the primary files]: whether the method or the node path explains the 1.6 to 1.7x
  • Proposed: the CMN home-node miss event (hns_cache_miss_all) around the 2 MiB chase beside its request counts [not run; source: peer transcript, not in the primary files]: whether part of the 2 MiB chain misses the SLC
  • /dev/ocm mapping attributes: question to Jesse [answered in the platform facts of every README: /dev/ocm maps a region as Normal write-back in 4 KiB pages [001 README line 24; 002 README line 32; 004 README line 37]. Run 4 boot C (007) mapped OCM with the contiguous hint in 64 KiB translations, both the hint and the 64 KiB alignment at once [007 README lines 3 and 33]; it ran no bandwidth rows]: whether the OCM mapping caps stores (the write rate was not re-measured under the 64 KiB mapping)
  • Table 4.6.1 on the core page, combining one-core read and write by level [present on asimov-c1nano-perf.html (section 4.6.1); the edit date 2026-11-04 is from the peer transcript]: presentation only
  • OCM streaming write through the CME (run 3); OCM and DRAM-address bandwidth rows repeated with the L3 on (run 6 boot F1) [run 3 (004) cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv; run 6 F1 (011) bandwidth-ocm-*.csv, cme-bandwidth-ocm-*.csv, bandwidth-dram-1core.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]: the OCM write rate from the CME store path; both read rates with the L3 on

What the tests showed. - Run 3: the CME writes OCM at 19.795 GB/s, like the core's 20.326, while it writes DRAM addresses at 61.971 to 63.865 GB/s [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv, cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. So the OCM write cap is not the core's store path alone. - Run 6 boot F1 (011, the L3 on): the core's OCM read rose to 20.143, 20.042, 19.883, 20.086 and 20.128 GB/s (all five within 1.3 %; the distance dependence vanished) and the all-five read to 19.822 [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, bandwidth-ocm-all5.csv of 011]. The SLC-served 256 KiB read rose to 26.297 GB/s, the 2 MiB read to 25.044 and the 32 MiB read to 24.575 [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011], overtaking the OCM read. So the run 3 ratio of 1.6 to 1.7 belongs partly to the read-stream item (read-stream-rise-l3-on): the OCM reads rose 1.21 to 1.36 times, the DRAM-address reads 2.6 to 2.7 times [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 10]. - F1: the core's OCM write stayed at 20.326 GB/s [bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011]. The CME's OCM write rose to 30.659 GB/s (1.55 times run 3) [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011], while the CME's DRAM-address writes fell to 40.445 to 52.530 GB/s [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]. - F1: the CME's OCM read rose to 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s per region (34.356 over all five), 1.45 to 1.71 times run 3 [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv, -all5.csv of 011; asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]. Against the CME's same-size warm 256 KiB DRAM row (41.562) every region still reads lower (0.81 to 0.96); against its 32 MiB row (36.583) only OCM0 (33.6) and the all-five (34.4) read lower [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011]. The CME's OCM reps spread up to 19.5 % on F1 [011 README line 206]. - Still Insufficient data: why one core writes OCM at 20.3 GB/s instead of 32.0 on every run (run 2 20.433, run 3 20.326, F1 20.326); why the per-region OCM chase reads 3.5 to 3.8 ns below the SLC chase while the all-five OCM chase reads 1.1 to 1.5 ns above it; and why the CME's OCM read sits below its same-size DRAM read. The page-size and flush-against-warm differences were never separated: the two proposed method-swap rows did not run.

4.26 CME L1 chain load 21.4 ns, ten times the core's 2.0 ns, and only 0.37 ns above the register round tripexplained

A CME L1 chain load costs 21.4 ns on run 3, 10.7 times the core's 2.0 ns, and only 0.37 ns above the no-load control.

What looked wrong

  • Through the CME (the Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit, one per DSU, with its own 64 KiB 4-way L1 of 1,024 lines), a 4 KiB chain load cost 21.376 ns per load on run 3. [004 cme-latency-dram-small.csv row 16]
  • That is the best of three reps (21.376, 21.453 and 21.473 ns). [004 cme-latency-dram-small.csv row 16]
  • The core's own 4 KiB chain read 2.002 ns per load on run 3. The CME load is 10.7 times slower. [004 latency-dram-small.csv row 8]
  • The no-load control cme-roundtrip (a DUP then a LASTB, 65,536 round trips per rep) read 21.004 to 21.006 ns per load, 42.00 to 42.01 CME cycles. [cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 012, column cme_cycles_per_load]
  • That held in all 417 reps of the eight boots from run 3 to boot F2. [cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 012, column cme_cycles_per_load]
  • Chain load minus control is 0.372 ns on run 3 and 0.367 ns on boot E. [arithmetic on the rows above]
  • The Arm LLVM scheduling model lists CLASTB (the instruction that copies the last active vector element into a general register) at 12 cycles in streaming mode. [refs/C1Nano-streaming-cme-instructions.s line 104]

Why it looked wrong

  • A 21 ns cost for a hit in a 64 KiB L1 fits no cache-level model. The core's L1 hit costs 2.0 ns on run 3.
  • The run 3 page first said that the 21.0 ns control is part of the 21.4 ns, that every CME instruction pays it, and that it is a floor.
  • Codex review R1 rejected that reading. The chain runs LD1D then LASTB. The control runs DUP then LASTB. [codex-review-run3.md lines 24 to 32, CME-plan.md line 473]
  • No calibration shows that the two dependency chains have the same non-memory cost. So the 0.372 ns difference is valid arithmetic but not a memory latency. [codex-review-run3.md lines 24 to 32, CME-plan.md line 473]
  • The page now calls it 'chain load minus round-trip baseline 0.37 ns, a derived number, not the memory latency'. [asimov-cme-perf.html, Short version]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
cme-roundtrip and cme-call controls in every CME latency filerun 3, boot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot E, boot F1, boot F2The core-to-CME-to-core path with no memory load (cme-roundtrip: 65,536 DUP/LASTB round trips per rep, cme-call: 64 one-load calls per rep), kept as a control and not as a floor [004 README.md line 62].
Chain rows 4 to 64 KiB with data prefetchers offboot B, boot D, boot F2The CME L1 hit with no prefetch refills (IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 set on CPUs 2 to 9 and their CMEs, cme_l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load 0.0000). A result near 21.0 ns would mean the load itself adds almost nothing to the round trip.

What the tests showed

  • Boot B (data prefetchers off): the chain read 21.021 ns per load at 4 KiB and 21.263 ns per load at 64 KiB, best rows. That is 0.02 to 0.26 ns above the 21.004 ns control. [006 bootB cme-latency-dram-small.csv rows 13 to 46]
  • Demand refills were 0.0010 to 0.0156 per load. [006 bootB cme-latency-dram-small.csv rows 13 to 46]
  • Boot D read 21.021 to 21.262 ns per load on the same rows. Boot F2 (the L3 on) read 21.015 to 21.240 ns per load. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 008 and 012, rows 16 and 46]
  • So an L1 hit load costs the round trip plus 0.02 to 0.26 ns. Most of a load's time is the core-to-CME link in both directions. [asimov-cme-run4.html, boot B section]
  • One run 3 cme-call rep read 82.641 ns per call, against 43.609 ns per call in the next rep. That is 39.0 ns more per call, or 2.50 us more per 64-call rep. [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv row 8]
  • The slow rep cost 168.52 core cycles per call against 90.02 (5,024 extra core cycles per rep against the next rep, 5,033 by the README). [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv row 8, 004 README.md line 90]
  • It cost 87.59 CME cycles per call against 81.05 (419 extra CME cycles per rep). [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv row 8]
  • The run 3 README reads the slow rep as a stall while the CME powers up (an inference, not a measurement). [004 README.md lines 89 to 90]
  • In dynamic mode the CME switches itself off about 1.2 to 1.5 us (est., from the RTL: 256 idle CME clocks, then a 1,024-tick timed wait) after both cores leave streaming mode. [004 README.md lines 89 to 90]
  • Those are the reset values of its power register, and nothing on this platform writes that register. [004 README.md lines 89 to 90]
  • The cme-call best values fall in two groups on every boot: 42.5 to 42.8 ns and 43.4 to 43.9 ns per call on run 3 and boots A to E. [007 README.md line 84, 008 README.md line 86, cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 012]
  • On boots A to D the group medians are 42.586 to 42.703 ns and 43.453 to 43.579 ns, 0.86 to 0.90 ns apart. [007 README.md line 84, 008 README.md line 86]
  • Run 6 moved the clock reads into the timed span. Its cme-call reads 124.5 to 125.6 ns per call, again in two groups 1.0 ns apart. [cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 012]

Still open

What part of the 21 ns is memory stays Insufficient data. No row separates the core-to-CME link from the CME L1. A calibration showing that the LD1D chain and the DUP chain have the same non-memory cost would settle it. The cause of the two cme-call groups 0.86 to 1.0 ns apart is also open.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. asimov-bench run 3969 (21.56 ns, quoted in CME-plan.md lines 62 to 63 and the run 3 README line 136); run 3 (membench-jibin-004), ran 2026-11-03 UTC [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 3]

What looked wrong. Through the CME (Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit, one per DSU, with its own 64 KiB 4-way L1 of 1,024 lines) a 4 KiB chain costs 21.376 ns per load [results/membench-jibin-004/results/19700101T000000Z/cme-latency-dram-small.csv row 16, the best of three reps 21.376, 21.453 and 21.473]. The core's 4 KiB row reads 2.002 ns [results/membench-jibin-004/results/19700101T000000Z/latency-dram-small.csv row 8], 10.7 times less. The register-only control (cme-roundtrip: DUP then LASTB, no load, 65,536 round trips per rep) reads 21.004 to 21.006 ns per load in all 417 reps across the eight boots from run 3 to F2, at 42.00 to 42.01 CME cycles per load [cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 012, column cme_cycles_per_load]. Chase minus control is 0.372 ns on run 3 and 0.367 ns on boot E. The Arm LLVM scheduling model lists CLASTB into a general register at 12 cycles in streaming mode [refs/C1Nano-streaming-cme-instructions.s line 104].

Why it looked wrong. A 21 ns cost for a hit in a 64 KiB L1 fits no cache-level model (the core's L1 hit is 2.0 ns). The run 3 page first said that 21.0 ns is part of the 21.4 ns, that every CME instruction pays it, and that it is a floor. Codex review R1 of the run 3 report rejected that: the chase runs LD1D then LASTB, the control runs DUP then LASTB, and no calibration shows the two dependency chains have the same non-memory cost, so the 0.372 ns difference is valid arithmetic but not a memory latency [codex-review-run3.md lines 24 to 32; the same caveat is R2 of the plan review, CME-plan.md line 473]. The page now calls it 'chain load minus round-trip baseline 0.37 ns, a derived number, not the memory latency' [asimov-cme-perf.html, Short version].

Tests added.

  • cme-roundtrip (65,536 DUP/LASTB round trips per rep) and cme-call (64 one-load calls per rep) controls in every --cme latency file [run 3 (004) onward; every CME latency file of 004 to 012]: the core-to-CME-to-core path with no load, kept as a control, not a floor [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 62]
  • Boot B: data prefetchers off on CPUs 2 to 9 and their CMEs (IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28), chain rows 4 to 64 KiB [run 4 boot B (006); repeated on boot D (008) and boot F2 (012, the L3 on)]: the CME L1 hit with no prefetch refills (cme_l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load 0.0000)

What the tests showed. Boot B: 21.021 ns at 4 KiB to 21.263 ns at 64 KiB, best rows, 0.02 to 0.26 ns above the 21.004 ns baseline, with 0.0010 to 0.0156 demand refills per load [results/membench-jibin-006/results/bootB/cme-latency-dram-small.csv rows 13 to 46]. Boot D reads 21.021 to 21.262 ns and boot F2 (L3 on) 21.015 to 21.240 ns on the same rows [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 008 and 012, rows 16 and 46]. So the L1 hit load costs the round trip plus 0.02 to 0.26 ns [asimov-cme-run4.html section on boot B], and most of a load's time is the core-to-CME link both ways. What part of the 21 ns is memory stays Insufficient data: no row separates the link from the CME L1. One run 3 cme-call rep read 82.641 ns per call (39.0 ns per call, 2.50 us per 64-call rep, above the next rep's 43.609 ns), with 168.52 core cycles per call against 90.02 (5,024 extra core cycles per rep by the next rep, 5,033 by the README) and 87.59 CME cycles against 81.05 (419 extra CME cycles) [results/membench-jibin-004/results/19700101T000000Z/cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv row 8]. The run 3 README reads this as a stall while the CME powers up (inference): in dynamic mode the CME switches itself off after about 1.2 to 1.5 us with both cores out of streaming mode (256 idle CME clocks, then a 1,024-tick timed wait, the reset values of its power register, which nothing on this platform writes) [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md lines 89 to 90]. The cme-call best values fall in two groups on every boot: 42.5 to 42.8 ns and 43.4 to 43.9 ns on run 3 and boots A to E, group medians 0.86 to 0.90 ns apart (boot D 42.703 and 43.562; B 42.586 and 43.484; A 42.703 and 43.579; C 42.586 and 43.453) [results/membench-jibin-008/README.md line 86; results/membench-jibin-007/README.md line 84; recomputed from cme-latency-*.csv of 004 to 010]. Run 6 moved the clock reads into the span, so its cme-call reads 124.5 to 125.6 ns, again in two groups 1.0 ns apart [cme-latency-*.csv of 011 and 012]. The cause of the two groups is open.

4.27 CME chain load climbs from 8 KiB with no step at its 64 KiB L1, and refills reach 17 per loadexplained

The CME chain load climbed from 8 KiB with no step at its 64 KiB L1. Refills reached 17 per load.

What looked wrong

  • In run 3 the repeated chain load through the CME (the Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit) read 21.4 ns per load at 4 KiB, 24.2 ns at 8 KiB and 31.6 ns at 16 KiB. [004 cme-latency-dram-small.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv, cme-best rows]
  • It read 47.6 ns at 64 KiB, 53.1 ns at 256 KiB and 70.3 ns at 32 MiB (best rep per footprint). [004 cme-latency-dram-small.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv, cme-best rows]
  • Jesse's README (the result notes of run 3) described the climb as +2.9 ns at 8 KiB, +7.4 ns at 16 KiB, +7.7 ns at 24 KiB and +6.4 ns at 48 KiB. [004 README.md line 63]
  • From 48 to 64 KiB the load rose only +1.5 ns. From 64 to 96 KiB, the first size past the CME L1, it rose +3.4 ns. [004 README.md line 63]
  • The outer-refill event (0x327E, lines brought in from beyond the cluster) read 1.65 to 3.43 per load at 8 KiB and 14.67 to 16.58 per load at 64 to 128 KiB in run 3. [004 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, rows 8192, 65536, 98304, 131072]
  • A chain load does one load per step. So at most one refill per load was expected.
  • Within one footprint the slowest rep had the most outer refills in 7 of the 9 sizes from 4 to 128 KiB in run 3. [004 README.md line 63]

Why it looked wrong

  • The CME L1 (the CME's own first-level data cache) is 64 KiB, 4-way, with 64-byte lines, so 1,024 lines. A chain up to 64 KiB fits in it. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 5.1, citing Arm TRM (technical reference manual) 107831 table 6-1]
  • The load should read flat to 64 KiB and step up after it. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 5.1, citing Arm TRM (technical reference manual) 107831 table 6-1]
  • Run 3 counted only inner refills (event 0x327D, lines from inside the cluster) and outer refills (event 0x327E). These two events cannot tell a demand miss from a prefetch fill.
  • Hypothesis at the time: the CME hardware prefetcher (128 streams, indexed by instruction address, with its own TLB, the address-translation cache) fetches lines a random chain never uses. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 3, citing TRM 107831]
  • Those lines evict the chain's own lines. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 3, citing TRM 107831]

Demand plus prefetch can then be checked against inner plus outer. A high prefetch count would support the prefetcher hypothesis.

What the tests showed

  • Boot A: demand-read plus prefetch refills equal inner plus outer refills within 0.047 per load on every one of the 151 counted CME rows. [recomputed from 005 cme-latency-*.csv, asimov-cme-run4.html section 4]

  • On the DRAM chain-load rows alone the match is within 0.0011 per load (0.03 %). [recomputed from 005 cme-latency-*.csv, asimov-cme-run4.html section 4]
  • Boot A: prefetch refills read 3.1 per load at 8 KiB, 14.7 per load at 32 KiB and 16.0 per load at 64 KiB (means of 3 reps, the best rep at 8 KiB reads 1.89 per load). [005 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, asimov-cme-run4.html section 8]

  • The prefetch count is 2,546 lines or 159 KiB per pass of the 256-line chain, through a 64 KiB cache that needs to hold only 16 KiB. [010 and 006 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, size 16384]
  • The load reads 35.07 ns per load against boot B's 21.07 ns, a gap of 13.99 ns. [010 and 006 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, size 16384]

Still open

The 13.99 ns gap at 16 KiB splits into 7.4 ns est. of demand misses (0.46 misses per load x 16.1 ns per miss, the miss price taken from boot B's 96 KiB row at 16.09 ns above its 16 KiB row) and 6.6 ns est. that no measurement explains. The only explanation on record is the peer session's 2026-11-06 hypothesis that the demand miss queues behind the prefetch fills. This split is not on the generated page. The record names no test that would settle the 6.6 ns est. remainder.

Why it looked wrong. The CME L1 is 64 KiB, 4-way, 64-byte lines, so 1,024 lines [asimov-cme-perf.html section 5.1, citing TRM 107831 table 6-1]. A chain up to 64 KiB fits, so the load should read flat to 64 KiB and step after. Run 3 counted only inner (0x327D) and outer (0x327E) refills, which cannot tell a demand miss from a prefetch fill. What the tests showed. Boot A (005): the demand-read plus prefetch refills equal the inner plus outer refills within 0.047 per load on every one of the 151 counted CME rows, 2.1 % at most where the sum exceeds 0.1 (the worst row is cme-latency-ocm-region3-vary.csv, 256 KiB, rep 2); on the DRAM chase rows alone the match is within 0.0011 per load (0.03 %) [recomputed from cme-latency-*.csv of 005]. Highlighted: CME, CME-prefetcher.

4.28 CME refills counted 'from inside the cluster' while the L3 held no data: zero on 19 of 104 run 3 rows, 2.1 to 2.8 per load at 32 to 64 KiB on boot Apartly explained

The CME counted 2 to 3 inner refills per load on boot A, although the L3 held no data and the partner core was offline.

What looked wrong

  • Run 3 (results folder 004, ran 2026-11-03 UTC) has 104 timed CME load rows (the CME is the per-cluster streaming unit that walks a chain of loads). 19 of them count zero inner refills (event 0x327D, line fills served from inside the cluster). [gen_run3.py lines 361 to 366, and codex-review-run3.md R10a]
  • The outer event (0x327E, line fills served from outside the cluster) is above zero in all 104 rows. [gen_run3.py lines 361 to 366]
  • All 19 zero rows are sparse OCM (on-chip memory) passes: 6 in the all5 file (lines 14 to 19, the 1.25 MiB chain), 3 each in region0, region1 and region2, and 4 in region3. [004 cme-latency-ocm-*.csv: region0 lines 14, 16, 19, region1 lines 16, 17, 19, region2 lines 14, 16, 18, region3 lines 14, 15, 16, 19]
  • The run 3 CME page had said both refill events are nonzero wherever the CME loads memory. [codex-review-run3.md section 2 counter validity row]
  • The same run 3 per-region sparse OCM passes count 1.0000 to 1.0312 outer refills per load. The all5 sparse passes count 1.0375 to 1.1031 outer refills per load. [004 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv and cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv, the 7 cme-fresh rows of each]
  • Boot A (005, ran 2026-11-04 UTC): the best rep (the best of three repetitions) counts 2.413 inner and 12.964 outer refills per load at 32 KiB (15.4 refills per load in all). [005 cme-latency-dram-small.csv lines 34, 38, 43, and asimov-cme-run4.html table 3.1]
  • The best rep counts 2.811 inner refills per load at 48 KiB and 2.079 at 64 KiB. [005 cme-latency-dram-small.csv lines 34, 38, 43, and asimov-cme-run4.html table 3.1]
  • As a mean over three reps, the inner share (inner refills divided by inner plus outer) on boot A is 15.8 / 15.2 / 15.8 / 14.8 % at 8 / 16 / 32 / 48 KiB. [005 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, recomputed]
  • On boot C (007) the inner share is 15.1 / 16.8 / 15.8 / 15.7 / 15.6 % at 8 / 16 / 24 / 32 / 48 KiB. [007 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, recomputed]
  • On runs 1 to 3 and boots A to D the DSU (a two-core cluster with a shared L3) L3s of CPUs 2 to 9 were in snoop-filter-only mode (the L3 tracks which lines other caches hold but stores no data). [Jesse's boot B README]
  • Boot B's core counter l3d_hit_rd_per_load reads 0.0000 L3 read hits per load in all 21 rows. [006 latency-dram-small-l3.csv]
  • CPU 3, the other core of CPU 2's cluster, was offline for the whole script on run 3 and on every boot. [run 3 README line 45, and boot A README line 17]

Why it looked wrong

  • With the L3 holding no data and the partner core offline, nothing inside the cluster should supply a line. So inner refills were expected near zero on every row.
  • The zero-inner rows on the run 3 sparse OCM passes fit service from outside the cluster. They contradicted only the page wording. So the page needed a fix, not the data.
  • The 2 to 3 inner refills per load on boot A (about 15 % of all refills at 8 to 48 KiB) had no named source in the result files.
  • The run 4 CME page does not agree with itself. Section 4 labels boot A's 2.4 inner refills per load at 32 KiB as "(the DSU's L3)". [asimov-cme-run4.html section 4]
  • Section 9.1 says boot A's inner refills "were read as the other core's caches or nothing (section 4)". [asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Run 3 report wording fixed to state the refill countsrun 3No measurement. The run 3 CME report's section 2 now states the counts (outer nonzero in all 104 timed load rows, inner zero on 19 OCM passes). Outside-cluster service fits those counts. The count lives in gen_run3.py (CME_TIMED, CME_INNER_ZERO, lines 361 to 366). The current asimov-cme-perf.html is the boot E version and no longer carries this count. [codex-review-run3.md, R10a response, 2026-11-03]
Boot E, L3 full mode: inner against outer refills by chain sizeboot EMeasures the inner share with the L3 holding data (SCP, the system control processor, firmware 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1, local commit 28663ab). The comparison is with boot C (same program, stock SCP firmware). A rise in the inner share would mean the L3 now supplies lines. No rise would mean the inner refills come from something else. [010, 2026-11-05]
L3 events 0x328E hit, 0x328F miss, 0x3290 refill beside 0x327D, 0x327Eboot F1, boot F2Measures which inner refills are L3 hits and which are something else inside the cluster, with the prefetchers on (F1) and off (F2). A nonzero 'miss minus refill' would mean lines came from a source that is neither the L3 nor outside the cluster. [011 and 012, 2026-11-06 and 2026-11-07, exploratory]

What the tests showed

  • On boot E (010, L3 full mode) the inner share as a mean over three reps rises to 99.5 / 88.0 / 53.0 / 48.8 / 33.4 % at 8 / 16 / 32 / 48 / 64 KiB (the page rounds these to 100 / 88 / 53 / 33 %). [010 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, and asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]
  • At 8 KiB boot E counts 3.98 inner and 0.02 outer refills per load. Boot C (007) counts 0.59 inner and 3.33 outer refills per load at 8 KiB. [010 and 007 cme-latency-dram-small.csv]
  • The page reads boot E's inner refills as L3 hits. [asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]
  • On F2 (012), hit plus miss equals inner plus outer in every row. [Jesse's F2 README, 'The CME L3 events']
  • Refill equals outer in every row, by construction (the reading of the RTL, the hardware design source: event 0x3290 is the same signal as 0x327E). [Jesse's F2 README, 'The CME L3 events']
  • On F2 'miss minus refill' in the best rep is 0.845 per load at 96 KiB and 0.321 per load at 384 KiB. [012 cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv lines 50 and 68, and asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.7]
  • The L3 hit count at the same rows is 0.141 and 0.637 per load. [012 cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv lines 50 and 68, and asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.7]
  • By the pre-queue check's reading of the RTL, 'miss minus refill' lines are lines a core's cache supplied.
  • CPU 2 wrote the chain with core stores. So a small chain is still in CPU 2's L2 when the CME walks it.
  • By that reading, boot A's inner refills were snoops (reads served by another cache inside the cluster) from CPU 2's caches.
  • A least-squares split over F2's 15 reps from 96 to 384 KiB (ns per load = a + hits x h + snoops x s + outer x o) gives a 23.4, h 6.7, s 13.9, o 20.4 ns est. per load, with rms 0.019 ns. [012 cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv, recomputed]
  • The three count columns sum to about one per row. So the split is collinear and is a hypothesis, not a measurement. [asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.7 caption]

Still open

The run 4 CME page leaves boot A's inner-refill source unresolved ("the other core's caches or nothing", section 9.1). No row isolates the snoop cost from the L3 hit cost. A chain the core never wrote (a hit-only control) is in no run. That measurement would separate the two. [asimov-cme-perf.html, 'Insufficient data: the L3-event split']

All 19 zero rows are sparse OCM passes: 6 in cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv (lines 14 to 19, the 1.25 MiB chain), 3 each in cme-latency-ocm-region0.csv (lines 14, 16, 19: passes 2, 4, 7), region1 (lines 16, 17, 19), region2 (lines 14, 16, 18) and 4 in region3 (lines 14, 15, 16, 19) of 004. The run 3 CME page had said both refill events are nonzero wherever the CME loads memory [codex-review-run3.md, section 2 counter validity row]. The same run 3 per-region sparse OCM passes count 1.0000 to 1.0312 outer refills per load (the all5 passes 1.0375 to 1.1031). Boot A: the repeated chase counts 2.413 inner and 12.964 outer refills per load in the best rep at 32 KiB (15.4 in all), 2.811 inner at 48 KiB and 2.079 at 64 KiB [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, lines 34, 38, 43]. As a mean over the three reps the inner share on boot A is 15.8 / 15.2 / 15.8 / 14.8 % at 8 / 16 / 32 / 48 KiB, and on boot C 15.1 / 16.8 / 15.8 / 15.7 / 15.6 % at 8 / 16 / 24 / 32 / 48 KiB [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005 and 007]. On runs 1 to 3 and boots A to D the DSU L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 was in snoop-filter-only mode: boot B's core hit counters read l3d_hit_rd_per_load 0.0000 in all 21 rows of latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 006 [Jesse's boot B README, 'What his rows show']. CPU 3, the cluster's other core, was offline for the whole script on run 3 and on every boot [Jesse's run 3 README line 45; boot A README line 17].

Why it looked wrong. With the L3 holding no data and the partner core offline, nothing inside the cluster should supply a line. So inner refills were expected near zero on every row. The zero-inner rows on sparse OCM passes fit service from outside the cluster and only needed the page wording fixed. The 2 to 3 inner refills per load on boot A (about 15 % of all refills at 8 to 48 KiB) had no named source in the files. The run 4 CME page section 4 labels the 2.4 inner refills per load at 32 KiB as '(the DSU's L3)', and its section 9.1 says boot A's inner refills 'were read as the other core's caches or nothing (section 4)'. The two sections do not agree.

Tests added.

  • Page wording fixed: the run 3 CME report's section 2 states the counts (outer nonzero in all 104 timed load rows, inner zero on 19 OCM passes, which outside-cluster service fits). The count is computed in gen_run3.py (CME_TIMED, CME_INNER_ZERO, lines 361 to 366). The current asimov-cme-perf.html is the boot E version and no longer carries this count. [run 3 report fix, 2026-11-03 (codex-review-run3.md, R10a response)]: none
  • Boot E: L3 full mode (SCP 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1, local commit 28663ab), inner against outer refills per load by footprint, compared with boot C (same program, stock SCP) [run 4 boot E (010), 2026-11-05]: the inner share with the L3 holding data
  • CME L3 events 0x328E hit, 0x328F miss, 0x3290 refill (exploratory) beside 0x327D and 0x327E, with the prefetchers on (F1) and off (F2) [run 6 boots F1 (011) and F2 (012), 2026-11-06 and 07]: which inner refills are L3 hits and which are something else inside the cluster

What the tests showed. On boot E the inner share (mean over three reps) rises to 99.5 / 88.0 / 53.0 / 48.8 / 33.4 % at 8 / 16 / 32 / 48 / 64 KiB (the page rounds these to 100 / 88 / 53 / 33 %). At 8 KiB boot E counts 3.98 inner and 0.02 outer refills per load, boot C 0.59 and 3.33 [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007; asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]. The page reads boot E's inner refills as L3 hits. On F2 hit plus miss equals inner plus outer in every row, and refill equals outer, by construction (the RTL reading: 0x3290 is the same signal as 0x327E) [Jesse's F2 README, 'The CME L3 events']. 'Miss minus refill' in the best rep is 0.845 per load at 96 KiB and 0.321 at 384 KiB (the hit count 0.141 and 0.637) [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012, lines 50 and 68; asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.7]. By the pre-queue check's reading of the RTL these are lines a core's cache supplied: CPU 2 wrote the chain with core stores, so a small chain is still in CPU 2's L2 when the CME walks it. By that reading boot A's inner refills were snoops from CPU 2's caches. The run 4 CME page leaves boot A's source unresolved ('the other core's caches or nothing', section 9.1). No row isolates the snoop cost from the L3 hit. The least-squares split over F2's 15 reps from 96 to 384 KiB, ns per load = a + hits x h + snoops x s + outer x o, recomputed: a 23.4, h 6.7, s 13.9, o 20.4 ns est., rms 0.019 ns; the three count columns sum to about one per row, so the split is collinear and a hypothesis [asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.7 caption]. A chain the core never wrote (a hit-only control) is in no run [asimov-cme-perf.html, 'Insufficient data: the L3-event split'].
