4.29 CME flushed 8 MiB row (62.6 ns) reads below the walked-once 32 MiB row (70.3 ns), the reverse of the coreexplained

In run 3 the CME's flushed 8 MiB chain read 62.6 ns per load, below the walked-once 32 MiB chain at 70.3 ns.

What looked wrong

  • In run 3 the CME's flushed 8 MiB chain read 62.576 ns per load. The walked-once 8 MiB chain read 66.246 ns per load. [004 cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv, cme-best rows]
  • So the flushed row sat 3.7 ns per load below the walked-once row of the same size.
  • The CME's walked-once chains kept getting slower past every cache, 68.709 ns per load at 16 MiB and 70.345 ns per load at 32 MiB. [004 cme-latency-dram-large.csv, cme-best rows]
  • The core showed the opposite order in run 3. Its flushed 8 MiB row read 52.738 ns per load, 7.7 ns per load above its walked-once 8 MiB row at 45.077 ns. [004 latency-dram-flushed.csv and latency-dram-large.csv, best rows]
  • It was level with the core's walked-once 32 MiB row at 52.185 ns per load. [004 latency-dram-flushed.csv and latency-dram-large.csv, best rows]
  • The flushed CME row counted 3.48 to 3.52 outer refills per load in run 3. Jesse's run 3 README expected about 1 per load. [004 cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv rows cme-fresh1 and cme-fresh2, column cme_l1d_refill_outer_per_load, and 004 README.md line 64]
  • The CME's walked-once 512 KiB, 768 KiB and 1 MiB chains read 44.893, 47.405 and 50.827 ns per load in run 3. [004 cme-latency-dram-large.csv, cme-best rows]
  • The repeated 96 to 384 KiB walks read 50.966 to 55.412 ns per load. [004 cme-latency-dram-small.csv, cme-best rows]
  • So a larger footprint read faster than a smaller one.

Why it looked wrong

  • Beyond the SLC (the 3.75 MiB cache on the mesh) both chain forms should pay the same DRAM time per load.
  • A flushed chain cannot read faster than a never-seen chain unless something fills its lines before the load arrives.
  • A footprint that outgrows a cache should not read faster than a footprint that fits in that cache.
  • A flushed walk should count about one outer refill per load, not 3.5.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
CME refill-cause counters on every CME chain rowboot ASplits the refills per load into demand reads (event 0x3280), hardware prefetches (event 0x32B2) and writes (event 0x3281). A count above one per load can then be assigned to the prefetcher or to demand misses.
Address-order 8 MiB flushed chain through the CMEboot A, boot B, boot EShows whether the CME prefetcher hides the DRAM time on a chain whose addresses rise in order, as a reference for the random chain (file cme-latency-dram-seq.csv).
CME and core data prefetchers off, L3 offboot BGives the demand-only reading of the flushed row and of every other CME chain row. Any drop with the prefetchers on is then the prefetcher's work. The prefetchers are turned off through a TF-A hook.
L3 on, prefetchers on (F1) and off (F2)boot F1, boot F2Separates the prefetcher from the L3 as the cause of the flushed row's value. Also gives the L3-served reading of the 96 to 384 KiB rows.

What the tests showed

  • On boot A the CME made 0.9931 demand and 2.5532 to 2.5925 prefetch refills per load on the flushed 8 MiB row. [005 bootA cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
  • The core made 0.0000 prefetch refills per load on its flushed row. [005 bootA latency-dram-flushed.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
  • So the CME prefetcher runs on a random chain and the core's prefetcher does not.
  • With the prefetchers off the flushed 8 MiB row read 71.711 ns per load (boot B) and 71.714 ns per load (boot F2). [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv cme-best rows of 005, 006, 010, 011, 012]
  • The boot B value is 18.972 ns per load above the core's 52.739 ns per load. [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv cme-best rows of 005, 006, 010, 011, 012, and 006 bootB latency-dram-flushed.csv best row]
  • With the prefetchers on it read 62.551 ns (boot A), 62.053 ns (boot E) and 62.080 ns (boot F1). [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv cme-best rows of 005, 006, 010, 011, 012]
  • So the prefetcher cuts the flushed row by 12.8 % (B against A), 13.4 % (F2 against F1) and 13.5 % (B against E) of the prefetcher-off value. [computed from the flushed cme-best rows of 005, 006, 010, 011, 012]
  • The L3 does not set the row. Boot B (L3 off) and boot F2 (L3 on) agree within 0.003 ns per load. [computed from the flushed cme-best rows of 005, 006, 010, 011, 012]
  • On boot A the prefetcher filled 15.14 to 17.05 lines per load on the repeated 96 to 384 KiB walks (14.2 to 15.1 lines per load on boot E). [005 bootA cme-latency-dram-small.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv, column cme_l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load, and the asimov-cme-perf.html refill chart for boot E]
  • The walked-once 512 KiB to 4 MiB rows carried 5.17 to 6.52 prefetch fills per load on boot A. [005 bootA cme-latency-dram-small.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv, column cme_l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load, and the asimov-cme-perf.html refill chart for boot E]
  • That extra traffic is why the small repeated walks were slow.
  • With the prefetchers off (boot F2) the rows read in the expected order, slower as the footprint grows.
  • The CME read 32.779 to 35.979 ns per load at 96 to 384 KiB (one outer refill per load), 37.691 ns at 512 KiB and 42.960 ns at 2 MiB. [012 bootF2 cme-latency-dram-small.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv, cme-best rows]
  • It read 62.826 ns at 8 MiB walked once, 71.068 ns at 32 MiB, and 71.714 ns at 8 MiB flushed. [012 bootF2 cme-latency-dram-large.csv and cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv, cme-best rows]
  • The address-order 8 MiB flushed chain read 21.417 ns per load with the prefetcher on (boots A and E) and 71.740 ns per load with it off (boot B). [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv cme-best rows of 005, 006, 010]
  • So on an address-order chain the prefetcher hides the whole DRAM time.

Still open

The files do not show which of the prefetched lines the random flushed walk used. A count of prefetched lines that a later demand load hit would settle that [012 README.md line 140]. On boot F2 the flushed row still reads 0.65 ns per load above the 32 MiB walked-once row (71.714 against 71.068 ns per load). The sources do not explain that small gap.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 (membench-jibin-004). Jesse's run 3 README raised the refill count on the flushed row (README.md of 004, line 64). The user asked the peer session on 2026-11-03 23:26 whether fresh and flushed rows should read alike (transcript-peer, the scratch copy, line 1331).

What looked wrong. Through the CME (the C1-SME2 streaming unit of the cluster) the flushed 8 MiB chain (every line cleaned and invalidated before each timed pass) reads 62.576 ns per load. The walked-once 8 MiB chain reads 66.246 ns, the 16 MiB 68.709 and the 32 MiB 70.345. So the flushed row is 3.7 ns below the unflushed 8 MiB row, and the latency keeps rising past every cache. The core's rows do the opposite. On the core the flushed 8 MiB row (52.738 ns) is 7.7 ns above its walked-once 8 MiB row (45.077 ns), and it meets the 32 MiB row (52.185 ns). The flushed CME row counts 3.48 to 3.52 outer refills per load, where Jesse's README expected about 1. The CME's walked-once 512 KiB to 1 MiB chains (44.9 to 50.8 ns) also read below the repeated 96 to 384 KiB walks (51.0 to 55.4 ns), a larger footprint reading faster than a smaller one.

Why it looked wrong. Beyond the SLC (the 3.75 MiB mesh cache) both chain forms should pay the same DRAM time. A flushed chain cannot be faster than an unseen one unless something fills its lines ahead of the load. A footprint that outgrows a cache should not read faster than one that fits it. And a flushed walk should count about one outer refill per load, not 3.5.

Tests added.

  • CME refill-cause events (demand read 0x3280, hardware prefetch 0x32B2, write 0x3281) on every CME chain row, beside the inner and outer refill counts [run 4 boot A (005)]: how many of the refills per load are prefetches and how many are demand misses
  • Sequential (address-order) 8 MiB flushed chain through the CME (cme-latency-dram-seq.csv) [run 4 boot A (005), boot B (006), boot E (010)]: whether the CME prefetcher hides DRAM on an address-order chain, as a reference for the random one
  • CME and core data prefetchers off through a TF-A hook, the L3 off [run 4 boot B (006)]: the demand-only reading of the flushed row and of every other CME chain row
  • L3 on with the prefetchers on (F1) and off (F2) [run 6 boots F1 (011) and F2 (012)]: whether the prefetcher or the L3 sets the flushed row; the L3-served reading of the 96 to 384 KiB rows

What the tests showed. Boot A counted the cause of the refills. On the flushed 8 MiB row the CME made 0.99 demand refills and 2.55 to 2.59 prefetch refills per load. On the 32 MiB row it made 1.00 demand and 2.68 prefetch refills per load. The core made 0.0000 prefetch refills per load on its flushed row. So the CME prefetcher runs on a random chain and the core's does not. With the prefetchers off the flushed row reads 71.711 ns (boot B) and 71.714 ns (F2). With them on it reads 62.551 ns (A), 62.053 (E) and 62.080 (F1). So the prefetcher cuts the flushed row by 12.8 to 13.5 % (B against A 12.8 %, F2 against F1 13.4 %). The L3 does not set it: B (L3 off) and F2 (L3 on) agree within 0.003 ns. The repeated 96 to 384 KiB walks were slow because the prefetcher filled 15.1 to 17.1 lines per load there on boot A (14.2 to 15.1 on boot E). The walked-once 512 KiB to 4 MiB rows carried 5.2 to 6.5 prefetch fills per load. With the prefetchers off (F2) the order of the hierarchy returns: 32.8 to 36.0 ns at 96 to 384 KiB (one outer refill per load, served inside the cluster), 37.7 at 512 KiB, 43.0 at 2 MiB, 62.8 at 8 MiB walked once, 71.1 at 32 MiB, 71.7 flushed. The sequential 8 MiB flushed chain reads 21.417 ns with the prefetcher on (A, E) and 71.740 with it off (B), so on an address-order chain the prefetcher hides the whole DRAM time. Which of the prefetched lines the random flushed walk used, the files do not show (README of 012, line 140). On F2 the flushed row still reads 0.65 ns above the 32 MiB walked-once row (71.714 against 71.068); the sources do not explain that small gap. The CME path adds 19.0 ns to a DRAM load over the core's (71.711 against 52.739 on boot B).

4.30 OCM through the CME: 9.6 to 18.0 ns above the core, sparse fastest, no order by mesh distanceexplained

OCM loads through the CME read 9.6 to 18.0 ns above the core. The sparse chain was fastest. The rows showed no order by mesh distance.

What looked wrong

  • On run 3 the one-line-per-page (sparse) OCM (on-chip memory, held at the mesh home nodes) rows were read through the CME (the streaming unit attached to each core cluster).
  • Those rows read 35.469 to 38.516 ns per load, best of 7 passes. [004 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • CPU 2's own loads of the same chains read 21.359 to 25.781 ns per load. [004 latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv]
  • The all-five every-line (dense) row read 44.688 ns per load through the CME against 25.340 ns on the core. [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5-dense.csv, latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv]
  • The run 3 rows did not order by mesh distance (the number of crosspoints between the cluster and the home node). [004 README line 66]
  • By pass median, OCM4 (3 crosspoints away) was lowest at 38.609 ns per load. OCM0 (1 crosspoint) was highest at 42.984 ns. [medians from the 7 cme-fresh rows]
  • By best pass, OCM2 (1 crosspoint) was fastest at 35.469 ns. OCM0 (1 crosspoint) was slowest at 38.516 ns. [004 README line 66]
  • The 7 passes of one region on run 3 spread 6.1 to 10.7 ns per load. Two extra crosspoints cost the core only 2.2 to 2.8 ns per load on run 2. [004 README line 66]
  • On run 4 boot A the chain shapes ordered the reverse of the core. [005 cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv, asimov-cme-run4.html section 6]
  • Sparse rows read 34.625 to 35.906 ns per load. Dense rows read 38.318 to 42.171 ns (3.2 to 6.3 ns above sparse). [005 cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv]
  • Vary rows read 45.391 to 48.813 ns (10.5 to 12.9 ns above sparse). [005 cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv]
  • On the core the dense chain is fastest. The sparse chain is slowest. [asimov-cme-run4.html section 6]
  • On run 4 boot E the OCM1 row read 28.984 ns per load. OCM0 and OCM2, at the same distance, read 37.156 and 35.969 ns. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region0..2.csv]
  • On boot E, OCM through the CME cost 9.62 ns (OCM1) to 18.03 ns (OCM4) more per load than from the core on the sparse rows. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region0..2.csv, asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]

Why it looked wrong

  • Rows at one mesh distance should read alike. On run 3, OCM0 and OCM2 are both 1 crosspoint away.
  • Their best passes differed (38.516 against 35.469 ns per load). [004 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • The CME path should add a fixed amount over the core's path. Instead the gap changed from region to region and from pass to pass. [004 README line 66]
  • The refill-cause counters of boot A show why. [005 cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv, asimov-cme-run4.html table 3.2 and section 6]
  • On the sparse rows the CME counted 0.46 to 0.63 demand-read refills (L1 lines fetched because a load missed) per load, as pass means.
  • It also counted 0.39 to 0.56 hardware-prefetch refills (L1 lines fetched by the CME prefetcher ahead of any load) per load, as pass means.
  • So 37 to 54 percent of the sparse loads were L1 hits on lines the prefetcher had already fetched (the page's hypothesis).
  • The dense rows counted 0.80 to 0.81 demand and 1.40 to 1.47 prefetch refills per load. The vary rows counted 0.92 to 0.94 demand refills per load. [005 cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv]
  • The prefetcher's fills hid the demand latency by a different fraction on each pass and each region. [asimov-cme-run4.html section 6]
  • The best pass of a row is therefore the pass where the prefetcher caught the most lines, not the demand latency. [asimov-cme-run4.html section 6]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
CME sparse, dense and vary OCM rows with refill-cause eventsboot ACounts demand-read refills (event 0x3280), hardware-prefetch refills (0x32B2) and write refills (0x3281) per load for each chain shape. Fewer than 1.0 demand refills per load means some loads hit lines the prefetcher had already fetched. [005 cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv]
CME prefetcher off, then off with L3 on and in-span stampsboot B, boot F2Reads the demand-only OCM latency through the CME, by the bracket (the whole timed call) and inside the streaming span (the loads alone). Rows that order by distance with 1.000 demand refills per load mean the prefetcher caused the run 3 disorder. [006 and 012 cme-latency-ocm-region*.csv]
OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations, prefetchers on and offboot C, boot DChecks the TLB (address translation cache) effect through the CME. A ratio near 1.0 against boots A and B means page translations do not explain the CME's extra cost. [007 and 008 cme-latency-ocm-*.csv]
L3 on through a rebuilt SCP, prefetchers onboot E, boot F1Checks whether the L3 (the per-cluster cache) serves the CME's OCM loads, by comparing inner refills (event 0x327D) with outer refills (0x327E). Inner refills near 0 per load mean the L3 does not serve them. [010 and 011 cme-latency-ocm-*.csv]

What the tests showed

  • With the CME prefetcher off, every pass counted 1.000 demand refills and 0.000 prefetch refills per load. The rows ordered by distance. [006 and 012 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • Boot B read 46.984 to 48.047 ns per load at 1 crosspoint and 50.328 to 52.047 ns at 3 crosspoints. [006 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • Boot F2 read 47.906 to 48.859 ns at 1 crosspoint and 51.734 to 52.109 ns at 3. [012 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • The pass spread fell to 0.1 to 0.7 ns per region on boots B and F2, from 6.1 to 10.7 ns on run 3. [006 and 012 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • On boot F2 the demand-only OCM load through the CME read 47.906 to 52.109 ns per load by the bracket and 43.453 to 47.734 ns inside the streaming span. [012 ns_per_load_span column, asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]
  • The difference, 4.375 to 4.468 ns per load of a 64-load pass, is call cost outside the span. [012 ns_per_load_span column, asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]
  • Boot F2 read 1.001 to 1.028 times boot B per region. So the L3 does not change OCM through the CME. [006 and 012 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • F2 counted 1.000 outer refills per load, none served by the L3. With the prefetchers on, F2 read 1.257 to 1.343 times F1 per region. [012 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, 012 README line 141]
  • The 64 KiB contiguous translations changed little through the CME. Boot D against boot B read 0.978 to 1.000 on the sparse rows, boot C against boot A 0.962 to 1.069. [007 and 008 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • Boot C sparse rows read 33.359 to 37.953 ns per load, boot D 46.641 to 51.328 ns. [007 and 008 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv]
  • The page gives the CME's own TLB as the reason. [asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.2, C1-SME2 TRM 107831]
  • Boot E's OCM1 best pass, 28.984 ns per load, is pass cme-fresh5. That pass counted 0.125 demand refills and 0.906 prefetch refills per load. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region1.csv rows cme-fresh1..7]
  • The other six passes of the row read 36.625 to 42.531 ns per load with 0.469 to 0.797 demand refills per load. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region1.csv rows cme-fresh1..7]
  • So on that one pass the prefetcher fetched about 0.9 of the chain's lines before the demand loads reached them.
  • On run 3 the OCM read through the CME ran at 0.62 times its warm DRAM-buffer rate, the reverse of the core. [004 README line 84]
  • The two rows differ in page size and in flushing. So the data do not say which of the two costs the CME. [CME-plan.md lines 64 and 439]
  • The asimov-bench reference OCM chase through the CME is 34.8 ns per load. The page compares it with boot E's 29.0 to 37.7 ns. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 8]

Still open

Why the prefetcher caught about 0.9 of the lines on boot E's OCM1 pass cme-fresh5 is not in the files. The pages do not name this counter reading. A repeat of that row with the refill-cause events on every pass would show whether a 0.125 demand-refill pass recurs. A run with the page size and the flushing changed one at a time would show which of the two costs the CME on the 0.62 bandwidth ratio.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 (004), 2026-11-03 (UTC) [results/membench-jibin-004/README.md line 66]; the three chain shapes compared on run 4 boot A (005), 2026-11-04 (UTC) [asimov-cme-run4.html section 3.2 and 6]

What looked wrong. On run 3 the one line per page (sparse) OCM rows read 35.469 to 38.516 ns per load through the CME [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 004, cme-best rows]. CPU 2's own loads of the same chains read 21.359 to 25.781 ns [latency-ocm-region0..4-cpu2.csv of 004]. The per-region pass medians did not order by mesh distance: OCM4 (3 crosspoints away) had the lowest median, 38.609 ns, and OCM0 (1 crosspoint) the highest, 42.984 ns [README 004 line 66; medians recomputed from the 7 cme-fresh rows]. By best pass OCM2 (1 crosspoint) was fastest at 35.469 ns and OCM0 (1 crosspoint) slowest at 38.516 ns. The 7 passes of one region spread 6.1 to 10.7 ns, more than the 2.2 to 2.8 ns that two extra crosspoints cost the core [README 004 line 66]. The every-line (dense) all-five row read 44.688 ns through the CME against the core's 25.340 ns [cme-latency-ocm-all5-dense.csv and latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 004]. On boot A the sparse rows read 34.625 to 35.906 ns, the dense rows 38.318 to 42.171 ns (3.2 to 6.3 ns above sparse) and the vary rows 45.391 to 48.813 ns (10.5 to 12.9 ns above sparse) [cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv of 005]. On the core the dense chain is fastest and the sparse slowest, so the CME's order is the reverse [asimov-cme-run4.html section 6]. On boot E the OCM1 row read 28.984 ns while OCM0 and OCM2, at the same distance, read 37.156 and 35.969 ns [cme-latency-ocm-region0..2.csv of 010]. On boot E OCM through the CME costs 9.6 to 18.0 ns more per load than from the core on the one line per page rows [asimov-cme-perf.html section 7].

Why it looked wrong. Rows at one mesh distance should read alike. The CME path should add a fixed amount over the core's path. The refill-cause counters of boot A show why they did not. On the sparse rows the CME counted only 0.46 to 0.63 demand-read refills per load (pass means) and 0.39 to 0.56 hardware-prefetch refills per load [asimov-cme-run4.html table 3.2; recomputed from the 7 cme-fresh rows of cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 005]. So 37 to 54 % of the sparse loads were L1 hits on lines the CME prefetcher had already fetched (page hypothesis, section 6). The dense rows counted 0.80 to 0.81 demand and 1.40 to 1.47 prefetch refills per load, and the vary rows 0.92 to 0.94 demand refills per load [same files]. The prefetcher's fills hid the demand latency, by a different fraction on each pass and each region. The best pass of a row is therefore the pass where the prefetcher caught the most lines, not the demand latency.

Tests added.

  • CME sparse, dense and vary OCM rows with the refill-cause events (0x3280 demand read, 0x32B2 hardware prefetch, 0x3281 write) [run 4 boot A (005), 2026-11-04]: demand against prefetch refills per load for each chain shape [cme-latency-ocm-region*{,-dense,-vary}.csv of 005]
  • CME prefetcher off (boot B); prefetcher off with the L3 on and in-span clock stamps (F2) [run 4 boot B (006, 2026-11-04 and 05); run 6 boot F2 (012)]: demand-only OCM latency through the CME, by the bracket and inside the streaming span [cme-latency-ocm-region*.csv of 006 and 012]
  • OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations, prefetchers on (C) and off (D) [run 4 boots C (007) and D (008), 2026-11-05]: the TLB effect through the CME [cme-latency-ocm-*.csv of 007 and 008]
  • L3 on through a rebuilt SCP, prefetchers on (E, F1) [run 4 boot E (010), run 6 boot F1 (011)]: whether the L3 serves the CME's OCM loads (inner refills 0x327D against outer 0x327E) [cme-latency-ocm-*.csv of 010 and 011]

What the tests showed. With the CME prefetcher off, every pass counts 1.000 demand refills and 0.000 prefetch refills per load, and the rows order by distance. Boot B: 46.984 to 48.047 ns at 1 crosspoint and 50.328 to 52.047 ns at 3 crosspoints [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 006]. F2: 47.906 to 48.813 ns at 1 crosspoint and 51.734 to 52.109 ns at 3 [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 012]. The pass spread falls to 0.1 to 0.7 ns per region (boot B and F2) from 6.1 to 10.7 ns on run 3. The demand-only OCM load through the CME is 47.906 to 52.109 ns by the bracket on F2, and 43.453 to 47.734 ns inside the streaming span; 4.4 to 4.5 ns per load of each 64-load pass is call cost outside the span [ns_per_load_span column of 012; asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]. F2 reads 1.001 to 1.028 times boot B, so the L3 does not change OCM through the CME; F2 counts 1.000 outer refills per load, none served by the L3 [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 006 and 012]. With the prefetchers on, F2 reads 1.257 to 1.343 times F1 per region [README 012 line 141]. The 64 KiB contiguous translations change little through the CME: boot D against boot B reads 0.978 to 1.000 on the sparse rows, boot C against boot A 0.962 to 1.069; boot C sparse 33.359 to 37.953 ns, boot D 46.641 to 51.328 ns [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 007 and 008; asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.2]. The page gives the CME's own TLB as the reason [C1-SME2 TRM 107831]. Boot E's OCM1 best pass, 28.984 ns, is the pass cme-fresh5, which counts 0.125 demand refills and 0.906 prefetch refills per load; the other six passes of that row read 36.625 to 42.531 ns with 0.469 to 0.797 demand refills per load [cme-latency-ocm-region1.csv of 010]. So on that one pass the prefetcher fetched about 0.9 of the chain's lines before the demand loads reached them. Why the prefetcher caught so many lines on that pass is not in the files. The pages do not name this counter reading. The OCM read through the CME runs at 0.62 times its warm DRAM-buffer rate on run 3, the reverse of the core; the rows differ in page size and in flushing, so the data do not say which costs the CME [README 004 line 84].

Highlighted: CME, CME-prefetcher, OCM, home-node, mesh.

4.31 CME OCM reads put 1.42 to 1.52 times the core's requests on the home node (run 3); with the L3 on, the dense OCM chains through the CME read 7 to 15 % faster, and the CME OCM reads' home-node requests fall to about halfpartly explained

CME OCM reads sent 1.42 to 1.52 times the core's requests to the home node (run 3). With the L3 on (F1) they sent about half.

What looked wrong

  • Run 3 (004): around the CME's OCM read commands the region's home node received 108,075 to 109,528 requests. Around the core's same commands it received 71,687 to 76,534 requests. [004 cmn-counts.csv rows cme-ocm-read-region<r> and ocm-read-region<r>, event hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all, own node]
  • That is 1.42 to 1.52 times (regions 0 to 4: 1.505, 1.508, 1.511, 1.424, 1.519). [asimov-cme-perf.html table 4.6]
  • Run 3 (004): the dense all-five chase through the CME put 940,974 requests on the five home nodes together. The core's same chase put 709,388 requests (1.33 times). [004 cmn-counts.csv rows cme-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2 and ocm-all5-dense-cpu2]
  • The all-five OCM read through the CME put 512,465 requests against the core's 371,186 (1.38 times). [004 cmn-counts.csv rows cme-ocm-read-all5 and ocm-read-all5]
  • The sparse OCM chains through the CME put only 0.86 to 1.07 times the core's requests on the home node. [004 cmn-counts.csv rows cme-ocm-region<r>-cpu2 and ocm-region<r>-cpu2]
  • Boot E (010, the L3 on) against boot A (005): the dense OCM chains through the CME read 0.85 to 0.93 times boot A.
  • Per region, best of 2 fresh passes: OCM0 35.92 vs 38.67 ns per load, OCM1 35.25 vs 38.32, OCM2 34.44 vs 38.87, OCM3 35.06 vs 41.22, OCM4 36.97 vs 42.17.
  • The all-five dense chain read 43.28 ns per load on E, 44.77 on A and 44.28 on boot C (007).
  • E's dense rows count 1.01 to 1.32 outer refills (event 0x327E) per load, mean of the two fresh passes. C's dense rows count 2.13 to 2.66.
  • The all-five dense row counts 2.07 on E, 2.46 on A and 2.05 on C. [cme-latency-ocm-region<r>-dense.csv and -all5-dense.csv of 010, 005, 007, cme-fresh rows, and asimov-cme-run4.html 9.2]
  • Boot F1 (011, the L3 on): the CME OCM reads reached 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s per region (best of 3 reps). Run 3 read 23.178 to 23.352 GB/s.
  • That is 1.45 to 1.71 times (regions 0 to 4: 1.451, 1.642, 1.611, 1.714, 1.664). [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region<r>.csv of 011 and 004, column aggregate_GBps]
  • Their home-node requests were 50,227 to 50,893 for regions 1 to 4 against 108,075 to 109,528 on run 3 (0.46 to 0.47 times). Region 0 counted 84,080 against 108,176 (0.78 times). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004, rows cme-ocm-read-region<r>]
  • The all-five read put 0.758 times run 3's requests on the five nodes. [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004, rows cme-ocm-read-all5]
  • The write put 1.050 times. Its rate rose from 19.795 to 30.659 GB/s (1.549 times). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004, rows cme-ocm-write-all5, and cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011 and 004, column aggregate_GBps]
  • F1's region read reps spread up to 19.5 % (region 3: 34.547, 33.33, 39.846 GB/s). [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region<r>.csv of 011 and 011 README, CME rows]
  • Boot F2 (012, the L3 on, the prefetchers off): the CME OCM reads fell to 0.723 to 0.906 times F1 (27.708 to 33.934 GB/s). Per region 0 to 4: 0.839, 0.723, 0.906, 0.780, 0.778. [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region<r>.csv of 012 and 011]
  • Own-node requests were 0.882, 1.521, 1.149, 0.889 and 0.894 times F1 for regions 0 to 4 (requests: 74,192 / 76,768 / 58,464 / 44,978 / 44,909).
  • Requests on each other node were 0.650 to 0.733 times F1. [cmn-counts.csv of 012 and 011, rows cme-ocm-read-region<r>]
  • Each region read command lived 1.046 to 1.085 times as long as on F1 (child_elapsed_ns). [cmn-counts.csv of 012 and 011, rows cme-ocm-read-region<r>, and 012 README, CME rows against boot F1]

Why it looked wrong

  • The same bytes read from the same region should produce about the same number of requests at the owning home node, whichever unit issues them. Run 3 counted 1.42 to 1.52 times more for the CME. [004 cmn-counts.csv]
  • OCM lives in 4 locked ways of each SLC home node on the mesh. A cluster-local L3 was therefore not expected to change OCM rows through the CME, or to take OCM reads off the mesh. [004 README, Read first]
  • The sparse OCM chains through the CME count only 0.00 to 0.03 inner refills (event 0x327D) per load on run 3. So their lines come from outside the cluster. [cme-latency-ocm-region<r>.csv of 004, column cme_l1d_refill_inner_per_load]
  • Region 0 behaves unlike regions 1 to 4 on F1 (0.78 times run 3's requests against 0.46 to 0.47). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004]
  • The write got faster on F1 (1.549 times run 3). Its request count rose at the same time (1.050 times). [cmn-counts.csv and cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011 and 004]
  • The mesh counts cover the whole command (buffer fill, chain build, flushes, controls, timed walks), not the timed loads alone. So they cannot isolate the CME's own traffic.

Tests added to clarify it

Refill-cause counts on the dense OCM chains through the CMEboot E, boot A, boot COuter refill count (event 0x327E) beside the demand (0x3280) and prefetch (0x32B2) refill counts on the dense OCM chains through the CME, boot E (010) against boots C (007) and A (005). The dense per-region rows exist on boots A to E (005 to 010), not on run 3. It measures how many of the dense chase's refills still come from outside the cluster with the L3 on. It also measures how many come from inside it. Fewer outer refills on E would mean the L3 serves part of them.
Mesh counters around the CME OCM commands, L3 onboot F1Mesh counters (cmncount, the mesh counter tool, event hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all, requests received per home node) around the same seven CME OCM bandwidth commands and the seven CME OCM chase commands on boot F1 (011). The chase rows carry the refill-cause events. The bandwidth rows carry no CME counters. Bandwidth refuses --perf with --cme. Run 4 ran no mesh counters around a CME command. It measures requests per home node with the L3 on, beside prefetch refills per load on the chase rows. Fewer requests than run 3 would mean some level in the cluster serves part of the reads.
The same CME OCM commands with the prefetchers off, the L3 onboot F2The same CME OCM commands on boot F2 (012) with the prefetchers off (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1, the boot firmware build that disables the prefetchers) and the L3 on. It measures the prefetcher's share of the OCM read rate and of the home-node requests. A drop in both against F1 would mean the prefetcher produced them.

What the tests showed

  • Hypothesis (Jesse's inference, run 3 README, Mesh counts): the extra run 3 requests are the CME's refills above one per load, its prefetches, seen at the home node.
  • Boot E (010) counts 0.36 to 0.45 prefetch refills (event 0x32B2) per load on the sparse OCM chains through the CME (mean over 7 passes per region). F1 (011) counts 0.41 to 0.47.
  • Those counts fit run 3's 1.42 to 1.52 ratios. [cme-latency-ocm-region<r>.csv of 010 and 011, column cme_l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load, cme-fresh rows]
  • On boot E the dense rows' outer refills about halve: 1.01 to 1.32 per load against C's 2.13 to 2.66.
  • Their inner refills rise to 0.87 to 1.52 per load (boots A and C: 0.00). [cme-latency-ocm-region<r>-dense.csv of 010, 007, 005, columns cme_l1d_refill_outer_per_load and cme_l1d_refill_inner_per_load]
  • So part of the prefetcher's fills come from the L3.
  • The 3-crosspoint regions gain most: OCM3 -6.2 ns per load and OCM4 -5.2 ns per load against boot A. [asimov-cme-run4.html 9.2]
  • On F1 fewer requests reached the home node (0.46 to 0.47 times run 3 for regions 1 to 4). So some level in the cluster served the rest. Which level, the counts do not show. [011 README, CME rows]
  • With the prefetchers off (F2, 012) the sparse OCM chains through the CME read 1.001 to 1.028 times boot B (006, the prefetchers off on both) per region, and 1.003 times for all five. [cme-latency-ocm-region<r>.csv and -all5.csv of 012 and 006]
  • So the L3 does not serve demand OCM loads through the CME. [012 README, Pointer: this boot against boot B]
  • With the prefetchers off (F2) the CME OCM reads still ran at 0.723 to 0.906 times F1 (27.708 to 33.934 GB/s). That is above run 3's 23.2 to 23.4 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region<r>.csv of 012 and 011]
  • Their own-node counts moved both ways (0.88 to 1.52 times F1). So the counts do not say which level served F1's reads. [cmn-counts.csv of 012 and 011]
  • The sessions grouped the OCM read rate's rise with the L3 on with the open read-stream item (read-stream-rise-l3-on).
  • The flushed 8 MiB CME command spread its requests evenly over the five nodes: 1,451,065 to 1,461,104 per node on run 3, 1,407,799 to 1,414,866 on F1, and 904,587 to 905,781 on F2. [cmn-counts.csv of 004, 011, 012, row cme-dram-flushed-8M-cpu2]
  • That is what the address hash predicts.

Still open

Which level inside the cluster served F1's CME OCM reads is still open. Why region 0 counted 0.78 times run 3 while regions 1 to 4 counted 0.46 to 0.47 is also open. A refill-cause count (inner 0x327D, outer 0x327E, prefetch 0x32B2) on the timed CME OCM read command itself would settle the first question. That count does not exist yet. The bandwidth command refuses --perf with --cme.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 (004) mesh counts, 2026-11-03; run 4 boot E (010) dense rows, 2026-11-05; run 6 boot F1 (011), 2026-11-06; boot F2 (012), 2026-11-07

What looked wrong. Run 3 (004): around the CME's OCM read commands the region's home node received 108,075 to 109,528 requests. Around the core's same commands it received 71,687 to 76,534. That is 1.42 to 1.52 times. The dense all-five chase through the CME put 1.33 times the core's requests on the five home nodes together (940,974 against 709,388). The sparse chains through the CME put 0.86 to 1.07 times the core's requests on the home node. Boot E (010, the L3 on) against boot A (005): the dense OCM chains through the CME read 0.85 to 0.93 times boot A (OCM0 35.92 vs 38.67 ns, OCM1 35.25 vs 38.32, OCM2 34.44 vs 38.87, OCM3 35.06 vs 41.22, OCM4 36.97 vs 42.17 ns per load). The all-five dense chain read 43.28 ns on E against 44.77 on A and 44.28 on C. E's dense rows count 1.01 to 1.32 outer refills per load (mean of the two fresh passes) against C's 2.13 to 2.66; the all-five dense row 2.07 on E against 2.46 on A and 2.05 on C. F1 (011): the CME OCM reads reached 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s per region (run 3: 23.178 to 23.352), 1.45 to 1.71 times. Their home-node requests were 50,227 to 50,893 for regions 1 to 4 against 108,075 to 109,528 on run 3 (0.46 to 0.47 times), but 84,080 for region 0 against 108,176 (0.78 times). The all-five read put 0.76 times run 3's requests on the five nodes. The write put 1.05 times while its rate rose from 19.795 to 30.659 GB/s. F1's region reps spread up to 19.5 %. F2 (012, prefetchers off): the reads fell to 0.723 to 0.906 times F1 (27.708 to 33.934 GB/s). Own-node requests were 0.882, 1.521, 1.149, 0.889 and 0.894 times F1 for regions 0 to 4 (74,192; 76,768; 58,464; 44,978; 44,909) and 0.650 to 0.733 times on each other node. Each region read lived 1.046 to 1.085 times as long.

Why it looked wrong. The same bytes read from the same region should produce about the same number of requests at the owning home node, whichever unit issues them. OCM lives in 4 locked ways of each SLC home node on the mesh. A cluster-local L3 was therefore not expected to change OCM rows through the CME, or to take OCM reads off the mesh. The sparse OCM chain rows through the CME count only 0.00 to 0.03 inner refills per load on run 3, so their lines come from outside the cluster. Region 0 behaves unlike regions 1 to 4 on F1. The write got faster on F1 while its request count rose. The mesh counts cover the whole command (buffer fill, chain build, flushes, controls, timed walks), not the timed loads alone, so they cannot isolate the CME's own traffic.

4.32 CME read calls carry about 100 ns of fixed cost per call, write calls none; run 6's in-span clock stamps added about 82 ns per callpartly explained

On run 3 CME read calls cost about 100 ns each and write calls none. Run 6's clock stamps added about 82 ns more.

What looked wrong

  • Run 3 (boot 004, 2026-11-03) timed every CME bandwidth pass as one kernel call.
  • A line through the 16 KiB and 48 KiB read rows gives the read kernel a fixed cost of 100.6 ns per call at a slope rate of 133.5 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, cme-read best rows 73.377 and 104.865 GB/s]
  • The same line through the write rows gives 0.5 ns per call at 63.9 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, cme-write best rows 63.731 and 63.821 GB/s]
  • The fixed cost is 45 % of the 16 KiB read pass (100.6 of 223.3 ns).
  • The 1 KiB read call takes 97.1 ns on run 3. The 1 KiB write call takes 39.1 ns on run 3. [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 004, best rows 10.549 and 26.213 GB/s]
  • The write call is 23.0 ns est. above its 16.0 ns of stores at 63.9 GB/s.
  • The one-load control cme-call minus the cme-roundtrip chain is only 21.7 ns per call on run 3 (42.703 minus 21.004 ns). [cme-latency-dram-large.csv of 004, rows 7 and 11]
  • That contradicts the 100 ns read intercept.
  • In run 6 the cme-call control tripled.
  • The best rows read 124.516 to 125.609 ns per call on boots F1 and F2 (reps up to 125.656 ns), with 61.000 to 61.250 ns of it inside the span. [cme-latency-*.csv of 011 and 012 (24 files)]
  • Boot E read 42.516 to 43.609 ns per call by the best rows (reps to 43.922 ns). [cme-latency-*.csv of 010 (21 files)]
  • The 1 KiB read call read 186.1 ns on F1 and 191.1 ns on F2 (108.0 ns in span on both) against 97.1 ns on run 3. [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 011 and 012, cme-read 1024 best rows]
  • Two run 6 forms also fit no line or no twin.
  • The looped write rows at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB do not lie on a line (largest residual 27.9 ns on F1 and 26.6 ns on F2). [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]
  • The single-call 96 KiB read reads 1.56 times its looped twin (the same size in the looped form) on F1 (68.249 against 43.713 GB/s).
  • On F2 it reads 1.07 times its looped twin (42.773 against 39.950 GB/s). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, 98304 best rows]

Why it looked wrong

  • Every call pays the same register save, SMSTART, SMSTOP (the Arm instructions that enter and leave streaming mode) and register restore.
  • So a read call and a write call should carry the same fixed cost. Run 3 gave 100.6 ns for read and 0.5 ns for write, a 100 ns gap.
  • Hypothesis H10 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 13): stores are posted (the core does not wait for a store to finish).
  • The last stores of one call drain while the kernel leaves streaming mode and the next call enters. From 16 KiB up the mode switch hides behind those stores.
  • Hypothesis H11: the read kernel ends with a fold of its 16 accumulators (15 EOR, one EORV, one FMOV).
  • The fold waits for every load to return. So most of the read call's cost would be the fold and its return dependency.
  • Run 6's cme-call tripled for a known reason.
  • The run 6 kernels are run 3's plus exactly 15 instructions (2 ISB, 2 MRS of CNTVCT_EL0, 2 ADRP, 3 ADD, 1 SUB, 2 LDR, 3 STR) by Jesse's disassembly. [README 011 lines 153 and 155, and cme_kern.S header lines 11 to 23]
  • The ISB (an instruction barrier) before the second stamp waits for earlier instructions. So the bracket of every call now holds the stamps' own cost.
  • Bracket minus span is the instrumented outside-span interval (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call, return and the second stamp's eight instructions), not the mode switch alone.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
In-span CNTVCT_EL0 stamps after SMSTART and before SMSTOPboot F1, boot F2Kernel time inside the streaming span (latency column 7 ns_per_load_span, bandwidth columns 11 and 12 span_s and span_GBps) against the caller's bracket around the call. Bracket minus span is the instrumented outside-span interval of one call (commit 0c190a1, five commits aa408ed to 0c190a1 on b79dffa).
Single-call CME form, no-fold read, DSB ST write, per-call write rowsboot F1, boot F2Each form's fitted cost per pass (four points, 2 % residual rule). Single-call at 4 to 24 KiB (cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv) and 48 to 256 KiB (cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv). Looped minus no-fold (--no-fold, cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv) as the net effect of the fold. DSB ST minus looped write (--dsb-st, cme-bandwidth-l1-dsb.csv) as the barrier's measured effect (consistent with H10 if positive, not a proof). The per-call write size at 1, 2, 4 and 8 KiB (cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv) at which the 23 ns est. disappears.
Matched control without the stampsnot runThe isolated stamp cost per call, from the same kernel with an empty span or the pre-run-6 binary on one boot. Plan section 13 G-k reading 1 says this control would be needed, and run 6 does not carry it. Section 14 for run 7 holds no such row.

What the tests showed

  • Single-call CME L1 read: 108.9 to 131.6 GB/s on F1 and 110.8 to 132.4 GB/s on F2 at 4 to 24 KiB. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012, cme-read best rows]
  • That is one 64-byte load per CME cycle, measured. It replaces the run 3 slope rate (133.5 GB/s, quoted earlier as 134 GB/s est.).
  • Single-call write: fitted rate 51.8 GB/s on F1 and 52.0 GB/s on F2 by the bracket (52.1 and 52.2 GB/s in span).
  • The single-call write intercept is -2.2 ns per pass. The per-size rows read 52.0 to 53.7 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]
  • Looped read intercept on F1: 186.2 ns per pass by the bracket, 103.9 ns in span, 134.2 ns without the fold. [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv and cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv of 011, cme-read best rows at 4096 to 24576]
  • On F2: 182.1, 101.1 and 138.8 ns (the F2 looped read line fails the 2 % rule, residual 6.6 ns). [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv and cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv of 012, cme-read best rows at 4096 to 24576]
  • So the fold costs 52.0 ns on F1 (43.3 ns on F2). Bracket minus span is 82.3 ns per call on F1 (81.0 ns on F2).
  • Boot E's whole cme-call without stamps took 42.5 to 43.9 ns. So most of the 82 ns is the stamps. [cme-latency-*.csv of 010, cme-call rows]
  • Net of the stamps a read call costs about 104 ns est. (186.1 minus 82.3 ns), near run 3's 97.1 ns 1 KiB read call.
  • The CME itself counted 242.7 to 246.3 cycles per cme-call on F1 and F2 against 78.8 to 87.6 cycles on run 3. So the added time runs inside the CME. [cme-latency-*.csv of 011, 012 and 004, cme_cycles_per_load column of the cme-call rows]
  • DSB ST (a barrier that waits for all earlier stores to finish) adds 47.4 ns per pass at 4 KiB, 97.8 ns at 8 KiB, 76.9 ns at 16 KiB and 74.3 ns at 24 KiB on F1 (48.9 to 101.5 ns on F2). [cme-bandwidth-l1-dsb.csv minus cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]
  • So stores are posted. This is consistent with H10, not a proof.
  • Per-call writes of 1, 2, 4 and 8 KiB take 124.1, 128.6, 149.8 and 182.1 ns on F1, with 76.1, 76.1, 76.3 and 90.5 ns of each outside the span. [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 011]
  • The write call's own cost stays open. The looped write gives no line to read it from. [README 012 line 176]
  • A call alone in its bracket spends 281.1 to 535.7 ns outside its span on F1 (280.0 to 523.6 ns on F2) in the single-call reps.
  • Back-to-back cme-call calls spend 63.5 to 64.6 ns outside the span. [README 011 lines 160 and 168, and README 012 line 144]
  • The chain rows (8,192 to 524,288 loads per span) carry 0.001 to 0.042 ns per load outside the span. The round trip reads 21.005 ns as before. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 011 and 012]
  • The 64-load OCM (on-chip memory at the mesh home nodes) region rows carry 4.4 to 4.8 ns per load of outside-span time over all passes (4.4 to 4.5 ns on the best passes). [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011 and 012]
  • So those rows are not directly comparable with boot E's bracket values.

Still open

Two items stay open: the stamps' own cost per call, and the write call's own cost (the looped write gives no line to read it from). A matched control without the stamps (the same kernel with an empty span, or the pre-run-6 binary on one boot) would settle the first. Run 6 does not carry it (plan section 13 G-k reading 1, no row in section 14 for run 7).

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 (membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03) two-point fits; Wade's SMSTART/SMSTOP comment 2026-11-05 12:24 PST (jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md line 233); plan section 13 2026-11-05 evening; run 6 boots F1 (011, 2026-11-06) and F2 (012, 2026-11-06 and 07)

What looked wrong. Run 3 timed every CME bandwidth pass as one kernel call. A line through the 16 and 48 KiB rows gives the read kernel a fixed cost of 100.6 ns per call at a slope rate of 133.5 GB/s [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, cme-read 16384 and 49152 best rows: 73.377 and 104.865 GB/s, so 223.3 and 468.7 ns per pass]. The same line through the write rows gives 0.5 ns per call at 63.9 GB/s [same file, cme-write best rows 63.731 and 63.821 GB/s]. Both kernels pay the same register save, SMSTART, SMSTOP and restore, so the two intercepts should not differ by 100 ns. The fixed cost is 45 % of the 16 KiB read pass (100.6 of 223.3 ns). The 1 KiB read call takes 97.1 ns and the 1 KiB write call 39.1 ns [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 004, best rows 10.549 and 26.213 GB/s]; the write call is 23.0 ns est. above its 16.0 ns of stores at 63.9 GB/s. The one-load control cme-call minus the cme-roundtrip chain is only 21.7 ns per call on run 3 (42.703 minus 21.004 ns) [cme-latency-dram-large.csv of 004, rows 7 and 11], which contradicts the 100 ns read intercept. In run 6 the cme-call control tripled: 124.516 to 125.609 ns per call by the best rows (reps up to 125.656), 61.000 to 61.250 ns of it inside the span [cme-latency-*.csv of 011 and 012, 24 files], against 42.516 to 43.609 ns best (reps to 43.922) on boot E [cme-latency-*.csv of 010, 21 files]. The 1 KiB read call read 186.1 ns on F1 and 191.1 ns on F2 (108.0 ns in span on both) against 97.1 ns on run 3 [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 011 and 012, cme-read 1024 best rows]. The looped write rows at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB do not lie on a line: largest residual 27.9 ns on F1 and 26.6 ns on F2 [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv of 011 and 012, cme-write best rows]. The single-call 96 KiB read reads 1.56 times its looped twin on F1 (68.249 against 43.713 GB/s) and 1.07 times on F2 (42.773 against 39.950) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, 98304 best rows].

Why it looked wrong. Every call pays the register save, SMSTART, SMSTOP and the restore, so a read call and a write call should carry the same fixed cost. Hypothesis H10 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 13): stores are posted, so the last stores of one call drain while the kernel leaves streaming mode and the next call enters, and the switch hides behind them from 16 KiB up. Hypothesis H11: the read kernel ends with a fold of its 16 accumulators (15 EOR, EORV, FMOV), which waits for every load to return, so most of the read call's cost is the fold and its return dependency. Run 6's cme-call tripled because the run 6 kernels are run 3's plus exactly 15 instructions (2 ISB, 2 MRS of CNTVCT_EL0, 2 ADRP, 3 ADD, 1 SUB, 2 LDR, 3 STR) by Jesse's disassembly [README 011 line 153], and the ISB before the second stamp waits for earlier instructions, so the bracket of every call now holds the stamps' own cost. Bracket minus span is the instrumented outside-span interval (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call, return and the second stamp's eight instructions), not the switch alone [cme_kern.S header lines 11 to 23; README 011 line 155].

Tests added.

  • In-span CNTVCT_EL0 stamps after SMSTART and before SMSTOP, printed as ns_per_load_span (latency, column 7) and span_s, span_GBps (bandwidth, columns 11 and 12) [run 6, commit 0c190a1 (five commits aa408ed, b345288, 0c424d7, 2fff008, 0c190a1 on b79dffa; follow-up-run-plan.md line 170), boots F1 (011) and F2 (012)]: kernel time inside the streaming span against the caller's bracket around the call; bracket minus span is the instrumented outside-span interval of one call
  • Single-call CME form (--asm-passes --cme) at 4, 8, 16, 24 KiB (cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv) and 48, 96, 160, 256 KiB (cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv); looped read without the fold (--no-fold, cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv); looped write with DSB ST before SMSTOP (--dsb-st, cme-bandwidth-l1-dsb.csv); per-call write rows at 1, 2, 4 and 8 KiB (cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv) [run 6 F1 (011) and F2 (012)]: each form's fitted cost per pass (four points, 2 % residual rule); looped minus no-fold is the net effect of the fold; DSB ST minus looped write is the barrier's measured effect (consistent with H10 if positive, not a proof); the per-call write size at which the 23 ns est. disappears
  • A matched control without the stamps (the same kernel with an empty span, or the pre-run-6 binary on one boot) [not drafted: plan section 13 G-k reading 1 says isolating the stamps' own effect would need such a control and run 6 does not carry it; section 14 (run 7) holds no such row]: the isolated stamp cost per call

What the tests showed. Single-call CME L1 read: 108.9 to 131.6 GB/s on F1 and 110.8 to 132.4 GB/s on F2 at 4 to 24 KiB, one 64-byte load per CME cycle, measured (replaces the 134 GB/s est. slope) [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012, cme-read best rows]. Single-call write: fitted rate 51.8 GB/s on F1 and 52.0 on F2 by the bracket (52.1 and 52.2 in span), intercept -2.2 ns per pass, the per-size rows 52.0 to 53.7 GB/s [same files, cme-write best rows]. Looped read intercept on F1: 186.2 ns per pass by the bracket, 103.9 ns in span, 134.2 ns without the fold [cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv and cme-bandwidth-l1-nofold.csv of 011, cme-read best rows at 4096 to 24576]; F2: 182.1, 101.1 and 138.8 ns (the F2 looped read fails the 2 % rule, residual 6.6 ns). So the fold costs 52.0 ns on F1 (43.3 on F2). Bracket minus span is 82.3 ns per call on F1 (81.0 on F2). Boot E's whole cme-call without stamps took 42.5 to 43.9 ns, so most of the 82 ns is the stamps. Net of them a read call costs about 104 ns est. (186.1 minus 82.3), near run 3's 97.1 ns 1 KiB read call. The CME itself counted 242.7 to 246.3 cycles per cme-call on F1 and F2 against 78.8 to 87.6 on run 3 [cme-latency-*.csv of 011, 012 and 004, cme_cycles_per_load column of the cme-call rows], so the added time runs inside the CME. DSB ST adds 47.4 ns per pass at 4 KiB, 97.8 at 8 KiB, 76.9 at 16 KiB and 74.3 at 24 KiB on F1 (48.9 to 101.5 on F2) [cme-bandwidth-l1-dsb.csv minus cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv, cme-write best rows], so stores are posted (consistent with H10, not a proof). Per-call writes of 1, 2, 4 and 8 KiB take 124.1, 128.6, 149.8 and 182.1 ns on F1, with 76.1, 76.1, 76.3 and 90.5 ns of each outside the span [cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv of 011; README 012 line 176]. The write call's own cost stays open: the looped write gives no line to read it from. A call alone in its bracket spends 281.1 to 535.7 ns outside its span on F1 (280.0 to 523.6 on F2) in the single-call reps, against 63.5 to 64.6 ns for back-to-back cme-call calls [README 011 line 168; README 012 line 144]. The chain rows (8,192 to 524,288 loads per span) carry 0.001 to 0.042 ns per load outside the span and the round trip reads 21.005 ns as before [README 011 line 160; cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 011 and 012]. The 64-load OCM region rows carry 4.4 to 4.8 ns per load of outside-span time over all passes (4.4 to 4.5 ns on the best passes) [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011 and 012, ns_per_load minus ns_per_load_span], so they are not directly comparable with boot E's bracket values.

Highlighted: CME, core, harness.

4.33 Read streams run 2.7 times faster with the L3 on, at footprints the L3 cannot holdopen

Read streams far larger than the L3 run 2.7 times faster when the L3 is on. The counters do not show why.

What looked wrong

  • One core reads a 32 MiB stream at 24.546 GB/s on boot E (L3 on) and 9.196 GB/s on boot C (L3 in snoop-filter-only mode). That is 2.669 times. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010 and 007]
  • The two boots share one build. The L3 mode is the one change.
  • Boot F1 (L3 on) against run 3 (L3 off) shows the same rise on every read stream of 48 KiB and above. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
  • One-core reads rise 1.561 times at 48 KiB (17.483 to 27.299 GB/s) and 2.690 times at 2 MiB (9.311 to 25.044 GB/s). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
  • At 32 MiB they rise from 9.172 to 24.575 GB/s. One-core copies rise 1.31 to 1.75 times (17.962 to 31.438 GB/s at 32 MiB). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
  • Four readers on four DSUs rise from 33.957 to 98.072 GB/s at 16 MiB (2.888 times). Eight readers rise from 66.673 to 107.593 GB/s at 16 MiB (1.614 times). [bandwidth-perdsu.csv and bandwidth-all8.csv of 011 and 004]
  • OCM reads rose too. One-core OCM reads rise 1.206 to 1.358 times (14.817 to 16.619 GB/s on run 3, 19.883 to 20.143 GB/s on F1). [bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011 and 004]
  • CME OCM reads rise 1.451 to 1.714 times (23.178 to 23.352 GB/s on run 3, 33.638 to 39.846 GB/s on F1). [cme-bandwidth-ocm-region0..4.csv of 011 and 004]
  • On F1 the region's home node receives 0.46 to 0.47 times run 3's requests for regions 1 to 4 (50,227 to 50,893 against 108,075 to 109,528 per command). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004]
  • For region 0 it receives 0.78 times run 3's requests (84,080 against 108,176). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004]
  • No core write stream moved. One-core writes are 1.000 to 1.003 times (31.996 GB/s on run 3, 31.997 GB/s on F1 at 32 MiB). [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
  • Four-DSU writes are 1.000 times (127.98 GB/s). The six writer-placement rows are 1.000 times. The all-eight write is 1.064 times at 2 MiB and 1.005 times at 16 MiB.
  • The CME's writes did move. Its OCM write rose from 19.795 to 30.659 GB/s (1.549 times). [cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv of 011 and 004]
  • Its DRAM write fell from 63.865 to 42.639 GB/s at 2 MiB (0.67 times). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
  • No DRAM-sized chain moved. The 32 MiB random chain reads 52.185 ns per load on run 3, 52.212 ns on F1, 52.238 ns on boot C and 52.875 ns on boot E. [latency-dram-large.csv of 004, 011, 007 and 010]

Why it looked wrong

  • A 32 MiB stream is 128 times the 256 KiB L3. The L3 cannot hold it. A cache that cannot hold the data was expected to leave the read rate unchanged.
  • The refill counters per 64-byte line are the same on both boots at 32 MiB. L1 refills are 0.9998 on boot C and 0.9998 on boot E. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, 33554432 B rep rows]
  • L2 refills are 0.9997 on C and 0.9998 on E. L1 prefetch refills are 0.9994 on both. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, 33554432 B rep rows]
  • L3 read refills from the mesh are 0.0004 on C and 0.00003 to 0.00005 on E. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, 33554432 B rep rows]
  • So each line still enters the L1 and the L2 once. The prefetcher still asks for every line.
  • F1's counted 2 MiB read put 0.975 times run 3's requests on the five home nodes (427,991 against 438,961 over the whole command). [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004, row dram-read-2M-cpu2]
  • It did so in 0.648 times the command time (1,391,056 ns against 2,147,182 ns). So the L3 did not take these reads off the mesh. [cmn-counts.csv of 011 and 004, row dram-read-2M-cpu2]
  • One DRAM load costs 52.185 ns on run 3, 52.212 ns on F1, 52.238 ns on boot C and 52.875 ns on boot E. [latency-dram-large.csv of 004, 011, 007, 010]
  • At 9.196 GB/s the 32 MiB stream must overlap about 7.5 loads est. with the L3 off. At 24.546 GB/s it must overlap about 20 loads est. with the L3 on.
  • The core spends 13.78 to 13.93 cycles per line on boot C and 5.13 to 5.22 cycles per line on boot E. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007 and 010, column cycles_per_line]
  • The files do not record how many reads are in flight. So they do not show the mechanism.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
One-core read, boot C against boot E, with refill countersboot C, boot EIt measures the one-core read rate at 2 and 32 MiB in five variants (plain, PRFM 4, 8 and 16 lines ahead, two streams). It records the refill and prefetch counters per line on two boots of one build. A rise on E with equal refills means the L3 mode, not the cache contents, changes the rate.
Run 3's 67 core command lines rerun on boot F1boot F1, run 3It measures every one-core, pair, per-DSU, all-eight and OCM read, write and copy stream with the L3 on against run 3 with the L3 off. It also counts the home-node requests of the counted 2 MiB read. A lower request count would mean the L3 serves part of the stream.
Core page section 2.3: setup differences, speed ratios, hypothesesotherOn asimov-c1nano-perf.html (the core page) it lists which of 112 rows in 29 groups moved. It lists the nine setup items that differed between the two boots, marked high, mid or low impact. It lists three hypotheses, each with a test. A non-L3 item marked high impact would be an alternative cause.
Proposed: reads in flight at the mesh port, prefetchers off, reader pairsnot runIt would count read requests in flight at the DSU's mesh port (a CMN-S3 PMU event, to be checked in the event list) on an L3-on boot and an L3-off boot. It would rerun run 3's one-core read lines with the prefetchers off on an L3-on boot with boot F2's firmware. F2 ran only run_cme.sh. It would compare two 16 MiB readers on CPUs 2 and 3 against CPUs 2 and 4. These three tests would separate the three hypotheses listed under open.

What the tests showed

  • The build, the boards and run-to-run noise are ruled out. k_read, k_write and k_copy (the three stream kernels) are byte for byte the same in both builds. [run 4 boots C and E, and run 6 boot F1 against run 3]
  • Boot E against boot C (one build) shows the rise. [run 4 boots C and E]
  • The controls and the one-core writes from 48 KiB on repeat within 0.3 %. The read reps spread 1.8 % or less inside each boot. [run 4 boots C and E, and run 6 boot F1 against run 3]
  • Page placement is ruled out for the DRAM rows and only partly for the OCM rows.
  • A PRFM hint (a software prefetch instruction placed ahead of the load) lowers the rate on boot E. With the hint 4 lines ahead one core reads 20.196 GB/s against 24.945 GB/s plain at 2 MiB, and 20.353 GB/s against 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010]
  • On boot C the hint adds 4 % or less. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007]
  • With the prefetchers off and the L3 off (boots B and D) one core reads 2.377 GB/s at 32 MiB. So the hardware prefetcher supplies almost all the overlap. [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 006 and 008]
  • The sequential 8 MiB chain fell from 6.917 ns per load on boot C to 2.492 ns per load on boot E. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 007 and 010]
  • L1 prefetch refills per load are 0.9999 to 1.0000 on C and 0.9997 on E. That chain has its own entry. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 007 and 010]
  • Four readers on four DSUs read 24.5 to 24.6 GB/s each on F1. That is the one-core rate. So four clusters do not share one limit. [bandwidth-perdsu.csv of 011]
  • Eight readers (two per cluster) read 13.4 GB/s each on F1. [bandwidth-all8.csv of 011]
  • The README of folder 011 (boot F1), written by Jesse, states that the home-node counts do not show the L3 taking the counted read off the mesh. It does not name a cause. [README of 011, lines 143 to 147]
  • The run 4 page adds a fourth reading, marked hypothesis: the prefetched lines wait in the L3 (about 11 ns from the core, est.) instead of in the SLC across the mesh. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 14.3]

Still open

Three hypotheses stand, each with a test not yet run. The L3's miss handling keeps more reads in flight per cluster. The prefetcher's requests overlap more with the L3 on. Or a per-cluster cap on reads in flight applies. A count of read requests in flight at the DSU's mesh port (a CMN-S3 PMU event) on an L3-on boot and an L3-off boot would settle which one holds.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boot E against boot C (010 against 007), both run 2026-11-05 UTC; confirmed by run 6 boot F1 (011, run 2026-11-06 UTC) against run 3 (004, run 2026-11-03)

What looked wrong. One core reads 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB on boot E against 9.196 GB/s on boot C (2.669 times). The two boots share one build, and the L3 mode is the one change. F1 against run 3 shows the same on every read stream of 48 KiB and above: one-core reads 1.561 times at 48 KiB up to 2.690 times at 2 MiB (24.575 to 27.299 GB/s against 9.172 to 17.483), four readers on four DSUs 33.957 to 98.072 GB/s at 16 MiB (2.888 times), eight readers 66.673 to 107.593 GB/s at 16 MiB (1.614 times), one-core copies 1.31 to 1.75 times, one-core OCM reads 1.206 to 1.358 times (14.817 to 16.619 GB/s up to 19.883 to 20.143), CME OCM reads 1.451 to 1.714 times (23.178 to 23.352 GB/s up to 33.638 to 39.846) with 0.46 to 0.47 times the requests on the region's home node (regions 1 to 4; 0.78 for region 0). No core write stream moved: one-core writes 1.000 to 1.003 times (31.996 to 31.997 GB/s at 32 MiB), four-DSU writes 1.000 (127.98 GB/s), the six writer-placement rows 1.000; the all-eight write read 1.064 at 2 MiB and 1.005 at 16 MiB. The CME's writes did move: its OCM write 19.795 to 30.659 GB/s (1.549 times) and its DRAM write 63.865 down to 42.639 GB/s at 2 MiB (0.67 times). No DRAM-sized chain moved: the 32 MiB random chain reads 52.185 ns on run 3 and 52.212 on F1; 52.238 on boot C and 52.875 on boot E.

Why it looked wrong. A 32 MiB stream is 128 times the 256 KiB L3, so the L3 cannot hold it. The refill counters per 64-byte line are the same on both boots at 32 MiB: L1 refills 0.9998 and 0.9998, L2 refills 0.9997 and 0.9998, L1 prefetch refills 0.9994 and 0.9994; L3 read refills from the mesh 0.0004 on C and 0.00003 to 0.00005 on E. So each line still enters the L1 and L2 once, and the prefetcher still asks for every line. F1's counted 2 MiB read put 0.975 times run 3's requests on the five home nodes (427,991 against 438,961 over the whole command) in 0.648 times the command time (1,391,056 against 2,147,182 ns). So the L3 did not take these reads off the mesh. One DRAM load costs 52.2 ns on run 3 and F1 (52.185 and 52.212 ns) and 52.2 and 52.9 ns on boots C and E. At 9.196 GB/s the 32 MiB stream must overlap about 7.5 loads est. with the L3 off, and at 24.546 GB/s about 20 est. with it on. The core spends 13.78 to 13.93 cycles per line on C and 5.13 to 5.22 on E. The files do not record how many reads are in flight, so they do not show the mechanism.

  • Run 6 boot F1: run 3's whole core command set (67 command lines, byte for byte) on boot E's firmware, with the mesh counters around the same commands [run 6 boot F1 (011) against run 3 (004)]: every one-core, pair, per-DSU, all-eight and OCM read, write and copy stream with the L3 on, and the home-node requests of the counted 2 MiB read
  • Core page section 2.3: the setup-difference table (nine items, each marked high, mid or low impact), the 112-row speed-ratio figure in 29 groups, the counter readings, three hypotheses each with a test [analysis on asimov-c1nano-perf.html, no new run]: which rows moved, what else than the L3 differed between the two boots, and what would settle the cause
  • Proposed, not run: count the read requests in flight at the DSU's mesh port (a CMN-S3 PMU event, to be checked in the event list) on an L3-on and an L3-off boot; run 3's one-core read lines with the prefetchers off on an L3-on boot (boot F2's firmware; F2 ran run_cme.sh only); two readers at 16 MiB on CPUs 2 and 3 against CPUs 2 and 4 [not run]: more reads in flight through the L3's miss handling, against the prefetcher's requests overlapping more, against a per-cluster cap on reads in flight

What the tests showed. The build is ruled out: k_read, k_write and k_copy are byte for byte the same in both builds, and boot E against boot C (one build) shows the rise. Boards and run-to-run noise are ruled out: the controls repeat within 0.3 %, the one-core writes from 48 KiB on within 0.3 %, and the read reps spread 1.8 % or less inside each boot. Page placement is ruled out for the DRAM rows and only partly for the OCM rows. A PRFM hint lowers the rate on E (20.196 GB/s with the hint 4 lines ahead against 24.945 plain at 2 MiB; 20.353 against 24.546 at 32 MiB), while on C it adds 4 % or less. With the prefetchers off and the L3 off (boots B and D) one core reads 2.377 GB/s at 32 MiB, so the prefetcher supplies almost all the overlap. The sequential 8 MiB chain fell from 6.917 to 2.492 ns per load on E with 0.9997 to 1.0000 L1 prefetch refills per load on both boots (its own entry). Four readers on four DSUs read 24.5 to 24.6 GB/s each, the one-core rate, so four clusters do not share one limit; eight readers (two per cluster) read 13.4 GB/s each. Jesse's F1 README states that the home-node counts do not show the L3 taking the counted read off the mesh, and it does not name a cause. Three hypotheses stand, each with a test not yet run: the L3's miss handling keeps more reads in flight per cluster; the prefetcher's requests overlap more with the L3 on; a per-cluster cap on reads in flight. The run 4 page adds a fourth reading, marked hypothesis: the prefetched lines wait in the L3 (about 11 ns from the core, est.) instead of in the SLC across the mesh.

4.34 L3 on moves the CME's refills inside the cluster, but the chain is slower at 8 to 32 KiB; the L3-served CME load is 32.8 to 33.9 ns with a hit/snoop splitpartly explained

L3 on made CME chain loads slower at 8 and 16 KiB. The L3-served load is 6.2 to 7.3 ns per load above asimov-bench.

What looked wrong

  • On boot E (run 4, DSU L3 on) the CME's L1 refills at 8 KiB were 3.98 inner and 0.02 outer per load, 99.5 % inside the cluster. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007, the 8192 rows]
  • On boot C (run 4, L3 off) they were 0.59 inner and 3.33 outer per load. Means over 3 reps. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007, the 8192 rows]
  • Yet the chain was not faster on boot E. At 8 KiB it read 24.932 ns per load against 24.466 ns per load on boot C, best rep, ratio 1.019. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007]
  • At 16 KiB it read 35.065 against 31.303 ns per load, ratio 1.120. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007 and README.md of 010 line 109]
  • On boot F2 (run 6, L3 on, prefetchers off) the exploratory L3-hit event 0x328E counted 0.14 to 0.64 hits per load at 96 to 384 KiB, best rep. [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
  • Inner refills in the same rows: 0.96 to 1.00 per load, best rep (0.88 to 1.00 over all reps). [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
  • On boot F2 the latency fell as the chain grew: 36.0 ns per load at 96 KiB down to 32.8 ns per load at 256 KiB, best reps. [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
  • The L3-served load on boot F2 was 32.8 to 33.9 ns per load at 192 to 384 KiB. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 012]
  • That is 6.2 to 7.3 ns per load above the 26.6 ns per load that asimov-bench measured for the DSU L3 through the CME. [CME-plan.md line 63 and asimov-cme-perf.html open items]

Why it looked wrong

  • An L3 hit inside the cluster should cost less than a refill from the mesh (the interconnect outside the cluster).
  • So refills moving inside the cluster should lower the chain time. Instead the chain read 1.019 times boot C at 8 KiB and 1.120 times at 16 KiB (boot E, best rep).
  • With the prefetchers off, every inner refill was expected to be an L3 hit. So the hit count should have been near 1.00 per load, not 0.14 to 0.64 (boot F2, best rep).
  • The L3-served load was expected near asimov-bench's 26.6 ns per load for the same path. It read 32.8 to 33.9 ns per load (boot F2, 192 to 384 KiB).

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Boot E against boot C: inner and outer CME refill split by footprintboot C, boot EIt measures the L3's effect on the CME chain with the CME prefetcher on. It uses the inner (event 0x327D) and outer (event 0x327E) refill counters on the same commit b79dffa with only the SCP differing. A lower chain time on boot E would mean the L3 helps the CME. [README.md of 010, 'Against boot C: the L3 alone' and line 109]
Boot F2: L3 on, prefetchers off, CME L3 events plus least-squares fitboot F2It measures the L3-served chain load through the CME with no prefetch refills. It also measures which level served each refill, using the exploratory events 0x328E (L3 hit), 0x328F (L3 miss) and 0x3290 (L3 refill). A least-squares fit ns per load = a + hits x h + snoops x s + outer x o runs over the 15 rep rows from 96 to 384 KiB. A hit count near 1.00 per load would mean the L3 served every load. [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012 and README.md of 012, 'The CME L3 events' and gen_run6.py l3_fit]

What the tests showed

  • Boot E against boot C: the CME prefetcher's fills set the chain time on both boots. At 16 KiB boot E counted 10.4 refills per load against 7.9 on boot C (inner plus outer, means over reps). [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007]
  • The prefetch-refill event alone read 9.95 against 7.44 per load. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007]
  • So no boot E against boot C row isolates one L3 hit through the CME. The run 4 CME page lists that number as 'Insufficient data'. [asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]
  • Boot F2: the 192, 256 and 384 KiB chains read 33.910, 32.779 and 33.014 ns per load, best rep. That is 11.8 to 12.9 ns per load above the 21.005 ns per load round-trip baseline. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 012, cme-best and cme-roundtrip rows]
  • The core's own L3 hit on boot E was 10.6 to 11.0 ns est. per load (256 and 384 KiB rows). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, 'An L3 hit costs about 10.8 ns']
  • Boot B (006, L3 off, prefetchers off) read 39.525, 40.700 and 41.677 ns per load for the same three chains. It counted 0.34 to 0.74 outer refills per load over the reps. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 006]
  • The L3 events agree with the inner/outer split by construction. Hit plus miss equals inner plus outer within 0.0001 per load, and refill equals outer, in every row. [recomputed from cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]
  • So the events validate nothing on their own. [README.md of 012 line 182]
  • Hypothesis from the pre-queue check's reading of the C1-SME2 RTL: miss minus refill counts lines snooped from CPU 2's own L2, which wrote the chain with core stores while CPU 3 was offline. [evidence/jibin/prequeue-0c190a1.txt]
  • The least-squares fit over the 15 rep rows gives constant 23.4, L3 hit 6.7, snoop 13.9 and outer 20.4 ns est. per load, rms 0.02 ns. [README.md of 012 line 181 and gen_run6.py l3_fit]
  • The fit columns are near-collinear, so the split is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

Still open

The control for the events, a chain written through the CME that no core ever touched, is not in any run. It would settle whether the hit/snoop split is real [asimov-cme-perf.html section 5.2 and README.md of 012 line 211]. The 6.2 to 7.3 ns per load gap between the boot F2 L3-served load and asimov-bench's 26.6 ns per load is not attributed [asimov-cme-perf.html open items].

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boot E against boot C (010 against 007), boot E ran 2026-11-05 UTC [README.md of 010, line 3]; run 6 boot F2 L3-event sweep (012), ran 2026-11-06 and 07 UTC [README.md of 012, line 3]

What looked wrong. On boot E (the DSU L3 on) 99.5 % of the CME's L1 refills at 8 KiB come from inside the cluster: 3.98 inner and 0.02 outer refills per load, mean over 3 reps (boot C, the L3 off: 0.59 inner and 3.33 outer) [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007, the 8192 rows]. Yet the chain reads 1.019 times boot C at 8 KiB (24.932 against 24.466 ns per load, best rep) and 1.120 times at 16 KiB (35.065 against 31.303 ns) [same files; README.md of 010, line 109]. On boot F2 (the prefetchers off, the L3 on) the exploratory L3-hit event 0x328E counts only 0.14 to 0.64 hits per load at 96 to 384 KiB at the best rep (0.12 to 0.64 over all reps), while the inner refills are 0.96 to 1.00 per load at the best rep (0.88 to 1.00 over the reps) [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012]. The latency falls as the chain grows: 36.0 ns at 96 KiB to 32.8 ns at 256 KiB [same file, best reps]. The L3-served load of 32.8 to 33.9 ns [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 012, 192 to 384 KiB] is 6.2 to 7.3 ns above asimov-bench's 26.6 ns for the DSU L3 through the CME [CME-plan.md line 63; asimov-cme-perf.html open items].

Why it looked wrong. An L3 hit inside the cluster should cost less than a refill from the mesh. Refills moving inside the cluster should lower the chain time, not raise it. With the prefetchers off, every inner refill was expected to be an L3 hit, so the hit count should have been near 1.00 per load, not 0.14 to 0.64.

Tests added.

  • Boot E against boot C: inner (0x327D) and outer (0x327E) CME refill split by footprint, same commit b79dffa, only the SCP differs [run 4 boots C (007) and E (010)]: the L3's effect on the CME chain with the CME prefetcher on [README.md of 010, sections 'Against boot C: the L3 alone' and line 109]
  • Boot F2: L3 on, prefetchers off (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1 with SCP 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1), the CME chases under --events cme-l3 (0x328E L3 hit, 0x328F L3 miss, 0x3290 L3 refill), exploratory; least-squares fit ns per load = a + hits x h + snoops x s + outer x o over the 15 rep rows from 96 to 384 KiB [run 6 boot F2 (012)]: the L3-served chain load through the CME with no prefetch refills, and which level served each refill [cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012; README.md of 012, 'The CME L3 events'; gen_run6.py l3_fit]

What the tests showed. E against C: the CME prefetcher's fills set the chain time on both boots. At 16 KiB E counts 10.4 refills per load (inner plus outer, mean over reps) against C's 7.9, and the prefetch-refill event alone reads 9.95 against 7.44 [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 007]. So no E-against-C row isolates one L3 hit through the CME; the run 4 CME page calls that number 'Insufficient data' [asimov-cme-run4.html section 9.1]. F2: the 192, 256 and 384 KiB chains read 33.910, 32.779 and 33.014 ns per load (best rep) [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 012], 11.8 to 12.9 ns above the 21.005 ns round-trip baseline [same file, cme-roundtrip rows]. The core's own L3 hit was estimated at 10.6 to 11.0 ns est. from boot E's hit set (256 and 384 KiB rows) [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, 'An L3 hit costs about 10.8 ns']. Boot B, the same chains with the L3 off, read 39.525, 40.700 and 41.677 ns with 0.34 to 0.74 outer refills per load [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 006]. The L3 events agree with the inner/outer split by construction: hit plus miss equals inner plus outer within 0.0001 per load, and refill equals outer, in every row [recomputed from cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 012; README.md of 012 line 182]. So they validate nothing on their own. Hypothesis (the pre-queue check's reading of the C1-SME2 RTL, evidence/jibin/prequeue-0c190a1.txt, quoted in README.md of 012 line 181): miss minus refill counts lines snooped from a core's cache in the cluster, here CPU 2's own L2, which wrote the chain with core stores (CPU 3 was offline). Least squares over the 15 rep rows: constant 23.4, L3 hit 6.7, snoop 13.9, outer 20.4 ns est., rms 0.02 ns, columns near-collinear [gen_run6.py l3_fit; recomputed]. The control for the events, a chain the core never touched (written through the CME), is not in any run [asimov-cme-perf.html section 5.2; README.md of 012 line 211].
