4.35 CME wake-up cost per timed span, the OCM pass spread through the CME, and a lone CME call's 280 to 536 ns outside its spanpartly explained

A lone CME call spends 280 to 536 ns outside its timed span on boots F1 and F2, against 64 ns for back-to-back calls.

What looked wrong

  • Jesse's run 3 README (membench-jibin-004) bound a fixed CME (the streaming compute unit, one per core cluster) cost per timed span at 0.1 to 0.3 us est. [004 README lines 13 and 90]
  • That bound came from three views of the data. [004 README lines 13 and 90]
  • On boot E the 7 CME passes of one OCM region (on-chip memory at the mesh home nodes) spread 7.25 to 13.55 ns per load, region 2 to region 1. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-fresh1..7 rows and asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]
  • The medians sat 3.63 to 12.66 ns per load above the bests. [010 cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv, cme-fresh1..7 rows and asimov-cme-perf.html section 7]
  • In run 3 one cme-call rep ran 82.641 ns per call, against 43.609 and 43.625 ns in the other two reps. [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv rows ocm,0,cme-call,0..2]
  • That is 2,498 ns over 64 calls: 5,033 extra core cycles but only 419 extra CME cycles. [004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv rows ocm,0,cme-call,0..2]
  • On boot F1, bracket minus span gave 63.5 to 64.6 ns per call for back-to-back cme-call calls (36 reps). [011 README lines 157-168 and cme-latency-*.csv of 011]
  • The same measure gave 76.0 to 106.2 ns per call for looped bandwidth calls of 1 to 256 KiB. [011 README lines 157-168 and looped cme-bandwidth-*.csv of 011]
  • Each of the 42 sparse OCM passes spent 285.8 to 292.2 ns outside its span. [011 README lines 157-168 and cme-latency-*.csv of 011]
  • The F1 single-call rows spent 281.1 to 535.7 ns per call outside the span: reads 281.1 to 300.9 ns and writes 354.6 to 427.8 ns after their first rep. [011 README line 168 and cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]
  • Every first rep spent more, reads 348.5 to 408.0 ns and writes 476.3 to 535.7 ns. [011 README line 168 and cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]

Why it looked wrong

  • The SCP (the system control processor) sets every cluster's CME power controller to dynamic mode as each core powers on. [011 README line 349]
  • By the RTL (the chip's hardware description, read but not measured) a CME in dynamic mode switches itself off after about 1.2 to 1.5 us est. with both cores out of streaming mode. [004 README line 89]
  • Switching off cleans and invalidates its L1, and switching on invalidates the L1 again. [004 README line 89]
  • Every timed span follows an untimed gap outside streaming mode. Whether the CME was off at a span's start is therefore unknown. [004 README lines 13, 89 and 90]
  • A 64-load OCM pass would carry up to about 5 ns est. per load of such a cost, a 320-load pass 0.3 to 1 ns est. [004 README lines 13, 89 and 90]
  • After the bracket's two clock reads (39.0 ns, bracket_overhead_ns) and one back-to-back call are taken out, the F1 sparse passes' excess is 0.18 to 0.19 us, inside run 3's 0.3 us bound. [011 README lines 155 and 168]
  • The first single-call write reps' excess of 0.33 to 0.42 us is outside it. [011 README lines 155 and 168]
  • The files do not separate a wake-up from the rest of a call's entry and exit (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call and return). [011 README lines 155 and 168]

Still open

A wake-up inside a span's first loads is bounded, not measured. The 0.33 to 0.42 us first-rep excess of the single-call writes on F1 is unassigned. A row that times the first load of a span apart from the rest would settle it [asimov-cme-perf.html section 10].

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 3 README (membench-jibin-004, run of 2026-11-03), CME power section, lines 13 and 87-91; run 6 span data (011 boot F1, run of 2026-11-06; 012 boot F2, run of 2026-11-07)

What looked wrong. Three views in Jesse's run 3 README bound a fixed CME cost per timed span at 0.1 to 0.3 us est. [membench-jibin-004/README.md lines 13 and 90]. On boot E the 7 CME passes of one OCM region spread 7.25 to 13.55 ns per load (region 2 to region 1), and the medians sit 3.6 to 12.7 ns above the bests [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv of 010, cme-fresh1..7 rows; asimov-cme-perf.html section 7 quotes 7.2 to 13.5]. One run 3 cme-call rep ran 82.641 ns per call against 43.609 and 43.625 in the other two reps: 2.5 us longer over 64 calls, with 5,033 extra core cycles (168.52 minus the mean of 90.02 and 89.73 cycles per call, times 64) and only 419 extra CME cycles (87.5938 minus 81.0469, times 64) [membench-jibin-004 cme-latency-ocm-all5.csv, rows 'ocm,0,cme-call,0..2']. By bracket minus span on F1, back-to-back cme-call calls spend 63.5 to 64.6 ns outside the span (36 reps) and looped bandwidth calls of 1 to 256 KiB 76.0 to 106.2 ns, but a call alone in its bracket spends 285.8 to 292.2 ns on the 42 sparse OCM passes (after a flush and a counter start) and 281.1 to 535.7 ns in the single-call rows: reads 281 to 301 ns and writes 355 to 428 ns after their first rep, and every first rep more (reads 348 to 408, writes 476 to 536) [membench-jibin-011/README.md lines 157-168; recomputed from cme-latency-*.csv, cme-bandwidth-*-asmpasses.csv and the looped cme-bandwidth-*.csv of 011]. About 39 ns of a one-call figure is the bracket's own two clock reads (bracket_overhead_ns=39.0, comment line 3 of every CME latency CSV of 011 and 012).

Why it looked wrong. The SCP sets every cluster's CME power controller to dynamic mode as each core powers on [membench-jibin-011/README.md line 349]. By the RTL (read, not measured) the CME in dynamic mode switches itself off after about 1.2 to 1.5 us with both cores out of streaming mode, cleaning and invalidating its L1 on the way, and switching on invalidates the L1 again [membench-jibin-004/README.md line 89]. Every timed span follows an untimed gap outside streaming mode, so whether the CME was off at the start of a span is unknown [same line]. A 64-load OCM pass would carry up to about 5 ns est. per load of such a cost, a 320-load pass 0.3 to 1 ns est. [004 README lines 13 and 90]. With the clock reads and a back-to-back call taken out, the sparse passes' excess (0.18 to 0.19 us) fits run 3's 0.3 us bound, but the first single-call write reps' excess (0.33 to 0.42 us) does not [011 README line 168]. The files do not separate a wake-up from the rest of a call's entry and exit (save, SMSTART, SMSTOP, restore, call and return) [011 README lines 155 and 168].

Tests added.

  • In-span clock stamps (CNTVCT_EL0) in every CME kernel: ns_per_load_span beside ns_per_load in latency rows, span_s and span_GBps in bandwidth rows [run 6 F1/F2 (membench-jibin-011 bootF1, 012 bootF2) [011 README lines 153-155]]: the outside-span time of a call by row type (bracket minus span), and whether the OCM pass-to-pass spread sits inside or outside the span
  • F2 repeat of the CME rows with the data prefetchers off (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1), the L3 on [run 6 F2 (membench-jibin-012) [012 README lines 7 and 67]]: outside-span ns per call by row type without prefetch, and the pass spread without prefetch
  • A row timing the first load of a span apart from the rest [not added; asimov-cme-perf.html section 10 lists it as the row that would decide the open item (the primary files do not say who chose to leave it)]: the wake cost itself, inside the span's first loads

What the tests showed. On F1 the best pass of each OCM region spends 286.0 to 289.0 ns outside its span (all 42 sparse passes: 285.8 to 292.2 ns); on F2 the best pass 280.0 to 286.0 ns (all passes 280.0 to 304.0 ns) [cme-latency-ocm-region0..4.csv and -all5.csv of 011 and 012, (ns_per_load minus ns_per_load_span) times loads; 012 README line 141]. The pass-to-pass spread is inside the span: on F1 the 7 passes of a region spread 3.19 to 8.75 ns per load by ns_per_load_span (3.14 to 8.73 by the bracket), on F2 0.16 to 0.36 ns per load in span (0.16 to 0.66 by the bracket, the F2 bracket maximum including one 304 ns outside-span pass of region 4) [same files; asimov-cme-perf.html section 10 quotes the bracket spreads 3.1 to 8.7 and 0.2 to 0.7]. So the spread is the prefetcher's, and it vanishes with the prefetchers off. F2's outside-span times match F1's by row type: cme-call 63.53 to 64.64 vs 63.52 to 64.61 ns (36 reps each); looped 1 to 256 KiB calls 75.8 to 105.6 vs 76.0 to 106.2 ns; single-call reps 280.0 to 523.6 vs 281.1 to 535.7 ns (F2 reads 280.0 to 293.1 after the first rep and 339.9 to 397.4 on the first rep, writes 371.0 to 421.0 and 452.3 to 523.6) [012 README line 144; recomputed from the same CSVs of 012]. So the prefetchers are not the cause of the lone-call excess either. A wake-up inside a span's first loads is bounded, not measured; the first-rep excess of the single-call writes stays unassigned.

4.36 8 MiB chain in address order through the CME reads 21.4 ns, like a CME L1 hitexplained

An 8 MiB in-order chain through the CME read 21.417 ns per load on boot A, the CME L1-hit time, not the DRAM time.

What looked wrong

  • An 8 MiB chain in address order, every line flushed from the caches first, read 21.417 ns per load through the CME on run 4 boots A, C and E. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010, cme-best rows]
  • The CME's 4 KiB repeated chain (a CME L1 hit) read 21.453 ns per load on boot A, 21.481 ns on boot C and 21.371 ns on boot E. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, 007, 010]
  • The 8 MiB row is within 0.07 ns of the 4 KiB row on every boot. [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, 007, 010]
  • The CME round-trip control (a CME call that does no memory load at all) read 21.004 to 21.005 ns per call on boots A to E. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 010, cme-roundtrip-best rows]
  • The 8 MiB row is only 0.41 ns above the round-trip control. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 010, cme-roundtrip-best rows]
  • The row counted 1.00 outer refills per load (an outer refill is a line fetched from outside the cluster) on boots A, C and E. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]
  • So every line still came from outside the cluster.
  • The core's own walk of the same chain read 6.917 ns per load on boots A and C and 2.492 ns on boot E. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]

Why it looked wrong

  • Every line of the chain is flushed before the pass. The chain is 8,388,608 bytes, 131,072 lines of 64 B. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, comment line '# size=8388608 lines=131072']
  • 8 MiB is larger than the SLC (the system level cache, 3.75 MiB). So every line must come from DRAM once per walk.
  • A chain with a DRAM footprint should read at the DRAM time, not at the CME L1-hit time of 21.453 ns per load (boot A).
  • The measured DRAM time through the CME is 71.711 ns per load (random flushed 8 MiB chain, boot B). [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006]
  • The result contradicts the footprint unless something fetches each line before the load reaches it.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
CME in-order row with refill-by-cause eventsboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot ECounts prefetch refills (event 0x32B2, cme_l1d_refill_hwprf) against demand refills (event 0x3280, cme_l1d_refill_rd) per load, plus inner (0x327D) and outer (0x327E) refills. A prefetch count near 1.0 per load means the CME prefetcher fetched each line before its load arrived.
Same row with the CME prefetcher offboot B, boot DReads the row with IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 set by TF-A (the boot firmware), which turns the CME hardware prefetcher off. A rise to the DRAM time would mean the prefetcher caused the 21.4 ns.
Row repeated on all five bootsboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EChecks repeatability. The same value on every boot with the same prefetcher setting means the result is not measurement noise.

What the tests showed

  • On boots A, C and E every refill was a prefetch: 1.0000 prefetch refills per load and 2.289e-05 demand refills per load (3 demand refills in 131,072 loads). [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]
  • The same boots counted 1.0000 outer refills per load. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]
  • So the CME prefetcher fetched each line before its load arrived. Each load then hit the CME L1.
  • With the prefetcher off the row read 71.740 ns per load on boot B and 71.738 ns on boot D, with 0.0000 prefetch refills and 1.0000 demand refills per load. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 008]
  • That is 3.35 times boot A's 21.417 ns. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 008]
  • The random flushed 8 MiB chain through the CME (the DRAM time through the CME) read 71.711 ns per load on boot B and 71.712 ns on boot D. [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008]
  • The in-order row with the prefetcher off is 0.03 ns above the random flushed chain. [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008]
  • The core's chain moved the same way: 6.917 ns per load with the prefetchers on (boot A) against 52.762 ns on boot B and 52.763 ns on boot D with them off. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 008]
  • That is 7.63 times. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 008]
  • The in-order row is the stimulus a hardware prefetcher is built for.
  • The run-4 CME page uses it to show whether the CME prefetch event counts at all. [asimov-cme-run4.html, Words used here and section 5 chart caption]

Still open

Open on the core side only. The core's in-order chain reads 6.917 ns per load on boot A, about one L2 hit (6.1 ns for the 128 KiB row). The core page's hypothesis is that the core's L1 prefetcher runs ahead by about one L2 hit, and the CME's runs far enough ahead for an L1 hit [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 5]. The record names no measurement that would settle this.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boot A (005), measured 2026-11-04 (UTC); the row is new in run 4 (run 3, 004, has no cme-latency-dram-seq.csv). Jesse's README 005 does not mention the row; the first written comparison is README 006 (boot B) and the run-4 CME page.

What looked wrong. An 8 MiB chain in address order, every line flushed first, reads 21.417 ns per load through the CME on boots A, C and E [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010, cme-best rows]. That is within 0.07 ns of the CME's 4 KiB L1-hit row (21.453 ns on A, 21.481 on C, 21.371 on E: 0.036 and 0.064 ns below on A and C, 0.046 ns above on E) [cme-latency-dram-small.csv of 005, 007, 010]. It is 0.41 ns above the 21.005 ns CME round-trip control (no memory load at all) [cme-roundtrip-best rows of the same files]. The row counts 1.00 outer refills per load, so every line still came from outside the cluster. The core's same chain reads 6.917 ns on A and C and 2.492 ns on E [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010].

Why it looked wrong. Every line of the 8 MiB chain is flushed before the pass, and 8 MiB is larger than the SLC (3.75 MiB). So every line must come from DRAM once per walk. A DRAM-footprint chain at the CME L1-hit time contradicts the footprint unless something fetches each line before the load reaches it.

Tests added.

  • CME sequential row with refill-by-cause events (demand read 0x3280 = cme_l1d_refill_rd, hardware prefetch 0x32B2 = cme_l1d_refill_hwprf, inner 0x327D, outer 0x327E); boots B and D with the CME prefetcher off (IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28 set by TF-A); the row repeated on all five boots [run 4 boots A, B, C, D, E (005, 006, 007, 008, 010)]: prefetch refills against demand refills per load on the row; the same row with the CME prefetcher off; repeatability across boots

What the tests showed. On boots A, C and E every refill is a prefetch: cme_l1d_refill_hwprf_per_load 1.0000, cme_l1d_refill_rd_per_load 2.289e-05 (3 demand refills in 131,072 loads), outer 1.0000 [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]. So the CME prefetcher fetches each line before its load arrives, and each load hits the CME L1. With the prefetcher off the row reads 71.740 ns on B and 71.738 ns on D, with hwprf 0.0000 and rd 1.0000 per load [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 008]. That is 3.35 times boot A's 21.417 ns and is 0.03 ns above the random flushed 8 MiB chain on the same boots (71.711 ns on B, 71.712 on D), the DRAM time through the CME [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008]. The core's chain moved the same way: 6.917 ns with the prefetchers on against 52.762 ns on B and 52.763 on D, 7.63 times [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 to 008]. The row is the stimulus a hardware prefetcher is built for, so it shows whether the CME prefetch event counts at all; the run-4 CME page uses it for that [asimov-cme-run4.html, Words used here; section 5 chart caption]. Open point on the core side only: the core's chain sits at about an L2 hit (6.9 ns against 6.1 ns for the 128 KiB row), so the core's L1 prefetcher runs ahead by about one L2 hit, while the CME's runs far enough ahead for an L1 hit; the core page marks this a hypothesis [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 5].

Highlighted: CME-prefetcher, CME, DRAM.

4.37 CME writes fall from 64 to 52 and 40 GB/s with the L3 on; CME stores stop at half a store per cycleopen

With the L3 on, CME writes fall from 64 to 52 and 40 GB/s. CME stores run at half a store per cycle.

What looked wrong

  • With the L3 on, the CME writes DRAM slower than with the L3 off.
  • Boot F1 (L3 on) writes 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
  • Run 3 (L3 off) wrote 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s at 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB. Both are bracket values, best rep. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 004]
  • The drop also holds in span from 48 KiB on. On F1 the in-span write is 53.5 to 56.3 GB/s at 48 to 256 KiB and 40.5 to 42.8 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB. [span_GBps column of 011]
  • Only the 16 KiB row reads higher in span (69.5 GB/s) than run 3's bracket (63.7 GB/s). [span_GBps column of 011]
  • The core's own writes and the CME's large reads did not move. One core writes 30.1 to 32.0 GB/s in run 3 and 30.6 to 32.0 GB/s on F1. [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011]
  • The CME reads 36.6 to 37.0 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB on both. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011]
  • The one exception: at 160 and 256 KiB, F1's CME reads are 1.114 to 1.117 times run 3's. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011 and README 011 lines 109 and 204]
  • Separate from the L3 question: the CME's store rate is below its load rate on every boot.
  • In run 3 at 48 KiB the CME read 104.9 GB/s and wrote 63.8 GB/s. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, 49152-byte rows]
  • That is 52 and 32 bytes per cycle at 2.003 GHz. The write rate is half of one 64-byte store per cycle. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, 49152-byte rows]
  • With the L3 on, the single-call form on F1 reads 109 to 132 GB/s, that is 54 to 66 bytes per cycle, one 64-byte load per cycle. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]
  • The same form writes only 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s, that is 26 bytes per cycle, 0.42 of a store per cycle. [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011]
  • No source on disk gives the CME store path width.

Why it looked wrong

  • A cache that is turned on should not slow a streaming write that cannot fit in it. The L3 holds 256 KiB, and the write footprint is 1 to 32 MiB.
  • The kernels are run 3's byte for byte (checked by disassembly on the machine under test). So the change is the platform's, not the code's. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]
  • Run 6's in-span clock stamps do not explain the drop at 1 to 32 MiB. The outside-span interval is at most 0.5 % of a call there (118.5 to 357.8 ns of calls of 25 to 1,644 us). [README 011, bandwidth rows note]
  • Bracket over span is 0.995 to 1.000 at 1 to 32 MiB. [recomputed from 011 and 012]
  • Hypothesis on the CME page: with the L3 on, the CME's stores allocate in the L3 and drain through it at the L3's write rate. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]
  • The same hypothesis: with the L3 holding no data, the stores went straight to the mesh. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]
  • No source gives the L3's write rate as a number.
  • The measured CME store rate with the L3 on is 27 bytes per cycle at 48 to 256 KiB in span (53.5 to 54.8 GB/s). [span_GBps column of 011]
  • At 1 to 32 MiB it is 20 to 21 bytes per cycle (40.4 to 42.8 GB/s). [span_GBps column of 011]
  • A supporting match: one CME writing 32 MiB on F1 (40.4 GB/s) is 0.99 times the 40.9 GB/s that CPUs 2 and 3 write together (16 MiB each) on the same boot. [bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv of 011 and 004]
  • Run 3 also gave 40.9 GB/s for the two cores, against the CME's 62.0 GB/s then. [bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv of 011 and 004]
  • The page's reading (hypothesis): if the CME's stores leave through the same cluster port, the two-core write limit is on the cores' side, not the port's. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Boot F2: CME bandwidth sweep with the data prefetchers offboot F2Whether the prefetcher causes the write drop. F2 (prefetchers off by a TF-A hook) writes 51.5 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB. That is 0.927 to 1.000 times F1 (2 MiB 0.927, the rest 0.992 to 1.000). So the prefetcher is not the cause [README 012 line 93 and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012].
Single-call writes 48-256 KiB, L1 write forms 4-24 KiBboot F1, boot F2The store rate without per-call cost. The single-call write (--asm-passes) is 51.4 to 52.4 GB/s at 48 to 256 KiB on F1 and 51.6 to 52.4 GB/s on F2. The L1 write forms (looped, single-call, looped with DSB ST) give 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 to 24 KiB on F1. So the store rate with the L3 on is 26 to 27 bytes per cycle in every form [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012 and cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011].
Proposed: L3-event write row, L3-off write row, mixed two-core writenot runA CME write row with the exploratory L3 events 0x328E and 0x328F on, a write row on an L3-off boot with run 6's kernels, a two-core write with one core in streaming mode, and Arm's statement of the CME L1 write policy. These would show where the stores drain (L3 allocation or not). They would also show whether any of the change is the in-span clock reads. And they would show whether the 40.9 GB/s two-core write limit is on the cores' side or the cluster port's [asimov-cme-perf.html sections 6 and 10].

What the tests showed

  • Cause unknown. The CME page lists it as open ('open: why the CME's writes fall with the L3 on'). [asimov-cme-perf.html section 10]
  • Two causes are ruled out. F2 rules out the prefetcher: its writes are 0.927 to 1.000 times F1's at 16 KiB to 32 MiB. [README 012 line 93]
  • The stamp check rules out run 6's clock reads at 1 to 32 MiB: the outside-span interval is at most 0.5 % of a call there. [README 011, bandwidth rows note]
  • The CME bandwidth rows carry no CME counters. The bandwidth program refuses --perf together with --cme. So no refill count sits beside the drop. [README 012 line 142]
  • Side result from F2: the CME prefetcher carries about half of a streaming DRAM read. The CME read at 32 MiB is 17.7 GB/s on F2 against 36.6 GB/s on F1 (0.48 times). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 012 and 011]
  • Copies fell with the writes. CME DRAM writes and copies on F1 are 0.65 to 0.84 times run 3's by the bracket at every size, and 0.65 to 0.89 times in span from 48 KiB on. [README 011 line 11]
  • Page defect found during verification: the 'CME L1 on its own' row of asimov-cme-perf.html prints an unrendered template, '{BPC6 * max(SINGLE_WR) / 64:.1f} of a store per cycle', where the number 0.42 should appear. [asimov-cme-perf.html table 'The CME L1 on its own']
  • The generator should be fixed.

Still open

Where the CME's stores drain with the L3 on is still unknown. The 40.9 GB/s two-core write limit is not yet assigned to the cores or to the cluster port. A CME write row with the exploratory L3 events 0x328E and 0x328F on, and a write row on an L3-off boot with run 6's kernels, would settle whether the stores allocate in the L3.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 6 boots F1 (membench-jibin-011, 2026-11-06 UTC) and F2 (012, 2026-11-06/07 UTC); the half-rate stores were first seen in run 3 (004, 2026-11-03 UTC)

What looked wrong. With the L3 on, the CME (the cluster's Arm C1-SME2 streaming unit) writes DRAM slower than it did with the L3 off. On boot F1 the CME write reads 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s by the bracket at 16 to 256 KiB and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB; boot F2 (prefetchers off) reads 51.5 to 52.5 and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at the same sizes [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, best rep]. Run 3 (L3 off) wrote 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s at 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004]. The drop also holds in span (the clock stamps inside the streaming span) from 48 KiB on: 53.5 to 56.3 GB/s at 48 to 256 KiB and 40.5 to 42.8 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB on F1; only the 16 KiB row reads higher in span (69.5 GB/s) than run 3's bracket (63.7) [span_GBps column of 011]. The core's own writes did not move: one core writes 30.1 to 32.0 GB/s in run 3 and 30.6 to 32.0 on F1 [bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011; README 011 line 109: 1.000 to 1.003 times at 48 KiB to 32 MiB]. The CME's reads did not move either where they can be compared: 36.6 to 37.0 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB on both (36.6 at 32 MiB on both), and 73.8 and 104.6 GB/s in span at 16 and 48 KiB on F1 against run 3's 73.4 and 104.9 by the bracket [README 011 line 204]; at 160 and 256 KiB the F1 reads are 1.114 to 1.117 times run 3's (41.4 and 41.6 against 37.1 and 37.2). Separate from the L3 question: the CME's store rate is below its load rate on every boot. In run 3 at 48 KiB the CME read 104.9 GB/s and wrote 63.8 GB/s, that is 52 and 32 bytes per 2.003 GHz cycle, so half of one 64-byte store per cycle. With the L3 on, the single-call form (every pass of a rep inside one call) reads 109 to 132 GB/s (one 64-byte load per cycle, 54 to 66 bytes per cycle) but writes only 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s (26 bytes per cycle, 0.42 of a store per cycle) [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011; asimov-cme-perf.html table 'The CME L1 on its own']. No source on disk gives the CME store path width.

Why it looked wrong. A cache that is turned on should not slow a streaming write whose footprint (1 to 32 MiB) cannot fit it (the L3 is 256 KiB). The kernels are run 3's byte for byte by the box's disassembly check [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6], so the change is the platform's, not the code's. Run 6's clock stamps do not explain the drop at 1 to 32 MiB: the outside-span interval is at most 0.5 % of a call there (118.5 to 357.8 ns of calls of 25 to 1,644 us) [README 011, bandwidth rows note], and bracket over span is 0.995 to 1.000 at 1 to 32 MiB (recomputed from 011 and 012). Hypothesis on the CME page: with the L3 on the CME's stores allocate in the L3 and drain through it at the L3's write rate, which is below the CME's store path; with the L3 holding no data the stores went straight to the mesh [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6]. No source gives the L3's write rate as a number. The measured CME store rate with the L3 on is 27 bytes per cycle at 48 to 256 KiB in span (53.5 to 54.8 GB/s) and 20 to 21 bytes per cycle at 1 to 32 MiB (40.4 to 42.8 GB/s). Supporting match: one CME writing 32 MiB on F1 (40.4 GB/s) is 0.99 times the 40.9 GB/s that CPUs 2 and 3 write together (16 MiB each) through the same cluster on the same boot [bandwidth-write-cpus2-3.csv of 011; run 3 also 40.9 GB/s, against the CME's 62.0 then]. The page's reading: if the CME's stores leave through the same cluster port, the two-core write limit is on the cores' side, not the port's (hypothesis).

Tests added.

  • Boot F2: the same CME bandwidth sweep with the data prefetchers off (TF-A hook sets IMP_CPUECTLR_EL1 bit 48 and IMP_CMECFG_EL1 bit 28) [run 6 boot F2 (membench-jibin-012)]: whether the prefetcher causes the write drop: F2 writes 0.927 to 1.000 times F1 at 16 KiB to 32 MiB (2 MiB 0.927, the rest 0.992 to 1.000) [README 012 line 93; cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012], so the prefetcher is not the cause
  • Single-call write rows at 48 to 256 KiB (--asm-passes) and the L1 write forms at 4 to 24 KiB (looped, single-call, looped with DSB ST) [run 6 boots F1 and F2 (011, 012)]: the store rate without per-call cost: single-call write 51.4 to 52.4 GB/s at 48 to 256 KiB on F1 and 51.6 to 52.4 on F2 [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv], 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 to 24 KiB [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011]; the store rate with the L3 on is 26 to 27 bytes per cycle in every form
  • Proposed: a CME write row with the exploratory L3 events (0x328E, 0x328F) on; a write row on an L3-off boot with run 6's kernels; a two-core write with one core in streaming mode; Arm's statement of the CME L1 write policy [not run]: where the stores drain (L3 allocation or not), whether any of the change is the in-span clock reads, and whether the 40.9 GB/s two-core write limit is on the cores' side or the cluster port's [asimov-cme-perf.html sections 6 and 10]

What the tests showed. Cause unknown; listed as open on the CME page ('open: why the CME's writes fall with the L3 on') [asimov-cme-perf.html section 10]. F2 rules out the prefetcher (writes 0.927 to 1.000 times F1). The stamp check rules out run 6's clock reads at 1 to 32 MiB (under 0.5 % of a call). The CME bandwidth rows carry no CME counters (bandwidth refuses --perf with --cme) [README 012 line 142], so no refill count sits beside the drop. Side result from F2: the CME prefetcher carries about half of a streaming DRAM read, 17.7 GB/s on F2 against 36.6 GB/s on F1 at 32 MiB (0.48 times) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 012 and 011]. Copies fell with the writes: 0.65 to 0.84 times run 3's by the bracket at every size (writes and copies together), 0.65 to 0.89 in span from 48 KiB on [README 011 line 11]. 4.38 Core sequential 8 MiB chain reads 6.9 ns with the L3 off and 2.5 ns with it on, faster than the L2 hitopen

On boot E an 8 MiB chain of flushed DRAM lines reads 2.492 ns per load, under the L2 hit's 6.023 ns.

What looked wrong

  • The sequential chain is an 8 MiB chain (a list of loads where each load returns the address of the next) over the 64-byte lines in address order.
  • Every line is flushed from every cache before each pass. So every load of it is a DRAM read [core page glossary, latency-dram-seq.csv header flush=1 seq=1].
  • On boots A and C (run 4, prefetchers on, L3 off) the chain reads 6.917 ns per load, best of two fresh passes [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 and 007].
  • On boot E (run 4, prefetchers on, L3 on) it reads 2.492 ns per load (fresh1 2.501 ns, fresh2 2.492 ns) [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010].
  • The prefetch counters are the same on all three boots: 1.0000 L1 refills and 1.0000 L2 refills per load [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010, 005, 007].
  • The L1 refills requested by the hardware prefetcher read 0.9997 per load on E, 0.9999 on A, and 1.0000 and 0.9999 on C [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010, 005, 007].
  • On boot E the 4 KiB repeated chain (an L1 hit) reads 2.002 ns per load (4.01 cycles).
  • The 128 KiB repeated chain (an L2 hit) reads 6.023 ns per load on E and 6.096 ns on A [latency-dram-small.csv of 010 and 005].
  • So on boot A the DRAM stream costs about an L2 hit. On boot E it costs 4.99 cycles at 2.003 GHz, one cycle above the L1 hit.
  • The L3 read refill event 0xA2 reads 0.0001 per load on boot E's sequential chain. Yet every line was flushed and came from outside the DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit, the cluster block that holds the L3).
  • On the random flushed chain of the same boot it reads 1.0001 per load [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010].

Why it looked wrong

  • Every load is a DRAM read: the line is flushed first, and one L2 refill per load is counted.
  • Yet one load costs an L2 hit on boots A and C (6.917 ns against the 6.096 ns L2 hit on A).
  • On boot E one load costs an L1 hit plus one cycle (2.492 ns against the 2.002 ns L1 hit) [latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-small.csv of 005 and 010].
  • One DRAM read costs 52.659 ns on boot E's random flushed chain [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010]. A 2.492 ns load cannot be waiting for its own line.
  • The L3 is 256 KiB per cluster. It cannot hold an 8 MiB stream.
  • So the 2.78 times change from boot A to boot E (6.917 / 2.492) with the same prefetch counts per load has no cause in the counters on disk.
  • Jesse's boot E README says the same: "These files do not show why its latency fell" [results/membench-jibin-010/README.md line 113].
  • The excess over the L1 chain on boot E is 0.490 ns (2.492 minus 2.002). That is 0.98 cycles at 2.003 GHz, close to one whole cycle.
  • A wait for a late line would not average to a whole cycle [core page section 8].

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Sequential 8 MiB chain (--seq), prefetch event set, core and CMEboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EIt measures ns per load and demand against prefetch refills per load at L1, L2 and L3 (events 0x03, 0x17, 0xA2, 0x81BC, 0x81BD, 0x0111) on results 005 to 010. The same row runs through the CME (the Arm C1-SME2 matrix engine, one per cluster, file cme-latency-dram-seq.csv). It also checks that the prefetch events count at all. The sequential chain is the prefetch stimulus [follow-up-run-plan.md line 16].
Sequential row with prefetchers off and L3 on (boot F2 firmware)not runIt would show how much of the 2.492 ns per load on boot E is the prefetcher's. Neither run 6 boot measured that. F2 (results 012) ran run_cme.sh only. F1 (results 011) ran run_all.sh at commit 0c190a1 with no latency-dram-seq.csv [run 4 core page section 14.2, README of 012 line 3].
Sequential chain with two members per line (32-byte stride)not runA per-line cost would halve per load, and a per-load cost would not [core page section 8].
Sequential-chain row under the L1 hit countersnot runIt would show whether any load waited for a line that had not yet arrived. The refill counters cannot say that [core page section 8].

What the tests showed

  • The DRAM time is overlapped, not missing.
  • With the prefetchers off (boots B and D, L3 off) the same chain costs the full DRAM time, 52.762 and 52.763 ns per load.
  • That matches the random flushed chain (52.659 ns on boot E, 52.739 ns on boot B) [latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008, 010].
  • So address order alone gives no gain. The prefetcher does the overlap.
  • On boot E the prefetcher issues a new DRAM read every 2.492 ns. Each read takes about 52.7 ns.
  • So it keeps about 21.2 reads in flight (issued and not yet returned) (est., 52.762 / 2.492).
  • On boot A it keeps about 7.6 reads in flight (est., 52.762 / 6.917) [derived from latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 005, 010, core page section 8].
  • The stream rate on boot E is 64 bytes per 2.492 ns, 25.7 GB/s (derived, GB = 1e9 bytes).
  • That is about the plain one-core DRAM read of the same boot: 24.945 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010, best rows].
  • On boot C the plain read moves 9.294 GB/s at 2 MiB and 9.196 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007].
  • By the same arithmetic boot C keeps about 2.8 times fewer reads in flight (est.).
  • The CME's own sequential row is unchanged by the L3: 21.417 ns per load on boots A, C and E alike, with 1.0000 prefetch refills per load [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010].
  • Four hypotheses are on the pages, none tested.
  • (1) With the L3 holding data, the prefetcher's stream drains into the L3 and the L2 refills complete sooner [run 4 core page 14.2].
  • (2) The full-L3 mode lets the cluster keep more read requests in flight toward the mesh [core page 2.3].
  • (3) The extra whole cycle per load is the prefetched line's write into L1 taking the cache for one cycle per line [core page section 8].
  • (4) Either the L1 prefetcher's fills do not allocate in the L3, or event 0xA2 counts demand reads only. The TRM (the Arm Technical Reference Manual) text does not say which [run 4 core page 3.1].

Still open

What the L3 changes in how far ahead the prefetcher runs is unknown (Insufficient data) [core page section 8]. The sequential row with the prefetchers off and the L3 on (boot F2's firmware) would show how much of the 2.492 ns per load is the prefetcher's. A 32-byte-stride chain would show whether the cost is per line or per load.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boot A (membench-jibin-005, run on 2026-11-04 UTC): 6.917 ns per load [results/membench-jibin-005/results/bootA/latency-dram-seq.csv, best row]. Boot E (membench-jibin-010, run on 2026-11-05 UTC): 2.492 ns per load [results/membench-jibin-010/results/bootE/latency-dram-seq.csv, best row]. The 0.49 ns excess over the L1 chain was written up on the core page section 8 on 2026-11-05 (memory asimov-cme-test-state.md). Jibin's question of 2026-11-06 ("you missed the DRAM load time; how did you get 0.49 ns of waiting") is not in the primary files; it comes from the transcript sources only (not verified here).

What looked wrong. The sequential chain is an 8 MiB chain whose members are the 64-byte lines in address order, every line flushed from every cache before each pass [core page glossary; latency-dram-seq.csv header: flush=1 seq=1]. Every load of it is a DRAM read. On boots A and C (prefetchers on, L3 off) it reads 6.917 ns per load, best of two fresh passes [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 and 007]. On boot E (prefetchers on, L3 on) it reads 2.492 ns per load (fresh1 2.501, fresh2 2.492) [latency-dram-seq.csv of 010]. The prefetch counters are the same on all three boots: 1.0000 L1 refills per load, 0.9997 (E), 0.9999 (A) and 1.0000 / 0.9999 (C) L1 refills requested by the hardware prefetcher, 1.0000 L2 refills per load. With the prefetchers off (boots B and D) the same chain reads 52.762 and 52.763 ns per load with 0.0000 prefetch refills [latency-dram-seq.csv of 006 and 008]. For comparison on boot E: the 4 KiB repeated chain (an L1 hit) reads 2.002 ns per load (4.01 cycles), and the 128 KiB repeated chain (an L2 hit) reads 6.023 ns [latency-dram-small.csv of 010]. So on A the DRAM stream costs about an L2 hit, and on E it costs 2.492 ns, which is 4.99 cycles at 2.003 GHz (cycles_per_load column 4.99), one cycle above the L1 hit's 4.01 cycles. The L3 read refill event 0xA2 reads 0.0001 per load on the sequential chain although every line was flushed and came from outside the DSU; on the random flushed chain of the same boot it reads 1.0001 [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010].

Why it looked wrong. Every load is a DRAM read (the line is flushed first and one L2 refill per load is counted), yet it costs an L2 hit (A, C) or an L1 hit plus one cycle (E). One DRAM read costs 52.659 ns on boot E's random flushed chain [latency-dram-flushed.csv of 010], so a 2.492 ns load cannot be waiting for its own line. The L3 is 256 KiB per cluster and cannot hold an 8 MiB stream, so the 2.78 times change from A to E (6.917 / 2.492) with the same prefetch counts per load has no cause in the counters on disk. Jesse's boot E README says the same: "These files do not show why its latency fell" [results/membench-jibin-010/README.md line 113]. The excess over the L1 chain is 0.49 ns, 0.98 cycles, close to one whole cycle. A wait for a late line would not average to a whole cycle [core page section 8].

Tests added.

  • Sequential 8 MiB chain (--seq) on every run 4 boot with the prefetch event set (0x03, 0x17, 0xA2, 0x81BC, 0x81BD, 0x0111) [run 4 boots A to E (005, 006, 007, 008, 010); the same row through the CME (cme-latency-dram-seq.csv)]: ns per load and demand against prefetch refills per load at each level; whether the prefetch events count at all (follow-up-run-plan.md line 16: the sequential chain is the prefetch stimulus used to validate the events)
  • Proposed, not run: the sequential row with the prefetchers off and the L3 on (boot F2's firmware). F2 (012) ran run_cme.sh only, so the core row did not run; F1 (011) ran run_all.sh at commit 0c190a1 and also has no latency-dram-seq.csv [not run (no latency-dram-seq.csv under results/membench-jibin-011 or -012)]: how much of the 2.49 ns is the prefetcher's [run 4 core page section 14.2]
  • Proposed, not run: a sequential chain with two members per line (32-byte stride) [not run]: a per-line cost would halve per load, a per-load cost would not [core page section 8]
  • Proposed, not run: a sequential-chain row under the L1 hit counters [not run]: whether any load waited for a line that had not yet arrived; the refill counters cannot say [core page section 8]

What the tests showed. The DRAM time is overlapped, not missing. With the prefetchers off (boots B and D) the same chain costs the full DRAM time, 52.762 and 52.763 ns per load, the same as the random flushed chain (52.659 ns on E, 52.739 ns on B) [latency-dram-seq.csv and latency-dram-flushed.csv of 006, 008, 010]. So the address order alone buys nothing; the prefetcher does the overlap. On boot E the prefetcher issues a new DRAM read every 2.492 ns while each read takes about 52.7 ns, so it keeps about 21 reads in flight (est., 52.762 / 2.492 = 21.2); on boot A about 7.6 (est., 52.762 / 6.917) [derived from latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 005, 010; core page section 8 draws this as wall-clock lanes]. The stream rate on E is 64 bytes per 2.492 ns, 25.7 GB/s (derived), about the plain one-core DRAM read of the same boot: 24.945 GB/s at 2 MiB and 24.546 GB/s at 32 MiB [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 010, best rows]. On boot C the plain read moves 9.294 GB/s (2 MiB) and 9.196 GB/s (32 MiB) [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv of 007], so by the same arithmetic C keeps about 2.8 times fewer reads in flight (est.). The CME's own sequential row is unchanged by the L3: 21.417 ns per load on A, C and E alike, with 1.0000 prefetch refills per load [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, 007, 010]. Hypotheses on the pages, none tested: (1) with the L3 holding data the prefetcher's stream drains into the L3 and the L2 refills complete sooner [run 4 core page 14.2]; (2) the full-L3 mode lets the cluster keep more read requests in flight toward the mesh [core page 2.3]; (3) the extra whole cycle per load is the prefetched line's write into L1 taking the cache for one cycle per line [core page section 8]; (4) either the L1 prefetcher's fills do not allocate in the L3, or 0xA2 counts demand reads only; the TRM text ('level 3 accesses that receive data from outside the L3 cache due to a memory-read operation') does not say which [run 4 core page 3.1]. What the L3 changes in how far ahead the prefetcher runs is Insufficient data [core page section 8].

4.39 Boot E's sparse per-region OCM rows got faster with fewer outside refills: the L3 serves part of their loadsexplained

Boot E's sparse OCM rows read faster than on the L3-off boots, with fewer outside refills per load. The L3 serves part of their loads.

What looked wrong

  • Boot E (run 4, membench-jibin-010, 2026-11-05) is the first boot with the L3 in full mode for CPUs 2 to 9.
  • Its sparse per-region OCM rows from CPU 2 read 19.078 to 20.391 ns per load. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu2.csv of 010, best row]
  • On run 3 (L3 off) the same rows read 21.359 to 25.781 ns per load, and on boot A (L3 off) 22.859 to 27.594 ns per load. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu2.csv of 004 and 005, best row]
  • Against boot A, the 10 sparse cells of CPUs 2 and 8 on E read 0.69 to 1.10 times A's time.
  • The one cell above A was CPU 8 to OCM4. It read 23.906 ns per load on E, against 20.141 ns on run 3 (+18.7 %) and 21.813 ns on A (+9.6 %). [latency-ocm-region4-cpu8.csv of 010, 004 and 005, best row, and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 14]
  • The dense all-five control row did not move.
  • From CPU 2 it read 26.082 ns per load on E, against 26.009 ns on A, 24.959 ns on C and 25.340 ns on run 3. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 010, 005, 007 and 004, best row]
  • The sparse rows counted fewer L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load on E. They counted 0.33 to 1.00 over the 10 cells of CPUs 2 and 8, 9 of them below 0.8. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,8}.csv of 010, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]
  • CPU 2 alone counted 0.330 to 0.589 per load on E, 0.739 to 0.772 on A and 0.703 to 0.830 on C. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,8}.csv of 010, 005 and 007, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]
  • The anomaly is this drop in outside refills together with the drop in time.
  • Two more signs on E.
  • Jesse's boot E README counts up to 0.48 L2 refills per load on the OCM passes that neither prefetch event nor 0xA2 accounts for, against at most 0.0157 on A. [membench-jibin-010/README.md line 153]
  • The route rows read 13.972 to 23.190 ns per load with 0.415 to 0.824 outside refills per load. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-route-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 010, best row]

Why it looked wrong

  • Every OCM load should cross the mesh to the region's home node. So each load should count one outside refill, that is 1.0 L3 read refills (event 0xA2) per load.
  • The L3 is 256 KiB per two-core cluster. One OCM region is also 256 KiB.
  • The /dev/ocm module maps a region as Normal write-back memory, the cacheable memory type. So the L3 may hold OCM lines. [membench-jibin-004/README.md lines 34 and 37, membench-jibin-010/README.md lines 318 and 319]
  • A sparse chain touches 64 lines per pass. Lines from the pass before can still be in the L3 when the next pass runs.
  • An L3 hit costs about 10.8 ns est. (from boot E's hit set, 10.6 ns at 256 KiB and 11.0 ns at 384 KiB). A mesh round trip costs about 26 ns. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 5, derived from latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 010 and 007]
  • So a row with part L3 hits reads below the true OCM latency.

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Dense all-five control row kept on every boot with the 0xA2 counterboot E, boot F1Whether every load still comes from outside the cluster when the L3 is on. A count of 0xA2 per load at 1.0 means no L3 hits. This row is then the OCM number to quote. On F1 it ran from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8.
Run 3's 20 sparse rows repeated byte for byte on L3-on firmwareboot F1The share of sparse-row loads served from the mesh (0xA2 per load) against run 3. The L2 refills per load serve as the control that the chains miss the L2 the same way. It ran from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8.
Proposed: sparse rows run under the L3 hit event (0x81C6)not runWhich loads hit the L3, as a direct count instead of the difference in 0xA2 counts. 0x81C6 is the hit event of boot E's hit-set event group.
Proposed: hit-set row from CPUs 4, 6 and 8, L3 onnot runWhether the L3 of the other clusters is in full mode too. Boot E's register read and hit counter cover CPU 2's cluster only.

What the tests showed

  • On E the dense all-five chain from CPU 2 counts 1.0010 and 1.0005 outside refills per load in its two passes (mean 1.0008). CPU 8 counts 1.0009 per load. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu{2,8}.csv of 010, fresh1 and fresh2 rows, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]
  • So none of the dense chain's loads is an L3 hit. This row is the OCM number to quote.
  • Boot F1 (run 6, membench-jibin-011, 2026-11-06) repeats the dense all-five row from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8 at 25.536, 25.932, 25.445 and 27.702 ns per load. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 011, best row]
  • It counts 1.0007 to 1.0009 outside refills per load. [latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 011, best row]
  • F1's sparse passes count 0xA2 at 0.425 per load, mean over 140 passes (5 regions x 4 CPUs x 7 passes), against 0.710 per load on run 3. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 004 and 011, and membench-jibin-011/README.md line 146]
  • The L2 refills per load are the same, 2.802 on F1 against 2.779 on run 3. So the chains miss the L2 the same way. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 004 and 011, and membench-jibin-011/README.md line 146]
  • Part of the sparse-row loads were therefore filled inside the cluster on F1.
  • Per row, F1's sparse 0xA2 pass means range from 0.299 to 0.652 per load over the 20 rows. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 011, and membench-jibin-011/README.md line 146]
  • F1's sparse per-region bests are 0.693 to 0.953 times run 3's in the 20 cells, geometric mean 0.834. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu{2,4,6,8}.csv of 011, and membench-jibin-011/README.md line 146]
  • The pages read this as the L3 serving part of the sparse-row loads. The per-region rows on the L3-on boots are below the true OCM latency.
  • The pages use them only for the order of the regions by mesh distance. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html Short version and table 6 caption, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 14]
  • On the L3-off firmware, reading below the dense all-five row was never the anomaly. Run 3's CPU 2 sparse bests were below it (25.340 ns per load) in 4 of 5 regions. [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 004, best row, and membench-jibin-004/README.md line 110]
  • Run 3's sparse bests did read higher than run 2's dense per-region rows in 18 of 20 cells, by 2.31 ns per load on average (-0.47 to +4.55 ns). [latency-ocm-region{0..4}-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-all5-dense-cpu2.csv of 004, best row, and membench-jibin-004/README.md line 110]

Still open

Which loads hit the L3 is a hypothesis. No OCM row on E or F1 ran under the L3 hit event (0x81C6). Running the sparse rows under that event on an L3-on boot would count the hits directly. A hit-set row from CPUs 4, 6 and 8 would show whether their clusters' L3 is in full mode too.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boot E (membench-jibin-010), 2026-11-05; repeated on run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011), 2026-11-06

What looked wrong. Boot E is the first boot with the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 in full mode. Its sparse per-region OCM rows (one line per 4 KiB page, 64 loads per pass, 7 passes) read faster than on the L3-off boots. From CPU 2 they read 19.078 to 20.391 ns per load (run 3: 21.359 to 25.781 ns; boot A: 22.859 to 27.594 ns). Against boot A, the 10 sparse cells of CPUs 2 and 8 read 0.69 to 1.10 times A's. One cell went the other way: CPU 8 to OCM4 read 23.906 ns on E, +18.7 % over run 3's 20.141 ns and +9.6 % over A's 21.813 ns. The dense all-five control did not move (26.082 ns on E, 26.009 ns on A). The sparse rows counted only 0.33 to 1.00 L3 read refills (event 0xA2, a line fetched from outside the cluster) per load on E, 9 of the 10 cells below 0.8, against 0.70 to 0.96 on A and C. On CPU 2 alone: 0.330 to 0.589 per load on E, 0.739 to 0.772 on A, 0.703 to 0.830 on C. Jesse's boot E README adds that E's OCM passes count up to 0.48 L2 refills per load that neither prefetch event nor 0xA2 accounts for (A: at most 0.0157). The route rows (the dense chase of one region under the mesh counters, CPUs 2 to 8) read 13.972 to 23.190 ns on E, also below the dense all-five row. Note: on the L3-off boots the sparse per-region bests were mostly below the dense all-five row too (run 3 CPU 2: 4 of 5 regions below 25.340 ns), so 'below the dense row' alone was never the anomaly. The anomaly is the drop in time with the drop in outside refills.

Why it looked wrong. Every OCM load should cross the mesh to the region's home node, so each load should count one outside refill. The L3 is 256 KiB per two-core cluster, the size of one OCM region. The /dev/ocm module maps a region as Normal write-back memory, the cacheable type, so the L3 may hold OCM lines. The sparse chain touches 64 lines per pass, so lines from the pass before can still be in the L3 when the next pass runs. A load that hits the L3 costs about 10.8 ns est. (from boot E's hit set), less than the 26 ns mesh round trip, so a row with part L3 hits reads below the true OCM latency.

Tests added.

  • The dense all-five control row (run 2's chain over all five regions, 1.25 MiB, 20,480 loads per pass, 2 passes) kept on every boot with the 0xA2 counter; rule: this row is the OCM number to quote [run 4 boot E (010), run 6 boot F1 (011, from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8)]: whether every load still comes from outside the cluster when the L3 is on (0xA2 per load stays at 1.0)
  • Run 3's 20 sparse per-region rows repeated byte for byte on the L3-on firmware from CPUs 2, 4, 6 and 8, with the 0xA2 and L2 refill counters [run 6 boot F1 (011)]: the share of sparse-row loads served from the mesh (0xA2 per load) against run 3, with the L2 refills as the control that the chains miss the L2 the same way
  • Proposed: the sparse rows run with the L3 hit event (0x81C6, boot E's hit-set event group) on an L3-on boot [not run]: which loads hit the L3 (a direct count instead of the 0xA2 difference)
  • Proposed: a hit-set row from CPUs 4, 6 and 8 on an L3-on boot [not run]: whether the L3 of the other clusters is in full mode (boot E's register read and hit counter cover CPU 2's cluster only)

What the tests showed. The dense all-five chain from CPU 2 reads 26.082 ns on E (A 26.009, C 24.959, run 3 25.340) and counts 1.0010 and 1.0005 outside refills per load in its two passes (mean 1.0008; CPU 8: 1.0009). So none of its loads is an L3 hit and it is the OCM number to quote. F1 repeats it from all four CPUs at 25.445 to 27.702 ns with 1.0007 to 1.0009 refills per load. F1's sparse passes count 0xA2 at 0.425 per load (mean over 140 passes) against run 3's 0.710, with the same L2 refills (2.802 against 2.779). So part of the sparse-row loads were filled inside the cluster on F1, by the L3 on the pages' reading. Which loads hit the L3 is a hypothesis until the hit event is counted on those rows: no OCM row on E or F1 ran under the L3 hit event. The per-region rows on the L3-on boots are below the true OCM latency, and the pages use them only for the order of the regions by mesh distance.

4.40 Table-walk rate on the 32 MiB chain differs 129 times between two processes of one boot; 0x8188 never countsopen

On boot D, two processes running the same 32 MiB chain counted 0.0034 and 0.4376 table walks per load, a 129 times gap.

What looked wrong

  • Boot D ran one 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB DRAM pages in two processes.
  • The first process (the TLB-set row) counted 0.0033 and 0.0035 walks per load (event 0x34, DTLB_WALK), mean 0.0034. Its best pass ran at 53.266 ns per load. [008 bootD latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1, fresh2, best, column dtlb_walk_per_load]
  • The second process (the walk row) counted 0.4381 and 0.4371 walks per load, mean 0.4376. Its best pass ran at 58.725 ns per load. [008 bootD latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1, fresh2, best]
  • That is 128.7 times more by pass means. By the best passes it is 132.8 times more (0.4381 against 0.0033). [008 bootD latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1, fresh2, best]
  • Boots C and E showed smaller gaps.
  • Boot C's gap went the other way: 0.3669 and 0.3655 walks per load in the TLB-set row against 0.1849 and 0.1850 in the walk row. [007 bootC latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
  • Boot E read 0.3662 and 0.3655 against 0.5113 and 0.5118. [010 bootE latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
  • Event 0x8188 (DTLB_WALK_BLOCK) read 0.0000 in all 37 pass rows of each boot's six walk files on boots C, D and E. [007, 008, 010 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]
  • Event 0x818A (DTLB_WALK_PAGE) equalled 0x34 to four decimals on every 32 MiB pass. [007, 008, 010 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv and latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]
  • On the five sparse OCM walk rows of boots C and E (prefetchers on), 0x34 counted up to 2.6094 and 2.7969 walks per load. [007, 010 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]
  • On those rows 0x8188 read 0.0000 in all 70 passes. 0x818A read 0.0156 (one walk in 64 loads) in two boot C passes only. [007, 010 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4, the two 0.0156 readings in 007 region1 row fresh5 and region2 row fresh7]
  • On boot D (prefetchers off) all three events read 0.0000 in all 35 OCM passes. [008 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]

Why it looked wrong

  • A walk rate on one chain was expected to belong to the boot (its page size and firmware), not to the process.
  • Boot D's 0.003 walks per load looked like the effect of the contiguous hint (boot D mapped the OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations).
  • But the hint changes only the /dev/ocm mappings. The 32 MiB chain lives on 4 KiB DRAM pages.
  • The rate was already spread across boots before the hint. Boot B read 0.3657 and 0.3661 walks per load on this row (58.509 ns best). Boot A read 0.5204 and 0.5210 (58.810 ns best). [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13, 008 README section Against boot B, and 005 and 006 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv]
  • A counter that never reads nonzero (0x8188) cannot be told from one that does not count.
  • By the RTL (the chip's hardware source code), 0x34 counts a data-side walk when it starts. Walks for the prefetch requesters (ids TLBID_PF0 to TLBID_PF3) are included. [nevis0_tlb_request_slot.sv:1359 and :1368, nevis0_tlb_pkg.sv:369-371, nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3374-3376 and :3405-3414, as cited in 007 README, The walk rows]
  • 0x8188 and 0x818A count a walk only when it returns a fault-free translation to the core. [nevis0_tlb_request_slot.sv:1359 and :1368, nevis0_tlb_pkg.sv:369-371, nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3374-3376 and :3405-3414, as cited in 007 README, The walk rows]
  • On this RTL a walk that ends in a page entry with the contiguous bit counts in 0x8188, not 0x818A. [nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3147]
  • A nonzero 0x8188 on a boot C or D OCM row would have shown the walker using the hint. It read 0 there. [007 and 008 READMEs, The walk rows]
  • But the OCM-row walks that only 0x34 counted returned no translation to the core. So those zeros do not test 0x8188. [007 and 008 READMEs, The walk rows]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Walk counter set on six rows from CPU 2 (run 5b addition)boot C, boot D, boot ECounts 0x34, 0x8188 and 0x818A in a second process of six chains the TLB-set rows already ran (the 32 MiB stimulus and the five sparse per-region OCM chains, commands 40 to 45). A nonzero 0x8188 on a boot C or D OCM row would mean the walker used the contiguous entry (goal G-i). The two walk rates of one boot become comparable as a by-product. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11, 2026-11-04, commits c3e5c49 and ed6056a in codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md lines 1067 and 1081, boot D ran ed6056a and boots C and E ran b79dffa per the 007 and 008 READMEs]

What the tests showed

  • The rate belongs to the process, not the boot. The walk rows' rates are 0.5, 129 and 1.4 times the TLB-set rows' rates on boots C, D and E. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13]
  • In all three boots the faster process walked less. [007, 008, 010 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, and 007 README, line on the 32 MiB stimulus]
  • Boot C: 56.726 ns per load at 0.185 walks per load against 59.081 ns at 0.366. [007 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, and 007 README, line on the 32 MiB stimulus]
  • Boot D: 53.266 ns at 0.0034 against 58.725 ns at 0.4376. [008 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv]
  • Boot E: 57.611 ns at 0.366 against 58.705 ns at 0.512. [010 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv and latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv]
  • 0x818A is validated. On the 4 KiB-page stimulus it equals 0x34 on every pass of boots C, D and E. [007, 008, 010 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, columns dtlb_walk_per_load and dtlb_walk_page_per_load]
  • The readings in both columns are C 0.1849 and 0.1850, D 0.4381 and 0.4371, E 0.5113 and 0.5118. That is what it must read when every walk ends in a page entry. [007, 008, 010 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, columns dtlb_walk_per_load and dtlb_walk_page_per_load]
  • 0x8188 stays unvalidated. It read 0 in every pass of every boot, and no row ever had a counted walk that ended in a block or contiguous entry. [007, 008, 010 READMEs, The walk rows]
  • The OCM-row walks that only 0x34 counts are the prefetchers' walks. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.3, and 007 README, The walk rows]
  • Boots B and D (prefetchers off) count 0 walks per load on the sparse chains. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.3, and 007 README, The walk rows]
  • Boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) count 0.27 to 1.24, 0.41 to 0.75 and 0.56 to 1.62 walks per load on the sparse TLB-set rows. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.3, and 007 README, The walk rows]
  • Rule: never quote boot D's 0.003 walks per load as the contiguous hint's effect.

Still open

Why two processes of one boot differ is Insufficient data. The DRAM chain's physical pages are not logged (the dmesg map lines cover /dev/ocm mappings only). No file shows what started each walk or how it ended [007 README, OCM mappings]. Running the same chain in several walk-counted processes of one boot would show whether the rate follows the process's page placement. Adding 0x813C (DTLB_WALK_RW, a demand-only walk event that no run's counter set included) would separate the program's walks from the prefetchers' walks [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, open items, and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 7].

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boots C, D, E (membench-jibin-007, 008, 010), 2026-11-05 UTC; boot D's README (008, The walk rows) is the first file that puts the two rates of one boot side by side

What looked wrong. Boot D ran the same 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB DRAM pages in two processes. The TLB-set row counted 0.0033 and 0.0035 table walks per load (0x34 DTLB_WALK) in its two passes, 0.0034 on average, at 53.266 ns per load best [results/membench-jibin-008/results/bootD/latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2, column dtlb_walk_per_load]. The walk row of the same chain counted 0.4381 and 0.4371 walks per load, 0.4376 on average, at 58.725 ns best [008 latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]. That is 129 times more walks (128.7 by the pass means; 132.8 by the best passes, 0.4381 against 0.0033). Boot C read 0.3669 and 0.3655 (TLB-set row, 59.081 ns best) against 0.1849 and 0.1850 (walk row, 56.726 ns best) [007 bootC, same two files]. Boot E read 0.3662 and 0.3655 (57.611 ns) against 0.5113 and 0.5118 (58.705 ns) [010 bootE, same two files]. Event 0x8188 DTLB_WALK_BLOCK read 0.0000 in all 37 pass rows of each boot's six walk files (C, D, E), while 0x818A DTLB_WALK_PAGE equalled 0x34 to four decimals on every 32 MiB stimulus pass. On the five sparse OCM walk rows with the prefetchers on, 0x34 counted up to 2.6094 walks per load on C (region 1, fresh7) and 2.7969 on E (region 3, fresh7), in 33 of 35 and 32 of 35 passes, while 0x8188 read 0.0000 in all 70 passes and 0x818A read 0.0156 per load (one walk in 64 loads) in two passes of C (region 1 fresh5, region 2 fresh7) and 0.0000 in the other 68 [007 and 010 latency-ocm-region<r>-walk-cpu2.csv, r = 0 to 4]. On boot D, prefetchers off, all three events read 0.0000 in all 35 OCM passes [008, same files].

Why it looked wrong. A walk rate on one chain was expected to belong to the boot (its page size and firmware), not to the process. Boot D's 0.003 walks per load looked like the contiguous hint's effect (boot D mapped the OCM in 64 KiB contiguous translations). But the hint changes only the /dev/ocm mappings, and the 32 MiB chain lives on 4 KiB DRAM pages, which the hint does not reach [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, section 13, line on the 32 MiB stimulus; 008 README, Against boot B]. Boot B, with no hint, read 0.3657 and 0.3661 walks per load on the same row (58.509 ns best) and boot A 0.5204 and 0.5210 (58.810 ns) [006 and 005 latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv], so the rate was already spread across boots before the hint. A counter that never reads nonzero (0x8188) cannot be told from a counter that does not count. By the RTL, 0x34 counts a data-side walk when it starts, including walks for TLB requests with the prefetch requester ids TLBID_PF0 to TLBID_PF3, and leaves out the TLB's own prefetch walks [nevis0_tlb_request_slot.sv:1359, :1368; nevis0_tlb_pkg.sv:369-371, as cited in 007 README, The walk rows]. 0x8188 and 0x818A count a walk only when it returns a fault-free translation to the core [nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3374-3376, :3405-3414, same README]. So the OCM-row walks that only 0x34 counted returned no translation to the core. On this RTL a walk that ends in a page entry with the contiguous bit counts in 0x8188, not 0x818A [nevis0_tlb_pagewalk.sv:3147, 007 and 008 READMEs], so a nonzero 0x8188 on a boot C or D OCM row would have shown the walker using the hint. It read 0 there, but the 0x34-only walks returned no translation, so these zeros do not test 0x8188.

Tests added.

  • Walk counter set (--events walk: cycles, 0x03, 0x17, 0xA2, 0x34 DTLB_WALK, 0x8188 DTLB_WALK_BLOCK, 0x818A DTLB_WALK_PAGE) on six rows from CPU 2: the 32 MiB stimulus and the five sparse per-region OCM chains, commands 40 to 45, each a second process of a chain the TLB-set rows already ran [run 5b additions, plan section 11 (2026-11-04), implementation commit c3e5c49 on 7921962 and comment-only revision ed6056a; boot D ran ed6056a, boots C and E ran b79dffa (ed6056a plus e024d57 and b79dffa) [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11; codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md lines 1067 and 1081; 007 and 008 READMEs]]: Designed for goal G-i: which descriptor (block or page) each walk ended in, to show whether the walker used the contiguous entry on boots C and D. The walk rate in a second process was a by-product: the walk row repeats the TLB-set row's chain in another process, so the two rates of one boot became comparable.

What the tests showed. The rate is the process's, not the boot's. In all three boots the faster of the two processes is the one that walked less: C 56.726 ns at 0.185 walks per load against 59.081 ns at 0.366; D 53.266 ns at 0.0034 against 58.725 ns at 0.4376; E 57.611 ns at 0.366 against 58.705 ns at 0.512 [the two files per boot named above; 007 README line on the 32 MiB stimulus]. The walk rows' rates are 0.5, 129 and 1.4 times the TLB-set rows' on C, D and E [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13]. Why two processes of one boot differ is Insufficient data: the DRAM chain's physical pages are not logged (the dmesg map lines cover /dev/ocm mappings only [007 README, OCM mappings]); the same chain in several walk-counted processes of one boot would show whether the rate is the process's page placement [asimov-c1nano-perf.html, open items]. 0x818A is validated: on the 4 KiB-page stimulus it equals 0x34 on every pass of C, D and E, as it must when every walk ends in a page entry. 0x8188 stays unvalidated: it read 0 in every pass of every boot, and no row ever had a counted walk that ended in a block or contiguous entry [007, 008, 010 READMEs, The walk rows]. The OCM-row walks that only 0x34 counts are the prefetchers': boots B and D (prefetchers off) count 0 walks per load on the sparse chains, boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) count 0.27 to 1.24, 0.41 to 0.75 and 0.56 to 1.62 per load on the sparse TLB-set rows, and by the RTL 0x34 includes the walks that prefetch-requester TLB requests start [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 13.3; 007 README, The walk rows]. The files do not show what started each walk or how it ended [007 README]. A demand-only walk event, 0x813C DTLB_WALK_RW, would separate the program's walks from the prefetchers' [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 7]; it was not in any run's counter set. Rule: never quote boot D's 0.003 walks per load as the contiguous hint's effect.
