4.41 Software prefetch 4 and 8 lines ahead at 2 MiB reads slower with the hardware prefetchers on than off (C vs D), and all four hint rows read below the plain loop with the L3 on (E)open

With the hardware prefetchers on, a software prefetch 4 or 8 lines ahead reads a 2 MiB buffer slower than with them off.

What looked wrong

  • G7 (the one-core read test, file bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv) reads 2 MiB and 32 MiB on CPU 2 with five kernels, best of 3 reps.
  • Boot C (007) has the hardware prefetchers on. Boot D (008) has them off.
  • Over the 10 G7 rows, boot C reads 0.795 to 3.869 times boot D. [007 README lines 107 and 109]
  • The plain 32 MiB read is 9.196 GB/s on C against 2.377 GB/s on D (3.869 times faster on C). [007 README line 109 and 007 and 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • The 2 MiB read with PRFM 4 lines ahead is 9.651 GB/s on C against 12.145 GB/s on D (0.795 times). [007 README line 109]
  • The same read with PRFM 8 ahead is 9.862 GB/s on C against 10.890 GB/s on D (0.906 times). [007 README line 109]
  • These are the only two G7 rows slower on C. [007 README line 109]
  • On C the hint adds little over the plain loop: 9.651 against 9.294 GB/s at 2 MiB (+3.8 %), and 9.339 against 9.196 GB/s at 32 MiB (+1.6 %). [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • On boot E (010, L3 on, prefetchers on) every hint row reads below the plain loop. [010 README line 114]
  • Plain: 24.945 / 24.546 GB/s at 2 / 32 MiB. PRFM 4 ahead: 20.196 / 20.353 GB/s. PRFM 8 ahead: 18.425 / 18.486 GB/s. [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • PRFM 16 ahead: 18.446 / 18.285 GB/s. Two streams: 17.982 / 18.911 GB/s. [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]

Why it looked wrong

  • The hardware prefetchers were expected to help a sequential read, or at worst to add nothing.
  • Instead, at 2 MiB the hint plus the hardware prefetcher reads 9 to 21 % slower than the hint alone. [007 and 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • PRFM 8 ahead is 9.4 % lower (9.862 against 10.890 GB/s, boot C against boot D). PRFM 4 ahead is 20.5 % lower (9.651 against 12.145 GB/s). [007 and 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • On boot E the hint 4 lines ahead costs 19.0 % at 2 MiB (20.196 against 24.945 GB/s) and 17.1 % at 32 MiB (20.353 against 24.546 GB/s). [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • The run 4 page (asimov-c1nano-run4.html) expected the hint to raise the rate. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4]
  • On boot B (006, prefetchers off) PRFM 4 ahead more than doubled the plain loop: 12.146 against 5.031 GB/s at 2 MiB. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4]
  • That result supported H7 (the hypothesis that the plain loop keeps too few lines in flight). [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4]
  • No counter in the files names the cause.
  • For the plain loop the refill counters per line are about the same on C and E (L1 0.99 and 0.99, L2 0.96 and 0.97, L1 prefetch 0.99 and 0.99 at 2 MiB). [asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html]
  • So they do not show the mechanism.
  • Boot C also ran a different bandwidth build (commit b79dffa) from B (commit 7921962) and D (commit ed6056a). The read kernels are the same bytes at the same offsets in their 64 B lines. [007 README lines 91 and 140]
  • Jesse (the author of the boot READMEs) calls the per-pass loop difference negligible for G7 (passes of 0.2 to 3.6 ms). [007 README lines 91 and 140]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
G7 read variants, the plan's "run 5" rows, with --perf countersboot B, boot C, boot D, boot EIt measures the one-core read rate per kernel with the hardware prefetcher off (B, D), on (C), or on with the L3 in full mode (E). It also records the counters l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line, l2d_refill_hwprf_per_line, l2d_refill_l1dhwprf_per_line and l3d_refill_rd_per_line (fills per line that were prefetches or came from the L3). A hint row above the plain loop on C would mean the hint adds to the hardware prefetcher's rate [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10 and bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv header and asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4].
Run 7 plan: one-core read sweep, L3 on against off, prefetchers offrun 7 (proposed)It measures whether the L3 mode changes the plain read rate without the prefetcher, on the two prefetchers-off boots with the same build. It does not test the PRFM rows directly [follow-up-run-plan.md section 14 item 2, planned 2026-11-08].

What the tests showed

  • The prefetcher setting is confirmed by the counter l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line (L1 data refills caused by the hardware prefetcher, per 64 B line). [007 README line 21]
  • It reads 0.8524 to 0.9994 in all 30 reps on boot C, and at most 0.0001 on boots B and D. [007 README line 21 and 006, 007, 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • Boots B and D (both prefetchers off) agree on all 10 G7 rows within 0.5 %: D reads 0.995 to 1.001 times B. [008 README line 56]
  • So the OCM (on-chip memory) translation hint, the only other change between B and D, does not touch these DRAM rows. [008 README line 56]
  • On boot C the hint rows lower l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line from 0.9921 to 0.9934 (plain loop, 2 MiB) to 0.9066 to 0.9072 (PRFM 4), 0.8599 to 0.8625 (PRFM 8) and 0.8524 to 0.8536 (PRFM 16). [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • They raise l3d_refill_rd_per_line (L3 read refills per 64 B line) from 0.0008 to 0.0012 (plain) to 0.0888 to 0.1437 (hint rows). [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • On boot E the hint rows lower l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line to 0.4532 to 0.4650 (PRFM 4), 0.2814 to 0.2855 (PRFM 8) and 0.3209 to 0.3427 (PRFM 16), against 0.9927 to 0.9932 for the plain loop. [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • l3d_refill_rd_per_line is at most 0.0032 in every E rep. [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]
  • With the hint in place, fewer L1 refills are credited to the hardware prefetcher. The total L1 refills per line stay at about 1.0000. [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv and 010 README line 114]
  • The plain loop costs 13.78 to 13.93 core cycles per 64 B line on boot C against 5.13 to 5.22 on boot E. [007 and 010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv and 010 README line 114]
  • Run 3's plain loop with the L3 off read 9.311 GB/s at 2 MiB and 9.172 GB/s at 32 MiB, the rate that H7 set out to explain. [004 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • The pages state the result without a cause. The run 4 page says "The software hint adds little with the hardware prefetcher on" (section 14.3). [asimov-c1nano-run4.html]
  • The core full page (asimov-c1nano-perf.html) says "The PRFM variants read below the plain loop on E" (section 7). [asimov-c1nano-perf.html]
  • Jesse's boot C README lists the two slower rows among "the largest moves" and gives no cause. [007 README line 109]
  • The brief page (asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html) marks the L3-on speedup of the plain loop as Insufficient data. [asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html]

Still open

No page, README or counter names a mechanism for the slower hint rows with the hardware prefetcher on (boot C) or for the hint rows below the plain loop on boot E. No counter in the files reports requests in flight. The planned run 7 sweep tests only the plain loop with the L3 on against off on the prefetchers-off boots. A run that measures the PRFM rows with a requests-in-flight counter would settle it.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boot C (membench-jibin-007) against boot D (008), Jesse's boot C README section "Against boot D" (lines 107 to 109), 2026-11-05; boot E (010) README line 114, 2026-11-05. The question itself was posed earlier, on the run 4 page after boot B: "Whether the hint adds to the hardware prefetcher's rate is boot C's question" [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4].

What looked wrong. G7 is the one-core read test (bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv): the plain read loop, the loop with a PRFM PLDL1KEEP software prefetch 4, 8 or 16 lines ahead, and a two-stream loop, at 2 MiB and 32 MiB on CPU 2, best of 3 reps. Boot C has the hardware prefetchers on. Boot D has them off. Over the 10 G7 rows C reads 0.795 to 3.869 times D [007 README line 107; recomputed from 007 and 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv best rows]. The plain read of 32 MiB reads 9.196 GB/s on C against 2.377 GB/s on D (3.869 times). But the 2 MiB reads with a software prefetch 4 and 8 lines ahead read 9.651 and 9.862 GB/s on C against 12.145 and 10.890 GB/s on D (0.795 and 0.906 times). Those are the only two G7 rows slower on C [007 README line 109]. On C the hint adds little over the plain loop: 9.651 against 9.294 GB/s at 2 MiB (+3.8 %) and 9.339 against 9.196 GB/s at 32 MiB (+1.6 %). On E (L3 on, prefetchers on) every hint row reads below the plain loop: plain 24.945 / 24.546 GB/s at 2 / 32 MiB, PRFM 4 ahead 20.196 / 20.353 GB/s, PRFM 8 ahead 18.425 / 18.486 GB/s, PRFM 16 ahead 18.446 / 18.285 GB/s, two streams 17.982 / 18.911 GB/s [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv best rows; 010 README line 114: "on E the plain read is the fastest of the five kernels at both sizes"]. The counter l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line (L1 data refills caused by the hardware prefetcher, per 64 B line) reads 0.8524 to 0.9994 in all 30 reps on C, and at most 0.0001 on B and D [007 README line 21; 006, 007, 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv].

Why it looked wrong. The hardware prefetchers were expected to help a sequential read, or at worst to add nothing. Here the software hint plus the hardware prefetcher reads 9 to 21 % slower than the hint alone at 2 MiB (pf8: 9.862 against 10.890 GB/s, 9.4 % lower; pf4: 9.651 against 12.145 GB/s, 20.5 % lower) [007 and 008 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. On E the hint 4 lines ahead costs 19.0 % at 2 MiB (20.196 against 24.945 GB/s) and 17.1 % at 32 MiB (20.353 against 24.546 GB/s) [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. The run 4 page had expected the hint to raise the rate: on boot B (prefetchers off) PRFM 4 ahead more than doubled the plain loop (12.146 against 5.031 GB/s at 2 MiB), which supported H7, the hypothesis that the plain loop keeps too few lines in flight [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.4 and the hypothesis list]. No counter in the files names the cause of the slowdown. The brief page states this for the plain loop: the refill counters per line are about the same on C and E (L1 0.99 and 0.99, L2 0.96 and 0.97, L1 prefetch 0.99 and 0.99 at 2 MiB), "so they do not show the mechanism" [asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html, item "One core reads 2.7 times more from DRAM with the L3 on"]. C's G7 rows also compare two bandwidth builds: C's bandwidth is rebuilt from b79dffa's bandwidth.c, while B and D ran 7921962's and ed6056a's builds. The read kernels are the same bytes at the same offsets in their 64 B lines; the per-pass loop differs, which Jesse calls negligible for G7's rows (passes of 0.2 to 3.6 ms) [007 README lines 91 and 140].

Tests added.

  • G7 read variants (plain, PRFM 4/8/16 lines ahead, two streams) at 2 MiB and 32 MiB with the prefetch counter set (--perf) [added as "run 5" in the plan (follow-up-run-plan.md section 10, table row "G7 (run 5)", commit 7921962 reviewed in codex round 8; cd1e6fd was the round 6 commit). Ran in run 4 on boots B (006, commit 7921962), C (007, b79dffa), D (008, ed6056a) and E (010, b79dffa).]: the one-core read rate with each hint, with the hardware prefetcher off (B, D), on (C), and on with the L3 in full mode (E); the columns l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line, l2d_refill_hwprf_per_line, l2d_refill_l1dhwprf_per_line and l3d_refill_rd_per_line say how many fills per line were prefetches and how many came from the L3 [bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv header]
  • run 7 plan: run 3's one-core read sweep on the two prefetchers-off boots, L3 on against L3 off, same build [planned 2026-11-08, not yet run [follow-up-run-plan.md section 14, item 2]]: whether the L3 mode changes the read rate without the prefetcher; it does not test the PRFM rows directly

What the tests showed. B and D (prefetchers off) agree on all 10 G7 rows within 0.5 %: D reads 0.995 to 1.001 times B [008 README line 56; recomputed]. So the OCM translation hint (the only other change between B and D) does not touch these DRAM rows. With the prefetcher on (C), the hint rows at 2 MiB are below the prefetcher-off hint rows, and on E they are below the plain loop. What the counters add: on C the hint rows lower l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line from 0.9921 to 0.9934 (plain loop, 2 MiB) to 0.9066 to 0.9072 (pf4), 0.8599 to 0.8625 (pf8) and 0.8524 to 0.8536 (pf16), and raise l3d_refill_rd_per_line from 0.0008 to 0.0012 (plain) to 0.0888 to 0.1437 (hint rows) [007 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv]. On E the hint rows lower l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line to 0.4532 to 0.4650 (pf4), 0.2814 to 0.2855 (pf8) and 0.3209 to 0.3427 (pf16) against 0.9927 to 0.9932 for the plain loop, with l3d_refill_rd_per_line at most 0.0032 in every E rep [010 bandwidth-read-prefetch.csv; 010 README line 114]. So with the hint in place, fewer L1 refills are credited to the hardware prefetcher, and the total L1 refills per line stay at about 1.0000. The pages state the result without a cause: "The software hint adds little with the hardware prefetcher on" (run 4 page section 14.3) and "The PRFM variants read below the plain loop on E" (core full page, figure in section 7). Jesse's boot C README lists the two slower rows among "the largest moves" and gives no cause. The brief page marks the L3-on speedup of the plain loop as Insufficient data. No page or README offers a mechanism for the hint rows, and no counter in the files reports requests in flight.

4.42 Boot E's 16 and 32 MiB chains read 0.4 to 0.7 ns above every earlier boot; F1's 2, 6, 8 and 16 MiB passes sit below every earlier passopen

Boot E's 16 and 32 MiB chains read 0.4 to 0.7 ns above every earlier boot. The rise did not repeat on F1.

What looked wrong

  • The 32 MiB chain read 52.875 ns per load on boot E (run 4, 010). Boots A, B, C, D and run 3 read 52.181, 52.248, 52.238, 52.249 and 52.185 ns per load on the same row, a spread of 0.068 ns.
  • So E sat 0.626 to 0.694 ns above every earlier best. [latency-dram-large.csv row 47 of 010, 005, 006, 007, 008, 004]
  • The 16 MiB chain read 51.167 ns per load on E. Boots A, B, C, D and run 3 read 50.692, 50.694, 50.686, 50.682 and 50.785 ns per load.
  • So E sat 0.382 to 0.485 ns above every earlier best. [latency-dram-large.csv row 43 of 010, 005, 006, 007, 008, 004]
  • Both of E's passes at 16 MiB (51.167 and 51.239 ns) and at 32 MiB (52.875 and 52.881 ns) sat above every pass of the four earlier boots. [latency-dram-large.csv rows 41-42, 45-46 of 010, 005, 006, 007, 008, 004, and README.md of 010 line 111]
  • Two rows at the same latency level did not move. The flushed 8 MiB row read 52.659 ns per load on E against 52.657 ns on boot C. [latency-dram-flushed.csv row 7 of 010 and 007]
  • The 8 MiB chain read 45.077 ns per load on E against 45.130 ns on C. [latency-dram-large.csv row 39 of 010 and 007]
  • On boot F1 (run 6, 011) the rise did not repeat. The 32 MiB chain read 52.212 ns per load and the 16 MiB chain 50.551 ns per load.
  • Instead both F1 passes at 2, 6, 8 and 16 MiB lay below every earlier pass from run 3 and boots A to E.
  • The gaps to the nearest earlier pass were 0.053 ns at 2 MiB (F1 23.835 and 23.714 ns against D's 23.888 ns) and 0.468 ns at 6 MiB (F1 39.085 and 39.116 ns against E's 39.584 ns).
  • The gaps were 0.411 ns at 8 MiB (F1 44.485 and 44.612 ns against B's 45.023 ns) and 0.119 ns at 16 MiB (F1 50.551 and 50.563 ns against D's 50.682 ns). [latency-dram-large.csv rows 21-22, 33-34, 37-38, 41-42 of 011, 008, 010, 006, and README.md of 011 line 143]
  • The verifier found that the 1.5 MiB row fits the same pattern. F1's passes read 23.502 and 23.593 ns per load, 0.179 ns below the lowest earlier pass (run 3's 23.772 ns). [latency-dram-large.csv rows 17-18 of 011 and 004]
  • The README of 011 does not list this row. The 2 MiB bests are 23.714 ns per load on F1, 24.096 ns on run 3 and 24.177 ns on E. [latency-dram-large.csv row 23 of 011, 004, 010]

Why it looked wrong

  • Turning the L3 on should not slow a DRAM-sized random chain. The flushed 8 MiB row at the same latency level read 52.659 ns per load on E against 52.657 ns on C.
  • So the flushed 8 MiB row did not move. [latency-dram-flushed.csv row 7 of 010 and 007]
  • The counters of the 16 and 32 MiB rows read the same on E and C. Both read 1.0000 L1 and L2 refills per load (every load missed both caches).
  • Both read 0.9995 to 1.0000 L3 read refills per load. [latency-dram-large.csv rows 41-42 and 45-46 of 010 and 007, and README.md of 010 line 111]
  • At 1.5 to 2 MiB the L3 serves almost nothing. It gives 0.962 to 0.965 L3 read refills per load at 1.5 MiB and 0.979 to 0.982 at 2 MiB, on both E and F1.
  • So the SLC and DRAM rows were expected unchanged on F1 too. A drop below every earlier pass had no counter to explain it. [latency-dram-large.csv rows 17-18 and 21-22 of 010 and 011, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Same command lines rerun on boot F1boot F1Whether E's rise at 16 and 32 MiB repeats on the same platform images (boot E's SCP, TF-A, kernel, OS images and /dev/ocm module byte for byte) with the new program build 0c190a1. A repeat would point to the shared platform. No repeat would leave boot E itself or the new build as the difference. [README.md of 011 lines 9 and 143]
Walk-counted 32 MiB chain on E and C in one processnot runWhether translation walks account for the 0.481 and 0.637 ns per load that E reads above C at 16 and 32 MiB. The test was proposed on the core page (asimov-c1nano-perf.html) but not run as of boot F2 (no latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv exists in 011 or 012).

What the tests showed

  • E's rise did not repeat on F1. F1 read 52.212 ns per load at 32 MiB, inside the 52.181 to 52.249 ns band of run 3 and boots A to D. [latency-dram-large.csv row 47 of 011]
  • F1 read 50.551 ns per load at 16 MiB, below every earlier pass. [latency-dram-large.csv row 43 of 011, and README.md of 011 line 143]
  • The core page's hypothesis for E alone: the 16 and 32 MiB chains carry translation walks.
  • E's 32 MiB walk row counted 0.5113 and 0.5118 walks per load (column dtlb_walk_per_load) at 58.705 and 58.722 ns per load. [latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv rows 5-6 of 010]
  • Verifier caveat: that walk row records backing=4k (4 KiB pages). The 16 and 32 MiB chain rows that rose record backing=hugetlb (large pages). [latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv row 4 and latency-dram-large.csv row 44 of 010]
  • So the 0.51 walks per load were measured on a different page size from the chain that rose. The hypothesis has no walk count on the hugetlb chain.
  • The walk rate also differs from process to process on one boot.
  • E's TLB-set row counted 0.3662 and 0.3655 walks per load on the same 4 KiB stimulus, at 57.658 and 57.611 ns per load. [latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv rows 5-6 of 010]
  • Both moves, E's rise and F1's drop, remain Insufficient data. The READMEs of 010 and 011 both say these files do not show the cause. [README.md of 010 line 111, and README.md of 011 line 143]

Still open

The cause of E's rise at 16 and 32 MiB and of F1's drop at 1.5 to 16 MiB is still open. A walk-counted 32 MiB chain row on the hugetlb chain, run on E and C in one process, would show whether translation walks account for the 0.481 and 0.637 ns per load that E reads above C.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boot E (010), run on 2026-11-05 [README.md of 010 line 299]; run 6 boot F1 (011), run on 2026-11-06 [README.md of 011 line 321]

What looked wrong. The 32 MiB chain reads 52.875 ns per load on boot E. Boots A, B, C, D and run 3 read 52.181, 52.248, 52.238, 52.249 and 52.185 ns on the same row, a spread of 0.068 ns [latency-dram-large.csv row 47 (best) of 010, 005, 006, 007, 008, 004]. So E sits 0.626 to 0.694 ns above every earlier best. The 16 MiB chain reads 51.167 ns on E against 50.692, 50.694, 50.686, 50.682 and 50.785 ns on A, B, C, D and run 3 [latency-dram-large.csv row 43 of the same files]. So E sits 0.382 to 0.485 ns above every earlier best. Both of E's passes at 16 and 32 MiB (51.167, 51.239; 52.875, 52.881) sit above every pass of the four earlier boots [rows 41-42 and 45-46; README.md of 010 line 111]. Two rows at the same latency level did not move: the flushed 8 MiB row reads 52.659 ns on E against 52.657 on C [latency-dram-flushed.csv row 7 of 010 and 007], and the 8 MiB chain reads 45.077 on E against 45.130 on C [latency-dram-large.csv row 39 of 010 and 007]. On F1 the rise did not repeat: the 32 MiB chain reads 52.212 ns and the 16 MiB chain 50.551 ns [latency-dram-large.csv rows 47 and 43 of 011]. Instead both of F1's passes at 2, 6, 8 and 16 MiB lie below every earlier pass (run 3 and boots A to E). The gaps to the nearest earlier pass are 0.053 ns at 2 MiB (F1 23.835 and 23.714 against D's 23.888), 0.468 ns at 6 MiB (F1 39.085 and 39.116 against E's 39.584), 0.411 ns at 8 MiB (F1 44.485 and 44.612 against B's 45.023) and 0.119 ns at 16 MiB (F1 50.551 and 50.563 against D's 50.682) [latency-dram-large.csv rows 21-22, 33-34, 37-38, 41-42 of 011, 008, 010, 006; README.md of 011 line 143]. Verifier note from the same CSVs: the 1.5 MiB row also fits this pattern, F1's passes 23.502 and 23.593 ns sit 0.179 ns below the lowest earlier pass (run 3's 23.772) [latency-dram-large.csv rows 17-18 of 011 and 004]; the README of 011 does not list it. The 2 MiB best values are 23.714 ns on F1, 24.096 on run 3 and 24.177 on E [latency-dram-large.csv row 23 of 011, 004, 010].

Why it looked wrong. Turning the L3 on should not slow a DRAM-sized random chain. The flushed 8 MiB row at the same latency level did not move on E. The counters of the 16 and 32 MiB rows read the same on E and C: 1.0000 L1 and L2 refills per load and 0.9995 to 1.0000 L3 read refills per load [latency-dram-large.csv rows 41-42 and 45-46 of 010 and 007; README.md of 010 line 111]. At 1.5 to 2 MiB the L3 serves almost nothing: 0.962 to 0.965 outside refills per load at 1.5 MiB and 0.979 to 0.982 at 2 MiB on both E and F1 [latency-dram-large.csv rows 17-18 and 21-22 of 010 and 011, column l3d_refill_rd_per_load]. So the SLC and DRAM rows were expected unchanged on F1 too, and a drop below every earlier pass had no counter to explain it.

Tests added.

  • Same command lines on boot F1 (boot E's SCP, TF-A, kernel, OS images and /dev/ocm module byte for byte; new program build 0c190a1) [run 6 F1 (011) [README.md of 011 lines 9 and 143]]: whether E's rise at 16 and 32 MiB repeats on the same platform
  • A walk-counted 32 MiB chain row on E and C in one process (proposed on the core page, not run as of F2) [not run; no latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv exists in 011 or 012]: whether translation walks account for the 0.48 and 0.64 ns that E reads above C

What the tests showed. E's rise did not repeat. F1 reads 52.212 ns at 32 MiB, within the 52.181 to 52.249 band of run 3 and boots A to D, and 50.551 ns at 16 MiB, below every earlier pass [latency-dram-large.csv rows 47 and 43 of 011; README.md of 011 line 143]. Hypothesis for E only, from the core page: the 16 and 32 MiB chains carry translation walks. E's 32 MiB walk row counts 0.5113 and 0.5118 walks per load (dtlb_walk_per_load) at 58.705 and 58.722 ns [latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv rows 5-6 of 010]. Verifier caveat: that walk row records backing=4k [latency-dram-walk-cpu2.csv row 4 of 010], while the 16 and 32 MiB chain rows that rose record backing=hugetlb [latency-dram-large.csv row 44 of 010]. So the 0.51 walks per load were measured on a different page size from the chain that rose, and the hypothesis has no walk count on the hugetlb chain. The walk rate also differs from process to process on one boot: E's TLB-set row counts 0.366 walks per load on the same 4k stimulus [latency-dram-tlb-cpu2.csv rows 5-6 of 010]. Both moves (E's rise, F1's drop) remain Insufficient data: the READMEs of 010 (line 111) and 011 (line 143) both say these files do not show the cause.

4.43 Boot E's 4 KiB looped L1 read reads 40.9 GB/s against boot C's 46.2open

Boot E's 4 KiB looped L1 read reads 40.9 GB/s against boot C's 46.2 GB/s on the same build, and the files do not show why.

What looked wrong

  • Boots C and E (run 4, folders membench-jibin-007 and 010, 2026-11-05 UTC) ran the same sixteen G8 rows (one-core L1 read and write rows).
  • The 4 KiB looped read reads 40.910 GB/s on E and 46.180 GB/s on C. [010 bootE and 007 bootC bandwidth-l1-passes.csv line 9, best row]
  • That is 0.886 times C, or 11.4 % lower. The same row costs 3.13 to 3.14 cycles per 64-byte line on E against 2.78 to 2.79 cycles per line on C. [bandwidth-l1-passes.csv column cycles_per_line, lines 4 to 8, of 010 bootE and 007 bootC, README of 010 line 170]
  • The gap is not rep noise (a rep is one repeat of the same row).
  • The five reps spread 0.16 % of the best on E (40.844 to 40.910 GB/s) and 0.53 % on C (45.936 to 46.180 GB/s). [bandwidth-l1-passes.csv lines 4 to 8 of 010 bootE and 007 bootC]
  • The other 15 G8 rows on E read 0.972 to 1.013 times C (largest deviation: the 4 KiB single-call write at 0.972). [README of 010 line 170]
  • The 4 KiB single-call read is equal on both boots, 53.096 GB/s on E and 53.103 GB/s on C. [bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv line 9 of 010 bootE and 007 bootC]
  • L1 data refills on the 4 KiB read rows are at most 0.0008 per line on both boots. [bandwidth-l1-passes.csv column l1d_refill_per_line of 007 bootC and 010 bootE]
  • Across all 16 G8 rows the largest value is 0.0199 per line on C and 0.0195 on E, on the 24 KiB read rep 0. [bandwidth-l1-passes.csv column l1d_refill_per_line of 007 bootC and 010 bootE]
  • So the 4 KiB buffer stayed in the L1 on both boots. [README of 010 lines 159 and 170]

Why it looked wrong

  • Boots E and C ran the same commit (b79dffa) and the same program build. The bandwidth binary on E is C's binary once stripped, 6 bytes of an assembler temporary name apart. [README of 010, section 'Against boot C: the L3 alone']
  • The 4 KiB buffer fits the 32 KiB L1 (the first-level data cache of one core). The refill counters show it stays there.
  • So the G8 rows on E are a repeat check of C's rows, not an L3 result. [README of 010, 'The G8 rows']
  • A repeat check on one build should give the same numbers. One row out of sixteen differs by 11.4 % with low rep noise. The README says 'these files do not show why'. [README of 010 line 170]

Tests added to clarify it

Related: run 6 boot F1 one-core 16 KiB read against run 3boot F1Whether another L1-resident row moves between boots. This is a weaker check than E against C. Run 3 and run 6 used different builds [README of 011, 'The 16 KiB rows', line 147].

What the tests showed

  • Insufficient data on the row itself. Run 6 boots F1 and F2 (membench-jibin-011 and 012) ran only the CME L1 rows. No second L3-on boot has repeated the G8 rows. [the 011 and 012 folders hold cme-bandwidth-l1-*.csv and no core bandwidth-l1-passes.csv or bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv]
  • A second L1-resident row moved between boots in run 6.
  • The one-core 16 KiB read on boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, 2026-11-06) reads 56.085 GB/s against run 3's 58.127 GB/s (0.965). [README of 011 line 147]
  • The reps spread 0.0 to 1.1 %, and the two runs used two builds. [README of 011 line 147]
  • Jesse's F1 README ties that row to this one: 'boot E against boot C, on one build, moved one L1 row too (the 4 KiB per-pass read, 0.886)'. [README of 011 line 147]
  • Those files do not show why either. [README of 011 line 147]
  • The row is listed as 'open' in the core page's open items (section 12), as 'Unexplained' in section 7.1, and on the run 4 page section 15. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html sections 7.1 and 12, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 15]
  • The brief page does not mention the row or 'G8'. A request from Jibin to remove it is not in the primary files checked. [asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html, jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md]
  • Wording differs between pages: the core full page says 'per-pass read', the run 4 page says 'looped-form read'. Jibin's wording rule is 'looped form'. [asimov-c1nano-perf.html sections 7.1 and 12, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 15, memory asimov-page-wording]

Still open

Why one L1-resident row on one build reads 11.4 % lower on boot E than on boot C is unexplained. The measurement that would settle it is the sixteen G8 rows with the perf columns on a second L3-on boot of the same firmware. That would show whether the 4 KiB looped read repeats 40.910 GB/s or 46.180 GB/s.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 4 boots C and E (membench-jibin-007 and 010), 2026-11-05 (UTC), both READMEs line 3

What looked wrong. Boots C and E ran the same sixteen G8 rows (one-core L1 read and write at 4, 8, 16 and 24 KiB, in a looped form and a single-call form). The 4 KiB looped read reads 40.910 GB/s on E and 46.180 GB/s on C. That is 0.886 times C, 11.4 % lower. The five reps of that row spread 0.16 % on E (40.844 to 40.910 GB/s) and 0.53 % on C (45.936 to 46.180 GB/s), so the gap is not rep noise. The row costs 3.13 to 3.14 cycles per line on E against 2.78 to 2.79 on C. The other 15 G8 rows read 0.972 to 1.013 times C's (the largest deviation is the 4 KiB single-call write, 0.972). The 4 KiB single-call read is equal on both boots (53.096 GB/s on E, 53.103 on C). The L1 data refills on the 4 KiB read rows are at most 0.0008 per line on both boots (all G8 rows: at most 0.0199 per line on C, 0.0195 on E).

Why it looked wrong. E and C ran the same commit (b79dffa) and the same program build (the bandwidth binary is C's once stripped, 6 bytes of an assembler temporary name apart) [README of 010, section 'Against boot C: the L3 alone']. The buffer fits the 32 KiB L1 and the refill counters show it stays there, so the G8 rows on E are a repeat check of C's rows, not an L3 result [README of 010, 'The G8 rows']. A repeat check that differs by 11 % on one row only, with low rep noise, has no explanation in the files: 'these files do not show why' [README of 010, line 170].

What the tests showed. Insufficient data. No second L3-on boot has run the G8 rows, so the row has not been repeated. The related run 6 observation (one-core 16 KiB read 0.965 times run 3 on boot F1, across two builds) shows a second L1-resident row moving between boots, and Jesse's F1 README ties it to this one: 'boot E against boot C, on one build, moved one L1 row too (the 4 KiB per-pass read, 0.886)'. These files do not show why either. The row is listed as 'open' in the core page's open items (section 12) and as 'Unexplained' in section 7.1, and on the run 4 page section 15. The brief page does not carry it (no mention of the row or of 'G8' in asimov-c1nano-perf-brief.html); a request from Jibin to remove it is not in the primary files checked (jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md has no such comment). 4.44 Boot F1 against run 3: L1-sized rows moved a few percent and counted latency commands ran 1.2 to 1.6 times longeropen

Boot F1 re-ran run 3's commands unchanged. Yet the 16 KiB reads fell 3.5 %. Latency commands ran 1.2 to 1.6 times longer.

What looked wrong

  • Boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, run 6, booted 2026-11-06 UTC) re-ran the 67 core command lines of run 3 (membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03 UTC) byte for byte.
  • The rows that fit the 32 KiB L1 (first-level cache) did not repeat.
  • The one-core 16 KiB read gave 56.085 GB/s on F1 against 58.127 GB/s on run 3 (0.965 times). The three reps were 55.715 to 56.085 GB/s on F1 against 57.654 to 58.127 GB/s on run 3. [004 and 011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • The pair 16 KiB read gave 112.409 GB/s on F1 against 116.407 GB/s on run 3 (0.966 times). [004 and 011 bandwidth-pair.csv]
  • The one-core 16 KiB write gave 30.608 GB/s on F1 against 30.127 GB/s on run 3 (1.016 times). The F1 write value is back at the 30.578 to 30.579 GB/s of runs 1 and 2. [001, 002, 004, 011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • The one-core writes of 48 KiB to 32 MiB repeated within 0.3 % (F1 over run 3: 1.000 to 1.003). [004 and 011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • The pair writes at 48 KiB and 160 KiB did not repeat (1.049 and 1.233). [004 and 011 bandwidth-pair.csv]
  • The mesh counters (cmn-counts.csv, column child_elapsed_ns, which spans the whole command) showed that F1's core latency commands ran longer.
  • The four counted 4 KiB controls took 1.310 to 1.423 times run 3's command time. The 20 single-region sparse OCM (on-chip memory) rows took 1.236 to 1.598 times.
  • The four sparse all-five rows took 1.167 to 1.208 times. The dense all-five rows took 1.028 to 1.044 times.
  • The three 2 MiB SLC (system level cache) chains took 1.010 to 1.024 times. The uncounted 4 KiB control took 1,269,307 ns on F1 against 883,269 ns on run 3 (1.437 times). [004 and 011 cmn-counts.csv]
  • The timed passes inside those commands did not grow. The four counted controls read 2.015 to 2.020 ns per load on F1 against 2.012 to 2.019 ns per load on run 3. [004 and 011 latency-control-cpu*.csv]
  • The 20 sparse OCM rows got faster: best 17.266 to 22.609 ns per load on F1 against 20.141 to 28.453 ns per load on run 3 (0.693 to 0.953 times, all 20 cells below 1). [004 and 011 latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv]
  • The counted core bandwidth commands ran 0.648 to 1.027 times run 3's command time. The counted 2 MiB read took 1,391,056 ns on F1 against 2,147,182 ns on run 3 (0.648 times). [004 and 011 cmn-counts.csv]

Why it looked wrong

  • A 16 KiB buffer fits the 32 KiB L1. The L3 (the third-level cache, the platform change that F1 was run for) should not touch it.
  • The kernels k_read, k_write and k_copy (the bandwidth inner loops) are byte for byte the same in both builds.
  • So an L1-sized row should repeat. It did not.
  • For the latency commands, the timed passes repeated or got faster. The whole command ran 1.2 to 1.6 times longer.
  • So something outside the timed passes grew.
  • The mesh counters give one time per whole command (chain build, flushes and unmap included). They cannot say which part grew.
  • Nine setup items differed between the two boots.
  • The SCP (system control processor) firmware was 0.48.0-nopcie.1 on run 3 with L3 full mode for cluster 0 only, and 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1 on F1 with L3 full mode for clusters 1 to 4 too.
  • The /dev/ocm module build differed (F1's adds debug map lines and the clusterpwrstat file, with the same 4 KiB mapping).
  • The binaries differed (commit ba834c0 on run 3 against 0c190a1 on F1): pass and worker differ, with the --asm-passes, --perf and CME paths.
  • chase (the latency program's loop) is the same 34 instructions. Its 48 B loop sits inside one 64 B line on F1 and across two lines on run 3.
  • k_write sits 16 B later in its line. [011 README lines 80-88, perf page section 2.3]
  • The latency rows on F1 carried three more prefetch counter columns (no multiplexing, perf_cov 1.0000).
  • The init differed: F1 ran the box's wrapper, which ran cme_test for about 0.012 s before run_all.sh.
  • Both boots ran on CPU 2 under SCHED_FIFO 10 (a real-time scheduling class and priority) with RT throttling off. So the scheduling is the same.
  • The emulator boards differed (ga13pd02 boards 6 to 9 on run 3 against 18 to 21 on F1, the same image copy). The dates differed. [011 README lines 80-88 and 322, perf page section 2.3]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Byte comparison of the two builds and the nine-item setup-difference tablerun 3, boot F1It lists which code (chase, k_read, k_write, k_copy, pass, worker, by the SDK's objdump of commits ba834c0 and 0c190a1) and which setup items differ between the boots and can touch an L1-sized row. A differing bandwidth kernel would point to the build. Identical kernels leave the cause outside the inner loop.
H6 / G5 write-cost check: two builds on one bootboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EIt runs the one-core 16 to 256 KiB write rows with bandwidth_r3 and bandwidth_r2 on one boot (bandwidth-write-small.csv and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv). A per-pass cost difference would mean a rebuild alone can move an L1-sized write row.
Counter-cost control: counted against uncounted 4 KiB control on CPU 2run 3, boot F1It takes helper_elapsed_ns of control-cpu2 minus control-nocount-cpu2 in cmn-counts.csv as the cost of the mesh counters per command. A higher cost on F1 would explain the longer commands. A lower cost would not.

What the tests showed

  • The build can move an L1-sized row by a few percent.
  • H6 (the hypothesis that run 3's rebuild added per-pass write cost) was supported on boots A, B and D: run 3's program was slower per pass than run 2's at 16 KiB by 11.2, 3.1 and 11.4 ns per pass.
  • It was not supported at 16 KiB on b79dffa's build. [run 4 page sections 3.8 and 9]
  • F1's 16 KiB write (30.608 GB/s) returned to the value of runs 1 and 2 (30.578 to 30.579 GB/s). So run 3's extra per-pass write cost did not appear in F1's build. [001, 002, 004, 011 bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]
  • Boot E against boot C, on one build, also moved one L1 row: the 4 KiB per-pass read, ratio 0.886. [run 4 page]
  • The counter cost per command fell on F1: 579,353 ns on F1 (1,907,513 minus 1,328,160) against 658,812 ns on run 3 (1,602,356 minus 943,544).
  • So the counters did not make the commands longer. [004 and 011 cmn-counts.csv, helper_elapsed_ns of control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2]
  • The counted 2 MiB read put 85,518 to 85,777 requests on each home node on F1 against 87,579 to 88,012 on run 3 (0.975 times). The command took 0.648 times as long.
  • So the counts do not show the L3 taking that read off the mesh. [004 and 011 cmn-counts.csv, hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all]
  • Boards and run-to-run noise were ruled out for the large moves: the controls repeat within 0.3 % and the one-core writes repeat within 0.3 %.
  • They were not measured for the 16 KiB rows. [perf page section 2.3, 'ruled out Boards or run-to-run noise']

Still open

Why the 16 KiB reads fell 3.5 % and which part of each latency command grew are both Insufficient data. The kernels are the same code. The files hold no counters for those rows. cmn-counts.csv gives only whole-command time. A repeat of the 16 KiB rows with both builds on one boot, with counters, would settle the first. A per-part timer (chain build, flushes, unmap, timed passes) on both builds would settle the second.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. run 6 boot F1 (membench-jibin-011, boot 2026-11-06 UTC) against run 3 (membench-jibin-004, 2026-11-03 UTC); written up in Jesse's F1 README (sections 'Core rows against round three' and 'Mesh counts') and in asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2.3. The date of the write-up is not in the primary files.

What looked wrong. Boot F1 ran run 3's 67 core command lines byte for byte. The rows that fit the 32 KiB L1 did not repeat run 3. The one-core 16 KiB read reads 56.085 GB/s on F1 against 58.127 on run 3 (0.965 times; reps 55.715 to 56.085 against 57.654 to 58.127). The pair's 16 KiB read reads 112.409 against 116.407 GB/s (0.966). The one-core 16 KiB write reads 30.608 against 30.127 GB/s (1.016), back at the 30.578 to 30.579 GB/s of runs 1 and 2. The one-core writes of 48 KiB to 32 MiB repeat within 0.3 % (1.000 to 1.003). The pair's writes at 48 and 160 KiB do not (1.049 and 1.233). Under the mesh counters (cmn-counts.csv, child_elapsed_ns, which spans the whole command) the F1 core latency commands ran longer: the four counted 4 KiB controls 1.310 to 1.423 times run 3's command time, the 20 single-region sparse OCM rows 1.236 to 1.598 times, the four sparse all-five rows 1.167 to 1.208, the dense all-five rows 1.028 to 1.044, the three 2 MiB SLC chains 1.010 to 1.024. The uncounted 4 KiB control ran 1,269,307 ns against 883,269 ns (1.437 times). The counted core bandwidth commands ran 0.648 to 1.027 times run 3's time (the counted 2 MiB read 1,391,056 ns against 2,147,182 ns, 0.648). The timed passes inside the latency commands did not grow: the four counted controls read 2.015 to 2.020 ns per load against 2.012 to 2.019, and the 20 sparse OCM rows read faster (best 17.266 to 22.609 ns per load against 20.141 to 28.453; 0.693 to 0.953 times, all 20 cells below 1).

Why it looked wrong. A 16 KiB buffer fits the L1, so the L3 (the platform change that F1 was run for) should not touch it. The kernels k_read, k_write and k_copy are byte for byte the same in both builds. So an L1-sized row should repeat, and it did not. For the latency commands, the timed passes repeated or got faster while the whole command ran 1.2 to 1.6 times longer, so something outside the timed passes grew. What differed between the two boots (Jesse's F1 README, 'Core rows against round three'; page section 2.3): the SCP firmware (0.48.0-nopcie.1 on run 3, L3 full mode for cluster 0 only; 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1 on F1, L3 full mode for clusters 1 to 4 too), the /dev/ocm module build (F1's adds debug map lines and the clusterpwrstat file; the same 4 KiB mapping), the binaries (commit ba834c0 against 0c190a1: pass and worker differ, with the --asm-passes, --perf and CME paths; chase is the same 34 instructions but its 48 B loop sits inside one 64 B line on F1 and across two on run 3; k_write sits 16 B later in its line), the counter columns on the latency rows (three more prefetch events, no multiplexing, perf_cov 1.0000), the init (F1 ran the box's wrapper, which ran cme_test for about 0.012 s before run_all.sh; both boots ran on CPU 2 under SCHED_FIFO 10 with RT throttling off, so the scheduling is the same), the emulator boards (ga13pd02 boards 6 to 9 against 18 to 21, the same image copy) and the date. The mesh counters give one time per whole command (chain build, flushes and unmap included), so they cannot say which part grew.

Tests added.

  • Byte comparison of the two builds (ba834c0 against 0c190a1) with the SDK's objdump: chase, k_read, k_write, k_copy, pass and worker; and section 2.3's setup-difference table (nine items, each with 'can it move a core row?' and a suspected impact) [analysis of membench-jibin-004 and -011 (Jesse's F1 README, 'Core rows against round three'; asimov-c1nano-perf.html section 2.3)]: which code and which setup items differ between the two boots, and which of them can touch an L1-sized row
  • H6 / G5 write-cost check: run 3's bandwidth program (bandwidth_r3) and run 2's (bandwidth_r2) run the one-core 16 to 256 KiB write rows on one boot (bandwidth-write-small.csv and bandwidth-write-small-r2prog.csv) [run 4 boots A to E (membench-jibin-005 to 008 and 010); a test added before run 6 that bears on the 16 KiB write row]: whether a rebuild alone moves the per-pass cost of an L1-sized write row
  • Counter-cost control: the counted and the uncounted 4 KiB control on CPU 2 (control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2 in cmn-counts.csv) [run 3 (004) and boot F1 (011)]: the cost of the mesh counters per command (helper_elapsed_ns minus the uncounted one's): 579,353 ns on F1 against 658,812 ns on run 3

What the tests showed. The build can move an L1-sized row by a few percent. H6 was supported on the builds of boots A, B and D (run 3's program slower per pass than run 2's at 16 KiB by 11.2, 3.1 and 11.4 ns) and not at 16 KiB on b79dffa's build (asimov-c1nano-run4.html, sections 3.8 and 9). F1's 16 KiB write (30.608 GB/s) returned to the value of runs 1 and 2 (30.578 to 30.579), so run 3's extra per-pass write cost did not appear in F1's build. Boot E against boot C, one build, also moved one L1 row (the 4 KiB per-pass read, 0.886). Why the 16 KiB reads fell 3.5 % is Insufficient data: the kernels are the same code and the files hold no counters for those rows (Jesse's F1 README: 'These files do not show why'). Which part of each latency command grew is Insufficient data: cmn-counts.csv gives only whole-command time, and the counter cost itself fell (579,353 ns against 658,812 ns). The counted 2 MiB read put 85,518 to 85,777 requests on each home node against run 3's 87,579 to 88,012 (0.975 times) while the command took 0.648 times as long, so the counts do not show the L3 taking that read off the mesh. Boards and run-to-run noise were ruled out for the large moves (controls repeat within 0.3 %, one-core writes within 0.3 %) but not measured for the 16 KiB rows.

4.45 Prefetcher-off boots take 0.28 s more per large CME sweep outside the timed walks; one OCM command lived 8.4 times longer with normal timed passesopen

Boots with the prefetchers off spend 0.28 s more per large CME sweep. The timed walks inside each sweep got faster.

What looked wrong

  • Boot F2 (run 6, folder membench-jibin-012: prefetchers off, L3 on) took 2.839 s of chip time. Jesse's estimator (est_chip_time.py, a script that prices each command from the log) gave 2.389 s.
  • Outside the two large sweeps the script ran about 0.58 s under the estimate. [012 README line 248, est_chip_time.py rerun on 012 log.txt]
  • Each of the two large CME chain sweeps (CME: the unit that runs the chain loads. Sweep: one command per chain size from 512 KiB to 32 MiB) took 0.91 s on F2 by the log's uptime stamps. [012 log.txt lines 5-6 and 68-69]
  • The same sweep took 0.63 s on boot F1 (membench-jibin-011: prefetchers on). The estimator gives 0.393 s per sweep. [011 log.txt lines 86-87 and 149-150]
  • Run 4 shows the same split. Boots B and D (prefetchers off) took 0.92 s per sweep.
  • Boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) took 0.64 s, 0.63 s and 0.63 s. [log.txt of membench-jibin-005, 006, 007, 008, 010]
  • The timed walks inside each sweep got faster with the prefetchers off.
  • The 22 timed walks of one sweep add up to 157.1 ms on F2 against 163.9 to 164.0 ms on F1. They add up to 158.0 ms on boot B against 164.2 ms on boot A. [cme-latency-dram-large.csv and -large-l3.csv of 012 and 011, cme-latency-dram-large.csv of 006 and 005]
  • So the extra 0.28 s per sweep sits outside the timed walks.
  • Two more oddities sit in boot F2. The command cme-ocm-region3-cpu2 (one OCM latency test, OCM: on-chip memory) lived 62.316 ms on F2 against 7.459 ms on F1, 8.35 times longer. [cmn-counts.csv child_elapsed_ns of 012 and 011]
  • Its best timed pass, 51.734 ns per load, is in line with the other four regions (47.906 to 52.109 ns per load). Those regions lived 7.509 to 7.574 ms on F2. [012 cme-latency-ocm-region3.csv]
  • The flushed 8 MiB CME command lived 102.733 ms on F2 against 70.428 ms on F1 (1.459 times). It sent each of the five home nodes only 0.639 to 0.643 times F1's requests. [cmn-counts.csv child_elapsed_ns of 012 and 011]

Why it looked wrong

  • Expectation: a prefetcher setting changes how fast the loads run. A slower sweep should then show slower timed walks.
  • The timed walks got faster instead (157.1 ms on F2 against 163.9 to 164.0 ms on F1).
  • So the extra 0.28 s per sweep lies in the untimed parts of each command: chain 0's untimed walks, the chain builds and the flushes. The files do not time those parts.
  • Expectation: the estimator should predict the sweep time. It prices every untimed part with one constant per boot: 10 ns est. per chain line built, 7 ns est. per flushed line, 14 ms est. per launch. [est_chip_time.py lines 18-33]
  • These constants do not depend on the prefetcher state. So the estimator cannot show a prefetcher-dependent untimed cost.
  • Expectation: a command's lifetime follows its timed passes and its mesh request counts.
  • cme-ocm-region3-cpu2 lived 8.35 times longer on F2 (62.316 ms against 7.459 ms). Its timed passes were in line with the other regions, and its mesh request counts were normal.
  • The files hold no explanation for it. [cmn-counts.csv of 012 and 011]
  • Expectation: the flushed 8 MiB command should live in proportion to its requests. It sent 2.54 million fewer requests over the five home nodes on F2 yet lived 32.3 ms longer.
  • The two timed walks account for only about 0.63 million of the fewer requests and 2.5 ms of the longer life. [cmn-counts.csv and cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 012 and 011]

Tests added to clarify it

TestRun or bootWhat it measures
Time the untimed parts of each large sweep commandnot runA timestamp or counter per untimed part (chain build, flush, chain 0's untimed walks) on a prefetcher-off boot would say which part carries the extra 0.28 s per sweep. The primary files hold no such row.

What the tests showed

  • Not tested. The 012 README lists where the time went, with an uptime stamp per command.
  • It marks the cause of the longer untimed parts and of the region 3 command as not shown by these files. [012 README lines 13, 143, 248, 249]
  • No follow-up row or counter for the untimed parts appears in the primary files of 012 or 011.
  • The closest on-disk measurement of the F2 chip time is the span of run_cme.sh (the test script) by CPU 3's absence from dmesg (the kernel log).
  • That span is 2.742 s on F2 and 2.169 s on F1. [012 dmesg.txt lines 203 and 234 (0.358 to 3.100 s), 011 dmesg.txt lines 286 and 317 (1.885 to 4.054 s)]
  • The 2.839 s figure exists only as a quote of the 'MB RUN end ns=2839351301' line in the 012 README.
  • The small sweeps (4 KiB to 384 KiB) do not show the split.
  • They took 0.11 s and 0.08 s on F2, 0.15 s and 0.15 s on F1, and 0.128 s by the estimator. [012 log.txt lines 4-5 and 66-68, 011 log.txt lines 85-86 and 147-149]
  • The flushed 8 MiB timed walks (2 x 131072 loads) took 18.8 ms on F2 against 16.3 ms on F1.
  • That is 71.715 and 71.714 ns per load against 62.104 and 62.080 ns per load. Outer refills per load were 1.0000 on F2 against 3.3681 and 3.4089 on F1. [cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv of 012 and 011]
  • Related: F1's counted core latency commands also lived 1.236 to 1.598 times as long as run 3's by child_elapsed_ns. [011 README line 149]

Still open

Which untimed part of each large sweep (chain builds, flushes, chain 0's untimed walks) carries the extra 0.28 s per sweep with the prefetchers off is still open. Why cme-ocm-region3-cpu2 lived 8.35 times longer on F2 with timed passes in line with the other regions is also open. A timestamp or counter per untimed part inside each command, on one prefetcher-off boot, would settle the first question.

Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

First seen. Noted in Jesse's README for run 6 boot F2 (membench-jibin-012, file dated 2026-11-07, section 'Where the time went'). The same 0.92 s sweeps already sit in the log.txt of run 4 boots B (006) and D (008), but no README noted them before the 012 README.

What looked wrong. Boot F2 (prefetchers off, L3 on) took 2.839 s of chip time. Jesse's estimator gave 2.389 s. Each of the two 512 KiB to 32 MiB CME chain sweeps took 0.91 s by the log's uptime stamps. The same sweep took 0.63 s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 0.393 s by the estimator. Run 4 shows the same split: boots B and D (prefetchers off) 0.92 s, boots A, C and E (prefetchers on) 0.64, 0.63 and 0.63 s. Yet the timed walks inside each sweep got faster with the prefetchers off: the 22 timed walks add up to 157.1 ms on F2 against 163.9 to 164.0 ms on F1 (boot B 158.0 ms against boot A 164.2 ms). So the extra 0.28 s per sweep is outside the timed walks. Two more oddities: the command cme-ocm-region3-cpu2 lived 62.316 ms on F2 against 7.459 ms on F1 (8.35 times), while its timed passes read 51.734 ns best, in line with the other four regions (47.906 to 52.109 ns). And the flushed 8 MiB CME command lived 1.459 times as long (102.733 against 70.428 ms) while putting only 0.639 to 0.643 times F1's requests on each of the five home nodes; the two timed walks account for about 0.63 million of the 2.54 million fewer requests and 2.5 ms of the 32.3 ms longer life. The rest of the script ran about 0.58 s under the estimate.

Why it looked wrong. The timed walks got faster with the prefetchers off. So the extra 0.28 s per sweep lies in untimed parts of each command: chain 0's untimed walks, the chain builds, the flushes. The files do not time those parts. The estimator (est_chip_time.py) prices every untimed part with one constant per boot (10 ns est. per chain line built, 7 ns est. per flushed line, 14 ms est. per launch), so it cannot show a prefetcher-dependent untimed cost. A single command living 8.35 times longer with unchanged timed passes has no explanation in the files: its timed passes and its mesh request counts look normal.

    4.46 CME bandwidth rows that moved with the prefetchers off: the 32 MiB read halves, the single-call 96 KiB read falls to 0.63x, the 16 KiB 64 B-load read rises to 1.20xpartly explained

    Prefetchers off: the 32 MiB CME read halved, the single-call 96 KiB read fell to 0.63x, the 16 KiB 64 B-load read rose 20 %.

    What looked wrong

    • Boot F2 (prefetchers off) against boot F1 (prefetchers on), best of 3 reps: the CME read at 32 MiB fell from 36.583 to 17.699 GB/s (0.484). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, line 112]
    • In span it fell from 36.591 to 17.702 GB/s (0.484). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, line 112]
    • Every F2 rep lay below every F1 rep. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, reps lines 109 to 111]
    • Other streaming rows fell less. ldr16 (64 B loads) at 32 MiB fell from 36.611 to 18.036 GB/s (0.493). Copy at 32 MiB fell from 41.235 to 34.192 GB/s (0.829). [same file, lines 155 and 120]
    • Read at 2 MiB fell from 36.921 to 32.758 GB/s (0.887). The looped 96 KiB read fell from 43.713 to 39.950 GB/s (0.914). [same file, lines 97 and 37]
    • The single-call 96 KiB read fell from 68.249 to 42.773 GB/s (0.627). In span it fell from 68.461 to 42.855 GB/s (0.626). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012, lines 18 to 21]
    • Every F2 rep (37.892 to 42.773 GB/s) lay below every F1 rep (60.136 to 68.249 GB/s). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012, lines 18 to 21]
    • On F1 the single-call 96 KiB read ran 1.561 times its looped twin (68.249 against 43.713 GB/s). On F2 it ran 1.071 times (42.773 against 39.950 GB/s). [asmpasses lines 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56 and dram-1core line 37 of 011 and 012]
    • The other single-call rows stayed at 0.996 to 1.010 times F1. One example is 127.468 against 128.768 GB/s at 48 KiB. [asmpasses lines 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56 and dram-1core line 37 of 011 and 012]
    • At 16 KiB (a buffer that fits the 64 KiB CME L1) ldr16 rose from 46.747 to 56.267 GB/s (1.204, in span 1.278). Every F2 rep lay above every F1 rep. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv line 127 of 011 and 012]
    • The 256 B-load read fell from 52.171 to 50.409 GB/s (0.966, in span 0.954). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv line 7 of 011 and 012]
    • Writes moved little. The 256 B-load write ran 0.927 to 1.000 times F1. str16 (64 B stores) ran 0.991 to 1.010 times F1. Single-call writes ran 0.996 to 1.003 times F1. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv lines 11 to 116 in steps of 15, 134, 148, 162 and asmpasses lines 14, 28, 42, 56]

    Why it looked wrong

    • A 16 KiB buffer fits the CME's 64 KiB L1 data cache. Turning the prefetcher off should not change a 16 KiB row. [membench-jibin-011/README.md line 349 and asimov-cme-perf.html, Words used here, CME]
    • Yet the 64 B-load read got 20 % faster (1.204) on F2 against F1. The 256 B-load read got 3 % slower (0.966).
    • 96 KiB is larger than the CME L1. On F1 the single-call form read 1.561 times its looped twin at 96 KiB. On F2 that advantage fell to 1.071 times. [asmpasses lines 7, 21, 28, 35 and dram-1core line 37 of 011 and 012]
    • So the prefetcher made the single-call form faster past the L1. The other single-call sizes (48, 160 and 256 KiB) did not move (0.996 to 1.010). [asmpasses lines 7, 21, 28, 35 and dram-1core line 37 of 011 and 012]
    • The bandwidth rows carry no CME counters. The bandwidth program refuses --perf (its counter option) together with --cme. So no refill count sits beside any of these moves. [bandwidth.c line 494 and membench-jibin-012/README.md line 142]
    • The nearest measurement with counters is run 4's sequential 8 MiB CME chase (a walk in address order). Boot B (prefetchers off) read 71.740 ns per load against boot A's 21.417 ns per load (3.35 times slower). [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 and 006, cme-fresh1 and cme-best rows]
    • Boot A's CME counted 1.0000 hardware-prefetch refill per load. Boot B's counted 0. [cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of 005 and 006, cme-fresh1 and cme-best rows]

    Tests added to clarify it

    TestRun or bootWhat it measures
    Single-call twin rows at 48 to 256 KiB, read and writeboot F1, boot F2Each sweep row below 256 KiB beside its single-call twin (bandwidth --cme --asm-passes, 3 reps) for the per-call cost. This row exposed the 1.561x gap at 96 KiB on F1 [run_cme.sh lines 117 to 122].
    F2 repeat of the CME bandwidth set, prefetchers offboot F2The CME prefetcher's share of each streaming row, as the F2 / F1 ratio of the best reps, in the bracket rate and the in-span rate.

    What the tests showed

    • The 32 MiB read halves with the prefetchers off (0.484 in the bracket rate and 0.484 in span). The 2 MiB read falls to 0.887. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, lines 112 and 97]
    • The 32 MiB write does not move: 40.445 GB/s on F1 against 40.357 GB/s on F2 (0.998). [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012, line 116]
    • The CME page reads this as: the CME's prefetcher carries half of a DRAM stream, and the writes do not change. [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6, Bandwidth by footprint]
    • No counter sits beside this reading. The bandwidth rows carry none.
    • The source entry keeps the halving as a side result under the entry cme-writes-fall-with-l3-on (not checked here).
    • The single-call 96 KiB read's advantage over the looped form fell from 1.561x on F1 to 1.071x on F2.
    • Jesse's F2 README says: "These rows carry no counters, so these files do not show why". [membench-jibin-012/README.md line 172]
    • For the 16 KiB ldr16 read, Jesse's F2 README says: "These files do not show why the 16 KiB 64 B-load row got faster". [membench-jibin-012/README.md line 142]
    • The in-span ratio (1.278) is larger than the bracket ratio (1.204). So the gain sits inside the streaming span, not in the call overhead. [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv line 127 of 011 and 012]
    • No further test for the 96 KiB single-call row or the 16 KiB ldr16 row appears in CME-plan.md or message-to-jesse-round6.md (searched for single-call, 96 KiB, ldr16).

    Still open

    Why the single-call 96 KiB read loses its 1.561x advantage without the prefetcher is open. Why the 16 KiB ldr16 read gets 20 % faster inside the CME L1 is also open. A CME refill counter beside these bandwidth rows would settle both. The bandwidth program has no CME counter set today [bandwidth.c line 494].

    4.47 PMU events that open but count zero: 0x2A on the C1-Nano, prefetch events on the CRB, 0x81C6 before boot Eexplained

    Several PMU events opened without error but read 0. A zero could not be told from an event that is not implemented.

    What looked wrong

    • Event 0x2A (L3D_CACHE_REFILL, the Arm event number for L3 refills) opens on the C1-Nano (the core in Asimov) with no error. It always reads 0. [common.h perf_open comment, 001 README.md line 26]
    • On the CRB (the Neoverse V3AE reference board) a 4 MiB sequential flushed chain ran at 2.7 ns per load, against 97.5 ns per load for the 8 MiB random flushed chain. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 8, CRB check of 2026-11-04]
    • The sequential chain had 0.056 L1D (L1 data cache) refills and 1.00 L2 refills per load. Those counts show that some prefetcher acted on it. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 8, CRB check of 2026-11-04]
    • The three prefetch events 0x81BC, 0x81BD and 0x0111 read 0.0000 per load there. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 8, CRB check of 2026-11-04]
    • On the CRB the hit set (0x81C5 L2 read hits, 0xA0 L3 read accesses, 0x81C6 L3 read hits) also opened and read 0.0000 in all three columns on a 1 MiB repeated row. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10, Verification of 2026-11-04]
    • That row had 1.00 L1 refills and 0 L2 refills per load. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10, Verification of 2026-11-04]
    • On Asimov, 0x81C6 read 0.0000 in all 21 rows of latency-dram-small-l3.csv on boot B (006), boot C (007) and boot D (008). [latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 006, 007 and 008, recomputed]
    • This kernel opens any raw event number except CHAIN (0x1E). A successful open proves nothing. [008 README.md line 14]

    Why it looked wrong

    • The expectation was that an event that opens without error also counts.
    • A zero count cannot be told from 'the event is not implemented' unless a row is built that must produce the activity.
    • On boots B, C and D the L3 held no data. IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1 (the cluster power-state register) read 0x0 on those boots. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]
    • Every L2 miss went to the mesh (the on-chip interconnect). [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]
    • So a zero 0x81C6 was a true absence of hits. It said nothing about the counter. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]
    • On the CRB the 1 MiB row fit that core's 2 MiB L2. Zero L3 accesses and zero L3 hits were expected there. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10]
    • Only 0x81C5 reading 0 beside 1.00 L1 refills per load showed an event that opens and does not count on that core. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10]
    • Without a validation rule, a zero prefetch count on Asimov would have been read as 'no prefetching'. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 6, line 136]

    Tests added to clarify it

    TestRun or bootWhat it measures
    Use 0xA2 (L3D_CACHE_REFILL_RD) instead of 0x2Arun 1L3 read refills from outside the cluster on the C1-Nano (column l3d_refill_rd_per_load). The TRM (the Arm technical reference manual) listed 0x2A as not implemented (PMCEID1_EL0 ID10 resets to 0). Run 1's group became cycles, 0x03, 0x17, 0xA2 [common.h perf_open_l3 comment, 001 README.md line 26].
    8 MiB sequential flushed chain as prefetch stimulus, random chain as controlboot A, boot B, boot C, boot D, boot EWhether 0x81BC, 0x81BD and 0x0111 count on the C1-Nano, as refills per load on latency-dram-seq.csv against latency-dram-flushed.csv. The per-event rule applies. An event is validated only when it counts on a row where its activity is established. A zero elsewhere means unvalidated, not broken. PERF_REQUIRED 4 keeps cycles and the three run 3 refill events required. The other three events open independently. A refused event then costs only its own column and prints '-' [follow-up-run-plan.md lines 16, 38 and 61, common.h line 229].
    Hit set (0x81C5, 0xA0, 0x81C6) on 64 KiB to 512 KiB repeated chasesboot B, boot C, boot D, boot EL2 and L3 demand read hits per load (latency-dram-small-l3.csv). The per-event rule was applied after codex review item R18. 0x81C5 is validated on the 64 KiB row, and 0xA0 on the 512 KiB row. 0x81C6 is validated only when nonzero beside a nonzero 0xA0, else unvalidated [codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md R18, follow-up-run-plan.md section 10].
    Walk set (0x34, 0x8188, 0x818A) on 32 MiB random chain, run 5bboot C, boot D, boot EWhich descriptor each page walk ended in (0x8188 DTLB_WALK_BLOCK, 0x818A DTLB_WALK_PAGE) on 4 KiB pages. Every walk there is a page walk. So 0x818A is validated there, and 0x8188 is expected to read 0 [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11, note 2].

    What the tests showed

    • Boot A (005), sequential chain: 0x81BC read 0.9999 and 0x0111 read 0.9999 refills per load, beside 1.0000 L1 refills and 1.0000 L2 refills per load, at 6.917 ns per load. [005 latency-dram-seq.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
    • 0x81BD read 0.0001 there. [005 latency-dram-seq.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
    • Boot A's random flushed control read 0.0000 in all three prefetch columns at 52.739 ns per load. So the three events count on the C1-Nano. [005 latency-dram-flushed.csv, rows fresh1 and fresh2]
    • 0x81BD was validated on the OCM rows of boot A, up to 2.98 refills per load. [005 latency-ocm-region4-vary-cpu8.csv, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 3.1]
    • Boot C (007) repeated this: 0x81BC 1.0000 and 0.9999, 0x0111 1.0000 and 0.9999 at 6.917 to 6.927 ns per load. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 007, 008 and 010]
    • Boot E (010) too: 0.9997 and 0.9997 at 2.492 to 2.501 ns per load with the L3 on. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 007, 008 and 010]
    • On boots B (006) and D (008), prefetchers off, the sequential chain read 52.76 ns per load with 0.0000 in all three columns. [latency-dram-seq.csv of 006, 007, 008 and 010]
    • 0x81C6 was validated on boot E (010), the first boot with the L3 on. [010 latency-dram-small-l3.csv, 010 README.md line 44]
    • It read 0.4651 to 0.4708 hits per load at 192 KiB, 0.7508 to 0.7712 at 256 KiB, 0.9152 to 0.9236 at 384 KiB and 0.4031 to 0.4118 at 512 KiB (3 repetitions per size). [010 latency-dram-small-l3.csv, 010 README.md line 44]
    • It read below 0.012 at 64 to 128 KiB. [010 latency-dram-small-l3.csv, 010 README.md line 44]
    • 0xA0 minus 0xA2 equals 0x81C6 within 0.0001 hits per load in all 21 rows of boot E. [010 README.md line 44]
    • On boots B, C and D 0x81C6 read 0.0000 in all 21 rows of each file. [latency-dram-small-l3.csv of 006, 007 and 008]
    • 0xA0's population was corrected on 2026-11-04 from Jesse's RTL (hardware design source) note. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11, note 1, common.h perf_open_l3 comment]
    • In this RTL it leaves out hardware-prefetch fills and prefetch-origin walks, and keeps the program's own page walks and software-prefetch reads. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11, note 1, common.h perf_open_l3 comment]
    • So 0x81C6 / 0xA0 is an estimate (est.) of the L3 demand hit rate. [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11, note 1, common.h perf_open_l3 comment]
    • 0x17 counts every L2 refill (data and instruction misses, translation walks, L1 write-backs and prefetches). So 0x17 minus the prefetch events is not a demand count. [common.h perf_open comment, asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 3.4]
    • 0x8188 read 0.0000 in every walk pass on boots C (007), D (008) and E (010). [007 README.md line 158, 008 README.md line 94, 010 README.md lines 187 to 189]
    • On the same passes 0x34 read 0.1849 to 0.1850, 0.4371 to 0.4381 and 0.5113 to 0.5118 walks per load. [007 README.md line 158, 008 README.md line 94, 010 README.md lines 187 to 189]
    • 0x8188 has read nonzero on no boot, and it stays unvalidated. [007 README.md line 158, 008 README.md line 94, 010 README.md lines 187 to 189]

    Still open

    Whether the V3AE implements the three prefetch events, or a prefetcher outside their scope did the work on the CRB, is Insufficient data (its manual was not at hand). The V3AE PMU manual would settle it [follow-up-run-plan.md section 8]. 0x8188 has read nonzero on no boot and stays unvalidated. A nonzero 0x8188 reading on any boot would settle it [010 README.md line 189].

    Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

    First seen. 2026-10-30 (Jesse: 0x2A opens and reads 0 on the C1-Nano, recorded in common.h and the run 1 README of 2026-10-31); CRB prefetch-event check 2026-11-04 (follow-up-run-plan.md section 8); CRB hit-set check 2026-11-04 (section 10); 0x81C6 zeros on boot B 2026-11-04 (membench-jibin-006)

    What looked wrong. Event 0x2A (L3D_CACHE_REFILL) opens on the C1-Nano without an error but always reads 0 [common.h perf_open comment; results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 26: '0x2A is not implemented here']. On the CRB (the Neoverse V3AE reference board) the three prefetch events 0x81BC, 0x81BD and 0x0111 read 0.0000 per load on a 4 MiB sequential flushed chain that ran at 2.7 ns per load, against 97.5 ns per load for the random flushed chain, with 0.056 L1D refills and 1.00 L2 refills per load. Some prefetcher clearly acted on that chain, yet the three events counted nothing [follow-up-run-plan.md section 8]. On the CRB the hit set (0x81C5, 0xA0, 0x81C6) also opened and read 0.0000 in all three columns on a 1 MiB repeated row with 1.00 L1 refills and 0 L2 refills per load [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10, 'Verification (2026-11-04)']. On Asimov, 0x81C6 (L3 read hits) read 0.0000 in all 21 rows of latency-dram-small-l3.csv on boot B (006), boot C (007) and boot D (008) [recomputed from the three CSVs]. This kernel opens any raw event number except CHAIN (0x1E), so a successful open proves nothing [results/membench-jibin-008/README.md line 14].

    Why it looked wrong. A zero count cannot be told from 'the event is not implemented' unless a row is built that must produce the activity. On boots B, C and D the L3 held no data (IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1 read 0x0, every L2 miss went to the mesh), so a zero 0x81C6 was a true absence of hits and said nothing about the counter [asimov-c1nano-run4.html section 11.1]. On the CRB the 1 MiB row fit that core's 2 MiB L2, so zero L3 accesses and zero L3 hits were expected there; only 0x81C5 reading 0 beside 1.00 L1 refills showed an event that opens and does not count on that core [follow-up-run-plan.md section 10]. Without a validation rule, a zero prefetch count on Asimov would have been read as 'no prefetching' [follow-up-run-plan.md section 6, line 136].

    Tests added.

    • Use 0xA2 L3D_CACHE_REFILL_RD instead of 0x2A. The TRM lists 0x2A as not implemented (PMCEID1_EL0 ID10 resets to 0) and it read 0 on the emulator [common.h perf_open_l3 comment]. [run 1 onward (run 1's group was cycles, 0x03, 0x17, 0xA2) [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md line 26]]: L3 read refills from outside the cluster on the C1-Nano (column l3d_refill_rd_per_load)
    • The --seq 8 MiB flushed sequential chain (latency-dram-seq.csv) on every boot as the prefetch stimulus, beside the 8 MiB random flushed chain (latency-dram-flushed.csv) as the control. Per-event validation rule: an event is validated only when it counts on a row where its activity is established; a zero elsewhere means unvalidated, not broken [follow-up-run-plan.md Words used here, line 16; goal G-a, line 38]. PERF_REQUIRED 4: cycles and the three run 3 refill events are required, the other three events open independently, so a refused event costs only its own column and prints '-' [common.h line 229; follow-up-run-plan.md line 61]. [run 4 boot A (005) onward]: whether 0x81BC, 0x81BD and 0x0111 count on the C1-Nano (refills per load on the sequential and random chains)
    • The hit set (--events l3: 0x81C5 L2 read hits, 0xA0 L3 read accesses, 0x81C6 L3 read hits) on the 64 KiB to 512 KiB repeated chases, with the same per-event rule applied after codex R18: 0x81C5 is validated on the 64 KiB row, 0xA0 on the 512 KiB row, 0x81C6 only when nonzero beside a nonzero 0xA0, else unvalidated [codex-review-follow-up-run-plan.md R18; follow-up-run-plan.md section 10]. [run 4 boots B, C, D (006, 007, 008) and boot E (010)]: L2 and L3 demand read hits per load (latency-dram-small-l3.csv)
    • The walk set (--events walk: 0x34, 0x8188 DTLB_WALK_BLOCK, 0x818A DTLB_WALK_PAGE) with a 32 MiB random chain on 4 KiB pages as the stimulus, where every walk is a page walk, so 0x818A is validated there and 0x8188 is expected to read 0 [follow-up-run-plan.md section 11, note 2]. [run 5b, boots C, D, E (007, 008, 010)]: which descriptor each page walk ended in

    What the tests showed. Boot A (005): on the sequential chain 0x81BC read 0.9999 and 0x0111 read 0.9999 refills per load beside 1.0000 L1 refills and 1.0000 L2 refills, at 6.917 ns per load; 0x81BD read 0.0001 there [latency-dram-seq.csv of 005, rows fresh1 and fresh2].     4.48 Harness measurement costs: chip-time estimate, mesh-counter helper cost, sparse-row counts and clock calibrationexplained

    Five harness numbers disagreed with expectations: chip-time estimates, the mesh-counter helper's cost, sparse-row request counts, clock calibration and two review findings.

    What looked wrong

    • The chip-time estimator (est_chip_time.py) gave 4.111 s est. for run 3. Run 3 then took 2.918 s of chip time. [CME-plan.md section 4.4 lines 398 and 642 and README of 004 line 19]
    • The estimator charged 14 ms est. per program start, a value taken from run 1. Jesse's run 2 README put each command at 3 to 5 ms est. [RUN2-PLAN.md line 360 and est_chip_time.py line 32 and README of 002 line 84]
    • Before run 3, the first CME plan budget claimed 0.5 s est. Its own parts summed to 0.99 s est. [codex-review-CME-plan.md line 58]
    • In run 2 the counted control row (a 4 KiB pointer chase run under the cmncount helper with the mesh counters on) read helper_elapsed_ns 1,163,263 ns.
    • The uncounted control read 540,889 ns. The gap is 622,374 ns. [cmn-counts.csv of 002, rows control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2]
    • Run 3's sparse OCM rows (one line touched per 4 KiB page) put 0.400 to 0.493 times run 2's dense request counts on the region's home node under the same labels. [README of 004 line 118 and cmn-counts.csv of 002 and 004]
    • The cycles column of a sparse per-region row read 2.068 to 2.259 cycles per ns over 140 passes. The clock runs at 2.00 cycles per ns. [README of 004 line 113 and latency-ocm-region*-cpu*.csv of 004]
    • Two review findings concern the harness itself. perf_cov (the running time divided by the enabled time of a counter group) was cumulative. One multiplexed row would then invalidate every later row. [CME-plan.md line 494, R4]
    • The mesh map in sysinfo.txt listed HN-S #0 to #4 (the five home nodes of the mesh) in an order that is not OCM0 to OCM4. [README of 002, Reading the numbers]

    Why it looked wrong

    • The launch assumption was 2.32 s of the 4.111 s est. for run 3, that is 56 % of the estimate. [CME-plan.md section 4.4, lines 403 and 495]
    • The 14 ms est. per launch is run 1's whole-run time minus its measured work, spread over its commands. Nothing in a run measures it. [RUN2-PLAN.md line 360]
    • Jesse's 3 to 5 ms est. is run 1's console timing minus a model of each command's work. The console polls every 10 ms. [README of 002 line 84]
    • The 0.99 s est. sum was 0.10 + 0.25 + 0.05 + 0.03 + 40 x 0.014 s. [codex-review-CME-plan.md line 58]
    • The counted helper makes 38 more sysfs reads (sysfs is the Linux kernel's file view of device settings) than the uncounted one to set its events up, 40 reads against 2.
    • The 622,374 ns gap in run 2 is therefore not the counters alone. [README of 002 line 74]
    • The mesh counters cover each whole command, with chain build, flushes and warm-up included. A sparse row times 448 loads (7 passes of 64 loads each) but flushes 4,096 lines 7 times.
    • If each line operation is one home-node request, the 7 full flushes make 61 to 73 % of a sparse row's excess and the 448 timed loads about 1 %. [README of 004 line 118]
    • Each pass also counts 150 to 400 user cycles (cycles spent in user mode) outside the clock bracket (the timed region between two clock reads). A 64-load pass spreads those cycles over only 64 loads.
    • A sparse row therefore cannot calibrate the clock as the long dense rows do. [README of 004 line 113]
    • PERF_EVENT_IOC_RESET (the kernel call that zeroes a perf counter) clears the counts but keeps the enabled and running times. A coverage ratio taken from the raw times was therefore cumulative over the group's life. [CME-plan.md line 494, R4]
    • The mesh map prints crosspoint numbers and each node's logical id within its type, not node ids. HN-S #0 to #4 are nodes 88, 216, 344, 160 and 288, that is OCM0, OCM2, OCM4, OCM1 and OCM3. [README of 002, Reading the numbers]

    Tests added to clarify it

    TestRun or bootWhat it measures
    --dry-run counts plus est_chip_time.py with labelled assumptionsotherChip time per command (est.) from exact counts of loads, lines, bytes, kernel calls and launches. The load and call costs are recalibrated to run 3's best rows, and the launch cost is kept as an unmeasured 14 ms est. allowance [CME-plan.md sections 3.6 and 4.4, R5 at line 476 and line 495 and follow-up-run-plan.md line 94 and est_chip_time.py lines 18 to 33].

The counted-minus-uncounted gap is the counters' cost as Jesse's README defines it [cmn-counts.csv rows control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2].
    per-row perf_cov in perf_read, checked by perf_cov_test.cotherWhether a multiplexed row is rejected on its own and the next quiet row is accepted, once perf_read takes each row's times as the change since the previous read. Tested on the CRB before run 3 and again for the run 4 plan.

    What the tests showed

    • Chip time measured: run 1 1.237 s, run 2 1.630 s (about 2 s est.), control run 1.610 s, run 3 2.918 s (2.5 to 4.1 s est.). [READMEs of 001 line 9, 002 line 16, 003 line 17 and 004 line 19]
    • Boot F1 took 3.803 s against 5.214 s est. Boot F2 took 2.839 s against 2.389 s est. [READMEs of 011 line 13 and 012 line 13]
    • Helper cost (counted minus uncounted helper_elapsed_ns): run 2 622,374 ns, control run 643,403 ns, run 3 658,812 ns, boot F1 579,353 ns. [cmn-counts.csv of 002, 003, 004 and 011, rows control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2]
    • The helper's own work (helper life minus child life) is 599,758 ns in run 2, 613,988 ns in run 3 and 609,192 ns in boot F1. [cmn-counts.csv of 002, 003, 004 and 011, rows control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2]
    • The counted child lived 22,616 ns longer in run 2 and 44,824 ns longer in run 3. In boot F1 the counted child lived 29,839 ns less than the uncounted one. [cmn-counts.csv of 002, 003, 004 and 011, rows control-cpu2 and control-nocount-cpu2 and README of 004 line 120]
    • Sparse rows: the dense all-five controls repeat run 2's counts node for node within -2.33 % to +1.40 %.
    • Every sparse row counts highest on its own node, at 5.1 to 6.2 times the other nodes' count, 47,972 to 57,204 requests against 8,566 to 10,516 requests per command. Own node minus others is 9.6 to 11.4 times 4,096 requests.
    • On the other four nodes the sparse rows read 0.89 to 1.06 times run 2's count, lower in 74 of 80 cells. [README of 004 lines 117, 118 and 130 and cmn-counts.csv of 002 and 004 and asimov-c1nano-perf.html table 4.7]
    • Clock: sparse per-region rows read 2.068 to 2.259 cycles per ns, sparse all-five rows 2.018 to 2.045, run 3's dense controls 2.000 to 2.001, run 2's OCM rows 2.000 to 2.011. [latency-ocm-*.csv of 004 and 002, cycles_per_load over ns_per_load]
    • perf_cov_test: PASS on the CRB. The crowded row was rejected as multiplexed with 3.70 ms running of 14.30 ms enabled, and the next row was accepted. PASS is recorded four times. [CME-plan.md lines 418, 502 and 623 and follow-up-run-plan.md line 157]
    • No counter was multiplexed in run 3: running_ns equals enabled_ns on every row. [README of 004 line 40]
    • Launch cost stays an estimate. helper_elapsed_ns spans the helper from main entry to exit and leaves out the loading of the helper itself.
    • The uncounted commands and the shell have no timing. [CME-plan.md lines 398 to 404 and 495]

    Still open

    The launch cost per program start is still 14 ms est. No run times the loading of the helper, the uncounted commands or the shell. Timing those three parts in one run would settle it. The files also do not say how many separate perf_cov_test runs produced the four PASS records.
