    4.49 CRB (reference board) lessons that shaped the Asimov method: learned random chains, first-touch cost, write collapse above 64 threadsexplained

    On the CRB, repeated random chains read 5.4 to 6.8 ns despite missing L2. Writers split across two meshes lost over half their bandwidth.

    What looked wrong

    • Learned chain. On the CRB (the Arm Phoenix reference server board: Neoverse V3AE cores, two CMN meshes, CMN being the Arm coherent mesh network) a random chain (a list of pointers walked one load at a time) walked a second time read 6.784, 5.626 and 5.424 ns per load at 8, 16 and 32 MiB in the main sweep of 2026-10-30. [crb/results/20261030T193108Z/latency.csv best rows]
    • The counters showed every load missing the 2 MiB L2 (the per-core second-level cache).
    • One pass over a chain never walked before read 26.093 ns per load at 8 MiB and 30.668 ns at 56 MiB. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/latency-fresh.csv best rows]
    • Cross-chiplet chain. A chain built on one chiplet (one of the two CRB dies, each with its own mesh) and walked from the other was first quoted as 2 to 7 ns extra per load.
    • That quote took the best of two 32 MiB walks: 32.72 to 37.29 ns per load against 30.22 to 30.25 ns on the same chiplet.
    • At 16 MiB the first walk cost 84.95 to 88.46 ns per load, the second 31.74 to 33.23 ns, and a same-chiplet walk 29.03 to 29.12 ns. [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv, fresh1, fresh2 and best rows]
    • Write collapse by thread count. In the CRB follow-up of 2026-10-30, DRAM write bandwidth fell as threads were added: 393.96 GB/s with 64 threads, 149.45 GB/s with 96 threads and 141.18 GB/s with 120 threads. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/asm.csv rows 259, 274, 289]
    • One writer at 8 MiB reached only 73.15 GB/s. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/asm.csv row 102]
    • Write collapse by placement. The placement grid of 2026-11-02 gave 394.15 GB/s with 64 writers on one mesh, 172.81 GB/s with 32 writers on each mesh and 346.49 GB/s with 16 writers on each mesh. [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv best rows]
    • Readers split 32+32 still gave 327.91 GB/s, against 346.05 GB/s with 64 readers on one mesh. [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/readgrid.csv best rows]
    • SLC capacity. The cache that sysfs (the Linux kernel's hardware description files) lists as L3 is the 128 MiB SLC (system level cache, held in the mesh home nodes).
    • In the CRB uncore run of 2026-10-30 (the run that read the mesh counters) a single buffer missed in the SLC 0.11 times per load at 64 MiB, 0.81 times per load at 96 MiB and 1.17 times per load at 128 MiB. [crb/results/uncore-20261030T203537Z/cmn-{64M,96M,128M}-{long,short}.csv, long minus short, over chase-long.csv minus chase-short.csv loads]
    • 96 MiB is well below the 128 MiB size.

    Why it looked wrong

    • A load that misses L2 cannot complete in 5 to 7 ns on this board. The never-walked chain shows the true miss cost: 26 to 31 ns per load at the same sizes.
    • The V3AE core has a temporal prefetcher (hardware that learns a repeated miss sequence and refills L2 before the next load arrives).
    • homelat.c (the CRB core-to-slice latency program) saw the same effect. With one fixed order its timed passes fell from 30 ns to 7 ns from the second repeat on. [bench/homelat.c:646-648]
    • Reporting the best of N walks hides the cost of the first touch (the first walk over lines held on the other chiplet).
    • At 16 MiB the two cross-chiplet walks differ by 53 to 56 ns per load. [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv]
    • Adding writers should not lower the total.
    • The CRB page (crb-memory-hierarchy.html) reads the fall as a placement effect: the collapse starts once both meshes carry about 32 writers or more. [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html, 'Writers on both meshes collapse DRAM write bandwidth']
    • The 64 MiB knee is the per-mesh SLC capacity.
    • Each mesh has 64 HN-S home nodes (mesh nodes that each own one slice of the SLC) of 1 MiB each (est.). [crb/results/cmn-map.txt, 64 numbered HN-S nodes per map]
    • A buffer is interleaved line by line, half on each mesh. [crb-hierarchy-findings.md, root run 2026-11-02]

    Tests added to clarify it

    TestRun or bootWhat it measures
    latency.c --fresh K and --flush: one pass over an unseen chainother, run 1Times one pass over a chain the core has never walked. --fresh K in bench/latency.c builds K = 2 to 8 chains per line. --flush in asimov/latency.c runs DC CIVAC (the Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction) on every line before the pass. A result near 26 to 31 ns per load means a true miss. A result far below it means a prefetcher learned the chain [bench/latency.c:166-183, 222 and asimov/latency.c:17-18, 348 and run 1 CSV headers 'fresh=3 flush=0' in latency-dram-large.csv and 'fresh=0 flush=1' in latency-dram-flushed.csv].
    latency.c --build-cpu with a per-walk report instead of best-of-NotherBuilds and first-touches the chain on one core and walks it from another, reporting each walk on its own. A large gap between the first and the second walk means a first-touch cost that best-of-N hid [bench/latency.c:140-161 and crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv].
    Writer and reader placement grid, 16 to 64 per meshotherMeasures DRAM write and read totals by how many threads sit on each mesh. A total that depends on placement rather than on thread count means a mesh-level effect [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv, readgrid.csv].
    homelat.c core-to-slice latency with a new random order per repeatotherMeasures latency from one core to the nearest and the farthest SLC slice with a new random order for the fill and the evictor on every repeat. The prefetcher then cannot learn the order. The result is the true slice latency [bench/homelat.c:51, 628-669 and crb/results/sudo-20261102T054936Z/full/latency.csv].
    Part 5 write-path counters on one writerotherCounts L1 and L2 refills-for-write, write-backs and crosspoint credit stalls while one writer runs. Zero stalls outside the core mean the single-writer limit sits inside the core [crb/results/sudo-20261102T211150Z/writepath.csv].
    Asimov fresh random chains, L2 prefetch-refill counter, prefetchers on and offboot A, boot BCounts L2 refills caused by a hardware prefetcher (PMU event 0x81BD, PMU being the performance monitoring unit) per load on fresh random chains with the prefetchers on (boot A). Re-times the same rows with them off (boot B). Zero refills with no timing change mean the C1-Nano (the Asimov core) does not learn a random chain [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.2 and section 11.2].

    What the tests showed

    • Never-walked chains on the CRB read 26.093 to 30.668 ns per load from 8 to 56 MiB. So the 5.4 to 6.8 ns learned-chain values were prefetcher hits, not misses. [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/latency-fresh.csv]
    • The cross-chiplet first walk cost 84.95 to 88.46 ns per load at 16 MiB. That is about 56 to 59 ns more than a same-chiplet walk. [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv]
    • The CRB page replaced its 2 to 7 ns claim with 'A first read of lines cached on the other chiplet costs 85 ns, later reads 32 ns'. [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html]
    • The write collapse is a placement effect across the two meshes: 394.15 GB/s with 64 writers on one mesh against 172.81 GB/s with 32 writers on each. [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv]
    • The root run of 2026-11-02 (run with root rights, so the mesh counters could be read) saw no retries and no throttling at the home nodes. So the bottleneck is somewhere else. [crb-hierarchy-findings.md]
    • The single-writer limit sits inside the core. Part 5 of the root run (the write-path counter test) counted zero L1 and L2 refills-for-write, zero write-backs and no crosspoint credit stalls while one writer ran.
    • That writer moved 69.18 to 71.34 GB/s at 8 MiB and 62.91 GB/s at 1 GiB. [crb/results/sudo-20261102T211150Z/writepath.csv best rows]
    • A partner on the same port raised the total to 80.62 to 82.05 GB/s, two ports to 118.85 to 122.06 GB/s, and four ports to 223.98 to 229.83 GB/s.
    • Core-to-slice latency ran 19 to 44 ns by distance. [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html, from sudo-20261102T054936Z/full/latency.csv]
    • On Asimov, boot A counted 0.000 L2 prefetch refills (event 0x81BD) per load on fresh random chains from 1.5 to 32 MiB. It counted 0.004 to 0.029 per load at 512 KiB to 1 MiB, and 0.124 to 0.212 per load on the repeat rows at 192 to 384 KiB.
    • With the prefetchers off (boot B) the 24 random rows moved only -5.6 % to +5.3 %. So the C1-Nano does not learn a random chain, unlike the V3AE. [asimov-c1nano-run4.html table 3.2 and section 11.2]
    • The CME (the Asimov per-cluster matrix engine) does prefetch on a repeated chain: 3.12 to 17.47 prefetch refills per load from 8 to 48 KiB. [asimov-cme-run4.html, 'CME L1 refills per load' chart]
    • A sparse 256 KiB chain on the CRB ran 145 to 158 ns per load with 3.8 to 7.3 L2 refills per load. The dense chain ran 28.9 ns per load with 1.00 refills per load.
    • That is 2.8 to 6.3 extra refills per load. The CME plan carried this as a warning about the method, not as an Asimov measurement. [asimov/CME-plan.md section 11, lines 596-599]

    Still open

    The CRB write collapse has no named bottleneck. A counter read at the mesh crosspoints or the memory controllers under the 32+32 writer placement would locate it. The raw CSV of the CRB sparse-chain run (145 to 158 ns per load) is not in the cache-perf tree. Those numbers rest on CME-plan.md alone.

    Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

    First seen. CRB main sweep 2026-10-30 (crb/results/20261030T193108Z), follow-ups 2026-10-31 to 2026-11-02 (followup2, followup3, root runs). Asimov run 1 ran on 2026-10-31 [results/membench-jibin-001/README.md, line 3], so the main sweep came before run 1 and the follow-ups ran beside Asimov runs 1 to 3.

    What looked wrong. Four CRB (Arm Phoenix reference server, Neoverse V3AE cores, two CMN meshes) results contradicted the hierarchy. (1) A repeated random chain read 5.4 to 6.8 ns per load at 8, 16 and 32 MiB (6.784, 5.626, 5.424 ns) while the counters showed every load missing the 2 MiB L2 [crb/results/20261030T193108Z/latency.csv, rows 8388608/16777216/33554432 'best']. A single pass over an unseen chain read 26.1 ns at 8 MiB and 30.7 ns at 56 MiB [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/latency-fresh.csv, 'best' rows]. (2) A chain built on one chiplet and walked from the other was first quoted as 2 to 7 ns extra (32 MiB second walk 32.7 to 37.3 ns against 30.2 ns same-chiplet), because the report took the best of two walks. The first walk at 16 MiB cost 85.0 to 88.5 ns per load, the second 31.7 to 33.2 ns, same-chiplet 29.0 to 29.1 ns [crb/results/followup2-20261031T073513Z/cross.csv, fresh1/fresh2 rows]. (3) DRAM write bandwidth fell with more threads: 64 threads 394 GB/s, 96 threads 149 GB/s, 120 threads 141 GB/s [crb/results/followup-20261030T194205Z/asm.csv rows 259, 274, 289]. The placement grid then showed 64 writers on one mesh 394.15 GB/s, 32+32 across the meshes 172.81 GB/s, 16+16 346.49 GB/s; reads with 32+32 still gave 327.91 GB/s [crb/results/followup3-20261102T031936Z/writegrid.csv and readgrid.csv, 'best' rows]. One writer at 8 MiB was limited to 73.15 GB/s [asm.csv row 102]. (4) The cache that sysfs calls L3 (the 128 MiB SLC, system level cache) missed on 0.81 of loads at 96 MiB and on 0.11 at 64 MiB, far below 128 MiB [crb/results/uncore-20261030T203537Z/cmn-96M-long.csv minus cmn-96M-short.csv, divided by the load difference from chase-long.csv and chase-short.csv].

    Why it looked wrong. (1) A load that misses L2 cannot complete in 5 to 7 ns on this board: the fresh chain shows 26 to 31 ns at the same sizes. The V3AE temporal prefetcher learns any repeated miss sequence and refills L2 just in time [bench/homelat.c:646-648: 'with one fixed order the timed passes fell from 30 ns to 7 ns from the second repeat on']. (2) Best-of-N hides a first-touch cost: the two walks differ by 53 to 56 ns at 16 MiB. (3) More writers should not lower the total. The CRB page reads the fall as a placement effect: the collapse starts once both meshes have about 32 writers or more [crb/crb-memory-hierarchy.html, 'Writers on both meshes collapse DRAM write bandwidth']. (4) The 64 MiB knee is the per-mesh capacity: each mesh has 64 HN-S home nodes [crb/results/cmn-map.txt, 64 numbered HN-S nodes per map], 1 MiB each (est.), and a buffer is interleaved line by line 50/50 over both meshes [crb-hierarchy-findings.md, root run 2026-11-02].

    Tests added.

    • latency.c --fresh K (K = 2 to 8 chains per line; warm on chain 0, time one pass of an unseen chain) [bench/latency.c:166-183, 222]; the Asimov latency.c adds --flush (DC CIVAC of every line before each timed pass, one pass) [asimov/latency.c:17-18, 348]. Run 1 already used both: latency-dram-large.csv header 'fresh=3 flush=0', latency-dram-flushed.csv header 'fresh=0 flush=1' [results/membench-jibin-001/results/*/]. [CRB followup 2026-10-30, then Asimov run 1 (2026-10-31) onward]: true miss latency beyond L2 (one pass over a chain the core has never walked)
    • latency.c --build-cpu (build and first-touch the chain on one core, chase on another) and the per-walk report instead of best-of-N [bench/latency.c:140-161]; the writer placement grid (16 to 64 writers per mesh, writegrid.csv/readgrid.csv); homelat.c core-to-slice latency with a new random order per repeat for fill and evictor [bench/homelat.c:51, 628-669]; part 5 write-path counters on one writer [crb/results/sudo-20261102T211150Z/writepath.csv]. [CRB follow-ups 2026-10-31 (followup2), 2026-11-02 (followup3, sudo-20261102T054936Z, sudo-20261102T211150Z)]: first-walk against second-walk cost across chiplets; write total by placement; nearest and farthest slice latency; where the single-writer limit sits

    What the tests showed. Fresh chains give 26.1 to 30.7 ns on the CRB from 8 to 56 MiB [latency-fresh.csv]. The cross-chiplet first walk costs 85.0 to 88.5 ns at 16 MiB, about 56 to 59 ns more than a local hit; the CRB page corrected its earlier 2 to 7 ns claim [crb-memory-hierarchy.html, 'A first read of lines cached on the other chiplet costs 85 ns, later reads 32 ns']. The write collapse is a placement effect across the two meshes: 394.15 GB/s with 64 writers on one mesh against 172.81 GB/s with 32 on each [writegrid.csv]; the root run saw no retries or throttling at the home nodes, so the bottleneck is elsewhere [crb-hierarchy-findings.md]. The single-writer limit sits inside the core: part 5 counted zero L1/L2 refills-for-write and write-backs and no crosspoint credit stalls while one writer moved 69.2 to 71.3 GB/s at 8 MiB (62.9 GB/s at 1 GiB), a same-port partner 80.6 to 82.1 GB/s total, two ports 118.9 to 122.1 GB/s, four ports 224.0 to 229.8 GB/s [writepath.csv, 'best' rows per block]. Core-to-slice latency ran 19 to 44 ns by distance [crb-memory-hierarchy.html, from sudo-20261102T054936Z/full/latency.csv]. On Asimov, boot A's fresh random chains from 1.5 MiB to 32 MiB counted 0.000 L2 refills by a hardware prefetcher (event 0x81BD) per load, 0.004 to 0.029 at 512 KiB to 1 MiB, and 0.124 to 0.212 on the repeat rows at 192 to 384 KiB [asimov-c1nano-run4.html, table 3.2]; with the prefetchers off (boot B) the 24 random rows moved only -5.6 % to +5.3 % [same page, section 11.2]. So the C1-Nano does not learn a random chain, unlike the V3AE. The CME does prefetch on a repeated chain: 3.12 to 17.47 prefetch refills per load from 8 to 48 KiB [asimov-cme-run4.html, CME L1 refills chart]. The sparse chain on the CRB ran 145 to 158 ns per load with 3.8 to 7.3 L2 refills per load, against 28.9 ns and 1.00 refills for the dense chain, that is 2.8 to 6.3 extra refills per load [CME-plan.md section 11, lines 596-599]; the plan carried it as a warning about the method, not an Asimov measurement. The raw CSV of that CRB sparse run is not in the cache-perf tree (not in this source).

    Highlighted: L2-prefetcher, core, SLC, mesh, DRAM, home-node.

    4.50 asimov-bench: CME matrix issue rate read 69 % of the ceiling by counters while the timer said 98 %; st1h at 3 cyclespartly explained

    CME hardware counters put the matrix issue rate at 69 % of its ceiling. A timer on a 4,096-FMOPA loop said 98 %.

    What looked wrong

    • The CME ceiling is 0.5 FMOPA issues per CME cycle (one FMOPA per 2 cycles).
    • The hardware counters gave CME_OP_MMDP_ISSUE / CME_CYCLES = 0.3455 issues per CME cycle on all five workers. That is 69 % of the ceiling [cme-survey.html section 4.3, asimov-bench dpa/stress, Spokane request 1504].
    • A timer gave 4,173 ns for 4,096 FMOPA (FP32, register operands) on one core, boot M2.
    • That is 1.019 ns per FMOPA, or 2.04 cycles per FMOPA. That is 98 % of the ceiling [cme-survey.html section 4.2, asimov-bench boot M2].
    • Two cores of DSU0 (the first cluster of two cores) issuing 2 x 4,096 FMOPA together took 8,909 ns, boot M2. That is 1.088 ns per FMOPA.
    • The pair got no more total work done than one core. Each instruction was 6.7 % slower [cme-survey.html section 4.2, boot M2].
    • Two st1h instructions (a CME store of 16-bit elements) issued back-to-back cost 3.0 CME cycles per instruction.
    • The RTL (the hardware design source) reading says 1 cycle [cme-survey.html section 9, Jacob Geldbach's run 4007 on GA13, RTL a10181848].

    Why it looked wrong

    • Two independent methods on the same unit disagreed by 29 percentage points: 98 % by the timer and 69 % by the counters.
    • Arm's own half-matmul test comment says one FMOPA per 2 cycles. The llvm-mca C1-Nano model (the LLVM instruction-timing model for this core) gives FMOPA 2.00 cycles per instruction [cme-survey.html sections 2 and 4.1].
    • For stores, the llvm-mca C1-Nano model lists ST1B (a CME store of 8-bit elements) of 2 vectors at 1.00 cycle per instruction and of 4 vectors at 2.00 cycles, with 2 cycles of latency [cme-survey.html section 4.1].
    • st1h is not in that table. A 3.0-cycle store is three times the model's rate [cme-survey.html section 4.1].

    Tests added to clarify it

    TestRun or bootWhat it measures
    Re-balanced loop with CME_CYCLES / CPU_CYCLES read beside the issue ratiootherThe loop was rearranged to 8 FMOPA + 8 LD1B (a CME vector load) + 12 FMLA (a vector multiply-add) per iteration, on asimov-bench dpa/stress, Spokane request 1511 (October 2026, not a membench-jibin run). It measures the MMDP issue ratio when the instruction stream does not starve the CME. It also records whether the CME stays allocated to the core for the whole window. A ratio near 0.5 would mean the 69 % came from the instruction stream, not from the CME.
    CME store rows by footprint, one thread on CPU 2run 3, boot F1, boot F2It runs cme-write (ST1B of four vectors, 256 B per instruction) at 16 KiB to 32 MiB. It runs cme-str16 (one 64 B vector per store) at 16 KiB, 2 MiB and 32 MiB. Both run in run 3 (004, the L3 off) and run 6 boots F1 and F2 (011/012, the L3 on, prefetchers on then off) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, 011 and 012]. It measures the sustained CME store rate in bytes per CME cycle. A rate of 0.5 stores per cycle would match the llvm-mca rate of 2.00 cycles for ST1B of four vectors. A rate of one store per 3.0 cycles would match the st1h cost.
    CME L1 write rows in the single-call form, 4 to 24 KiBboot F1, boot F2The single-call form runs every pass of a rep (one repetition of the kernel) inside one call. That removes the per-call cost. It measures the CME store rate in stores per cycle with the footprint inside L1 [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and 012].

    What the tests showed

    • The re-balanced loop gave 0.4916 to 0.4922 issues per CME cycle. That is 98 % of the 0.5 ceiling [cme-survey.html section 4.3, request 1511].
    • CME_CYCLES / CPU_CYCLES was 0.9993, so the CME stayed allocated to the core [cme-survey.html section 4.3, request 1511].
    • The bench authors attribute the original 69 % to the in-order front end: about 44 instructions per 8 FMOPA at an IPC of 1.9 in the verbatim loop [cme-survey.html section 4.3, kernels.h cme_fmopa_fit comment].
    • So the timer and the counters agree once the stream fits the front end.
    • The two-core result of 1.088 ns per FMOPA is explained by the one CME per DSU being time-shared between its two cores [cme-survey.html section 2].
    • cme-write in run 3 (004, the L3 off) gave 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s from 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB, best of 3 reps [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004].
    • That is 32 bytes per cycle at 2.003 GHz (derived), or 0.5 of a 64 B store per cycle. This matches the llvm-mca rate of 2.00 cycles for ST1B of four vectors [asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1].
    • cme-write in run 6 boot F1 (011, the L3 on) gave 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB (26 bytes per cycle) and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB (20 to 21 bytes per cycle), both derived [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011].
    • Boot F2 (012, prefetchers off) gave 51.5 to 52.5 and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at the same sizes [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 012].
    • cme-str16 gave 63.7, 63.9 and 62.0 GB/s in run 3 and 52.1, 42.7 and 40.6 GB/s in boot F1 at 16 KiB, 2 MiB and 32 MiB [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004 and 011].
    • The single-call L1 write rows on boot F1 read 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 to 24 KiB, or 0.42 of a 64 B store per cycle (derived) [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011 and asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1].

    Still open

    The st1h 3.0-cycle cost and the 0.5 ST1B stores per cycle stay open. No membench-jibin row uses st1h. No source on disk gives the CME store path width that would settle the ST1B rate. So both are Insufficient data [asimov-cme-perf.html, CME pipeline widths row]. The fall of cme-write from 63.7 GB/s (run 3, the L3 off) to 51.6 GB/s (boot F1, the L3 on) is a separate open item. The page's hypothesis is that the stores allocate in the L3 and drain at its rate [asimov-cme-perf.html open items].

    Full verified record (long form, with every number and source)

    First seen. Three measurements by other teams, all relayed through cme-survey.html (written 2026-11-02, section 9 added 2026-11-02 evening): (a) the timer rows of asimov-bench boots M2 and M3 on 2026-10-12 (engines/cme.py), (b) the counter rows of asimov-bench dpa/stress on Palladium, 2026-10-14 and 15 (Spokane requests 1504 and 1511, FORMAT.md section 6.4), (c) Jacob Geldbach's team on GA13, October 2026, run 4007 (RTL a10181848). Not from any membench-jibin results folder.

    What looked wrong. Three results did not fit the half-matmul rate of one FMOPA per 2 cycles (ceiling 0.5 issues per CME cycle). (1) The CME counters gave CME_OP_MMDP_ISSUE / CME_CYCLES = 0.3455 on all five workers, which is 69 % of the 0.5 ceiling, while the timer rows gave 1.019 ns per FMOPA = 2.04 cycles, 98 % of the ceiling [cme-survey.html sections 4.2 and 4.3]. (2) Two cores of DSU0 issuing 2 x 4,096 FMOPA together took 8,909 ns, 1.088 ns per FMOPA, against 1.019 ns for one core (4,173 ns for 4,096 FMOPA): the pair got no more total work done than one core, and each instruction was 6.7 % slower [cme-survey.html section 4.2, boot M2]. (3) Back-to-back st1h x2 cost 3.0 cycles per instruction where the RTL reading says 1 [cme-survey.html section 9, Jacob's run 4007].

    Why it looked wrong. Two independent methods on the same unit disagreed by 29 percentage points (98 % by the timer, 69 % by the counters). Arm's own half-matmul test comment says one FMOPA per 2 cycles, and the llvm-mca C1-Nano model gives FMOPA 2.00 cycles per instruction [cme-survey.html sections 2 and 4.1]. For the stores, the llvm-mca C1-Nano model lists ST1B of 2 vectors at 1.00 cycle per instruction and of 4 vectors at 2.00, with 2 cycles of latency; st1h is not in that table [cme-survey.html section 4.1; refs/C1Nano-streaming-cme-instructions.s cited on asimov-cme-perf.html, CME pipeline widths row]. A 3.0-cycle store is three times the model's rate.

    Tests added.

    • Loop re-balanced for the in-order C1-Nano front end: 8 FMOPA + 8 LD1B + 12 FMLA per loop, with CME_CYCLES / CPU_CYCLES read beside the issue ratio [asimov-bench dpa/stress, Spokane request 1511 (October 2026); not a membench-jibin run]: MMDP issue ratio when the instruction stream is arranged so the in-order front end does not starve the CME; whether the CME stays allocated to the core for the whole window
    • cme-write rows (ST1B of four vectors, 256 B per instruction) at 16 KiB to 32 MiB, plus cme-str16 (one 64 B vector) at 16 KiB, 2 MiB and 32 MiB, and cme-copy, one thread on CPU 2 [run 3 (004, the L3 off): cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv; run 6 boots F1 and F2 (011/012, the L3 on, prefetchers on/off): cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv]: the sustained CME store rate by footprint, in bytes per CME cycle
    • CME L1 write rows in the single-call form (every pass of a rep inside one call), 4 to 24 KiB [run 6 boots F1/F2 (011/012): cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv]: the CME store rate with the per-call cost removed, in stores per cycle

    What the tests showed. Re-balanced loop: 0.4916 to 0.4922 issues per CME cycle, 98 % of the 0.5 ceiling, and CME_CYCLES / CPU_CYCLES = 0.9993 (the CME stayed allocated to the core) [cme-survey.html section 4.3, request 1511]. The bench authors attribute the original 69 % to the in-order front end: about 44 instructions per 8 FMOPA at an IPC of 1.9 [cme-survey.html section 4.3, citing kernels.h cme_fmopa_fit comment]. So the timer and the counters agree once the stream fits the front end. The two-core result (1.088 ns per FMOPA) is explained by the one CME per DSU being time-shared [cme-survey.html section 2]. The st1h 3.0-cycle anomaly stays open: no membench-jibin row uses st1h. The cme-write rows use ST1B of four vectors and gave: run 3 (004, the L3 off) 63.7 to 63.9 GB/s from 16 KiB to 2 MiB and 62.0 GB/s at 32 MiB, which is 32 bytes per cycle or 0.5 of a 64 B store per cycle at 2.003 GHz (derived) [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 004, best of 3 reps; asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1 table]; run 6 boot F1 (011, the L3 on) 51.6 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 to 256 KiB (26 bytes per cycle) and 40.4 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 to 32 MiB (20 to 21 bytes per cycle); boot F2 (012) 51.5 to 52.5 and 39.5 to 40.4 GB/s at the same sizes [cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv of 011 and 012]. The single-call L1 write rows on F1 read 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 to 24 KiB, 0.42 of a store per cycle [cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv of 011; asimov-cme-perf.html section 6.1]. The 0.5 store per cycle of run 3 matches the llvm-mca rate for ST1B of four vectors (2.00 cycles). Why the stores stop at that rate is Insufficient data: no source on disk gives the CME store path width [asimov-cme-perf.html, CME pipeline widths row]. Why the writes fall with the L3 on is a separate open item (hypothesis on the page: the stores allocate in the L3 and drain at its rate) [asimov-cme-perf.html open items].

    Highlighted: CME, core, L3.

    5. Words used here

    --perf with --cme
    Two options of the bandwidth program. It refuses them together, so CME bandwidth rows carry no CME counters.
    /dev/ocm
    The Linux module that maps an OCM region into a process.
    all-five chain
    One chain that spans all five OCM regions. Its dense form is the OCM number the pages quote.
    asimov-bench
    A reference benchmark whose OCM chase through the CME read 34.8 ns per load.
    best of 3 reps
    Each kernel runs 3 times and the page quotes the fastest rate.
    best rep
    The highest aggregate_GBps over the 3 reps of a row.
    best row
    The fastest of the repeated runs of one test row.
    boot A to E (005 to 010)
    The five run-4 boots. 005, 006, 007, 008 and 010 are the result folders for boots A, B, C, D and E.
    boot A to F1
    Result sets 005 (A), 006 (B, prefetchers off), 007 (C), 008 (D), 010 (E) and 011 (F1, L3 on). Runs 1, 2, control and 3 are 001, 002, 003 and 004.
    boot C, boot E
    C1-Nano runs membench-jibin-007 and membench-jibin-010 of 2026-11-05.
    boot F1
    The first boot of run 6 (membench-jibin-011), with the L3 on.
    boot F1, boot F2
    Run 6 boots on the L3-on firmware. F2 also has the data prefetchers turned off.
    boot F2
    Run 6 boot of 2026-11-06/07 UTC (membench-jibin-012) with the L3 on and the data prefetchers off.
    bracket
    The timer around the whole call, so it includes per-call cost.
    bracket / span
    Bracket: the time between two timer reads around a whole call. Span: run 6's second pair of stamps inside the call, around the data loop only.
    bracket, in span
    Two timings reported for one CME write. On F1 they read 40.445 GB/s (bracket) and 40.459 GB/s (in span).
    C1-Nano
    The Arm core in the emulated Asimov chip.
    cell
    One CPU-to-OCM-region pair in the latency test. Four CPUs by five regions give 20 cells.
    chain
    A list of memory lines where each line holds the address of the next, read one load at a time.
    chain (chase)
    A list of loads where each load returns the address of the next load, so the loads cannot overlap on their own.
    chase
    A pointer-chase latency test. Each load waits for the previous one, so it measures one load's latency.
    chase (chain walk)
    A chain of dependent loads: each load's result is the next address, so one load must finish before the next starts. It measures latency.
    chip time
    The time the emulated chip spends on one run, read from the ns= line of that run's README.
    cluster
    The group of cores that share one L3. An L3 read refill counts a demand read that left this group.
    CME
    The Asimov per-cluster matrix engine. It does prefetch on a repeated chain.
    CME L1
    The CME's own first-level data cache: 64 KiB, 4-way, 64-byte lines, 1,024 lines.
    cme-call
    The one-load latency control: one CME call that performs a single load.
    cme-roundtrip
    The latency chain baseline whose per-load time is the CME round trip (21.0 ns).
    CMN
    The Arm mesh interconnect that joins the clusters to the home nodes.
    CMN S3
    Arm's coherent mesh network: a 6 by 6 grid of crosspoints that connects clusters, home nodes and memory bridges.
    cmncount
    The harness's counter reader. It opens one mesh counter per node id around a command and reports the counts in cmn-counts.csv.
    CNTVCT_EL0
    The Arm virtual counter register used for the in-span clock stamps.
    control run
    Run 003: run 1 firmware with run 2 code, used to separate firmware changes from code changes.
    control run (003)
    A run made to check whether the firmware change between run 1 and run 2 moved the numbers.
    core page
    The report page for the core's cache tests, asimov-c1nano-perf.html. The run 4 core page is asimov-c1nano-run4.html.
    CRB
    The Neoverse V3AE reference board. Its core has a 2 MiB L2.
    crosspoint
    A switch point on the mesh, named by its (x,y) position.
    cycles per line
    Core clock cycles spent per 64 B line read, at 2.003 GHz.
    data prefetcher
    Hardware that fetches cache lines ahead of demand. Boot F2 ran with it off (TF-A 0.35.0-pfoff.1).
    DC CIVAC
    The Arm clean-and-invalidate instruction.
    demand refill
    A refill caused by a load that needed the line (event 0x3280).
    dense all-five row
    The control row from run 2: one chain over all five regions, 1.25 MiB, 20,480 loads per pass, 2 passes.
    dense chain
    A pointer chain that loads every cache line of the region, 4,096 loads per pass.
    DSU
    DynamIQ Shared Unit. The cluster unit that holds the L3.
    dynamic mode
    The CME power-controller mode in which the CME switches itself off after both cores leave streaming mode.
    est
    An estimate, not a measurement.
    est.
    An estimate: a number derived from other measurements, not read from a counter or a timer.
    Flushed
    A test variant that flushes the caches before the timed walks.
    flushed chain
    A chain whose cache lines were evicted with DC CIVAC before the walk, so every load misses the caches.
    flushed row
    A test row whose chain lines were pushed out of the caches before the timed pass (--flush).
    footprint
    The buffer size a bandwidth row sweeps, here 16 KiB to 32 MiB.
    fresh chain
    A chain the core has never walked. One pass over it gives the true miss cost.
    G7
    The plan's name for the group of read variants (plain, PRFM 4/8/16 ahead, two streams).
    G8 rows
    The L1 read and write rows of the run plan that compare the two forms.
    H7
    The run 4 page's hypothesis that the plain read loop keeps too few lines in flight.
    hardware prefetcher
    A unit that guesses which lines a program will need next and fetches them before a load asks.
    hit set
    A latency row whose footprint fits in the L3, used to measure the L3 hit cost (10.8 ns est.).
    HN-S
    A home node on the CMN mesh. Each one owns one OCM region. This SoC has five.
    hns_cache_miss_all
    Mesh counter: SLC misses at a home node.
    hns_mc_reqs_local_all
    The home-node counter of requests sent on to memory.
    hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all
    Mesh counter: requests received at a home node.
    hns_pocq_retry_all
    Mesh counter: requests a home node retried. Proposed as the test for this outlier, never run.
    home node
    A node on the mesh that holds one SLC array. There are five.
    home node (HN-S)
    The mesh node that owns an address: it keeps the snoop filter and the SLC slice for that address. Asimov has five.
    IMP_CLUSTERPWRSTAT_EL1
    The cluster power-state register. A reading of 0x0 means the L3 held no data.
    in flight
    Issued and not yet returned: the number of reads a core, a prefetcher or a cluster keeps open at once.
    in-order core
    A core that cannot start later instructions before earlier ones finish. It cannot overlap a pass boundary with the next pass's loads.
    Jesse's README
    The README.md that the result-set author wrote inside each membench-jibin set.
    L1
    The level-1 cache of one core. A 16 KiB buffer sits in it.
    L1, L2, L3
    The three cache levels, from the one nearest the core (L1) to the farthest (L3). L1D is the L1 data cache.
    l1d_refill_hwprf_per_line
    L1 data-cache refills caused by the hardware prefetcher, divided by lines read. A value near 1 means the prefetcher fetched nearly every line.
    L2
    The per-core second-level cache, 2 MiB on the CRB.
    L2 refills per load
    How many lines the L2 cache fetched per measured load. A value above 1 means some lines arrived before their load.
    L3
    The level-3 cache. Boot E ran with it on.
    L3 read refill
    A cache line brought into the L3 by a read miss. A count of 1.0 per load means every load missed the L3.
    L3 read refill (event 0xA2)
    A hardware counter that counts one for each line the L3 fetched from outside the cluster.
    L3 read refills per load
    A core counter of lines brought into the L3 on reads, divided by the chain loads. 1.00 on both 8 MiB rows, so it cannot show SLC hits.
    looped form
    One call per pass over the buffer.
    membench-jibin-NNN
    The results folder of one run: 002 is run 2, 003 the control run, 004 run 3, 011 run 6 boot F1.
    mesh
    The on-chip interconnect that carries L2 misses to memory.
    mesh port
    The cluster's one link to the mesh (the on-chip interconnect). Traffic beyond the cluster caches leaves through it.
    ns per load
    Nanoseconds for one dependent pointer load in the chain.
    OCM
    On-chip memory held at the mesh home nodes.
    outer refill
    A line brought into the CME's L1 (its first-level cache) from a level beyond it, counted per load.
    pair
    Two cores in one DSU (CPUs 2+3) running the same kernel together, recorded in bandwidth-pair.csv.
    pass
    One full read of the buffer.
    perf_cov
    The counters' coverage fraction of the command, where 1.0000 means no multiplexing.
    PMU
    Performance monitoring unit, the hardware counters of the core or of the mesh.
    pointer chase
    A chain of loads where each load returns the address of the next load.
    prefetcher
    Hardware that fetches lines into a cache before the program asks for them.
    prefetchers
    The core's L1 and L2 hardware units that fetch lines before a load asks for them. Boots B, D and F2 ran with them off.
    PRFM PLDL1KEEP
    The Arm prefetch-hint instruction, asking for a line to be loaded into L1 before the loop reaches it. The tests issued it 4, 8 or 16 lines ahead.
    refill
    One cache line brought into the CME L1, for any reason.
    refills per load
    The count of L1 refill events divided by the number of chain loads in the pass.
    rep
    One execution of the bandwidth command.
    rep, best rep
    One repetition of a test. The best rep is the best of three repetitions, the value table 3.1 of the run 4 CME page quotes.
    repeated chain / fresh chain / flushed chain
    Repeated: the same random chain walked many times (later walks hit whatever cache holds it). Fresh: walked once. Flushed: every line cleaned and invalidated (DC CIVAC) first.
    rms
    Root-mean-square residual of a fit: the typical miss between the fit and the measured cells, in ns.
    route rows
    The G6 rows: each cell's dense chain run with 8 crosspoint counters and a best-of-2 latency.
    RTL
    The hardware design source of the chip.
    run / boot
    A run is one result set (membench-jibin-002 is run 2, 004 is run 3). Runs 4 and 6 have several boots (A to E, F1 and F2), each a fresh start of the platform.
    run 3
    The 2026-11-03 UTC run (membench-jibin-004) with the L3 off.
    SCP
    The system control processor, which sets the CME power mode as cores power on.
    SCP / TF-A
    SCP: the system control processor firmware, which stages each cluster's L3 mode. TF-A: Trusted Firmware-A, the EL3 firmware; a rebuilt TF-A turned the prefetchers off on boots B, D and F2.
    SCP firmware
    The system control processor firmware: 0.48.0-nopcie.1 on run 3, 0.48.0-nopcie-l3.1 on F1.
    SCP, TF-A
    The two firmware components whose versions changed between run 1 (SCP 0.34.0, TF-A 0.24.0) and run 2.
    single-call form
    Every pass of a rep inside one call (the --asm-passes rows), which removes per-call cost.
    single-call form (--asm-passes)
    The L1 read form that runs all passes of a rep inside one assembly call.
    SLC
    The 3.75 MiB cache on the mesh.
    snoop
    A read of a line out of another core's cache inside the cluster instead of from the L3 or the mesh.
    snoop-filter-only mode
    An L3 setting under which the L3 of CPUs 2 to 9 held no data.
    span
    The time between two CNTVCT_EL0 stamps placed after SMSTART and before SMSTOP, inside the kernel.
    sparse (one line per page) / dense (every line)
    Sparse OCM chains use one line per 4 KiB page, so a prefetcher cannot fetch a neighbour that the chain will use. Dense chains use every line of the region.
    sparse chain
    A chain on widely spaced addresses. On run 3 its loads count 0.00 to 0.03 inner refills per load.
    sparse OCM pass
    One timed CME load pass over an OCM chain, one of the 7 cme-fresh rows per OCM file in run 3.
    spread
    The gap between the highest and lowest per-node count in one row, as a percent of the lowest.
    streaming mode
    The Arm SME mode in which a core's loads and stores go through the CME.
    sysinfo.txt
    The file in a run's output that holds the mesh map.
    TF-A
    Trusted Firmware-A, the boot firmware. The pfoff build turns the prefetchers off.
    TLB
    Translation lookaside buffer, the cache of recent address translations in the core.
    TRM
    The Arm technical reference manual for the core.
    two streams
    The fifth G7 kernel, a two-stream read loop.
    V3AE
    The Arm Neoverse core on the CRB.

    6. Sources and method

    • The two session histories (asimov-04 and asimov-be, 2026-10-30 to 2026-11-08), distilled to their user and assistant turns.
    • Jesse's README.md in results/membench-jibin-001 to 012, and the result CSV files, log.txt, sysinfo.txt and uart logs in those folders.
    • The run plans and reviews: RUN2-PLAN.md, follow-up-run-plan.md, CME-plan.md, the codex review files, HANDOFF-2026-11-02.md, jibin-comments-perf-modeling.md.
    • The report pages: asimov-c1nano-perf.html, asimov-cme-perf.html, asimov-c1nano-run4.html, asimov-cme-run4.html, run1-report.html, ocm-interpretation.html, cme-survey.html.
    • Arm documents: C1-Nano Software Optimization Guide 109590 (on disk); C1-Nano TRM, C1-SME2 TRM 107831, C1-DSU TRM 107804 and CMN S3 TRM 107858 as cited by the pages (not on disk); Cortex-A520 TRM (predecessor core, public).
    • Method: 17 extraction passes (one per source slice) produced raw outlier lists; a merge pass joined duplicates into 50 entries; one verification pass per entry recomputed every number from the CSV files; one rewrite and one check pass per entry produced the bullets. Numbers the sources disagree on are kept with both sources in the full record.
